questionStem: A 35-year-old man has had recurrent episodes of dysuria and pelvic pain over the past 2 years. He is sexually active. Examination shows a tender prostate. Urinalysis shows 2-5 WBC/hpf . A urine culture is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
system: Renal/Urinary and Male and Female Reproductive

questionStem: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of moderate numbness and weakness of his left hand. There is no history of trauma to the hand . He has hypertension treated with enalapril and type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin . He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m 2• His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min , respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Examination shows atrophy of the hypothenar muscles . The middle , ring, and small fingers are held in flexion ; there is weakness of abduction of the small finger. The patient cannot prevent paper from being pulled through his fingers. All other intrinsic hand muscles are normal. Deep tendon reflexes are 1 + at the left brachioradialis, biceps , and triceps muscles . Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the palmar aspect of the left ring and small fingers and the hypothenar region of the hand. The remainder of the examination shows no other abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

choices.C: Lesion of the lower trunk of the brachia! plexus
choices.D: Lesion of the medial cord of the brachia! plexus

correctExplanation: This is most likely caused by neuropathy from the ulnar nerve .
incorrectExplanation: (A) Syringomyelia might cause similar symptoms but would typically affect both hands and cause deficits to temperature sensation. (B) CB nerve root compression and (C, D) lesions on the lower trunk and medial cord of the brachia! plexus would not cause this constellation of symptoms. ,.

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of light-headedness . She states that she feels as if she is going to pass out when she gets out of bed in the morning. She has not had chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations . She has hypertension and hypothyroidism . Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide, enalapril, and levothyroxine . She appears fatigued . She is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 26 kg/m2• Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 64/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg while supine and 135/85 mm Hg while standing . Examination shows dry skin. The thyroid gland is symmetrically enlarged, nodular, and nontender. Jugular venous pulsations are present 3 cm above the sternal angle and decrease by 2 cm with inspiration. The lungs are clear to auscultation . A grade 1/6 systolic murmur is heard best at the left sternal border without radiation. There is trace pitting edema of the ankles. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Results of a complete blood count are within the reference range. Her serum potassium concentration is 3.4 mEq/L, and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 1.5 µU/ml. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 64/min and is otherwise unchanged from an ECG 1 year ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause of this patient's light-headedness?

choices.A: Measurement of serum free thyroxine concentration
choices.B: Serial measurements of serum creatine kinase activity

correctExplanation: An ambulatory ECG is needed to confirm bradycardia when she has her current symptoms, and the treatment would ultimately be a pacemaker.
incorrectExplanation: (A, B, C, E) None of the other listed diagnostic studies would disclose that diagnosis. ,.

questionStem: A 52-year-old woman has decreased urine output 6 hours after admission to the hospital for treatment of a 3-day history of nausea and vomiting . She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and peripheral neuropathy. Her outpatient medications were glipizide, atorvastatin , lisinopril, and 81-mg aspirin; all medications were held on admission . Her blood pressure was 82/40 mm Hg on admission . After beginning intravenous administration of fluids, her blood pressure increased to 110/70 mm Hg. On examination now, the abdomen is soft, and there is diffuse mild tenderness with no guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds are decreased. There is decreased sensation to light touch over the feet. Laboratory studies show: On Admission Now Fingerstick blood glucose 4+ 4+ Serum Urea nitrogen (mg/dl) 38 54 Creatinine (mg/dl) 1.8 2.6 Urine Specific gravity 1.028 1.011 RBC (/hpf) 0-2 0-2 Casts None coarse granular Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's decreased urine output?
system: Renal/Urinary and Male and Female Reproductive

questionStem: A 42-year-old man with alcoholism is admitted to the hospital 12 hours after the onset of severe epigastric pain that radiates to the back. He has had several episodes of vomiting. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. There is tenderness to palpation in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant of the abdomen ; there are no signs of peritonitis. Bowel sounds are decreased . After 2 days, laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 13 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume102 µm3 Leukocyte count 12,000/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 76% Bands 4% Lymphocytes 20% Serum Ca2• Urea nitrogen Creatinine Albumin Amylase 6 mg/dL 20 mg/dL 1.4 mg/dL 3.5 g/dL 500 U/L His serum electrolyte concentrations are within the reference range. Which of the laboratory findings in this patient is associated with the worst prognosis?

A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of fever and cough with increasing production of purulent sputum for 24 hours. She has had asthma since childhood that is characterized by episodes of coughing and wheezing . Treatment with inhaled corticosteroids was begun 8 months ago. She has been hospitalized twice over the past 2 months for low-grade fever, increased sputum production , and a poorly resolving infiltrate in the left lower lobe; sputum cultures at that time grew normal flora and Aspergillus fumigatus . She is in moderate respiratory distress. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F) , pulse is 95/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Diffuse expiratory wheezes and crackles are heard at the left lung base. Cardiac examination shows a normal S 1 and S2 with no murmurs . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A previously healthy 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of progressive shortness of breath. During this period, she also has had intermittent nonproductive cough and wheezing, especially when she has colds during the winter. She has not had night sweats. She takes no medications . She has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 9 years. She is employed as a landscape architect. Her 60-year-old father has had emphysema since his early 40s. The patient appears well. Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Breath sounds are mildly decreased at the lung bases. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Spirometry shows an FEV 1 of 45% of predicted. X-rays of the chest are shown. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's lung injury?

choices.C: Chronic infection with respiratory syncytial virus
choices.D: Chronic irritation and inflammation from cigarette smoking
choices.E: Defective chloride secretion from respiratory epithelium

questionStem: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of moderate right leg pain for 2 days. He has metastatic non-small cell carcinoma of the lung and completed palliative chemotherapy 3 weeks ago . He takes no other medications . His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 146/80 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Hemog~~n 13g~L Platelet count 367,000/mm 3 Prothrombin time 12 sec (INR=1) Partial thromboplastin time28 sec Serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL Venous duplex ultrasonography of the right lower extremity shows thrombosis in the common femoral vein. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: Placement of an inferior vena cava filte

correctExplanation: An inferior vena cava filter would not treat the deep venous thrombosis and has not been shown to alter outcomes for patients with malignancy and thrombus . ,.

questionStem: A moderately obese 35-year-old woman has a 4-year history of recurrent abscesses in both axillae. These are progressively more frequent and severe. The episodes are interfering with her ability to work. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus that is fairly well controlled by diet and the use of oral hypoglycemic agents. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Institution of insulin therapy to improve glucose control
choices.E: Washing three times daily with pHisoHex and wate

correctExplanation: In this case, the patient's type 2 diabetes mellitus is well-controlled so insulin therapy is not needed and likely poor glycemic control would not substantially alter her risk for infection.
incorrectExplanation: (B) Long-term administration of antibiotics would not alter her clinical course and have side effects. (D) Silver sulfadiazine would not have an effect on her symptoms, and (E)/ daily washing may have a benefit but given her symptoms and disease burden (C) surgical excision would be the treatment of choice. ,.

questionStem: 1\.~ I- v-- I Ill a VF V3 V6 20. A 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of sharp anterior chest pain. She says that the pain is worse with inspiration and when she is supine and is relieved somewhat when she sits up. She took two acetaminophen tablets 1 hour ago, but they have not relieved the pain. She has no history of similar symptoms or serious illness. She takes no other medications. Her temperature is 37 .8°C (100°F), pulse is 100/min and regular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 114/76 mm Hg. A two-component friction rub is heard at the apex . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . An ECG is shown . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: In the setting of acute pericarditis, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, are the initial treatment of choice, usually in conjunction with colchicine.
incorrectExplanation: (B) Prednisone may be used for recalcitrant pericarditis or for pericarditis caused by an autoimmune disease, but not for this case as an initial therapy, unless a contraindication for NSAID therapy was present. (C, D, E) Heparin, nitroglycerin, and morphine would be treatments for myocardial infarction and so are not necessary. ,.

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman with osteoporosis and hypertension is admitted to the hospital because of progressive confusion during the past 5 days. Her husband reports that she has had constipation for the past week and abdominal pain for the past 3 days. She had right breast cancer treated with lumpectomy and radiation therapy 2 years ago. Medications are alendronate , hydrochlorothiazide, and a calcium supplement containing vitamin D. She is alert. Her temperature is 36.4°C (97.5°F}, pulse is 78/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 156/82 mm Hg. Pulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and tenderness throughout; there is no guarding or rebound. Rectal examination shows hard brown stool. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings . On mental status examination , she appears anxious and is not oriented to person , place, or time. Her serum calcium concentration is 14.8 mg/dl, and serum albumin concentration is 3 g/dl. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows multiple skull metastases. Which of the following is the strongest contributing factor for this patient's hypercalcemia?

A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood twice in the past hour. He appears robust and comfortable. His pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 100/80 mm Hg while supine. There is mild epigastric tenderness. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Hematocrit is 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Discharge him with instructions to return if the pain or vomiting recurs

questionStem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and decreased urine output over the past 48 hours. She has an 8-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glipizide . She has no history of renal disease . Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), and respirations are 24/min . While supine, her pulse is 106/min, and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. While sitting, her pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg. She appears acutely ill and slightly lethargic . Examination shows decreased skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, and flat neck veins. There is mild, generalized abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound tenderness. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 15,000/mm 3 Serum Na+ c1- K+ HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Glucose Creatinine Urine Na+ pH Specific gravity Glucose Ketones 146 mEq/L 100 mEq/L 2.9 mEq/L 28 mEq/L 72 mg/dL 254 mg/dL 3.4 mg/dL 8 mEq/L 5.0 1.028 2+ trace Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
system: Renal/Urinary and Male and Female Reproductive

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman has had progressively severe midback pain over the past month. She has been fatigued and less mentally alert for 3 weeks. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities except for impaired cognitive function. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin Hematocrit Leukocyte count Serum Ca 2+ Urea nitrogen Creatinine 8 g/dL 24% 12,500/mm3 12.4 mg/dL 35 mg/dL 2.4 mg/dL Serum electrolyte concentrations are within normal limits. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. A lateral x-ray of the skull is shown . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
correctExplanation: The elevated calcium concentration supports this diagnosis and the lytic lesion seen on the x-ray of the skull adds further support. The next step in diagnosis would be to measure a urine and serum protein electrophoresis, ideally with immunofixation.
incorrectExplanation: (B) Mammography would be reasonable as a routine study but not to diagnose melanoma. (C) Bone scan is not typically done but could be considered if there is concern for marrow uptake or lytic lesions not seen on a skeletal survey but is not typically done. (D) CT scan is not necessary as the lytic lesion is seen on x-ray. (E) A renal biopsy would not be the first diagnostic study to consider in a patient with this presentation, but could be considered if electrophoresis is within normal limits and there is still renal failure without a clear cause. ,.

questionStem: Two days after a myocardial infarction, a previously asymptomatic 60-year-old woman develops pulmonary edema. A grade 4/6 systolic murmur is heard at the apex. Oxygen saturation in the right atrium and pulmonary artery is 65%, and pulmonary artery diastolic pressure is 35 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Torn chordae tendineae of the tricuspid valve

correctExplanation: A ruptured interventricular septum might produce similar symptoms, but oxygenated blood from the left ventricle would enter the right and would make the oxygen saturation higher.
incorrectExplanation: (B) A ruptured left ventricular free wall would cause shock but not likely pulmonary edema and right-sided pressures would likely be lower. (D) A ruptured pulmonary valve would cause a diastolic murmur and would not lead to elevated pulmonary artery pressures. (E) A ruptured tricuspid valve would typically be heard on the sternal border compared to the apex and also would tend to have elevated vena caval pressure and lower pulmonary artery pressure. ,.

questionStem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was found unconscious on the floor of his apartment next to an open bottle of barbiturates . On arrival, his pulse is 118/min, respirations are 6/min, and blood pressure is 98/64 mm Hg. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated. Examination shows diffuse movement to painful stimuli. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ c1- K+ HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Creatinine Creatine kinase Urine 140 mEq/L 106 mEq/L 6.1 mEq/L 14 mEq/L 27 mg/dl 5.7 mg/dl 10,000 U/L pH 6 Specific gravity 1.010 Blood positive Glucose negative Protein trace RBC 3-4/hpf WBC 0-2/hpf Pigmented granular casts4-5/lpf Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's renal failure?
correctExplanation: This all suggests rhabdomyolysis, a breakdown of muscle and is characterized by a high serum potassium concentration and myoglobin present in urine (which activates the blood assay in a urine dipstick, but results in a negative erythrocyte count in urinalysis).
incorrectExplanation: (A) Glomerulonephritis would have evidence of nephritis with either erythrocytes or erythrocyte casts in the urine which is not present. (B) Acute interstitial nephritis is typically an allergic reaction to a drug, which is possible in this case, but would be manifested by leukocytes, leukocyte casts, and eosinophils present on urinalysis. (C) Bladder obstruction would typically have more azotemia and would be improved by removing the obstruction by placing a catheter, if possible. There is no evidence to suggest obstruction in this vignette, however. (D) Cholesterol emboli are usually released from atherosclerotic plaques during an invasive procedure such as angioplasty and are typically diagnosed by biopsy. This would be unlikely given the vignette. ,. "' , ~ r-- ,.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has been amenorrheic for 3 months. She has also had increased facial hair growth and multiple episodes of acne over the past year; she has had a 27-kg (60-lb) weight gain during this time despite no change in appetite . Menses had occurred at regular intervals until 1 year ago, when they became increasingly irregular . She is not sexually active. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 36 kg/m 2• Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. Examination shows truncal obesity with pink striae. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Urine 13-hCG test is negative . Measurement of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.E: Urine free cortisol concentration in a 24-hour specimen

questionStem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of increasing pain and redness of his left knee. Ten days ago, he spent several hours on his knees waxing a floor. His knee has been somewhat swollen and painful since then. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 120/85 mm Hg. The anterior aspect of the knee overlying the patella is erythematous , and there is fluctuance in this area. There is no effusion. Range of motion of the knee is full, and any movement of the knee produces minor discomfort . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.D: Inflammatory bursitis of the pes anserinus

correctExplanation: This suggests patellar septic bursitis, common for those on their knees for some time, and the fever suggests infection.
incorrectExplanation: (A) Deep venous thrombosis would show edema distal to where the clot would be. (D) The joint might be red but there are no other skin findings such as varicosities. The range of motion of the knee is intact which makes inflammatory bursitis of the pes anserinus unlikely and also making (B) gout and (G) septic arthritis even less likely. (C) A Baker cyst is located in the popliteal fossa, and (E) Osgood-Schlatter disease (osteochondritis of the tibial tubercle) typically presents in adolescents or young adults as an anterior knee pain that increases gradually over time and is typically not associated with swelling or erythema. ,. "' , ~ r-- ,.

questionStem: A previously healthy 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an itchy rash on her face, arms, and hands for 2 days. She notes that the rash appeared 2 days after working in her garden. Examination shows urticaria! and vesicular lesions over the face, upper extremities , and hands. Which of the following is the most likely pathologic process of this patient's rash?

choices.A: Chemotaxis of eosinophils caused by direct antibody reaction with plant sap
choices.B: Destruction of adhesion among epidermal cells caused by circulating lgG autoantibodies directed against the cell
choices.D: Photosensitivity of the epidermis caused by plant sap
choices.E: Squamous epithelial cell damage caused by plant sap

correctExplanation: This dermatitis is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to the toxin, which is a cell-mediated hypersensitivity, caused by helper T lymphocytes.
incorrectExplanation: (D) The sap does not cause photosensitivity or (E) direct injury, and (A) chemotaxis and (B) lgG antibody mediated destruction would be Type I and Type II hypersensitivity reactions. ,.

questionStem: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of progressive fatigue and shortness of breath with exertion . His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 56/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/92 mm Hg. Bilateral basilar crackles are heard on auscultation. Cardiac examination shows a laterally displaced point of maximal impulse. Echocardiography shows left ventricular dilation and an ejection fraction of 32%. In addition to furosemide , which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

An asymptomatic 32-year-old woman with HIV infection comes to the physician as a new patient. Her last visit to a physician was 14 months ago. She takes no medications . Examination shows hairy leukoplakia and cervical adenopathy. Her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 180/mm3 (Normal~500) , and plasma HIV viral load is 20,000 copies/ml. In addition to antiretroviral therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Mammography, Pap smear, and Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carinil) prophylaxis
choices.C: Pap smear and P. jiroveci pro h laxis
choices.D: P. jiroveci and Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus and anxiety disorder comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive numbness of her hands that has recently extended to her forearms . During the past 2 months , she has burned her fingers numerous times while cooking; she did not know that she had burned herself until she saw the development of blisters. She has no other neurologic symptoms . Her only medication is insulin . Cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is 5/5 in the upper and lower extremities . Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ bilaterally. Babinski sign is absent. Sensation to pinprick and temperature is absent over the hands and upper extremities extending to the neck and posterior scalp but is intact over the trunk and lower extremities . Proprioception and sensation to vibration are normal throughout. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The presence of hyperreflexia indicates that there are upper motor symptoms and would not likely be conversion disorder.
incorrectExplanation: (A) Brachia! plexopathy and (D) diabetic polyneuropathy would not have these symptoms and would likely affect vibratory sensation which is intact in this patient. (B) Cervical stenosis is possible, but would not likely affect temperature sensation, and is often accompanied by weakness that is not present in this patient. ,.

questionStem: A 62-year-old man with severe obstructive pulmonary disease has chronic disabling dyspnea . His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. He is plethoric, and jugular veins are distended . Breath sounds are distant, and the second component of S2 is accentuated. His FEV 1 is 0.5 L. An x-ray of the chest shows prominent pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary hypertension in this patient is most likely the result of which of the following?

A 57-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a painful, cold right leg for 4 hours. He has hypertension , type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia . Medications include metformin , triamterene-hydrochlorothiazide , and atorvastatin . He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. His blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Pulses are decreased in the right lower extremity. His serum creatinine concentration is 1.5 mg/dl. Angiography of the right lower extremity shows occlusion of the common femoral artery. Twenty-four hours later, his serum creatinine concentration increases to 3.6 mg/dl. Which of the following measures prior to his angiography is most likely to have prevented this patient's worsening azotemia?

choices.E: There are no known preventive measures

system: Renal/Urinary and Male and Female Reproductive

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increasingly severe pain of the fingers over the past 6 months. She has a 6-year history of cold sensitivity of the hands. On cold exposure , her fingers become initially pale and then turn blue; there is redness with recovery. She has a 3-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease . Examination shows tightening of the skin of the fingers, with erythema , scaling, and telangiectasias . Dry crepitant crackles are heard at both lung bases. X-rays of the hands show loss of tufts of some distal phalanges and scattered soft tissue calcifications . Serum antinuclear antibody testing is most likely to show which of the following?

choices.C: Positive findings for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody and negative findings for antinuclear antibody
choices.D: Positive findings for antiribonuclear protein antibody

questionStem: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician for a preoperative evaluation . He is scheduled to undergo partial colectomy in 5 days because of recurrent diverticulitis. He can carry groceries up two flights of stairs without stopping . He has no history of chest pain or heart disease. Two months ago, his serum total cholesterol concentration was 162 mg/dl. He takes no medications. He is adopted and has no information about his family history. He smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years but stopped 3 years ago. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 93 kg (205 lb); BMI is 30 kg/m2• His pulse is 78/min and regular, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation . S 1 and S2 are normal. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex with radiation toward the left axilla. The abdomen is soft. An ECG shows a normal sinus rhythm and left bundle branch block. Echocardiography shows mitral valve thickening with mild regurgitation . Which of the following diagnostic tests is indicated prior to the operation?
correctExplanation: The patient has a good exercise tolerance (manifested by walking two flights of stairs without breathlessness) and has a number of cardiovascular risk factors. He has a grade 2/6 systolic murmur.
incorrectExplanation: (B) Typically a grade 3/6 murmur or higher would suggest pathology and, as such, the patient has no signs of angina or cardiovascular decline. (C and D) None of the diagnostic studies listed would change immediate management prior to surgery and (E) would not require further testing. ,.

questionStem: A 52-year-old woman comes for a routine health maintenance examination . She feels well. Over the past 6 months, menses have occurred at irregular 2- to 3-month intervals . She takes no medications . She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years and drinks alcohol socially. Her father has hypertension , and her mother has osteoarthritis of the knees and is scheduled for bilateral knee replacements . The patient is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 72 kg (160 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m 2. Her pulse is 80/min and regular and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Range of motion of all joints is full and does not produce pain . She is concerned about her risk for arthritis . Which of the following is most likely to decrease this patient's risk for osteoarthritis?

choices.A: Begin a swimming program 30 minutes daily three times weekly
choices.B: Begin a walking program 30 minutes daily three times weekly

correctExplanation: There is no data that estrogen prevents osteoarthritis as well. ,.

questionStem: A 42-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of the recent onset of shortness of breath. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 25 years. He is emaciated and in moderate respiratory distress . There is dullness to percussion and egophony at the right lung base. He has a leukocyte count of 18,200/mm 3 (60% neutrophils, 17% band forms , 20% lymphocytes , and 3% monocytes). An x-ray of the chest shows a right lower lobe infiltrate with a pleural effusion . Thoracentesis shows purulent, foul-smelling fluid . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A 62-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for treatment of pneumonia . He has a 3-day history of fever, cough productive of greenish sputum , and mild shortness of breath. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease . Current medications include 81-mg aspirin, atenolol, isosorbide , glipizide, metformin , and rosiglitazone . He appears ill and has mild shortness of breath . His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 110/min and regular, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 195/64 mm Hg. Moist crackles are heard at the left lung base. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 16,700/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 90% Ban~ 2% Lymphocytes 8% Serum Na+ K+ c1- Hco3- Glucose Creatinine AST ALT 137 mEq/L 4.8 mEq/L 97 mEq/L 20 mEq/L 180 mg/dL 1.5 mg/dL 18 U/L 12 U/L An x-ray of the chest confirms left lower lobe pneumonia . Immediate discontinuation of which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-day history of increasingly severe left hip pain. She now has difficulty walking because of the pain. She has temporal arteritis and hypertension . Her medications are prednisone and enalapril. Vital signs are within normal limits. Internal and external range of motion of the left hip is limited by pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . An x-ray of the left hip shows no abnormalities . An MRI of the hips is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.D: x-rays show no finding, making hip fracture

questionStem: A study is conducted to compare a new stool test with mucosa! biopsy for diagnosing Helicobacter pylori infection. A total of 400 patients with suspected H. pylori infection are enrolled. Patients are screened using both methods. Results show that of the 100 patients who tested positive for H. pylori infection on biopsy, 80 also tested positive using the new stool test; 120 patients who tested negative for H. pylori infection on biopsy tested positive using the new stool test. Which of the following represents the sensitivity of the new stool test for H. pylori infection in this study?

A47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of soreness in the back of her throat and pain on swallowing. She has had recurrent episodes of tonsillitis during the past 2 years. Examination shows massive edema of the soft palate and enlarged tonsils with a purulent discharge from the right tonsil. Without treatment , this patient is at increased risk for which of the following?

A previously healthy 27-year-old intern comes to the emergency department 5 minutes after she was stuck in the left middle finger by a 20-gauge needle used on a 22-year-old patient with AIDS. The patient is currently being treated with zidovudine (AZT), indinavir, and lamivudine (3TC); his current plasma HIV viral load is undetectable . The patient's serum studies 2 days ago showed: Total bilirubin AST ALT 0.8 mg/dl 100 U/L 80 U/L Hepatitis B surface antibody positive Hepatitis B surface antigen negative The intern had completed hepatitis B immunizations 10 months ago. Examination shows a needle puncture wound. In addition to chemoprophylaxis for HIV exposure, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for this intern?

choices.B: Administering hyperimmune hepatitis B immune globulin

questionStem: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination. He has a 1-year history of hypertension controlled by a thiazide diuretic . He smokes one pack of cigarettes and drinks 3 ounces of alcohol daily. He has gained 6 kg (13 lb) since his last visit 1 year ago. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and now weighs 88 kg (195 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m 2• His blood pressure is 156/88 mm Hg. His serum LDL-cholesterol concentration is 150 mg/dl, and serum HDL-cholesterol concentration is 50 mg/dl. Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for coronary artery disease in this patient?

A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the emergency department because of an uncontrollable nosebleed for 6 hours. This is her fourth nosebleed over the past 2 weeks . Each of the previous nosebleeds stopped within approximately 2 hours. Her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals, but she did have heavier than usual bleeding during her last two menstrual periods . She takes no medications . She has no history of bleeding problems , including during an uncomplicated appendectomy at the age of 10 years and during delivery of her two children . There is no family history of bleeding problems. Examination shows scattered petechiae over the trunk and upper and lower extremities . There is fresh and clotted blood in the nares with continued oozing of blood. Her hemoglobin concentration is 9.8 g/dl, leukocyte count is 9000/mm 3 with a normal differential, and platelet count is 20,000/mm 3. Examination of bone marrow aspirate shows megakaryocytes . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: An initial first step for treatment is steroid therapy.
incorrectExplanation: (B) Methotrexate therapy has not been shown to have an effect on ITP. (C/D/E) Interventions on the spleen are reserved for severe cases that persist despite medical treatment and have relapses. This patient has a new diagnosis and thus deserves a course of steroids to see effect. ,.

questionStem: A 77-year-old man is brought by his wife for a follow-up examination 3 weeks after an episode of right middle lobe pneumonia. The pneumonia is improving with antibiotic therapy. Three months ago, he had a similar episode . His wife says that he swallows his food well, but he has had a slight increase in his chronic cough after meals. He has multi-infarct (vascular) dementia. He smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years, but he quit 15 years ago. He has never had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease . Rhonchi are heard over the right midlung field on auscultation ; the diaphragm has poor excursion . His speech is mildly dysarthric. His Mini-Mental State Examination score is 20/30. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Recommendation of a full liquid diet with liquid supplements

questionStem: A healthy 39-year-old man of German descent comes for a routine examination . He had a cholecystectomy at the age of 25 years. He has had several episodes of mild jaundice over the past 10 years that resolved spontaneously . He appears healthy . Examination shows no abnormalities except for splenomegaly . His hematocrit is 39%, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration is 36% Hb/cell, and mean corpuscular volume is 80 µm 3. Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative . A blood smear shows erythrocytes with loss of central pallor. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?

choices.A: Abnormal red blood cell membrane F) Globin chain mutation
choices.B: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia G) Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
choices.C: Congenital dihydrofolate reductase deficiency H) Lead poisoning
choices.D: Decreased erythropoietin concentration I} Pyruvate kinase deficiency
choices.E: Folic acid deficiency J) Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency

correctExplanation: There is no evidence of any autoimmune disease, and the negative result of the Coombs test makes autoimmune conditions unlikely.
incorrectExplanation: (C) The patient is in his 30s and takes no supplemental folic acid so a history of congenital dihydrofolate reductase deficiency is not likely. (D) There is no evidence of decreased erythropoietin concentration, and the patient has no known risk factors such as chronic kidney disease. (E) There is no reason to think the patient is deficient in folate or (J) vitamin B12 (cobalamin) because there is no evidence of macrocytosis. (G) Glucose 6- phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is unlikely in patients of northern European descent and would manifest after taking a substance known to stress the oxidative-reduction system (such as sulfa antibiotics) . (F) Globin chain mutations would result in smaller cells , typically a more profound anemia and auto-splenectomy at this age (rather than splenomegaly). (H) Lead poisoning is not likely given the information in the vignette, and (I) while pyruvate kinase deficiency certainly fits the clinical picture, it usually is more problematic in childhood and requires transfusions if the phenotype is significant. Neither has been included in the vignette, making spherocytosis more likely. ,.

questionStem: A 4 7-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of progressive swelling of both legs and generalized weakness . He says he now has some difficulty performing his usual activities . Last year, he received the diagnosis of hepatitis B and C. He has a long-standing history of intravenous drug use. He refused treatment for hepatitis C and currently takes no medications. He is not in acute distress. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 55 kg (121 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 160/99 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is nontender. There is no hepatomegaly. Muscle strength is normal. questionStem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever and confusion for 4 hours. She has a 5-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus. She had Neisseria meningitidis meningitis 3 years ago. Current medications include hydroxychloroquine. Her temperature is 40°C (104°F). Examination shows nuchal rigidity. Kernig sign is present. correctExplanation: Deficiency of terminal components of complement is the most likely cause of this patient's recent and recurrent infection with Neisseria meningitidis. The presence of fever, nuchal rigidity, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrating gram-negative diplococci is diagnostic for bacterial meningitis. Deficiency of terminal complement factors (eg, C5—C9) impairs the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) and predisposes patients to infection with Neisseria species, although infections tend to occur with uncommon serotypes. While the complement cascade can be activated via the classical, lectin, or alternative pathways, each pathway converges on the same point whereby C3 is cleaved to release C3a and C3b. The C3 convertase complex subsequently leads to activation of C5, with formation of C5a and C5b, the latter of which complexes with C6, C7, C8, and C9 to form the MAC. The MAC creates a transmembrane pore that interferes with the integrity of the cellular membrane, leading to cell lysis. Screening for terminal complement deficiency usually starts with determination of the CH50, a diagnostic test that measures the ability of the patient's serum to lyse sheep erythrocytes coated with antibodies directed against erythrocyte membrane proteins. Because this test measures the activity of factors C1—C9, a deficiency at any point will lead to an abnormal result, although in patients with terminal complement deficiency, the CH50 concentration will be very decreased or even zero. In addition to treating infections, further treatment should include vaccination against N. meningitidis, H. influenzae, and S. pneumoniae.

The time between infection and onset of symptoms is variable, with incubation time lasting several weeks or more. questionStem: Prior to discharge to a skilled nursing care facility, an 80-year-old woman is evaluated in the hospital because of a decreased hemoglobin concentration. She underwent hemicolectomy 10 days ago for gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to diverticulosis. Four units of packed red blood cells were transfused during the procedure. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her medications are lisinopril and metformin. Today, her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mucosal pallor and conjunctival icterus. Abdominal examination shows a well-healing incision. Baseline hemoglobin concentration on postoperative day 3 was 10.0 g/dL . Hemoglobin concentration today is 7.5 g/dL . Laboratory studies are most likely to show which of the following additional findings? Direct Antiglobulin Serum Bilirubin (Coombs) Test Concentration
correctExplanation: Laboratory studies are most likely to disclose a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test and an increased serum concentration of indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin, which is consistent with a hemolytic transfusion reaction. This patient's presentation 10 days following blood transfusion, and not immediately during transfusion, suggests a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR). In contrast to acute hemolytic transfusion reactions, which arise because of ABO incompatibility and can be life-threatening, DHTRs usually result from the presence of autoantibodies against minor erythrocyte antigens (eg, Rh antigens). In all cases, DHTR requires prior exposure to the antigen for the patient to produce antibodies, but in some instances, the antibodies may not be found in titers during routine blood bank screening to be appropriately recognized. The Coombs test involves incubating the patient's erythrocytes with anti-IgG and anti-complement antibody known as Coombs reagent. If an autoantibody or complement is bound to the surface of the erythrocytes, the Coombs reagent will bind to it and cause agglutination resulting in a positive test. The fixation of complement results in intravascular hemolysis and an increased indirect bilirubin while binding of antibodies to the surface of erythrocytes may mark them for removal in the reticuloendothelial system. In either case, patients present with anemia and evidence of hemolysis. Treatment is supportive.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 92-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her family because of a 1-year history of cognitive decline. correctExplanation: Alzheimer disease (AD) is the most common type of dementia. It typically presents with progressive cognitive deterioration that begins with short-term memory impairment and a decline in visuospatial abilities, which progresses to apraxia, language abnormalities, and dysexecutive syndrome. The disease culminates in behavioral and personality changes that prevent the patient from performing basic activities of daily living, such as bathing. Age is the strongest risk factor for AD. The incidence of AD approximately doubles every 5 years after age 65. Less significant risk factors include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and a sedentary lifestyle. AD may be treated with drugs that both directly and indirectly increase acetylcholine in synaptic clefts. These include donepezil and cholinesterase inhibitors, which non-competitively and reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, thereby increasing the amount of synaptic acetylcholine available for neurotransmission. Though these drugs may slow the rate of cognitive decline and modestly improve functionality, they are not curative for AD.

questionStem: A previously healthy 42-year-old man comes to the office because of severe right-sided headaches for the past 3 weeks. He says that he awakens every night at 3 AM with a sharp stabbing pain behind the right eye that usually lasts about 30 minutes. There is no associated nausea. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 25 years and drinks a six-pack of beer daily. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination during an episode shows ptosis on the right and tearing and conjunctival injection; the right pupil is 2 mm, and the left is 4 mm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Cluster headaches are primary headaches that typically present with brief (<120 minutes), unilateral, severe pain in the orbital, supraorbital, or temporal region of the head and are accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms. The pathogenesis is incompletely understood but likely involves activation of sensory fibers of the trigeminal nerve and parasympathetic nerves. Autonomic symptoms commonly include ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, and/or nasal congestion. Patients typically present between the ages of 20 and 50 years and are often male. Cigarette and alcohol use may be triggers for patients with a history of cluster headaches. The headaches often recur over a series of weeks to months, sometimes at the same time each year. Oxygen therapy with 100% oxygen is the most effective first-line abortive treatment, and verapamil is the first-line prophylactic treatment. The clinician should always distinguish primary headache types (eg, tension, cluster, migraine) from secondary headache types (eg, intracranial bleeding, tumors, glaucoma) because the treatment and prognosis differ greatly.

correctExplanation: Seborrheic keratosis is a benign proliferation of the epidermis. It is characterized histologically by a benign, acanthotic proliferation of keratinocytes with absence of cellular atypia. The lesions are typically round, raised, brown or tan in color, and sharply demarcated with an adherent or stuck-on appearance. Seborrheic keratosis is common in middle-aged and older adults and is most associated with increasing age. While seborrheic keratosis is benign, the sudden appearance of numerous seborrheic keratosis lesions on the back and trunk, known as the Leser-Trélat sign, can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of gastrointestinal malignancy. questionStem: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of persistent actinic keratosis despite treatment with 5-fluorouracil. Examination shows a 0.5 x 0.5-cm lesion. A photograph of the lesion is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctExplanation: Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion that may progress to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Clinically, lesions typically appear as light pink, ill-defined macules with a gritty texture in areas of prolonged sun exposure, such as the face, ears, and dorsal hands. Actinic keratosis may be treated with topical medications, such as 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod, excision, cryotherapy, or dermabrasion. Ablative therapies are best used when the diagnosis is relatively certain, and a histopathologic specimen is not required. Lack of response to topical therapy should raise suspicion for possible SCC and should prompt an excisional biopsy. A low threshold of suspicion for SCC should be maintained particularly in patients with a history of immunocompromise or solid organ transplantation. Excisional biopsy is preferable because of its ability to assess for invasive disease and curative potential if the entire lesion is removed.

SCC lesions that are incompletely excised usually require further excision with careful assessment of the margins. Radiation therapy (Choice D) is not typically used for lesions that are concerning for SCC. Radiation is sometimes used in conjunction with surgical excision in high-risk SCC tumors or in lesions that are not amenable to complete excision. Qualifying dental procedures for which prophylaxis is recommended include any procedures in which the manipulation of gingival tissue or periapical teeth occurs, or in any case of perforation of the oral mucosa. When indicated, antibiotics that cover oral flora should be administered 30 to 60 minutes before the time of the procedure as a single dose.

questionStem: A 48-year-old man has a 6-month history of pain in both buttocks when he walks and erectile dysfunction. He has been a heavy smoker for 20 years. His blood pressure in the lower extremities is less than half of that in his arms. His serum cholesterol concentration is 286 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Aortic atherosclerosis commonly occurs at the aortic arch, where it serves as a major risk factor for cerebral embolism, and in the abdominal aorta distal to the renal arteries. Aortic atherosclerosis may lead to ischemia of the lower extremities, presenting with claudication of the buttocks and legs, lower extremity pain, paresthesia, paraplegia, shiny, hairless skin, and erectile dysfunction. questionStem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of progressive shortness of breath and right upper abdominal pain. She has been unable to sleep while supine because of difficulty breathing. She underwent chemotherapy 1 year ago for breast cancer. She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 104/80 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous pulsations at the angle of the jaw with the patient sitting upright. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Heart sounds are distant. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard. Abdominal examination shows diffuse hepatomegaly. There is 2+ pedal edema. Her serum urea nitrogen concentration is 42 mg/dL, and serum creatinine concentration is 1.6 mg/dL. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: The presentation of pericardial effusion may range from asymptomatic to severe, symptomatic cardiac tamponade in large-volume or rapidly accumulating cases. Compression of the cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle, impairs cardiac filling and decreases cardiac output (low stroke volume). Presenting features include but are not limited to a history of chest discomfort, shortness of breath, decreased exercise tolerance, fluid retention, and lightheadedness, along with any historical feature that may explain the cause of effusion (eg, weight loss or history of malignancy in cases of malignant effusion). Vital signs may be normal in cases of small effusions or may include tachycardia and hypotension in cases of tamponade. Physical examination findings include Beck triad (hypotension, distended jugular veins, and distant heart sounds) in the case of tamponade. These findings occur because of the presence of fluid in the pericardial space muffling heart sounds and increasing collapsing pressure on the right ventricle, which is transmitted to the vena cavae and their tributaries. In such a manner, increased right heart pressure is reflected as increased jugular venous distention (JVD). ECG may disclose low voltage and/or electrical alternans. There may be pulsus paradoxus on evaluation of blood pressure. Confirmatory diagnosis requires visualization of the effusion, often on echocardiogram. Mild or asymptomatic cases may be managed conservatively with watchful waiting and treatment of any predisposing conditions, whereas moderate, symptomatic, or severe cases, especially if accompanied by hemodynamic instability require treatment with pericardiocentesis or a pericardial window to restore diastolic filling and cardiac output. questionStem: A previously healthy 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of severe abdominal and back pain. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 120/min and regular, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 160/105 mm Hg in the right arm and 80/50 mm Hg in the left arm. Breath sounds are normal. Cardiac examination shows a normal S, and S,. Femoral pulses are normal on the right and absent on the left. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 39% Leukocyte count 10,500/mm3 Serum Urea nitrogen 32 mg/dL Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL Liver function tests are within the reference range. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Aortic dissection classically presents with severe, acute, tearing chest or abdominal pain radiating to the back and differential blood pressures between extremities with asymmetric pulses. Dissection begins with a disruption of the tunica intima of the vessel, which permits blood to dissect the layers of the vessel wall with each heartbeat. A dissection flap may advance in any direction within the vessel, occluding or involving branch ostia. If vessel takeoffs supplying the limbs are affected, pulse deficits or differential blood pressures may arise. If splanchnic vessels are involved, end-organ dysfunction such as mesenteric ischemia or acute kidney injury may be seen. Management may be medical or surgical and depends on the location of the dissection within the vessel (eg, Type A vs Type B). Regardless of the need for surgery, all patients with dissection should receive immediate medical management to prevent further progression of the flap. Controlling the patient's heart rate and blood pressure is the priority in preventing progression. Intravenous B-adrenergic blocking medications should be used with a goal of lowering the heart rate to approximately 60 beats per minute and the blood pressure to less than 100 to 120 mm Hg systolic and 60 to 80 mm Hg diastolic. Lowering the heart rate helps prevent the advancement of the dissection flap and resultant occlusion of branch vessels by limiting the pulse pressure differential. Complications such as stroke, acute coronary syndrome, and cardiac tamponade may be immediately life-threatening. ¢ G € 6 t Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause

questionStem: A 67-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital 2 hours after the acute onset of pain in the left lower extremity. She has mild mitral insufficiency and chronic atrial fibrillation. She takes no medications. Examination shows a cool left lower extremity and mottling of the skin to the knee. Sensation is absent below the midthigh. She is unable to move her left foot. After undergoing left femoral embolectomy, sensorimotor function is intact, and left femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are palpable. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a dilated left atrium without a patent foramen ovale or atrioventricular thrombus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to prevent further embolization in this patient?
correctExplanation: Atrial fibrillation describes the uncoordinated contraction of the cardiac atria and is often the result of chronic left atrial enlargement caused by mitral regurgitation or increased left sided pressures (eg, in left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction). When the atria do not uniformly fill and contract, blood can become stagnant in areas of the atria, especially in the left atrial appendage. Blood in stasis is prone to coagulate, which results in the formation of a thrombus within the cardiac chambers. If a portion of such a thrombus embolizes, many clinical syndromes can result. For example, strokes occur when a thromboembolism occludes cerebral circulation, mesenteric ischemia occurs when the mesenteric arteries are occluded, and acute limb ischemia occurs when an artery supplying an extremity becomes occluded. Management of atrial fibrillation includes anticoagulation with warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant (eg, apixaban) to prevent the formation of atrial thrombus, which reduces the risk for thromboembolic complications.

The initial presentation is often nonspecific, including weight loss and fatigue. Once the tumor has invaded or involved neurosensory and vascular structures, patients may begin to experience coughing and hemoptysis. If the lesion is large enough to invade or obstruct a bronchus, patients may also experience post-obstructive or recurrent pneumonia in parenchyma distal to the lesion, caused by atelectasis and impaired endobronchial clearance of mucus, secretions, and inhaled pathogens. In this patient, the decreased breath sounds over the right posterior hemithorax suggest the presence of an endobronchial obstruction to airflow; this is further supported by atelectasis on x-ray in the corresponding area. questionStem: A 70-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath with exertion. Six months ago, he was able to walk five blocks before having shortness of breath. He now has shortness of breath after walking one block. He has not had chest pain, palpitations, swelling of his legs, or shortness of breath at night. He has hypertension. His medications are lisinopril and aspirin. He does not smoke cigarettes. He is a retired foundry worker. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 Ib); BMI is 24 kg/m2. His pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows no other abnormalities. There is no edema of the extremities. Results of pulmonary function testing show an FVC of 65% of predicted and an FEV ,:FVC ratio of 70%. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pneumoconiosis describes interstitial lung disease arising because of inhalation of small solid particulate matter such as dust or powder (eg, talc, silica, beryllium, and ores) that leads to the development of fibrosis with resultant restrictive lung disease. It is often seen in patients with chronic exposures, such as foundry workers, miners, shipyard workers, cotton workers, farmers, stone drillers, and sandblasters. The disease's progress is often worsened by smoking. It generally presents with chronic symptoms of cough and shortness of breath on exertion; when severe or advanced, it can be associated with the need for supplemental oxygen and symptoms of heart failure (eg, cor pulmonale). Diagnosis is based on clinical history, symptoms, examination, exposure history, characteristic imaging tests that show fibrosis (x-ray may show honeycombing and fibrosis, especially in the apices), and pulmonary function tests that disclose a restrictive pattern of lung disease marked by decreased overall volumes and capacities but a preserved or increased ratio of FEV ,:FVC. This ratio is a key distinguishing feature from obstructive lung disease, which generally presents with a decrease in the ratio.

questionStem: A previously healthy 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of abdominal cramps and diarrhea. During this period, she has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss and 8 to 10 loose stools daily that contain a small amount of mucus. Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness of the right lower quadrant. A Sudan black B fat stain of the stool is positive. Colonoscopy with biopsy of the terminal ileum shows inflammation with granuloma formation. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's steatorrhea?

correctExplanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, most frequently involving the terminal ileum. It can arise anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract and is a subclass of inflammatory bowel disease. Most patients experience chronic abdominal cramping, bloody diarrhea, and weight loss. Examination often shows generalized abdominal tenderness, sometimes worse in the right lower quadrant, and extraintestinal manifestations such as uveitis. Severe Crohn disease can result in intestinal obstruction from stricture or inflammation, bowel perforation, intraabdominal abscess, and the formation of fistulas. Crohn disease may manifest with steatorrhea caused by the impairment of bile salt resorption secondary to inflammation of the terminal ileum. Bile salts play a crucial role in the solubilization of fats in the enteric lumen, and are recycled through the enterohepatic circulation, which is dependent on the resorption of bile salts through an intact ileal mucosa. Impairment of bile salt resorption because of ileal inflammation can overwhelm the ability of the liver to synthesize de novo bile acids, resulting in a deficiency in fat-soluble vitamin absorption. questionStem: An obese 42-year-old woman has an episode of colicky pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen that lasts 2 hours and subsides spontaneously. She has no fever or leukocytosis and no signs of peritoneal irritation in the right upper quadrant. Liver function tests show no abnormalities. Ultrasonography shows gallstones. choices.A: Bacterial growth in bile within the common hepatic duct

The pain is typically dull, severe, triggered by meals, and may radiate to the right shoulder. Biliary colic can be distinguished from cholecystitis by a lack of fever, a normal abdominal examination, and a lack of leukocytosis. Abdominal ultrasonography can aid the diagnosis by identifying the presence of gallstones. Provided that the clinical picture and examination are improving, the acute management of biliary colic is generally conservative with oral analgesics. Elective cholecystectomy is recommended to prevent future complications from the gallstones. If symptoms of biliary colic progress to show features of jaundice, hepatic injury, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, choledocholithiasis, or cholangitis, operative (cholecystectomy) or interventional (eg, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) management should take place.

questionStem: A 23-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-week history of fatigue and swelling of her eyelids, ankles, and feet. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 Ib); BMI is 21 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows 2+ periorbital edema and 3+ pedal edema. No other abnormalities are noted. Fasting serum studies show a total cholesterol concentration of 348 mg/dL and triglyceride concentration of greater than 400 mg/dL. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
correctExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure. This occurs because of the loss of normal size and charge filtration of the glomerular capillary and Bowman capsule interface. Causes of nephrotic syndrome include minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and proteinuria. Complications include hypercoagulability caused by the urinary loss of proteins such as antithrombin-3, which functions to inhibit coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII. Deficiency of antithrombin-3 leads to hypercoagulability and would put this patient at high risk for thrombotic conditions such as deep venous thrombosis. Patients with nephrotic syndrome are also at an increased risk for infection because of the urinary loss of gamma globulins.

However, a positive result on a sensitive test must be verified by a highly specific test, which would have a decreased risk for false positive results. Therefore, sensitive tests are often used for screening, as in this patient, but must be verified by a more specific test. Therefore, a test with 99% specificity would be most likely to confirm or refute this patient's diagnosis. Cases and controls are interviewed after their conditions stabilize. The researchers conclude that regular use of alcohol reduced the risk of colon cancer. Which of the following is the most important reason to be concerned about the authors' conclusion?

For example, in this scenario, choosing a control population that consists of patients admitted to the hospital with acute injuries likely interferes with the interpreted results of the studies that the regular use of alcohol reduced the risk for colon cancer. This is because regular alcohol use can lead to acute injuries during intoxication, and thus the control group may have a higher baseline use of alcohol compared to the case group. This has likely led to the possible inappropriate conclusion in this study that regular use of alcohol reduced the risk for colon cancer. questionStem: A77-year-old man has had intermittent confusion since transfer from the hospital to hospice care 6 days ago. His blood pressure has ranged between 90/45 mm Hg and 70/20 mm Hg during this period. He was treated in the hospital for a myocardial infarction sustained 3 weeks ago. During the past 8 years, he has been admitted to the hospital four times for myocardial infarction. He has been treated unsuccessfully for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and has been unable to tolerate inotropic agents. He has had left hemiparesis since he sustained a stroke 30 years ago. His physician has explained to him and his family that he is not a candidate for cardiac transplant or implant of a left ventricular assistance device. The patient has severe chronic back pain. His only medication is morphine. The patient's advance directive designates his daughter as his health care proxy, and the patient has explained that he wants his daughter to make medical decisions for him. The daughter says that the hospice care is insufficient in controlling her father's pain and asks that he be admitted to the hospital. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Hospice care is a form of health care that aims to provide comfort and palliation to terminally ill patients in their last stages of life. As a terminally ill patient approaches the end of life, they may decide to focus on the quality of remaining life rather than on increasing the quantity of time remaining. Hospice is a multidisciplinary healthcare model that includes physicians, nurses, social workers, and chaplains and aids to eliminate suffering and provide spiritual and emotional support to patients and their family. Goals often include treating symptoms, such as pain and anxiety, and providing a patient as much time at home as possible by avoiding further hospital admissions. This patient has terminal heart failure associated with arrhythmias, as well as hemiparesis, and has opted to enroll in hospice care. Therefore, care should be taken to eliminate the symptoms related to this patient's chronic illnesses by discussing the patient's pain control with the hospice staff, rather than admitting him to the hospital again.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Spiritual counseling (Choice B) and psychiatric assessment (Choice C) are services provided by hospice care. However, neither would improve this patient's back pain to prevent another hospital admission. Titrating this patient's pain medications would be the more appropriate next step in management. Admission to the hospital (Choice D) would not be in line with this patient's goals. It would be more appropriate to try to manage his pain as an outpatient prior to admitting to the hospital, which would limit his remaining time at home. questionStem: A 54-year-old man is hospitalized because of a 5-day history of chills and moderate pain, edema, and erythema of the right foot. His symptoms began 2 days after he stepped on a nail. He has coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He has no known drug allergies. His medications are metformin, insulin, lisinopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, and aspirin. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 145/92 mm Hg. Examination of the right lower extremity shows erythema, warmth, and tenderness to palpation from the proximal aspect of the ankle to the dorsum of the foot. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam therapy is begun, and the patient’s home medication regimen is continued. While filling the prescription, the pharmacist notices a problem in the medication order. Investigation shows that the physician wrote the prescription in an immediate-release formulation instead of an extended-release formulation. Which of the following best characterizes this type of medical error?
correctExplanation: Medical errors are common in healthcare and are often the result of an interplay of individual and systemic factors. They range from medication administration errors to failures of equipment, among a variety of others. These errors or mistakes may or may not reach the patient. Adverse events occur from medical errors that reach the patient and cause unintended harm, whereas sentinel events are an extreme form of these events that lead to permanent disability or death. However, many safeguards are put into place to prevent errors from reaching patients. For example, as in this case, the medication ordered by the physician is checked by the pharmacist prior to being dispensed, and then it would be further checked by the bedside nurse before it is delivered to the patient. These medical errors that do not reach the patient are referred to as near miss events.

Adverse event (Choice B) is a medical error that reaches the patient and causes harm, such as giving the wrong medication to a patient. Symptoms include fever, chills, myalgias, malaise, headaches, cough, nausea, and vomiting. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) recommends annual influenza virus vaccination beginning at age greater than 6 months. The influenza vaccine is available as a trivalent or quadrivalent intramuscular injection of inactivated virus or as a nasal spray of live attenuated virus. Inactivated influenza vaccine can be safely administered via intramuscular injection to patients who are immunocompromised, who may be at higher risk for severe illness and influenza-related complications if they forego vaccination and are infected with influenza. Influenza is a seasonal illness, affecting patients in winter and early spring. This patient who is immunocompromised should receive annual vaccination for influenza virus.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of vaginal discharge and itching for 1 week. She has been sexually active with multiple partners for 3 years, and they use condoms occasionally. Over the past 3 years, she has had three episodes of candidal vaginitis and three episodes of genital herpes. Pelvic examination shows a white vaginal discharge with a cottage-cheese consistency. Examination shows no other abnormalities. A Pap smear is obtained. Topical antifungal medications are prescribed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: HIV testing is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis for this patient with high-risk sexual behavior and recurrent episodes of vaginal candidiasis and genital herpes. Routine, one-time screening is recommended for most sexually active individuals over the age of 13 years, but more frequent screening is indicated for those with a higher risk for contracting HIV. These populations include those with numerous sexual partners, especially if barrier protection is infrequently used, patients who exchange sex for money, injection drug users, those who have HIV-positive partners, and men who have sex with men, among others. This patient's high-risk sexual behavior and history of recurrent genital herpes and vaginal candidiasis strongly suggests the presence of underlying immunodeficiency as might occur with advanced HIV infection. As such, testing for HIV is prudent. Testing typically involves the use of a fourth-generation combined HIV 1/2 antigen and antibody test. If the test is positive, then further antibody testing to differentiate between infection with HIV-1 or HIV-2 is indicated. If the fourth-generation test is positive but the results of further antibody testing are negative or indeterminate, then the HIV viral load should be measured. While genotyping is usually recommended to determine resistance patterns for antiretroviral drugs, a positive HIV test should prompt immediate initiation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).

Vaginal candidiasis can be diagnosed without the use of a fungal culture as yeast forms are readily appreciated on microscopy of vaginal secretion thereby making fungal culture unnecessary. It can be diagnosed Clinically. Herpes culture (Choice C) is incorrect. Genital herpes infection can be diagnosed clinically in the setting of characteristic lesions, but laboratory confirmation is necessary as well with the first episode. Viral culture remains the gold standard but is not sensitive, so PCR-based tests are preferred. questionStem: Six hours after beginning dicloxacillin therapy for cellulitis of the right lower extremity, a 37-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of pruritic rash, dyspnea, and mild cough. She has a history of childhood asthma but no history of adverse reactions to medication. Six months ago, she had streptococcal pharyngitis treated with penicillin. She has otherwise been healthy. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 86/64 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Examination of the skin shows 1- to 2-cm areas of pink urticaria over the trunk and upper and lower extremities and a 3-cm, erythematous, mildly tender area over the distal right lower extremity. Air movement is poor, and inspiratory and expiratory wheezes are heard on auscultation. Her hemoglobin concentration is 13.1 g/dL, and leukocyte count is 9500/mm%. A chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. In addition to discontinuing dicloxacillin therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Administration of epinephrine is the most appropriate immediate step in management for this patient with clinical features of anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction that develops following exposure to an allergen; in this case, the presumed allergen is dicloxacillin. It is caused by widespread IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and is characterized by histaminergic responses within multiple organ systems leading to flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and vasodilation, which can lead to airway obstruction and circulatory collapse. If not managed promptly, death can occur from hypoxia and/or distributive shock. The diagnosis is made clinically, and the first treatment that should be given is intramuscular epinephrine. Adjunctive medications may include inhaled B-adrenergic agonists, glucocorticoids, histamine blockers, fluid resuscitation, and potentially invasive airway or vasopressor support. When medications are suspected as the cause of anaphylaxis an allergy warning should be placed in the patient's chart. At the time of discharge, all patients should be provided with an epinephrine autoinjector with instructions on how to use it. They should also be educated on the nature of their allergy and advised to avoid antibiotics within the same class in the future. In some instances, referral to an allergist may be appropriate.

While this medication may improve symptoms of pruritus and urticaria, it is considered an adjunct medication in anaphylaxis as it does not reverse the underlying process as epinephrine does. Prednisone (Choice C) is a steroid that is frequently given to patients with anaphylaxis even though it has little immediate effect on the disease process. questionStem: A previously healthy 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of progressively worsening fatigue; he has had a 14-kg (30-Ib) weight loss during this period. Vital signs are within normal limits. The spleen tip is palpated 8 cm below the left costal margin. Examination shows no other abnormalities. His hematocrit is 40%, leukocyte count is 36,000/mm%, and platelet count is 70,000/mm3. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy show 100% cellularity with an increase in all hematopoietic cell lines. The presence of which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The presence of the BCR/ABL fusion protein, the product of an abnormal chromosome known as the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome, will likely confirm the diagnosis of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). CML is diagnosed by the presence of the Ph chromosome, a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, which causes constitutive activation of the ABL kinase protein. Activation of ABL kinase leads to subsequent activation of the JAK/STAT and Ras/MAPK/ERK pathways, leading to increased hematopoietic proliferation, inhibition of normal checkpoint inhibition, and resistance to apoptosis. While the Ph chromosome is required for the diagnosis of CML, it can also be found in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Typical laboratory findings in CML include leukocytosis with an increase in nearly all cell lines. Basophilia and eosinophilia are characteristic. Leukostasis, a condition in which leukocytosis leads to end organ damage from occlusion of capillaries by malignant cells, is uncommon in CML. This contrasts with conditions such as acute leukemias in which circulating blasts, which are large and not particularly pliable, easily lodge in capillaries causing pulmonary and neurologic complications. Treatment of CML is primarily with tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib or dasatinib. Such medications are effective and often result in complete molecular response (remission) within several months of initiation.
