questionStem: An 8-year-old girl has had migrating polyarthralgia and fever for 4 days. She appears ill. Examination shows an evanescent rash. Her left knee is red, swollen , and tender. The chest is clear to auscultation . A grade 4/6, holosystolic apical murmur is heard with radiation to the axilla . There is no organomegaly . Which of the following is the most likely cardiac abnormality?
correctExplanation: Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) may present with migratory polyarthralgia, pancarditis (pericarditis, myocarditis, or endocarditis), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea, fever, increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and short PR interval following an infection from group A streptococci, most often pharyngitis. The mitral valve is the most commonly affected. Antibodies to M protein enhance host defenses against group A streptococci but can result in an autoimmune attack against self-antigens through molecular mimicry. This can result in valve inflammation and acute regurgitation. Chronic mitral regurgitation, prolapse, or stenosis can result as potential long-term sequelae.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aortic stenosis (Choice A) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that is heard best at the upper right sternal border and radiates to the carotid arteries. It classically occurs secondary to age-related fibrotic and calcific changes of the valve but can occur earlier in life in cases of bicuspid aortic valve or chronic rheumatic disease. Tetralogy of Fallo! (Choice C) consists of pulmonary infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect, and right ventricular hypertrophy, resulting in a right-to-left shunt with cyanosis first noted in infancy. The murmur heard with Tetralogy of Fallo! relates to the underlying ventricular septal defect, characterized by a holosystolic murmur heard best in the lower left sternal border, and to the pulmonic stenosis, characterized by a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur in the pulmonic listening area. Tricuspid regurgitation (Choice D) demonstrates a holosystolic murmur heard best in the lower left sternal border. The tricuspid valve is less commonly affected than the mitral or aortic valves in ARF. Ventricular septal defect (VSD) (Choice E) is characterized by a holosystolic murmur heard best in the lower left sternal border. VSD generally presents at birth and is not associated with ARF.

questionStem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department 60 minutes after the sudden onset of tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . He does not smoke. He is 190 cm (6 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 80 kg (176 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2• His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg in his right arm and 70/40 mm Hg in his left arm. Pulse oximetry on 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . The lungs are clear to auscultation . Heart sounds are normal. Pulses are difficult to palpate in the left upper extremity. Peripheral pulses are otherwise normal. A chest x-ray shows a widened upper mediastinum . An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no acute changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Labetalol is a first-line antihypertensive medication used to decrease blood pressure in the setting of presumed aortic dissection, which classically presents with severe, acute, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, differential blood pressures between extremities, and a widened mediastinum on a chest x-ray. To prevent further progression of the dissection flap, controlling the patient's heart rate and blood pressure is the first priority. An intravenous ~-adrenergic blocking agent should be used with a goal of decreasing the heart rate to approximately 60/min and the blood pressure to less than 100 to 120 mm Hg systolic and 60 to 80 mm Hg diastolic. Decreasing the heart rate helps prevent the advancement of the dissection flap and resultant occlusion of branch vessels by limiting the pulse pressure differential. Labetalol is a nonspecific adrenoreceptor blocker that targets both ar and ~radrenoreceptors, making it an ideal choice for the management of the patient's heart rate, cardiac contractility, and vascular resistance.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Administration of heparin (Choice A) would be appropriate in the management of an acute coronary syndrome. Administering therapeutic anticoagulation in the setting of an aortic dissection increases the risk for severe thoracic hemorrhage and exsanguination if there is an associated aneurysm and/or damage to the tunica adventitia. Administration of nitroglycerin (Choice C) may be appropriate in cases of aortic dissection for blood pressure control if the goal is not met with adrenoreceptor blockade; however, it would follow administration of a ~­ adrenergic blocking agent to prevent reflex tachycardia and widening of pulse pressure. Fiberoptic intubation (Choice D) may be appropriate for a patient with a compromised airway, but in cases without an impending threat to the airway would be superseded by management of the immediate life­ threatening condition, the patient's aortic dissection. Pericardiocentesis (Choice E) is appropriate in cases of pericardia! effusion and/or tamponade, which would present following symptoms of pericarditis, or with muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distention, and hypotension iftamponade from any cause is present. Pulsus paradoxus may be seen on examination.

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of ulcers on her right ankle for 6 months . There is no history of recent trauma . She has a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin for the past 4 years and a 2-year history of chronic bilateral ankle swelling . Her temperature is 37.?°C (99.9°F), pulse is 82/min , and blood pressure is 140/88 mm Hg. Examination shows ulceration of the medial aspect of the right ankle. There is bilateral lower leg and pedal edema with patches of brown pigmentation . Peripheral pulses are present and normal. Which of the following is the most likely pathogenesis of this condition?
correctExplanation: Venous insufficiency presents with dependent, pitting edema that improves with compression and elevation, along with paresthesia and hyperpigmentation of the skin (e.g., stasis dermatitis). In severe cases, chronic circulatory insufficiency can result in skin breakdown, leading to the development of open ulcers, classically along the medial aspect of the ankle. Venous insufficiency often results from deep venous thrombosis with resultant damage to the valves. When the thrombus resolves, the residual vessel may be dysfunctional from damage to the valve leaflets, valve annulus, or increased diameter of the native vessel. This prevents the vessel from functioning effectively and results in stagnant or retrograde venous flow secondary to gravity. Treatment includes wound care for the ulcer and measures to reverse the venous insufficiency such as optimizing venous return, diuresis, and improving circulatory function by optimizing cardiac, vascular, and kidney function.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Arterial insufficiency {Choice A) classically presents with claudication; thin, waxy, hairless skin; an absence of edema; and painful ulcers classically along the outer ankle, foot, or distal toes. Congestive heart failure {Choice B) presents with shortness of breath, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, peripheral edema, jugular venous distention, crackles on examination, and an S3 or S4 gallop. It may be an indirect cause of venous congestion through stasis and hypervolemia. Neurotrophic ulcer {Choice C) results from repetitive trauma or compression in areas of impaired sensation. Such ulcers are commonly seen overlying bony prominences (e.g., metatarsal heads) in cases of peripheral neuropathy from diabetes mellitus. Thromboangiitis obliterans {Choice D) is also known as Buerger disease and is a small vessel vasculitis associated with smoking. It typically presents with claudication symptoms that may progress to ulceration, gangrene, and autoamputation of digits. Ulcerations tend to occur in the tips of the fingers and toes.

questionStem: A 42-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of generalized itching and fatigue . He has chronic renal failure secondary to glomerulonephritis and receives hemodialysis three times weekly. Examination shows no abnormalities except for a patent arteriovenous fistula in the left forearm . His serum calcium concentration is 8.3 mg/dl , serum phosphorus concentration is 4.1 mg/dl , and serum intact parathyroid hormone concentration is 485 pg/ml (N=10-65) . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism typically presents with increased parathyroid hormone (PTH), hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia. It results from end-stage kidney disease because of the inability of the kidney to excrete phosphate and to produce active vitamin D, which results in hypocalcemia. Hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia result in the upregulation of PTH, which increases bony turnover to raise serum calcium and promotes renal excretion of phosphate. When unregulated, this process results in renal osteodystrophy which is the breakdown of bone because of excessive PTH stimulus of osteoclasts.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Familial hypercalcemic hypocalciuria {Choice A) arises from an abnormal calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells. As a result, PTH is not suppressed by normal or increased serum calcium. This leads to mild hypercalcemia with increased PTH because of the normal mechanism of action of PTH on osteoclasts and renal tubules. Cinacalcet is used to treat the condition, which increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor to the presence of serum calcium. Paraneoplastic syndrome {Choice B) defines a pathologic state that arises secondary to the presence of a malignancy; for example, squamous cell carcinoma of the lung may exogenously produce PTH-related peptide (PTH-rP) which functions in the same manner as PTH. Endogenous PTH is downregulated in the setting of exogenous PTH-rP. Primary hyperparathyroidism {Choice C) presents with hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and increased PTH. It occurs because of a parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism {Choice E) describes a state of chronic, refractory, autonomous production of PTH in the setting of long-standing kidney disease and presents with hypercalcemia, normal or increased serum phosphate, and increased PTH.

questionStem: A previously healthy 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of mild hearing loss and ringing in her right ear and a decreased sense of taste on the right. She also has had episodes of unsteadiness during this period and has had trouble understanding speech . She has not had nausea , vomiting , or vertigo . Examination shows no abnormalities . Audiometry shows predominantly high-frequency neural hearing loss on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) commonly presents with symptoms of hearing loss, vertigo, and ataxia, often slow in onset and progressive over a subacute to chronic period. Classically, these tumors occur at the cerebellopontine angle of the brain stem and are associated with neurofibromatosis. They may exert mass effect on cranial nerves within their proximity or invade the nerves from which they arise, often the facial nerve, vestibulocochlear nerve, or adjacent nerves. Facial nerve involvement manifests as facial asymmetry because of loss of skeletal muscle innervation and occasionally presents with diminished taste perception involving the ipsilateral anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Vestibulocochlear nerve palsy can present with diminished hearing or tinnitus (cochlear branch) on the ipsilateral side, and vertigo or ataxia may occur (vestibular branch) because of impaired proprioception from loss of input from the ipsilateral vestibule. In cases of larger masses, disruption of brain stem tracts and increased intracranial pressure can result.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Meniere disease (endolymphatic hydrops) (Choice B) presents with a classic triad of hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo, and is caused by fluid overload within the vestibulocochlear apparatus. It would not cause a decreased sense of taste. Meningitis (Choice C) typically presents with headache, fever, photophobia, phonophobia, and neck stiffness, as well as possible Kernig or Brudzinski signs noted on examination. It may be caused by bacterial, viral, fungal, or parasitic infections. Cranial nerve deficits may result, but a chronic presentation involving cranial nerves only would be rare. Otosclerosis (Choice D) results in dysfunction of the ossicles and causes conductive hearing loss; neurologic symptoms of ataxia would be unlikely. Pituitary adenoma (Choice E) can present with mass-like symptoms such as a headache or bitemporal hemianopsia, or with symptoms caused by the functional production of a hormone from the tumor (e.g., galactorrhea secondary to a prolactinoma). Because of the position of the pituitary gland within the sella turcica, symptoms involving the facial nerve or vestibulocochlear nerve would be unlikely.

questionStem: A previously healthy 15-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of difficulty breathing and sharp chest pain that began during track practice . She is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 55 kg (121 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m2. On arrival , her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) , pulse is 70/min , and respirations are 28/min . Breath sounds are decreased over the lateral chest on the right; there is hyperresonance to percussion . Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings?

choices.A: Air collection in the pleural space

correctExplanation: Pneumothorax results from air entering the intrapleural space from either an external (e.g., stab wound) or internal (e.g., ruptured bleb or bronchus, bronchopleural fistula) source. As the air accumulates within the space, the lung parenchyma becomes compressed, resulting in respiratory distress, reduced breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, and in severe cases, tension on the mediastinal structures impeding venous return resulting in hypotension. A spontaneous primary pneumothorax can occur in a tall, thin, young person because of the rupture of a pulmonary bleb, classically in a young athlete and often during physical exertion. Small pneumothoraces can be managed with serial examinations and repeat chest x-rays to confirm resolution. When the lesion is larger than 20 to 30% of the hemithoracic volume, a chest tube should be placed to evacuate the pneumothorax and reinflate the lung to prevent the development of a persistent or permanent pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax should be immediately decompressed with emergent needle thoracostomy to prevent hemodynamic collapse.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alveolar atelectasis (Choice B) may present with shortness of breath or be asymptomatic depending on the size and extent. A small, subsegmental atelectatic region may be completely asymptomatic, whereas if an entire lung is involved, the patient may present with shortness of breath, severe hypoxia, diminished ipsilateral breath sounds, and dullness to percussion. Narrowing of moderate-sized airways (Choice C) presents with poor air movement, wheezing or rhonchi, and cough, and describes the pathophysiology of bronchitis. Asthma classically results in narrowing of the small airways. Pleural inflammation (Choice D) presents with pleuritic chest pain, often following a viral respiratory infection. Occasionally, a friction rub may be heard on auscultation, but often the examination and vital signs are unremarkable. Pulmonary parenchymal inflammation (Choice E) describes pneumonitis or pneumonia, which typically presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and cough; hyperresonance to percussion would not be expected.

questionStem: A previously healthy 42-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of discharge from the left nipple. She is sexually active and uses an oral contraceptive . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) , pulse is 90/min , respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/75 mm Hg. Examination shows no breast masses . A serosanguineous discharge is easily expressed from the left nipple. Mammography shows no areas of microcalcification . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: lntraductal papilloma is the most common cause of unilateral bloody nipple discharge. Nipple discharge is concerning for underlying malignant pathology if presenting as spontaneous bloody, serosanguinous, or clear unilateral discharge or if there is discharge in the setting of a palpable breast mass. lntraductal papillomas are benign tumors originating from the walls of lactiferous ducts that typically grow and can result in local duct obstruction. Papillomas can be solitary or multiple, and while typically benign, can contain areas of atypia or carcinoma. Mammography is generally insensitive for intraductal papilloma, particularly when small. Galactography can be performed, involving cannulation and injection of contrast into a duct, which demonstrates a filling defect. Breast ultrasonography and MRI can also be utilized to evaluate the extent and characteristics of the papillomas. Treatment typically requires surgical excision to exclude components of atypia or neoplasia.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Breast abscess (Choice A) is a potential complication of mastitis, most commonly occurring in breast-feeding women. It typically presents following mastitis, with a localized region of indurated, fluctuant tissue. Breast cancer (Choice B) encompasses many types of breast carcinoma, including invasive ductal and lobular carcinoma, medullary carcinoma, inflammatory breast carcinoma, and cystosarcoma phyllodes. The most common type is invasive ductal carcinoma, which typically presents as a palpable, immobile breast mass, which may demonstrate features such as spiculated margins and microcalcifications on mammography. Malignancies can be associated with pathologic nipple discharge, although intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of unilateral bloody nipple discharge. Ductal ectasia (Choice C) more often occurs in perimenopausal women and is a widening of the lactiferous ducts with thickening of their walls, often near the nipple. Ectatic ducts are often asymptomatic until they become blocked, at which time they may become nodular or painful. Bloody discharge is uncommon. Fat necrosis (Choice D) is often detected in the breast as a palpable nodularity in an area of previous trauma. On imaging, peripheral calcifications are often seen. Fibroadenoma (Choice E) presents as a unilateral, nontender, mobile, rubbery mass in the breast. They are benign and are not associated with nipple discharge. Fibrocystic changes of the breast (Choice F) are a benign and cyclic cause of breast pain that presents with focal masses or nodules. Nipple discharge is uncommon in fibrocystic breast disease. Galactocele (Choice G) presents as a painless breast lump typically following the cessation of lactation. It does not present with pathologic nipple discharge and often resolves spontaneously. Mastitis (Choice I) presents with erythema and induration in an area of tender, warm skin. It classically occurs in breast-feeding mothers as a consequence of microtrauma to the nipple leading to inoculation from cutaneous or oral flora. Staphylococcus aureus is a common pathogen. It does not generally present with bloody nipple discharge.

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of severe cramping pain in the lower abdomen . The pain has been constant for the past 16 hours. The abdomen is markedly distended . A McBurney incisional scar is noted in the right lower quadrant. The x-ray shown was taken shortly after admission . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.C: Mechanical obstruction of the small intestine

correctExplanation: A sigmoid volvulus results from twisting of the sigmoid mesentery, which can lead to large bowel obstruction and perforation or intestinal necrosis if not treated. Patients commonly present with symptoms secondary to a large bowel obstruction such as constipation, abdominal bloating, distention, nausea, and vomiting. Sigmoid volvulus typically demonstrates a coffee-bean appearance on abdominal x-rays with severe distention of the sigmoid colon. In patients without complications such as bowel ischemia or perforation, treatment requires detorsion of the sigmoid colon and mesentery through sigmoidoscopy with placement of a rectal tube to facilitate stool passage and maintain decompression. Recurrent sigmoid volvulus may require surgical colopexy or sigmoid colectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cecal cancer (Choice A) is often asymptomatic until late in the course. It is classically associated with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and iron deficiency anemia. lleoileal intussusception (Choice B) describes telescoping of one segment of ileum into an adjacent segment, which can cause intestinal ischemia or obstruction. It typically occurs because of a pathologic lead point (e.g., malignancy, stricture, lymphadenopathy), and presents with colicky pain and bloating. Abdominal x-rays are often nondiagnostic for the condition, which is better detailed on ultrasonography (children) or CT scan (adults), which will disclose the intussusceptum. Mechanical obstruction of the small intestine (Choice C) is typically acute, occurring because of adhesions, inflammatory bowel disease, strictures, malignancies, or hernias. It typically presents with abdominal pain, nausea, nonbloody and sometimes bilious emesis, hyperactive and high-pitched bowel sounds, and abdominal distention. X-rays may show dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Paralytic ileus (Choice D) refers to intestinal hypomotility without a mechanical obstruction, most commonly occurring following surgery or in the setting of electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., end-stage kidney disease resulting in hyperkalemia). It typically presents with diffuse small and large bowel dilatation.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 24 hours after the onset of severe abdominal cramps and nausea . During this period , she has vomited yellow-green material once and has had only two bowel movements , which were small and liquid. During the past 6 months , she has had less severe abdominal cramps associated with diarrhea and a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. She says the cramps have become more severe during the past month. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . On arrival , she is in moderate distress . She appears pale. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 52 kg (114 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m 2. Her temperature is 37 .2°C (99°F), pulse is 90/min , and blood pressure is 116/78 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows moderate distention with mild right lower quadrant tenderness . Her leukocyte count is 14,000/mm 3• A CT scan of the abdomen shows thickening of the terminal ileum and air in the rectum. The colon is not dilated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Upper gastrointestinal series with a water-soluble contrast and small bowel follow-through

correctExplanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, most frequently involving the terminal ileum. It can arise anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract and is a subclass of inflammatory bowel disease. Most patients experience chronic abdominal cramping, bloody diarrhea, anemia, and weight loss. Examination often demonstrates generalized abdominal tenderness, sometimes worse in the right lower quadrant, and, depending on the severity and extent, may disclose complications such as enterocutaneous fistulas and extraintestinal manifestations such as uveitis. Severe Crohn disease can result in intestinal obstruction from stricture or inflammation, bowel perforation, intra-abdominal abscess, and the formation of additional fistulas. Diagnosis occurs through colonoscopy with biopsy, which is the best next step in the diagnosis of this patient. Laboratory analyses often disclose increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein concentration. Treatment is through anti-inflammatory medications, immunomodulators, and glucocorticoids, with complicated, severe cases sometimes requiring surgery including small bowel resection or colectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Barium enema (Choice A) is used to evaluate the lumen of the large bowel to assist in the diagnosis of colonic neoplasms, strictures, fistulas, or postsurgical complications. It does not reliably image the distal small bowel and does not permit sampling of tissue for biopsy. Upper gastrointestinal series with a water-soluble contrast and small bowel follow-through (Choice B) studies are indicated when structural lesions involving the stomach or small bowel are suspected. This is most commonly indicated for the evaluation of small bowel pathology, such as duodenal atresia, malrotation with volvulus, and Crohn disease; however, it would not offer the opportunity to sample tissue through biopsy. MRI of the abdomen (Choice C) offers high-contrast resolution detail of soft-tissue structures within the abdomen. It can be used for the evaluation of a variety of intra-abdominal pathologies. MRI enterography techniques can be utilized to investigate sites of active or chronic bowel inflammation, although this would not permit tissue sampling. Capsule endoscopy (Choice D) is used in the diagnosis of jejunal and proximal ileal pathology located outside of the reachable field of view of upper endoscopy or colonoscopy. It is most commonly used in the workup of small bowel sources of gastrointestinal bleeding or neoplasia. It offers images only and cannot be used for tissue sampling.

questionStem: A 66-year-old man with unresectable squamous cell lung cancer has the acute onset of severe shortness of breath. An x-ray of the chest shows a unilateral pleural effusion. The patient has been receiving hospice care at home. Which of the following management strategies is most consistent with the patient's preference for hospice care?
correctExplanation: Hospice care generally carries the goal of providing an improved quality of life for a patient when a terminal condition is present. While the criteria for hospice eligibility vary by state and sometimes by individual hospice organization, there are general universally agreed-upon conditions for eligibility such that a life-limiting condition must be present, often with a prognosis of 6 months or less to live. Additionally, frequent hospitalizations; progressive weight loss or failure to thrive; terminal malignancy; advanced dementia, Alzheimer type; end-stage kidney disease without dialysis or transplant; and end-stage heart, lung, or liver failure are often conditions for which hospice eligibility exists. In such cases, a focus is placed on the patient's goals of care related to quality of life, and procedures or medical treatments that would improve such quality are undertaken in lieu of those that would limit the quality of life or cause undue distress without changing prognosis. Thoracentesis in the setting of terminal lung cancer would improve the patient's respiratory status and comfort without adding undue risk for pain. This is an appropriate intervention for a patient with terminal lung cancer and a large, compromising pleural effusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Initiation of systemic chemotherapy (Choice A), radiation therapy (Choice B), open pleurodesis (Choice C), and tracheostomy (Choice E) would all add undue discomfort and suffering without altering the patient's prognosis. These are contraindicated in a hospice patient with a terminal malignancy.

questionStem: A previously healthy 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a motor vehicle collision . She was an unrestrained front seat passenger . On arrival, she has pain and tingling in her right leg and is unable to move it. Her pulse is 105/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 155/90 mm Hg. The right lower extremity is pale. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent on the right. There is a posterior dislocation of the right knee. Motor and sensory function is absent below the right knee. Following reduction of the dislocation and splinting of the right lower extremity, the patient is able to move the leg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Venous duplex ultrasonography of the right lower extremity
choices.B: CT scan of the right lower extremity

correctExplanation: Posterior knee dislocation places traction on the popliteal artery and branches of the sciatic nerve. Such an injury can result in potential circulatory insufficiency and neurological deficits to the leg distal to the level of the injury, resulting in permanent loss of function if untreated. Prompt reduction of the knee dislocation serves to limit the extent of injury by relieving neurovascular traction, thereby minimizing damage and restoring nerve function and arterial flow. Arterial injuries sustained during a posterior knee dislocation can include dissection, rupture, thrombosis, and intramural hematoma; pseudoaneurysms can also occur. Prompt arteriography or CT/MR angiography is indicated to further investigate the presence of underlying arterial injuries and to facilitate operative repair planning.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Venous duplex ultrasonography of the right lower extremity (Choice A) is appropriate to investigate the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis, which can result from stasis in the setting of orthopaedic injury. However, it is not the most likely immediate complication of a knee dislocation. CT scan of the right lower extremity (Choice B) provides detail about bony, vascular, and soft tissue structures; however, a CT angiography protocol would be required for appropriate vessel imaging detail. Arthroscopy (Choice C) may eventually be required in the diagnosis or repair of potentially damaged knee ligaments from the dislocation; however, this is not the most immediate limb-threatening complication. Nerve conduction studies (Choice E) may eventually be indicated to diagnose injury to the distal sciatic nerve branches such as the tibial and peroneal nerves but would not take precedence over arterial injury assessment in a patient where motor function had been restored. No further diagnostic studies necessary (Choice F) is inappropriate; posterior knee dislocation is highly associated with arterial injury and additional studies are indicated to prevent a delay in diagnosis and treatment.

questionStem: A 70-year-old man has a 2-year history of progressive dysphagia and intermittent regurgitation of undigested food . A barium swallow is shown . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: A pharyngoesophageal (Zenker) diverticulum occurs within the hypopharynx, just above or at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle. The mechanism of formation includes an uncoordinated swallowing mechanism, which results in muscle spasms of the cricopharyngeus leading to pulsion diverticula as the wall of the hypopharynx and superior esophagus weakens. Symptoms include halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food, and dysphagia. Barium swallow discloses a posterior, midline outpouching above or at the level of the cricopharyngeus. Treatment includes surgical repair and resection (diverticulectomy), plus dietary modifications to include soft or liquid foods.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Absence of peristalsis after swallowing (Choice A) occurs in the setting of autonomic neuropathy, cerebrovascular accident, and achalasia. It generally results in the failure of a food bolus to transit through the hypopharynx and/or esophagus, not in the focal formation of a hypopharyngeal diverticulum. Diffuse esophageal spasm (Choice C) presents with severe dysphagia and chest pain, often acutely in the setting of swallowing. It may also occur in the absence of swallowing, such as in association with gastroesophageal reflux disease. Barium swallow would disclose a "corkscrew" esophagus, not a focal hypopharyngeal diverticulum. Severe gastroesophageal reflux (Choice D) presents with cough, sour or metallic taste, chest discomfort, and nausea. It is often worse when supine or following the ingestion of trigger foods. It would not be expected to cause a focal hypopharyngeal diverticulum.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman is scheduled for operative treatment of an umbilical hernia with incarcerated omentum under general anesthesia . During the operation , a solid nodule is excised , and a frozen section shows metastatic carcinoma consistent with primary ovarian cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

choices.A: Close the operative site and discuss further treatment with the patient when she awakens
choices.B: Place a central venous catheter with a subcutaneous injection port for chemotherapy and discuss further treatment with the patient when she awakens
choices.C: Place a peritoneal dialysis catheter through the operative site for future chemotherapy and discuss further treatment with the patient when she awakens
choices.D: Obtain consent from the next of kin and place a central venous catheter with a subcutaneous injection port for chemotherapy
choices.E: Obtain consent from the next of kin and proceed with laparotomy and tumor debulking

correctExplanation: Incidental discoveries during unrelated surgery, when not immediately life-threatening, are appropriately managed by closing the operative site and discussing the findings with the patient when they regain decision­ making capacity following anesthesia. While discovery of malignancy in a young woman may immediately prompt the thought that treatment would be desired, the decision to pursue intervention is ultimately the patient's choice, upholding the ethical principle of autonomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Placing a central venous catheter with a subcutaneous injection port for chemotherapy and discussing further treatment with the patient when she awakens (Choice B) and placing a peritoneal dialysis catheter through the operative site for future chemotherapy and discussing further treatment with the patient when she awakens (Choice C) do not respect the patient's autonomy and do not consider her preferences in treatment. Obtain consent from the next of kin and place a central venous catheter with a subcutaneous injection port for chemotherapy (Choice D) and obtaining consent from the next of kin and proceeding with laparotomy and tumor debulking (Choice E) are also incorrect. These choices violate the patient's autonomy, and there is no suspicion of a lack of decision-making capacity outside of the time the patient is under anesthesia. In cases where the patient would not be able to make a decision because of an absence of capacity, a surrogate decision maker can be used. However, unless a procedure is urgent or emergent, there is no immediate need to consult a surrogate. The patient can recover capacity from the anesthesia with a decision made after further discussions.

questionStem: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination 2 months after she sustained a right hip fracture when she fell in her kitchen . Two years ago, she sustained a Colles fracture in a fall. Examination today shows a well-healed scar over the right hip. Range of motion of the hip joint is full. Her serum calcium concentration is within the reference ranges ; her serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration is decreased . A DEXA scan shows osteoporosis . Which of the following is the most likely additional serum abnormality in this patient?
correctExplanation: Osteoporosis occurs because of the loss of bone mineral density. The condition results from the interplay of three possible mechanisms: failure to achieve peak bone density, increased bone resorption, and decreased new bone formation. The condition is often asymptomatic until a traumatic injury results in a fracture, most commonly involving the hip, distal radius, or vertebrae. Classically, serum calcium, vitamin D, and magnesium concentrations are within the reference ranges; however, calcium handling in the bloodstream is key in the pathogenesis of osteoporosis. Hypocalcemia and hypovitaminosis D both lead to increased concentrations of parathyroid hormone (PTH), which results in increased osteoclast activity and bone resorption. Low concentrations of vitamin D are also associated with increased concentrations of PTH even when serum calcium is within the reference range. The diagnosis of osteoporosis is made based on DEXA scan once the bone density falls below 2.5 standard deviations of the mean for a young adult. Treatment includes correcting any modifiable risk factors, supplementing calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise therapy, and the use of osteoclast inhibitors (e.g., bisphosphonates).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Decreased 1 a-hydroxylase activity (Choice A) results in a low active vitamin D concentration in the setting of end-stage kidney disease because of loss of parenchymal cells that synthesize the enzyme and the resultant inability to convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, the active form. A deficiency of this enzyme would be uncommon outside of a primary kidney disease. Nutritional deficiency of vitamin D is more likely when the precursor 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration is low. Decreased thyroxine (T 4) concentration (Choice B) presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism including weight gain, lethargy, fatigue, constipation, hair loss, and cold intolerance. Thyroid hormone promotes bone mineral density; however, in the absence of additional symptoms of hypothyroidism, a deficiency of thyroxine is less likely. Increased calcitonin concentration (Choice C) classically presents with hypocalcemia, as calcitonin promotes osteoblast activity with resultant bone mineral deposition. Increased osteocalcin concentration (Choice D) is a marker of bone formation and is correlated with increases in bone mineral density, for example, when bone-forming medications such as teriparatide are used.

questionStem: A 25-year-old man comes for a routine health maintenance examination. A harsh systolic murmur is heard. Examination shows no other abnormalities . Echocardiography shows a bicuspid aortic valve . This patient is at increased risk for aortic stenosis as a result of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Calcification of the valve is a pathologic consequence of mechanical stresses on heart valves and results from repetitive microtrauma from the opening and closing of valve leaflets with associated chronic inflammation. Many people will develop some degree of valve stenosis because of chronic inflammation with resultant calcification and fibrosis over time, with the aortic valve most commonly affected. Structural abnormalities of the valve, such as a bicuspid aortic valve, alter the biomechanics of valve opening and closing, which increases the likelihood of earlier calcification and resultant stenosis because of increased mechanical trauma. Congenital bicuspid aortic valve classically presents with early signs and symptoms of aortic stenosis and left-sided diastolic heart failure. Patients may report fatigue, shortness of breath, cough, diminished exercise tolerance, or syncope with exertion. Examination findings include a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border, and pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed) may be noted on examination of peripheral pulses. Because of the chronic increased afterload from a fixed obstruction by the valve, left ventricular hypertrophy and resultant diastolic dysfunction can occur. If early aortic stenosis occurs, the patient may be a candidate for aortic valve replacement.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Formation of atherosclerotic plaque (Choice B) describes the principal risk factor for coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular accidents, and peripheral artery disease. The presence of a plaque within the arterial wall acts as a nidus for thrombus formation when the plaque ruptures. This does not play a role in the development of aortic stenosis. Rupture of the chordae tendineae (Choice C) may occur following a myocardial infarction. It typically leads to acute valvular regurgitation and is classically associated with acute pulmonary edema from mitral regurgitation. Streptococcal infection (Choice D) is associated with rheumatic heart disease, which results in inflammation of the valves of the heart, most commonly the mitral and aortic valves. This may present with acute regurgitant murmurs and chronically can result in stenosis. This patient's bicuspid aortic valve is his main risk factor for early-onset aortic stenosis. Thrombus deposition on the valve (Choice E) is commonly seen in cases of mechanical valve replacement with subtherapeutic anticoagulation. The nonendothelialized valve surface acts as a nidus for thrombus formation.

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after she sustained severe head injuries in a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which she was the unrestrained driver. Paramedics report finding a bottle of amphetamines inside the patient's vehicle . On arrival , her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 6, and she is immediately intubated . Her pulse is 50/min , and blood pressure is 180/90 mm Hg. Examination shows numerous ecchymoses ; lacerations over the face , trunk , and upper extremities ; and right-sided hemotympanum . There are obvious facial fractures . Except for an abrasion over the right upper quadrant , abdominal examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's increased blood pressure?

choices.F: Pain response related to the fractures

correctExplanation: The Cushing reflex presents with systemic hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations. It is observed during periods of increased intracranial pressure, often in the setting of impending herniation. As intracranial pressure rises, often because of intracranial bleeding (e.g., traumatic epidural or subdural hematoma) and/or cerebral edema, mean arterial pressure rises to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure. In response to rising mean arterial pressure, carotid baroreceptors trigger reflex bradycardia as an autoregulatory response. Irregular respirations occur because of compression of the pons and medulla, which control autonomic respiratory rate and pattern. The presence of the Cushing reflex suggests increased intracranial pressure in extremis and constitutes a neurosurgical emergency. Immediate treatment to decrease intracranial pressure is required, including administration of mannitol, hypertonic saline, hyperventilation, and elevation of the head of the bed with emergent decompressive surgery.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acute renal artery dissection (Choice A) can cause secondary hypertension from activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, though clinical evidence including thoracoabdominal trauma, flank bruising, or a bruit may be present. Bradycardia and head trauma with signs of a basilar skull fracture (hemotympanum) are more suggestive of intracranial bleeding. Amphetamine intoxication (Choice B) and increased serum catecholamine concentration (Choice E) present with signs of sympathomimetic toxicity including hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, and dilated pupils. Decreased minute ventilation (Choice C) does not generally have a direct causal relationship with mean arterial pressure; however, it can be associated with increased intracranial pressure through respiratory acidosis inducing cerebral vasodilation. Pain response related to the fractures (Choice F) is variably associated with signs of sympathetic or parasympathetic stimulus, which would include hypertension and tachycardia in the setting of increased sympathetic stimulus, or bradycardia and hypotension in the event of a vagal response to pain.

questionStem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician's office because of claudication . He smokes two packs of cigarettes per day and has no history of diabetes mellitus . The femoral pulses are palpable bilaterally, and distal pulses are absent. Capillary refill in both feet is less than 5 seconds . Ankle-arm indices are 0.75 on the right and 0.60 on the left. In addition to recommending that he quit smoking , which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in patient care?
correctExplanation: Prescription for an exercise program is the most appropriate initial step in management for this patient. Leg pain that occurs following exertion and improves with rest is known as claudication and indicates the presence of peripheral vascular disease. Claudication results from increased physiologic demand of the skeletal musculature for oxygen, which cannot be met because of the fixed obstruction to flow of stenotic arteries. As demand falls during rest, the pain typically improves. Peripheral vascular disease is common among older men who smoke cigarettes and have a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or hyperlipidemia. Active exercise improves collateral vascularization, which allows for improved arterial oxygenated blood flow to the skeletal musculature and is the best initial step in treatment along with the mitigation of risk factors. Additional therapeutic options include cilostazol and surgical revascularization (e.g., bypass, stenting), which can be employed following exercise therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Balloon angioplasty (Choice A) and femoropopliteal bypass (Choice B) are both invasive options that should be reserved for when noninvasive therapy is no longer sufficient. Sympathectomy (Choice C) refers to the removal of a sympathetic nerve root and is often used in hyperhidrosis, reflex sympathetic dystrophy, and Raynaud disease. The disease cause of claudication is generally not because of sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction, and sympathectomy does not generally play a role in treatment. Vasodilator therapy (Choice D) (e.g., cilostazol) may have a role in treating this patient's claudication, but it will not promote collateral vascularization which improves long-term symptoms. Because of this, initial treatment with a regimented exercise program is recommended.

questionStem: A 51-year-old man comes to the physician 10 days after discovering a nontender mass in his neck. His father and two older brothers were diagnosed with thyroid cancer at the ages of 46, 46, and 49 years , respectively . Examination shows a 2-cm nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid gland . A 1-cm, firm, nontender lymph node is palpable in the anterior cervical chain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and produces calcitonin. It often arises insidiously and is typically asymptomatic until a nodule is of palpable size. Symptoms of hypocalcemia may be present if severe. It is associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN), types 2A and 2B; as a result, familial association is common. It can spread hematogenously or lymphatically. Diagnosis occurs through thyroid ultrasonography and biopsy. Treatment includes thyroidectomy and chemoradiation. As well, additional neoplasms of MEN, types 2NB should also be investigated such as pheochromocytoma and parathyroid adenoma.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Anaplastic carcinoma (Choice A) is a rare, aggressive thyroid malignancy that invades local structures such as the esophagus and trachea. It generally only occurs in older persons and carries a poor prognosis. On examination, a "hard, woody mass" may be palpable along with symptoms of dysphagia or hoarseness. Follicular carcinoma (Choice B) also presents with a thyroid nodule and is the second most common thyroid malignancy after papillary carcinoma. It is diagnosed on biopsy, as the neoplastic cells are noted to invade the surrounding capsule, which differentiates it from a benign follicular adenoma. It typically carries a good prognosis. Hurthle cell adenoma (Choice C) is a less common type of benign thyroid adenoma arising from Hurthle cells. It most commonly occurs in older females. Papillary carcinoma (Choice E) is the most common type of thyroid cancer and carries an excellent prognosis. It typically demonstrates empty-appearing nuclei with central clearing, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies on histology. Early radiation exposure in childhood is a risk factor.

questionStem: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because he has been excessively sleepy for the past 2 days. He was hospitalized 3 weeks ago for an episode of acute pancreatitis . He has a long-standing history of alcoholism but has abstained for 8 weeks . He appears lethargic and does not respond to questions . His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1 °F). Examination shows severe jaundice and peripheral muscle wasting . There are spider angiomata across the neck. Abdominal examination shows distention and a fluid wave; tenderness cannot be assessed because of his somnolence . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Administration of vitamin B 12 (cyanocobalamin) and folic acid

correctExplanation: Leukocyte count 11 ,500/mm 3 Prothrombin time 17 sec (INR 1.4) Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine Albumin Alkaline phosphatase AST ALT 60 mg/dL 2.6 mg/dL 2.0 g/dL 182 U/L 56 U/L 94 U/L Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) occurs most frequently in cirrhotic states, although it can occur in any setting causing ascites. SBP describes an infection within ascitic fluid in the peritoneal cavity, most often from translocated enteric flora such as Escherichia coli. The classic presentation includes fever along with diffuse abdominal pain and tenderness in a patient with ascites. If there is clinical concern for SBP, the ascites fluid should be sampled through a paracentesis. Laboratory analysis of the ascitic fluid should include Gram stain, culture, and cell counts. A total leukocyte count of greater than 1000/mm 3 or greater than 250 neutrophils/mm 3 is generally diagnostic of SBP since culture results are variably positive. Antibiotics with gram-negative rod coverage (e.g., third-generation cephalosporins) are considered first-line.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Abdominal ultrasonography (Choice A) may provide detail as to the presence of ascites and the structural character of the liver. However, in cases with clear signs of liver failure and evidence of ascites on examination, it would delay sampling of the ascites fluid and administration of antibiotics. Administration of vitamin B 12 (cyanocobalamin) and folic acid (Choice B) is important in the repletion of deficient cofactors and coenzymes as a result of the patient's chronic malnutrition. However, such repletion should follow addressing more immediate infectious concerns from SBP. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (Choice C) is a diagnostic and potentially therapeutic intervention for the evaluation of the anatomy and patency of the hepatobiliary tree. It does not have an immediate role in the management of SBP. Hemodialysis (Choice D) is appropriate in cases of end-stage kidney disease or in emergent cases of acute kidney injury, severe acidosis, electrolyte derangements, toxic ingestions, fluid overload, or uremia. It does not have an immediate role in the management of SBP unless severe hepatorenal syndrome is concomitantly present.

questionStem: One week after undergoing laparotomy for a gunshot wound to the right upper quadrant of the abdomen , a 35-year-old man has increasing jaundice and hematemesis . His total serum bilirubin concentration is 8.0 mg/dl . During laparotomy , a through-and-through injury to the right lobe of the liver was found . The entrance and exit wounds of the liver were oversewn with liver sutures . No drain was placed . Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy now shows clots and blood in the duodenum , but no active site of bleeding is identified . Two units of packed red blood cells are administered . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: A liver injury from penetrating trauma can disrupt normal hepatic parenchyma and stroma, including bile ducts, hepatic arteries and veins, and the portal veins. If a drain is not placed into the liver during repair, hematomas can accumulate or drain into the biliary system, and ongoing bleeding may not be immediately detected. Blood in the duodenum without a clear source in the setting of a liver injury is consistent with a diagnosis of hematobilia, in which blood from a hepatic source drains into the biliary tree and through the sphincter of Oddi into the duodenum. An arteriovenous fistula involving the bile ducts must also be considered and repaired if present.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Duodenal ulcer (Choice A) and gastric ulcer (Choice C) classically present with worsening abdominal pain related to the consumption (gastric) or lack of consumption (duodenal) of food. Complications include perforation, stricture formation, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding, which can present with either melena or hematochezia depending on the rate of hemorrhage. Ulcers are visualized as erythematous discontinuities in the mucosa on upper endoscopy. Esophageal varices (Choice B) result from chronic portal hypertension and most commonly occur in the setting of alcoholic cirrhosis. Varices are typically seen as dilated submucosal blood vessels in the distal esophagus on upper endoscopy. Gastritis (Choice D) presents with abdominal pain, nausea, hematemesis, or melena, and often results from the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, cigarette smoking, or alcohol consumption. It presents as diffuse or patchy regions of erythematous mucosa on upper endoscopy.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of mild abdominal cramps, foul-smelling stools, and intermittent diarrhea after meals. He underwent distal pancreatectomy for pancreatitis and chronic pain 3 months ago. He has a history of major depressive disorder and alcoholism ; he has not had a drink for the past year. His medications are esomeprazole , sertraline , and vitamin B complex supplement. He has not had any recent changes to his diet. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is flat and nontender ; bowel sounds are hyperactive and high pitched. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 43% Leukocyte count 12,500/mm 3 Serum Amylase activity Lipase activity 90 U/L 100 U/L Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Exocrine and endocrine pancreatic insufficiency are associated with chronic pancreatitis and result from repeated episodes of acute pancreatitis leading to the destruction of acinar and islet cells. The loss of acinar and islet parenchyma can be further exacerbated if a distal pancreatectomy is performed to control symptoms or manage complications of chronic pancreatitis. The exocrine pancreas produces digestive enzymes, the absence of which leads to malnutrition (e.g., cachexia, muscle wasting), weight loss, vitamin deficiencies, and frequent, loose, foul-smelling, sometimes oily stools (steatorrhea). The diagnosis of pancreatic insufficiency is through clinical history, imaging, and biopsy. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is treated with oral pancreatic enzyme replacement such as pancrelipase. Endocrine pancreatic insufficiency, if present, typically results in diabetes mellitus, which requires insulin replacement therapy. Any modifiable inciting causes of pancreatitis (e.g., gallstones, alcohol use disorder, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia) should be mitigated to delay disease progression and preserve remaining native pancreatic function.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cholestyramine (Choice A) is used in the management of hyperlipidemia to decrease serum concentrations of LDL-cholesterol. Dicyclomine (Choice B) is an antispasmodic and diphenoxylate (Choice C) slows gut motility. Both are used in the management of irritable bowel syndrome. They do not play a role in the treatment of pancreatic insufficiency. Metronidazole (Choice D) is an antibiotic used in the management of anaerobic infections, notably C/ostridioides difficile (formerly C/ostridium difficile) and Giardia Jamblia.

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman is undergoing elective endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with 20% benzocaine spray for analgesia and intravenous meperidine and midazolam for sedation . She is receiving 100% oxygen (5 L/min) by nasal cannula . Ten minutes after initiation of the procedure , she becomes mildly confused and cyanotic . She does not have chest or abdominal pain. She has a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with metformin . She had a myocardial infarction and coronary artery bypass grafting 3 years ago and has not had cardiac symptoms since then . Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed 1 year ago; abdominal ultrasonography 2 weeks ago showed a dilated common bile duct with retained calculi. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years . Her pulse is 106/min, respirations are 30/min , and blood pressure is 116/78 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry shows a decrease in oxygen saturation from 99% to 84% during the past 10 minutes ; oxygen saturation improves significantly with 40% oxygen by face mask. A few crackles are heard at the lung bases. Laboratory studies show: Arterial blood gas analysis shows : Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Administration of 100% oxygen by nonrebreather face mask

correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Methemoglobin Carboxyhemoglobin Pco2 Po2 0 2 saturation 41% (N:51 .5) 2% (N:55) 43 mm Hg 282 mm Hg 99% Methemoglobinemia occurs when an abnormal fraction of hemoglobin in the blood exists in the ferric (Fe 3•) form (methemoglobin). Methemoglobin cannot effectively bind oxygen, which impairs tissue oxygen delivery. Most cases of methemoglobinemia are acquired, typically because of exposure to an oxidant stressor such as an anesthetic (e.g., benzocaine), nitrate, or dapsone. Symptoms include shortness of breath, fatigue, lethargy, light-headedness, and in severe cases, arrhythmia, seizure, and multisystem organ failure. Vital signs typically demonstrate reduced oxygen saturation, and examination may show cyanosis. Characteristically, blood appears darkened ("chocolate-colored blood") on gross visualization. Treatment includes supplemental oxygen plus intravenous administration of methylene blue, a reducing agent that donates electrons to heme. Reduction to the ferrous (Fe 2•) form restores the ability of hemoglobin to bind, carry, and deliver oxygen to tissues.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Administration of 100% oxygen by nonrebreather face mask (Choice A) is an acceptable strategy for supplemental oxygenation in cases of methemoglobinemia; however, this patient is already receiving oxygen by face mask, and the arterial blood gas analysis demonstrates appropriate partial pressure of oxygen in the bloodstream. Additional supplemental oxygen would have no further clinical benefit to the patient. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (Choice B) is appropriate in cases of carbon monoxide poisoning leading to hypoxia and end-organ damage. Methemoglobinemia results from oxidation of heme, not from competitive binding by carbon monoxide. Reduction of heme and improved transport of oxygen would not be achieved through hyperbaric therapy. Exchange transfusion (Choice C) can theoretically replace dysfunctional methemoglobin; however, the inciting factor may still be present within the patient, which could further convert replaced hemoglobin to methemoglobin, nullifying the value in any transfusion. Methylene blue is a safer and more effective treatment for methemoglobinemia. Mechanical ventilation (Choice E) is indicated in cases of hypoxemic or hypercapnic respiratory failure not responsive to noninvasive therapies. questionStem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after being involved in a motorcycle collision . On arrival , he is unconscious . His pulse is 132/min, respirations are 22/min , and blood pressure is 88/62 mm Hg. There are no visible external injuries . The pupils are 6 mm and sluggish . He moves his extremities in response to pain. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the hypotension?
correctExplanation: Blunt trauma with a moderate to high energy mechanism of injury is commonly associated with intracranial, intrathoracic, intra-abdominal, pelvic, and spinal injury. Shock (inadequate end-organ perfusion, typically marked by hypotension) is often classified by its cause. Cardiogenic, hypovolemic, obstructive, and distributive shock all present with distinctive features in the history and physical examination. Following trauma, hemorrhage, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and spinal cord injury leading to loss of sympathetic tone are all common causes of shock. Internal exsanguination from injury to the great vessels, intercostal vessels, liver, spleen, or pelvic arteries is the leading cause of hypotension in traumatically injured persons, which results in hypovolemia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aspiration (Choice A) results from the inhalation of liquid or semi-solid contents, often gastric contents, oral secretions, or blood. It presents with shortness of breath, cough, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Unless massive, it does not typically result in circulatory collapse. Cardiac contusion (Choice B) is a potential complication of blunt chest trauma. It is often evidenced by external signs of chest trauma such as bruising, rib fractures, or sternal fractures. Neurogenic shock (Choice D) is the result of a high cervical spinal cord injury (Choice E) and presents with bradycardia and hypotension.

questionStem: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination . He has had a mass on the back of his neck that has been enlarging over the past 8 months . His growth and development are appropriate for age. A photograph of the mass is shown . Examination shows no other abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign vascular neoplasm that may expand, ulcerate, and bleed. If they are present within the central nervous system, seizures, intracranial bleeding, and neurologic deficits can occur. Cavernous hemangiomas are often congenital, and familial inheritance is possible. Imaging can be obtained if the lesion cannot be visualized externally, and to determine the depth and extent of involvement. Diagnosis is based on clinical appearance and imaging features; if there is still uncertainty about the diagnosis, biopsy is done. Treatment includes excision, though bleeding is a known complication. Observation is also appropriate for superficial, small lesions.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cephalocele (Choice A) defines a protrusion of intracranial contents through a defect in the skull, typically covered by skin and dura. They do not classically appear vascular or expand with time. Fat necrosis (Choice B) generally results from a traumatic injury involving adipose tissue and appears erythematous, nodular, and often demonstrates calcifications on imaging. Lesions do not typically persist or expand over time. Lymphatic hypertrophy (Choice C) presents with enlarged lymph nodes or lymphedema and characteristically presents without erythema, except in cases of lymphangitis or chronic dermatitis. Malignant transformation (Choice D) describes the conversion of a benign lesion to a state of malignancy with the potential for metastasis and invasion, which is rare in hemangiomas. Retention cyst (Choice E) describes a benign lesion that arises when a gland is unable to excrete its product, for example, a mucous retention cyst in the oral cavity, or a sebaceous cyst of the skin. Their growth is typically slow and generally not accompanied by symptoms apart from the presence of the lesion.

questionStem: A 62-year-old man with alcoholism comes to the emergency department because he has vomited bright red blood three times during the past 6 hours. His pulse is 130/min, and blood pressure is 90/40 mm Hg. He becomes dizzy when he sits up. Abdominal examination shows marked distention, shifting dullness , and a fluid wave . Upper endoscopy shows esophageal varices and an ulcer with a blood clot on a visible vessel located on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.C: Intravenous fluid therapy and blood transfusion
choices.D: Endoscopic-guided sclerosis of the esophageal varices
choices.E: Placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portal shunt

correctExplanation: Tachycardia and hypotension in the setting of gastrointestinal bleeding is diagnostic of decompensated hemorrhagic shock, for which the appropriate immediate treatment includes intravenous fluid therapy and blood transfusion, regardless of the underlying cause of blood loss. Alcohol use disorder promotes the formation of gastric and duodenal ulcers through mucosal irritation and gastritis. If an ulcer erodes through the mucosa and submucosa, marked bleeding can occur from the underlying vessels. Posterior duodenal ulcers are often associated with erosion into the gastroduodenal artery. If bleeding is not promptly addressed with fluid resuscitation, blood transfusion, and endoscopic or surgical control, rapid exsanguination and death can result. Treatment should also include administration of an intravenous proton pump inhibitor.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous administration of ADH (vasopressin) (Choice A) would not take the place of immediate fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion in a patient with blood loss, tachycardia, and hypotension. It no longer has a recognized role in the immediate management of gastritis or peptic ulcer disease. Intravenous administration of esmolol (Choice B) may worsen the hemodynamics of a patient with hemorrhagic shock and is contraindicated, as it blocks beta-adrenergic receptors resulting in decreased heart rate and myocardial contractility, which in turn decreases cardiac output. In cases of hemorrhagic shock, mean arterial pressure is maintained by systemic vascular resistance and heart rate; stroke volume is often dramatically diminished because of low preload in the setting of blood loss. Endoscopic-guided sclerosis of the esophageal varices (Choice D) is incorrect, as the patient's hemorrhagic shock is secondary to a bleeding duodenal ulcer, not esophageal varices. Any active variceal bleeding would have been noted during the upper endoscopy. Placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portal shunt (Choice E) is used in the prevention of variceal bleeding by decreasing portal venous pressure. It does not have an immediate role in the management of a bleeding duodenal ulcer.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of episodes of headache , sweating , and rapid heartbeat. She has not had weight loss or chest pain. She has a 10-year history of hypertension that has been difficult to control despite trials of different drug classes . There is no family history of cancer. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 172/105 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities . A 24-hour urine collection shows increased catecholamine and metanephrine concentrations . An MRI of the abdomen shows a 4-cm enhancing mass in the right adrenal gland . Surgical excision of the mass is scheduled . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy to prepare this patient for surgical removal of the adrenal mass?
correctExplanation: Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations, tremors, agitation, tachycardia, tachypnea, and treatment-refractory hypertension. It is the most common tumor of the adrenal medulla, and is marked by the functional secretion of epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, which causes episodic hyperadrenergic symptoms. Physical examination may disclose diaphoresis, tremor, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hyperthermia during a symptomatic episode, and may be normal otherwise. Diagnosis is through laboratory evaluation and imaging studies. Laboratory evaluation may disclose increased urine and plasma catecholamines and metanephrines. Imaging studies may disclose a tumor within the adrenal gland, though 10% are extra-adrenal. Treatment includes a-adrenergic blocker such as phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible inhibitor, followed by 13-adrenergic blocker before resection. Failure to administer appropriate antiadrenergic therapy may result in hypertensive crisis or tachydysrhythmia at the time of resection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Atropine (Choice A), a cholinergic inhibitor, is used in the management of symptomatic bradycardia and in organophosphate toxicity. It has no role in the management of pheochromocytoma and would likely worsen the presentation as it would permit further unopposed sympathetic stimulus. Methylprednisolone (Choice B) is a glucocorticoid with trace mineralocorticoid activity used in the management of allergic reactions, anaphylaxis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, multiple sclerosis, and many other rheumatologic, autoimmune, infectious, and neoplastic conditions. It does not have an immediate role in the direct management of pheochromocytoma. Propranolol (Choice D) is a nonspecific 13-adrenergic blocker used in the management of panic disorder, social phobia, essential tremor, thyrotoxicosis, tachyarrhythmias, migraines, and portal venous hypertension. It previously had a role in the management of hypertension, angina pectoris, and myocardial infarction, but is no longer a first-line medication for these conditions. It has a potential role in the management of pheochromocytoma but should follow a-adrenergic blocker. Sodium nitroprusside (Choice E) is an intravenous, titratable vasodilator used in the management of hypertensive emergencies; however, it may result in reflex tachycardia in the setting of pheochromocytoma.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-month history of profuse , watery diarrhea with facial flushing . During this period , he has had fatigue and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss. The diarrhea has not resolved with use of over-the-counter antidiarrheal medications . He has no history of serious illness and takes no other medications . His pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities . Intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun . His stool output is 5 Lover the next 24 hours; his stool potassium concentration is increased . Serum studies show a pH of 7.56 and a potassium concentration of 2.8 mEq/L. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a pancreatic mass . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: VIPoma is a rare tumor often associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia that produces vasoactive intestinal peptide {VIP). Through its physiologic mechanism of action, VIP causes chronic and profound watery diarrhea, electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypokalemia, hypercalcemia), achlorhydria, alkalosis, flushing, and vasodilation. This syndrome is often termed WDHA syndrome (watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria). Diagnostic evaluation includes imaging of the abdomen with CT scan or MRI, somatostatin receptor scintigraphy, or PET scan to assist in localization of the tumor, and biopsy for tissue evaluation. Treatment includes correction of the associated fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base derangements, along with surgery and/or chemotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Gastrinoma {Choice A) is associated with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, the constellation of findings stemming from a gastrin-secreting tumor. It results in excessive production of acid by the gastric parietal cells. This can lead to recurrent, chronic duodenal or jejunal ulcers, which can present with abdominal pain, diarrhea secondary to malabsorption, and possible hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia. Glucagonoma {Choice B) is a rare functional malignancy that secretes glucagon, which increases serum glucose concentration. Symptoms are nonspecific and include mild diabetes mellitus, paraneoplastic rash (e.g., necrolytic migratory erythema), and weight loss. lnsulinoma {Choice C) is a rare neoplasm of pancreatic islet cells that functionally produces insulin in a dysregulated manner. Insulin is produced even in periods of hypoglycemia. Patients present with symptoms of hypoglycemia, which are generally neuroglycopenic (agitation, headache, blurry vision, diplopia, tremor), autonomic {diaphoresis, tremoring, nausea, vomiting, cramping, tachycardia, anxiety), and nonspecific (fatigue, weakness, lethargy), and are often exacerbated by periods of fasting or exercise. Somatostatinoma {Choice D) is an uncommon neuroendocrine malignancy that presents with weight loss, mild diabetes mellitus, steatorrhea caused by limited cholecystokinin release, and achlorhydria from inhibition of gastrin.

questionStem: A previously healthy 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of blurred vision for 2 weeks . His blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. Funduscopic examination shows slightly pale optic discs . Visual field testing shows bitemporal hemianopia . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pituitary adenoma is associated with bitemporal hemianopsia because of its proximity to the optic chiasm. The nasal (medial) retina receives light entering the eye from temporal (lateral) sources. The fibers from this area of the retina travel within the medial aspect of the optic nerve, and then cross at the optic chiasm to form the optic tract within the contralateral brain. Damage to these fibers anywhere along their course will prevent the patient from perceiving images projected on the retina from the temporal field of view. Classically, patients report poor peripheral vision and a resultant inability to walk or drive as they cannot see things lateral to their bodies. The optic chiasm sits directly superior to the sella turcica, and pituitary adenomas may grow superiorly, compressing the chiasm resulting in loss of a patient's bilateral temporal field of view.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Basilar artery aneurysms (Choice A), when small and unruptured, may be asymptomatic. In cases of rupture or thrombosis, the posterior intracranial circulation may be affected, and patients can present with headache, cranial nerve deficits, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, and ataxia. Cavernous sinus thrombosis (Choice B) classically follows an infection or injury involving a structure drained by the cavernous sinus (e.g., sinusitis), and results in cranial nerve deficits involving those that traverse the cavernous sinus (oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, and abducens nerves). Classic symptoms include ipsilateral orbit pain, proptosis, periorbital edema, and impairment in extraocular movement, pupil reactivity, or symmetry. Craniopharyngioma (Choice C) is a tumor seen in the sella turcica derived from remnants of Rathke pouch. It is the most common supratentorial tumor in childhood, although it is much less common than pituitary adenomas in adults. When large, they can compress the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopsia. Optic nerve glioma (Choice D) typically presents with unilateral vision loss or an afferent pupillary defect.

questionStem: While undergoing a splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenic purpura , a 49-year-old man aspirates during a difficult intubation . The diagnosis is confirmed when bile is aspirated from the trachea . Which of the following factors is most predictive of the severity of the resulting aspiration pneumonia?

choices.A: Amount of bile present in the aspirate
choices.C: Presence of solid material in the aspirate

correctExplanation: The inhalation of orogastric contents is known as aspiration, and it can occur from simple fluids such as water or stomach contents such as emesis or regurgitated products. Small volume, simple fluid aspiration may be resorbed by the lung without any consequence of infection, irritation, or compromised gas exchange. In other cases, large volume aspiration may sufficiently impair gas exchange resulting in refractory hypoxia. The aspiration of acidic stomach contents may cause aspiration pneumonitis, whereas the aspiration of gastrointestinal flora and additional bacteria can cause aspiration pneumonia. The volume of aspirate is the strongest predictor of complications from aspiration, especially in the case of pneumonia, as the bacterial inoculum may overwhelm the native ability of the pulmonary alveolar defenses (macrophages, cilia, mucus) to prevent colonization, replication, and infection. Aspiration pneumonia classically presents with cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, and rhonchi on examination. Imaging classically shows an infiltrate in the most dependent segments of lung at the time of aspiration (e.g., in the superior segment of the inferior lobe when supine or lower lobes when erect), and treatment includes broad-spectrum antibiotics with sufficient coverage of oral flora, gram-negative rods, and anaerobes.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Amount of bile present in the aspirate (Choice A) may be a factor in determining the severity of a noninfectious aspiration pneumonitis but would not play an immediate role in predicting the severity of an aspiration pneumonia. Duration of endotracheal intubation (Choice B) increases the risk for ventilator-associated pneumonia, which is not characteristically caused by oral flora. Typical organisms include Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Presence of solid material in the aspirate (Choice C) increases the risk for airway obstruction and atelectasis following aspiration, and also increases the risk for pneumonia, but to a lesser extent than the overall volume of aspiration fluid. Use of prophylactic antibiotics preoperatively (Choice D) is indicated to prevent skin and soft-tissue infections, contamination from the operative incision, sepsis, and peritonitis in the case of intra-abdominal surgery.

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 3-hour history of severe pain in his right testicle .
