questionStem: A 65-year-old man comes for a follow-up examination 1 week after excision of a small raised lesion with pearly margins from the lateral left naris. The pathology confirms basal cell carcinoma with the tumor extending to the resection margin in one section. Examination shows a well-healed incision. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

The primary risk factor for developing basal cell carcinoma is ultraviolet light exposure, though age, fair skin, and family history also contribute. Basal cell carcinomas typically present as pink, pearly papules or nodules with rolled borders and central ulceration most commonly on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck. Subtypes of basal cell carcinoma include those that are less invasive, such as superficial and nodular, and those that are more invasive, such as infiltrative and morpheaform. In all subtypes, the risk of metastasis is low, though the tumors can invade locally and cause significant tissue damage. Biopsy may be performed with a variety of techniques, including excisional, shave, or punch biopsy. Treatment of basal cell carcinoma requires complete surgical removal, either via excision or Mohs micrographic surgery. In the case of incomplete excision, re-excision with negative biopsy margins is indicated to reduce the risk of metastasis.

Complete excision with negative margins is required for definitive treatment of basal cell carcinoma. Delay of repeat excision increases the likelihood of tumor recurrence and metastasis. While electrodessication and curettage, as well as photodynamic therapy, are often used to treat basal cell carcinoma, laser therapy is not commonly employed and is inadequate in the setting of a prior excisional biopsy with a positive margin. questionStem: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after sustaining burns over 40% of his total body surface area in a house fire. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. The burned surface is anesthetic and covered with a thick, firm, brownish eschar; thrombosed vessels are visible through the burn surface. Over the next 24 hours, which of the following is the most urgent priority in management for this patient?
correctExplanation: Intravenous fluid resuscitation is the most urgent priority in management of this patient with a severe, full-thickness burn, which is often classified as a burn involving more than 20% of the total body surface area (TBSA) in adults. Severe burns can result in numerous complications, including compartment syndrome secondary to circumferential eschar formation, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy, and infection, but the priority within the first 24 hours is to replace the extensive fluid losses that occur during and immediately after a serious burn. The Parkland formula, which is calculated using the weight of the patient in kilograms and the percent of TBSA burned, is often used to calculate the estimated fluid requirements in the first 24 hours. Fifty percent of the total fluid requirements are given in the first 8 hours after the burn, and the rest is given over the next 16 hours. Ongoing fluid resuscitation following the first 24 hours is usually titrated to urine output, with a goal of 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/hr. Subsequent management should focus on providing temporary coverage of burned areas, ensuring adequate nutrition, managing pain, and treating or preventing complications such as compartment syndrome and infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (Choice A) has not been shown to improve outcomes in burn victims in acute settings, although it is sometimes used later in the course for compromised skin grafts. The most common use of hyperbaric oxygen therapy is for the treatment of carbon monoxide poisoning and dive-related injuries such as decompression sickness. Administration of tetanus toxoid (Choice B) vaccine is important for all patients with any burn that is more than superficial if their tetanus vaccine status needs to be updated, but it is less critical than immediate fluid resuscitation in a severely burned patient. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (Choice D) as a prophylactic measure is not indicated in patients with severe burns. Although many of these patients may develop infections during their treatment and recovery, the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics in the absence of suspected or proven infection does not improve outcomes. It does not innervate the intrinsic muscles of the hand. questionStem: Two months after undergoing an orthotopic liver transplant, a 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of persistent fever and shortness of breath. Breath sounds are decreased over the right hemithorax, and there is dullness to percussion. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray and a CT scan of the chest are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The chest x-ray shows reduced lung volumes with a large region of consolidation and effusion in the right lung base and periphery. This is further reflected in the CT scan as a loculated, heterogeneous fluid collection consistent with an empyema. correctExplanation: An inguinal hernia occurs when a loop of bowel protrudes through the abdominal wall at and around the inguinal canal. Symptoms include a bulge in the groin or scrotum, with associated heaviness or a dull pain, often worsened with increased abdominal pressure during straining. Risk factors for their development include male sex, advanced age, chronic cough or constipation, smoking, and abdominal wall injury. Congenital hernias are caused by failure of the processus vaginalis to close, whereas acquired hernias are caused by a weakness in the abdominal musculature. Indirect inguinal hernias are the most common type of hernia, often congenital, and occur when the hernia protrudes through the internal ring of the inguinal canal. questionStem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-month history of a mass in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. The patient says the mass fluctuates in size in relation to her menstrual cycle. She reports no pain or skin changes on or around the breast. Evaluation of a new breast mass includes a thorough history and physical examination. Further diagnostic evaluation of a breast mass depends on the patient's age, as well as the clinical concern for malignancy. In patients younger than age 30 years, such as this patient, ultrasonography is utilized as the initial imaging modality to further analyze a palpable breast mass. questionStem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a nonhealing lesion on her foot for 8 weeks. She has type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin. questionStem: A 29-year-old man with a 6-year history of end-stage renal disease undergoes uneventful renal transplantation. There is immediate diuresis of the kidney with urine output greater than 500 mL/h. Over the next several days, his serum creatinine concentration decreases to normal, and serum phosphorus concentration decreases to 1.5 mg/dL. The decrease in the serum phosphorus concentration is most likely because of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Chronic kidney disease results in secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism caused by derangement of calcium and phosphate homeostasis. As the failing kidney is unable to regulate the level of blood calcium and phosphorus, parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentrations increase to promote increased serum calcium from gut, renal, and bone absorption, and to promote renal excretion of phosphorus. PTH levels remain persistently high in renal failure, and even after transplantation, the increased level can persist for several months or even a year or more. Following renal transplantation, the graft kidney will appropriately respond to PTH, which will result in reabsorption of calcium, and excretion of phosphorus. There are multiple proposed mechanisms beyond PTH to explain post-transplant hypophosphatemia, though PTH is postulated to play a primary role. Post-transplant, the kidney is also able to produce active Vitamin D, a function also lost in end-stage kidney disease. Vitamin D promotes gastrointestinal absorption of calcium and phosphorus, further contributing to restored serum levels of both, and affecting feedback on the parathyroid gland to produce PTH. The mechanism of electrolyte homeostasis following transplant is complex, though PTH and Vitamin D, among several other factors, play key roles.

Patients with end-stage kidney disease, such as this patient prior to renal transplant, are usually hypocalcemic, as the kidney cannot reabsorb calcium. While rebound hypercalcemia may occur following renal transplantation, underlying hyperparathyroidism is a more likely etiology for this patient's decrease in serum phosphorus concentration. questionStem: A 37-year-old woman with stage IV breast cancer is admitted to the hospital because of lethargy and right thigh pain for the past 3 days. Acute hypercalcemia can present with a broad spectrum of symptoms and can be life-threatening because of its effect on neuronal conduction, the cardiac action potential, kidney function, and volume status. It commonly presents with constipation, lethargy, weakness, and altered mental status. It can result in a short QT interval and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, leading to significant dehydration. questionStem: A 62-year-old woman has shortness of breath immediately after beginning transfusion of fresh frozen plasma and 2 units of packed red blood cells to manage acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding. questionStem: A 67-year-old woman develops swelling of her left leg 3 days after Roux-en-Y choledochojejunostomy for an obstructing cancer of the head of the pancreas. Venous Doppler ultrasonography is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Elevation of the left lower extremity

correctExplanation: Leg swelling following recent surgery and known malignancy may provoke deep venous thrombosis (DVT). DVT, a thrombus within the deep veins of the body, generally the leg, is generally provoked by the features of Virchow’s triad: venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. In this case, risk factors such as surgery, malignancy, and prolonged immobilization likely contributed to the development of a DVT. While the distinction of provoked or unprovoked DVT matters in deciding long-term anticoagulation, in the immediate setting, the management is the same regardless of the reason for occurrence, and anticoagulation is the appropriate best next step. Recent surgery may be considered a relative contraindication to anticoagulation, and a careful assessment of bleeding risk should be performed. Clinical calculators, such as the HAS-BLED score, can be useful for quantifying the risk of bleeding with anticoagulation. Anticoagulation with heparin may be preferable for select patients, particularly those with a history of recent surgery or malignancy, due to greater ease of reversal of anticoagulation with heparin (short half-life, readily available reversal agent), compared to other agents.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Elevation of the lower extremity (Choice A) may alleviate discomfort and swelling associated with DVT but is not a substitute for anticoagulation. Use of compression stockings (Choice B) is often employed in patients with DVT but may be uncomfortable and lacks proven benefit. It would not take priority over anticoagulation to prevent propagation or embolization of a thrombus. Physical therapy (Choice C) may be useful in promoting early ambulation and is not known to increase the risk of embolization, but anticoagulation would take priority. Intravenous streptokinase therapy (Choice D) is a thrombolytic agent that may be used in extensive or proximal DVT or venous thromboembolism. Patients with uncomplicated DVT do not usually require thrombolysis. Additionally, high risk of bleeding (such as due to recent surgery) is a contraindication to administration of thrombolytics. questionStem: Two hours after admission to the hospital for injuries sustained in a motor vehicle collision, a 77-year-old woman has the onset of tachycardia. She was the restrained driver of a vehicle that struck a tree head on. She sustained bilateral anterior fractures of the 5th and 6th ribs. On admission, ECG showed occasional premature atrial contractions, and 1 L of lactated Ringer solution was administered. Vital signs on admission and now are: Two Hours Ago on soe Now Admission Temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F) 37.4°C (99.3°F) Pulse 86/min 100/min and irregular Respirations 20/min 24/min Blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg 110/60 mm Hg Examination shows no jugular venous distention or pulsus paradoxus. Posterior crackles are heard over the lower quarter of the lung fields bilaterally. Hematocrit is 43%. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the cardiovascular findings?
correctExplanation: Blunt cardiac injury (BCI) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient who recently sustained injuries in a motor vehicle accident (MVA) and now has evidence of an irregular cardiac rhythm. BCI is most often seen in the setting of MVAs, and the incidence is higher in those who sustain blunt trauma directly to the precordium or suffer rapid deceleration. BCI can result in a wide range of cardiac injuries from mild to life-threatening. Arrhythmias following BCI occur in approximately 5% of patients, and rhythm abnormalities range from premature ventricular contractions to supraventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. In most instances, the arrhythmias are mild and not life-threatening, although all patients should be admitted for cardiac monitoring. More severe complications of BCI include ventricular rupture leading to pericardial tamponade, valvular rupture, and myocardial infarction secondary to coronary artery dissection or thrombosis. Patients who suffer catastrophic injuries typically do not survive transport to the emergency department. questionStem: A 37-year-old man comes to the physician with his wife because of a 10-week history of severe shortness of breath after walking one block and swelling of his legs. His wife says that he has snored for many years and during the past 6 months has had many episodes every night in which he stops breathing for 15 seconds and then suddenly wakes up. He has had constant daytime fatigue for the past 3 months. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Current medications include insulin and an ACE inhibitor. He appears cyanotic and is in mild respiratory distress. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 145 kg (320 Ib); BMI is 49 kg/m2. His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 144/88 mm Hg. Examination shows decreased air movement at the lung bases. Scattered rhonchi are heard. Heart sounds are distant. Examination of the lower extremities shows brawny induration and 3-cm granulating ulcers above the medial malleoli. There is 3+ pitting edema to the midtibia bilaterally. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows a PCO, of 50 mm Hg and a Po, of 52 mm Hg. If this patient is not treated for the current findings, he will be at increased risk for which of the following?
correctExplanation: If this patient remains untreated for his obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), he is at risk of developing cor pulmonale. OSA is characterized by intermittent obstruction of the upper airway leading to hypoxia and apnea. A history of snoring, followed by periods of witnessed apnea in association with daytime somnolence or morning headaches, is common. The severity of OSA is determined using the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), and treatment of moderate to severe OSA is with the use of a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) device at night. The pressure supplied by a CPAP keeps the upper airway open, thereby preventing upper airway obstruction and apneic episodes. Severe, untreated OSA can lead to a variety of complications, including pulmonary hypertension. As the pulmonary circulation is usually a low-pressure system, the right ventricle is not equipped to pump against such increased pressures. Thus, pulmonary hypertension causes secondary right ventricular dysfunction, referred to as cor pulmonale. Cor pulmonale manifests in findings of right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy on ECG and chest x-ray with peripheral edema and hepatomegaly (signs of right-sided heart failure). The enlarged right ventricle is associated with a precordial heave on examination and a pronounced S,, given the increased pressure of the pulmonary system impacting the closure dynamics of the pulmonic valve. This patient has evidence of right ventricular dysfunction and should be treated with CPAP at night to prevent chronic hypoxia, pulmonary vasoconstriction, and irreversible right ventricular remodeling and failure.

questionStem: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the onset of shortness of breath at rest. One week ago, he was discharged from the hospital after undergoing a partial colectomy for a diverticular abscess. His postoperative course had been uncomplicated. On arrival, he is in mild respiratory distress. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 140/98 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Abdominal examination shows a well- healing incision with no erythema or tenderness. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 89%. Oxygen is administered via nasal cannula, and his symptoms improve. Laboratory studies are pending. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: Transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells

correctExplanation: The patient's presentation is concerning for acute pulmonary embolism (PE), and heparin therapy should be initiated immediately. PE can be difficult to diagnose as it often presents with nonspecific and varied symptoms. Several validated clinical decision-making aids are used in practice, such as the Wells’ Criteria. In a patient presenting with acute dyspnea, the presence of tachycardia, history of recent surgery within the past 4 weeks, and lack of a clear alternative diagnosis for his symptoms place him at a higher risk for acute PE, and his case should be managed accordingly. The Wells’ Criteria also include clinical evidence of a current deep venous thrombosis (DVT), prior history of DVT and/or PE, hemoptysis, and presence of malignancy within the past 6 months. Other symptoms and signs that are commonly associated with acute PE include pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, and hypoxemia.

questionStem: One hour after undergoing a colon resection for a sigmoid carcinoma, a 57-year-old woman is tachypneic and agitated in the recovery room. She was extubated in the operating room and is breathing 30% oxygen by nasal cannula. She is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 140 kg (308 Ib); BMI is 44 kg/m2. Her pulse is 120/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 135/90 mm Hg. Breath sounds are shallow and symmetrical. Heart sounds are normal. Arterial blood gas analysis shows: pH 7.25 Pco, 60 mm Hg Po, 70 mm Hg Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

The most appropriate next step is intubation and mechanical ventilation for respiratory support, regardless of the determined etiology of respiratory failure, as this patient requires immediate management of an acute life threat. Perioperative pulmonary complications are a major cause of mortality and morbidity in surgical patients. Thoracic and abdominal surgery reduce vital capacity and functional residual capacity significantly, due to diaphragm dysfunction, splinting, and postoperative pain. questionStem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being involved in a head-on motor vehicle collision. She was the unrestrained front seat passenger. She is alert. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg. Examination shows ecchymoses over the forehead, left side of the chest, and upper abdomen. Pupils are equal and reactive to light. There is no jugular venous distention. Breath sounds are decreased over the left lung base. Heart sounds are normal. Abdominal examination shows epigastric tenderness. X-rays of the chest are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia can occur after penetrating injury or blunt trauma, which is caused by a sudden increase in intraabdominal pressure that leads to rupture of the diaphragm. An opening in the diaphragm can lead to the presence of abdominal contents within the thorax, and presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and bowel sounds within the lung fields. It commonly occurs in the left hemithorax and may be visualized as intestinal loops or other abdominal organs in the thorax on x-ray. In this patient's chest x-ray, there is a gastric bubble visible in the left hemithorax. Other chest x-ray findings can include elevation of the hemidiaphragm, abnormal nasogastric tube positioning, atelectasis, or blunting of normal architecture. Management includes surgical exploration and repair of the ruptured diaphragm.

Flail chest (Choice C) generally results when two or more adjacent ribs are fractured at two or more locations, which results in paradoxical movement of that segment of the chest wall. questionStem: A previously healthy 25-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 4-month history of intermittent abdominal cramps. During this period, she has noticed occasional mucus mixed with her stools but has never noted any bright red blood. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 45 kg (100 Ib); BMI is 16 kg/m2. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness to palpation of the right lower quadrant; there is no distention, guarding, or rebound. Rectal examination shows normal sphincter tone, a noninflamed anal fistula, brown stool, and no masses. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Crohn disease is the most likely diagnosis in this young patient with a low BMI, positive fecal occult blood test, diarrhea with mucus, and the presence of an anal fistula on examination. Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, most frequently involving the terminal ileum. It can arise anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract and is a subclass of inflammatory bowel disease. Most patients experience chronic abdominal cramping, bloody diarrhea, and weight loss. Examination often demonstrates generalized abdominal tenderness, sometimes worse in the right lower quadrant, and, depending on the severity and extent, may disclose complications such as enterocutaneous fistulas and extraintestinal manifestations such as uveitis. Severe Crohn disease can result in intestinal obstruction from stricture or inflammation, bowel perforation, intraabdominal abscess, and the formation of additional fistulas. Diagnosis occurs through imaging and biopsy. Laboratory analyses often show increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Fluoroscopic small bowel follow through commonly shows narrowing of the intestinal lumen at the terminal ileum, along with other additional sites of stricture or fistulous formation. Treatment depends upon the severity and extent of disease but often includes 5-aminosalicylic acid derivatives, topical or oral steroids, and biologic agents such as anti-TNF- inhibitors. Surgery is sometimes required.

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-month history of intermittent bright red rectal bleeding. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Digital rectal examination shows blood in the rectal vault. Endoscopy shows scattered 1-cm to 2-cm polyps throughout the colon. Endoscopic polypectomy of the larger polyps is performed. Results of biopsy of the polyps show dilated, cystic, mucus-filled glands with abundant lamina propria and inflammatory infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Juvenile polyposis (JPS) is the most likely diagnosis in this pediatric patient with painless and intermittent hematochezia and polyps demonstrating dilated, cystic, mucus-filled glands. JPS is a genetic condition with incomplete penetrance that is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and occurs as the result of mutations in the SMAD4 or BMPR1A genes. Patients typically present within the first two decades of life with painless rectal bleeding secondary to polyps, although other more severe manifestations include intussusception and malabsorptive syndromes. Colonoscopy often discloses numerous polyps, but the histology is characteristic and sets JPS apart from many other polyposis syndromes. Polyps in JPS may be of many different varieties, but the most common type are called hamartomas. Hamartomatous polyps are made up of various tissues within the gastrointestinal tract, and histologically, they have inflammatory cells within the lamina propria in addition to mucin-filled, dilated glands. Other associated findings include telangiectasias of the skin, the gastrointestinal tract, the liver, and the lungs. Iron deficiency anemia may develop in patients with chronic gastrointestinal bleeding and should be monitored. Screening for colorectal cancer should be performed every 1 to 3 years after diagnosis, and in some cases, patients may require a colectomy.

Patients present with mucocutaneous findings including trichilemmomas, breast cancer, thyroid disease, endometrial or renal cell cancer, and a variety of gastrointestinal disorders including colonic, duodenal, and gastric polyps or colorectal cancer. questionStem: A 33-year-old man comes to the office as a new patient after he recently moved to the state. His last visit to a physician was 2 years ago. He has a 13-year history of ulcerative colitis well controlled with mesalamine. His mother has type 2 diabetes mellitus. His father was diagnosed with colon cancer at the age of 55 years. The patient does not smoke cigarettes. He drinks two 12-0z beers monthly. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate colon cancer screening for this patient?

choices.B: Colonoscopy at the age of 45 years
choices.C: Colonoscopy at the age of 50 years
choices.E: Virtual colonoscopy at the age of 45 years
choices.F: Virtual colonoscopy at the age of 50 years

correctExplanation: Colonoscopy now is the most appropriate cancer screening option for this patient. Colonoscopy guidelines differ based upon whether patients have an underlying genetic disorder that predisposes them to premature colorectal cancer (CRC) such as Lynch syndrome, a history of inflammatory bowel disease, or a family history of CRC. The risk for colon cancer in patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) increases with the duration, extent, and activity of disease. Patients with extensive colitis, a history of uncontrolled inflammation, or a disease duration of greater than 10 years are at the highest risk for CRC. Those with proctitis, left sided colitis, and a history of well-controlled disease are at a lower risk of CRC. Regardless, all patients should undergo screening colonoscopy 8 years from the date of their diagnosis as the risk of CRC increases dramatically after this time. The subsequent screening regimen is usually at 1- to 3-year intervals and is determined by findings at each colonoscopy.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force previously recommended starting routine colonoscopy screening at age 50 years for all individuals at average risk, or between ages 40 years and 45 years for individuals at higher risk. However, guidelines have recently been updated and recommend consideration for routine screening colonoscopy starting at age 40 years for average risk individuals. Virtual colonoscopy now (Choice D), at the age of 45 years (Choice E), or at the age of 50 years (Choice F) are all incorrect. Virtual colonoscopy, also known at CT colonography, involves placing a rectal tube to distend the colon with gas prior to obtaining CT images of the entire colon. questionStem: A 67-year-old man with a 2-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Treatment with the maximum dosage of proton pump inhibitors has not relieved his symptoms. He also has hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. His only other medication is hydrochlorothiazide. His blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) shows grade Ill esophagitis and Barrett esophagus. A biopsy specimen of the esophagus shows mild dysplasia. He undergoes Nissen fundoplication, and his symptoms resolve. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Repeat the EGD if the patient's symptoms recur
choices.D: Perform laser ablation of Barrett esophagus

correctExplanation: Repeat the EGD and biopsy in 6 months is the most appropriate next step in management. Barret esophagus refers to intestinal metaplasia of squamous epithelium in the esophagus and is usually a consequence of prolonged gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), which occurs when acidic gastric contents reflux backward through the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) into the esophagus. The mucosa of the esophagus is comprised of squamous epithelium and does not traditionally encounter such an acidic environment. Constant exposure to acidic intraluminal contents induces a change in cell type from squamous epithelium to the columnar glandular epithelium found in the intestines as an adaptive response. Metaplasia can eventually lead to dysplasia, which is premalignant. questionStem: A 62-year-old woman has had halitosis and progressive dysphagia with spontaneous regurgitation of undigested food over the past 2 years; she has lost 2.3 kg (5 Ib) during this period. questionStem: A 72-year-old man who is in the hospital has had abdominal cramps and bright red rectal bleeding for the past 6 hours. During this period, he has passed three bloody, moderately sized stools. Two days ago, he underwent surgical resection of an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. He had a hemorrhage during dissection of the aneurysm and had hypotension for the first 20 minutes of the operation. He received 6 units of packed red blood cells. Risk factors for acute ischemic colitis include older age, coronary artery disease, hypercoagulability, peripheral arterial disease, or recent endovascular surgery. Typical symptoms of patients with acute ischemic colitis include crampy abdominal pain, tenderness over the affected bowel, and hematochezia. Ischemic colitis can be complicated by necrosis, viscus perforation, or ileus. Treatment typically involves supportive care, anticoagulation, antibiotics, and surgery in cases of bowel infarction, necrosis, or perforation.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of moderate rectal pain, rectal itching, and bleeding with bowel movements. questionStem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of increasingly severe abdominal pain for the past 4 hours and a temperature of 39°C (102.2°F) and shaking chills for the past 2 hours. questionStem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-hour history of increasingly severe left-sided chest pain that is worse when she inhales. Six hours ago, she underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy because of a 1-month history of progressive dysphagia. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She appears anxious. Her temperature is 37.9°C (100.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg. Stretching of smooth muscle, stricture, and connective tissue, especially if chronic inflammation has resulted in compromise of the stromal strength of the esophageal wall, can lead to perforation. An esophageal perforation permits translocation of gastrointestinal contents such as food, stomach acid, and bacteria into the mediastinum, which can lead to fatal mediastinitis if untreated. questionStem: A 25-year-old man has postoperative pain 6 hours after a mesh repair of an inguinal hernia under local (lidocaine) anesthesia. Which of the following is the most appropriate analgesic pharmacotherapy for the incisional pain?

Oral administration of non-opiate medications may be helpful for pain control, but many patients may require opioid analgesics to control severe pain. Typically, the approach to adequately controlling pain is multimodal. While opioid medications can offer strong analgesia, opiates are central nervous system depressants and can lead to dependence, addiction, and death. Opiate intoxication causes sedation, bradycardia and hypotension, depressed respiratory drive, and constricted pupils. Opiates are commonly used for analgesia and act on receptors within the gastrointestinal tract, reducing gut motility and thus causing constipation. Adjunctive pain medications, such as acetaminophen, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications, gabapentin, and others, can help reduce the use of opiate medications and reduce the risk for its side effects, tolerance, and dependence. Short-term therapy following surgery with opiate compounds is indicated, though care should be taken to avoid prolonged use due to the risk of side effects and dependence.

questionStem: A 5-week-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-week history of progressive jaundice. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. His mother says that his stools are white. He is at the 50th percentiles for height and weight. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F). Examination shows moderate jaundice. The liver edge is palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin and is firm and slightly nodular. In contrast to benign causes of neonatal jaundice, biliary atresia presents with progressively worsening jaundice (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia), pale stools, dark urine, poor weight gain, and, in untreated cases, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, and portal hypertension. Classically, benign etiologies of neonatal jaundice will improve by the second to third week of life, whereas biliary atresia will persist and often worsen within the first 8 weeks of life. Intraoperative complications included a 30-minute period of hypotension and a total blood loss of 2.5 L requiring 4 units of packed red blood cells. Currently, her temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation, and breath sounds are heard bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows no distention. Bowel sounds are absent. correctExplanation: Acute kidney injury is defined as an acute increase in creatinine by greater than or equal to 0.3 mg/dL or 1.5 times above baseline creatinine, occasionally with oliguria or anuria. Acute kidney injury can be prerenal (because of dehydration, low vascular perfusion states such as congestive heart failure, or intrinsic such as acute tubular necrosis) or postrenal because of obstruction. A common cause is acute tubular necrosis, which can be caused by ischemia in the setting of prolonged hypoperfusion or toxins. A way to distinguish between the causes of acute kidney injury is by measuring the fractional excretion of sodium. The fractional excretion of a solute measures the percentage of the original filtered amount that is present in the excreted urine. The calculations are made using the plasma and urine concentrations of the sodium and creatinine. Prerenal and intrinsic kidney injury can be distinguished by the fractional excretion of sodium, which is <1% in prerenal and >2% in intrinsic kidney injury. In acute tubular necrosis, laboratory evaluation will show a blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio of less than 20, a fractional excretion of sodium greater than 2%, and muddy brown casts on urinalysis.

questionStem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after sustaining extensive injuries in a motor vehicle collision. Urethral injuries are characterized by difficulty voiding, blood at the urethral meatus, perineal ecchymosis, and may be associated with a pelvic fracture. Straddle injuries can cause trauma to the anterior urethra, while pelvic fractures may injure the posterior urethra. Urethral injuries are evaluated by retrograde urethrography, which involves the injection of contrast into the urethra to evaluate for the extravasation of contrast, indicating urethral discontinuity. questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of bloody discharge from the right nipple for 2 weeks. There are no breast masses or axillary or supraclavicular adenopathy. However, an intraductal papilloma itself is a benign lesion. Nipple discharge may be caused by lactation, physiologic mechanisms such as galactorrhea, or pathologic lesions such as breast cancer or infection. Evaluation includes a careful history and physical examination, with particular attention paid to whether the discharge is unilateral or bilateral, if it is from a single or multiple ducts, and whether it is associated with any breast abnormalities (eg, skin changes, breast lumps). Lactation and physiologic discharge are more commonly bilateral and from multiple ducts, whereas pathological lesions more commonly present unilaterally. Further diagnostic evaluation of pathologic discharge, as in this patient, often involves ultrasonography or mammography based on patient age. If an abnormality is detected, biopsy is recommended.

Fibroadenomas do not routinely present with nipple discharge. Paget disease of the breast (Choice D) describes skin changes of the nipple and areola that are often related to underlying malignancy. questionStem: An otherwise healthy 40-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the office 2 weeks after she noticed a tender mass on her left breast while showering. Menarche was at the age of 12 years. The patient had her first child at the age of 28 years and underwent tubal ligation after the birth of her second child 8 years ago. The patient's maternal aunt was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 75 years. Examination of the patient shows no lymphadenopathy. The breasts appear normal and symmetric. Palpation of the breasts shows normal breast tissue bilaterally; there is a 2-cm firm mass on the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with no skin or chest wall attachment. Mammography confirms a solitary, well-defined mass in the same location. Ultrasonography of the breasts shows that the mass is fluid-filled and compressible with posterior shadowing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Breast masses are common in women. Evaluation of a new breast mass includes a thorough history and physical examination. Benign masses are commonly small, well- circumscribed, and mobile, whereas malignant lesions are more likely to be large, poorly defined, adherent to underlying tissue, and associated with skin or nipple changes. Further diagnostic evaluation of a breast mass depends on the patient's age, as well as the clinical concern for malignancy. In patients younger than 30 years old, ultrasonography is utilized as the initial imaging modality to further analyze a palpable breast mass. In this case, the patient's mass visualized on mammography was confirmed with breast ultrasonography, which disclosed a cystic-appearing lesion. questionStem: A previously healthy 42-year-old woman comes to the office because of a painful mass in the right breast for 3 weeks. Menarche was at the age of 12 years. She had her first child at the age of 22 years. Examination shows a 1-cm, firm, tender mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast; there is no lymphadenopathy. Examination of a biopsy specimen shows fibroadenoma and lobular carcinoma in situ. Over the next 10 years, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?
correctExplanation: Breast masses are common in women, and breast cancer is the most common non-dermatologic malignancy in women. Evaluation of a new breast mass includes a thorough history and physical examination. Benign masses are commonly small, well-circumscribed, and mobile, whereas malignant lesions are more likely to be large, poorly defined, adherent to underlying tissue, and associated with skin or nipple changes. Further diagnostic evaluation of a breast mass depends on the patient’s age, as well as the clinical concern for malignancy, and typically includes mammography and/or ultrasonography, in addition to biopsy when indicated. Although a significant portion of breast masses are benign, they may be associated with future malignancy. Lobular carcinoma in situ is a benign proliferative lesion with atypical cell characteristics that most commonly occurs in pre- menopausal women. However, it is associated with an increase in the risk of development of invasive breast carcinoma, which may occur in either the ipsilateral or contralateral breast, although it is not considered a precursor lesion. Therefore, this patient is at greatest risk for developing invasive ductal carcinoma in the next 10 years. Other risk factors for the development of breast cancer include a family history of premenopausal breast cancer, genetic mutation (eg BRCA 1 or 2), early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, obesity, exogenous estrogen use, and African American ethnicity.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bone metastasis (Choice A) is often associated with breast, prostate, and lung cancer. Typical presentations include bone pain, hypercalcemia (eg, abdominal pain, altered mental status, nephrolithiasis), and pathologic fractures. Given this patient's history of lobular carcinoma in situ, she is most at risk for the development of invasive breast cancer in the future, which may or may not be associated with metastasis. Fibrocystic breast condition (Choice B) is a benign disease of the breasts characterized by multiple cystic masses that are often hormonally responsive and fluctuate in size. questionStem: A previously healthy 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after falling 12 feet from a barn loft. He landed straddling a wooden beam. His pulse is 120/min; other vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the scrotum and penis shows edema and ecchymoses. Urinalysis shows numerous RBCs. Doppler ultrasonography of the testes shows a scrotal hematoma; there is no blood flow to the testes. An analgesic is administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Blunt trauma of the external genitalia in a male can lead to injury to the testes, penis, and anterior urethra. Specifically, blunt trauma to the penis can result in penile fracture, whereas trauma to the scrotum can cause rupture of the testes, vascular injury, and testicular torsion and hematoma. A straddle injury, as in this patient, causes injury to the perineum with subsequent disruption of the bulbar urethra. Penile fractures result with pain, edema, and ecchymoses, whereas testicular rupture or vascular injury presents with testicular swelling and ecchymoses, with disruption of the testicular anatomy. Disruption of the bulbar urethra presents with hematuria on urinalysis. This patient has many genitourinary abnormalities following his straddle injury, including a possible penile fracture, scrotal hematoma, and possible testicular vascular injury and urethral injury. The absence of blood flow to the testes is a surgical emergency and requires prompt evaluation by surgical exploration to try to restore blood flow and prevent testicular necrosis and resultant infertility. The next most appropriate step in management of this patient is surgical exploration.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Renal ultrasonography (Choice A) may be used to evaluate the kidney if there was suspicion of upper genitourinary tract injury. questionStem: Twenty-four hours after undergoing total thyroidectomy and lymph node dissection for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma, a 57-year-old woman has circumoral paresthesia and tingling of the fingertips. Examination shows hyperreflexia when the facial nerve is tapped. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Intravenous calcium gluconate should be given to this patient with signs and symptoms of hypocalcemia following thyroidectomy. The parathyroid glands are located along the posterior aspect of the thyroid gland and, while not frequent, can sometimes be inadvertently removed during a thyroidectomy. The parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which has numerous actions, including the stimulation of vitamin D activation in the kidneys and resorption of calcium from the bones to maintain calcium homeostasis. Loss of appropriate PTH production leads to hypocalcemia, with resultant symptoms that include perioral paresthesia, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT interval. The Chvostek sign, in which tapping of the facial nerve leads to spasm of the facial muscles, and Trousseau sign, in which an inflated blood pressure cuff occluding the brachial artery causes carpopedal spasm, are two physical examination findings that may indicate hypocalcemia. Treatment is with intravenous calcium gluconate. For these reasons, calcium and PTH are often monitored immediately following total thyroidectomy to aid in the early detection and treatment of hypocalcemia.

questionStem: Two days after undergoing thoracotomy for a stab wound to the right hemithorax, a 25-year-old woman has oliguria despite adequate fluid replacement. During the operation, she received 4 units of packed red blood cells. Her hematocrit is 35%, serum urea nitrogen concentration is 12 mg/dL, and serum creatinine concentration is 0.9 mg/dL. Her oliguria is most likely caused by an increased concentration of which of the following hormones?
correctExplanation: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin, ADH) is a hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary that leads to water reabsorption in the collecting duct of the renal tubule by increasing the amount of aquaporin channels. It also increases systemic vascular resistance by causing peripheral vasoconstriction and consequently increases blood pressure. Its secretion is stimulated by increased plasma osmolality and decreased arterial blood volume. The syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH (SIADH) occurs when ADH is secreted independently of plasma osmolality or arterial blood volume. This most commonly occurs in neurologic injury, as a medication side effect, or because of ectopic production by a malignant tumor or lung disease. However, surgery can also cause an increase in secretion of ADH, thought to be secondary to pain. Inappropriate secretion of ADH in relation to plasma osmolality and blood volume results in decreased urine output; when this occurs, the residual urine is concentrated, with urine studies showing a urine osmolality above 100 mOsmol/kg and urine sodium above 40 mEq/L. While hypovolemia or obstruction can cause oliguria, these would likely also increase the patient’s serum urea nitrogen and creatinine. As these parameters are normal, this patient's oliguria is most likely secondary to an increased concentration of ADH.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cortisol (Choice B) is increased in Cushing syndrome, which presents with hypertension, central adiposity, moon facies, hirsutism, striae, proximal muscle weakness, and insulin resistance. This can be caused by Cushing disease, exogenous glucocorticoids, or a variety of other etiologies. However, Cushing syndrome more commonly presents with polyuria than oliguria. Epinephrine (Choice C) and norepinephrine (Choice E) excess would be expected to present with signs of sympathetic nervous system activation, such as tachycardia and hypertension. This consequently would lead to increased cardiac output and theoretically increased renal perfusion, which may be associated with increased rather than decreased urine output. questionStem: Eight hours after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, an obese 55-year-old man has a pulse of 150/min and blood pressure of 60/40 mm Hg. Hematocrit is 28% (42% preoperatively). Serum creatine kinase activity is 200 U/L. MB isoenzyme of creatine kinase fraction is less than 2% (N<5% of total). Arterial Po, is 70 mm Hg. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia without other changes. Central venous pressure is 2 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Sudden postoperative hypotension is presumed to be caused by bleeding until determined otherwise. Other causes of postoperative hypotension include under-resuscitation during the procedure, medication side effects, and sepsis. Hypovolemia, whether due to anemia or fluid depletion, results in a compensatory tachycardia to try to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP). However, with significant enough hypovolemia, the tachycardia is unable to maintain the MAP, the blood pressure subsequently falls, and the patient becomes hypotensive. Other evidence of postoperative bleeding in this patient includes a decrease in hematocrit from 42% to 28% (although a decrease in hematocrit may not always be present with an acute bleed), and a low central venous pressure indicating hypovolemia. Other signs of bleeding include pallor and swelling or ecchymoses of the surgical site. Management of postoperative hypotension caused by bleeding includes fluid resuscitation, blood product transfusion, pressor therapy, and prompt surgical re-exploration.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Addisonian crisis (Choice A) occurs in adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal insufficiency (depending on level — primary, secondary, tertiary) presents variably with weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Patients with Addison disease may develop an Addisonian crisis in response to a variety of stressors, such as severe infection or a surgical procedure. This often presents with lethargy, confusion, and hypotension. This patient has no other symptoms of Addison disease but does have a decreased central venous pressure and hematocrit, making postoperative bleeding a more likely cause of this patient's hypotension. Myocardial infarction (Choice B) classically presents with crushing substernal chest pain that radiates to the left shoulder and jaw, associated with shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and nausea. If the myocardial ischemia and infarction areas includes a significant portion of the myocardium, a decrease in cardiac output can occur with consequent hypotension. However, a myocardial infarction would be associated with a significantly higher concentration of CK-MB, which is an isoenzyme specific for myocardial damage. ¢ G € 6 o Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause

questionStem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 30 minutes after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision. He was the unrestrained driver. On arrival, he is oriented to person but not to place or time. He has no documentation in his wallet regarding his religious affiliation, but his friend says she thinks he might be a Jehovah's Witness. His family cannot be contacted. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Fifteen minutes later, his pulse is 135/min, and blood pressure is 75/40 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows distention and tenderness with rebound. Abdominal ultrasonography for trauma (FAST) shows blood in the hepatorenal recess. His hematocrit is 15%. One of the most common reasons for declining blood transfusion is identification as a Jehovah's witness. Many Jehovah’s witnesses will not accept transfusions of whole blood, red blood cells, platelets, or plasma, although many will accept albumin. Additionally, they often decline autologous blood transfusions, although they often accept cardiopulmonary bypass. This patient is most likely experiencing traumatic hemorrhagic shock, based on his tachycardia, hypotension, positive focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) exam, and hematocrit, and appropriate resuscitation should occur with fluid and blood products to restore hemodynamic stability while he undergoes emergent surgical exploration. This patient is unable to consent, as he is only alert and oriented to self, and has no records that identify him as being a Jehovah's witness. While his friend believes he may be a Jehovah’s witness, she is unsure, and there is no way to confirm this as his family is unable to be reached. questionStem: A 37-year-old woman remains ventilator-dependent 3 weeks after undergoing a gastric restrictive procedure. She has obstructive sleep apnea and restrictive lung disease. Preoperative arterial blood gas analysis on room air showed a pH of 7.35, PCO, of 65 mm Hg, and Po, of 45 mm Hg. She is currently receiving fentanyl and lorazepam for sedation to maintain acceptable arterial blood gas concentrations. Attempts to reduce the dosages of medication have resulted in life-threatening hypoxia and carbon dioxide retention. Tracheostomy is recommended to prevent permanent vocal cord damage from continued orotracheal intubation. Prior to the operation, no discussions took place concerning tracheostomy placement. She is unmarried, and her only living relative is a sister who resides in another state. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

choices.A: Continue current ventilator support with orotracheal intubation
choices.C: Contact the hospital ethics committee to give consent
choices.D: Discontinue sedation and determine if the patient can communicate her wishes
choices.E: Proceed with tracheostomy as a medical necessity

correctExplanation: Scenarios frequently arise in healthcare in which patients are unable to consent for themselves. For example, patients with altered mental status or who are intubated and sedated lack the capacity to make decisions, which may be caused by the inability to understand the consent process or the inability to vocalize their desires. In this situation, the healthcare provider must receive consent from the patient's health care proxy. While different states have varying laws about the hierarchy of decision-makers, spouses, parents, and siblings are often included. This patient has had ongoing mechanical ventilatory requirements, and she is unlikely to wean from the mechanical ventilator soon given her recurrent hypoxia and hypercarbia. Prolonged orotracheal intubation can lead to laryngeal edema, tracheal stenosis, and oropharyngeal ulcers, whereas the placement of a tracheostomy improves patient comfort, allows them to communicate, and facilitates the ventilator weaning process. Thus, it would be in this patient's best interest to undergo tracheostomy placement. As her wishes are unknown, the most appropriate next step in management would be to reach out to her next of kin, in this case her sister, to obtain consent for the procedure.

Transitioning this patient to ventilation through a tracheostomy tube would be in her best interest. 5α-reductase is most known for converting testosterone, the male sex hormone, into the more potent dihydrotestosterone. So more potent dihydrotestosterone = more hairs. More: General Rules: Testosterone comes from the ovaries, DHEA comes from the adrenal glands, 17-hydroxyprogesterone comes from the adrenal glands (mid-step product that appears in the urine in CAH). Work Up: For any patient coming with hirsutism or virilization symptoms, Next Best Step:  Laboratory Testing: o Testosterone  If abnormal  lesion is ovarian, do ultrasound   If lesion is bilateral, likely PCOS, do LH/FSH level to confirm  If lesion is unilateral, likely granulosa-theca cell tumor (secretes estrogen) o DHEA  If DHEA markedly elevated, likely adrenal tumor  do CT scan abdomen to check for "unilateral" lesion and confirm with adrenal vein sampling  If DHEA mildly elevated, likely congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)  do CT of abdomen to check for "bilateral" lesion and confirm with elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone level o 3-17-hydroxyprogesterone  If elevated, confirm congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH).  If you perform all initial laboratory test and all levels are within normal (as in our case in this question), then you are dealing with idiopathic type o Rationale: the existence of 5α-reductase activity (responsible of the conversion of testosterone into the very potent form of dihydrotestosterone – DHT) produces certain features in both genders secondary to high levels of DHT  Male  Pre-natal (results in external male genitalia)  Post-natal (results in scalp hair loss, increased hair in the axillary + pubic and extremities + prostate enlargement)  Female  Results in growth of hair on arms and legs beside axillary and pubic areas. Conclusion: The excessive hair growth in this girl in the absence of lab abnormalities, is suggestive of increased 5α-reductase activity (which is the idiopathic)

The initial presentation of HSV2 can be severe with painful genital ulcers, dysuria, fever, tender local inguinal lymphadenopathy, and headache. In other patients, however, the infection is mild, subclinical, or entirely asymptomatic. Other symptoms and signs in these first episode infections included systemic symptoms, including fever, headache, malaise, and myalgias (67%), local pain and itching (98%), dysuria (63%), tender lymphadenopathy (80%). Symptoms tended to be more severe in women than in men. Clinical recurrences of genital HSV are common (what this question is describing), but are typically less severe than primary or nonprimary infections. The mean duration of lesions is generally shorter with recurrences than in primary infection (10 versus 19 days) and the duration of viral shedding is usually two to five days. Systemic symptoms are infrequent and approximately 25% of recurrent episodes are completely asymptomatic. As many as 50% of patients with symptomatic recurrences have prodromal symptoms before eruption such as local mild tingling or shooting pains in the buttocks, legs, and hips (UTD).

Lactational mastitis is a condition in which a woman's breast becomes painful, swollen, and red; it is most common in the first three months of breastfeeding. Initially engorgement occurs because of poor milk drainage, probably related to nipple trauma with resultant swelling and compression of one or more milk ducts. If symptoms persist beyond 12 to 24 hours, the condition of infective lactational mastitis develops (since breast milk contains bacteria). Infective lactational mastitis typically presents as a firm, red, painful, swollen area of one breast associated with fever >38.3ºC in a nursing mother; milk secretion may be diminished. Systemic complaints may include myalgia, chills, malaise, and flu-like symptoms. In the early stages, the presentation can be subtle with few clinical signs; patients with advanced infection may present with a large area of breast swelling with overlying skin erythema. Reactive axillary lymphadenopathy may be associated with axillary pain and swelling (UTD).

Bleeding can occur in early pregnancy due to the following factors: Implantation bleeding can occur anywhere from 6-12 days after possible conception. Every woman will experience implantation bleeding differently - some will lightly spot for a few hours, while others may have some light spotting for a couple of days. Some type of infection in the pelvic cavity or urinary tract may cause bleeding. After intercourse, some women may bleed, because the cervix is very tender and sensitive. In this case a woman should discontinue intercourse until she has been seen by her doctor. This is to prevent any further irritation - having normal sexual intercourse does not cause a miscarriage. Signs of miscarriage include vaginal bleeding (usually heavy, a period or more), cramping pain felt low in the stomach (stronger than menstrual cramps), tissue passing through the vagina. Müllerian duct is responsible for the formation of 1. Uterus, 2. Fallopian tubes, and 3. Upper portion of the vagina. But in this patient, her secondary sexual characteristics are not fully developed (breast) therefore this patient is most likely an XY with decreased testosterone sensitivity which has led to the prominence of the estrogen and the formation of a rudimentary vagina (they usually have testes as well, but the testes should be removed to avoid malignancy).
