It also typically presents after 20 weeks of gestation. Measurement of bilirubin concentration in amniotic fluid (Choice D) can be used to determine whether the fetus is experiencing hemolysis. However, sampling would be unnecessary if Kell typing of the father disclosed that he was Kell-negative, making this an inappropriate initial action. Intravenous lgG therapy (Choice E) can be used to treat autoimmune diseases and could have possibly prevented the development of Kell antibodies if it had been given at the time of blood transfusion. However, it plays no role in the prevention of erythroblastosis fetalis in the setting of active anti-Kell antibodies. Intravenous Rh0(D) immune globulin therapy (Choice F) is used to prevent alloimmunization to the Rh(D) antigen in Rh(D)-negative women when they are potentially exposed to fetal blood. It plays no role in the prevention of erythroblastosis fetalis because of anti-Kell antibodies. Educational Objective: Antigens on the fetal RBCs depend on the antigens of each parent's RBCs. If the mother exhibits antibodies against a specific RBC antigen, whether from a previous pregnancy or a blood transfusion, the fetus is at risk for erythroblastosis fetalis if it carries that antigen, as maternal lgG antibodies can cross the placenta. The first step in determining the potential RBC antigens of a fetus is to determine the antigen type of each parent.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has never had a menstrual period . She is 150 cm (4 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (137 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m 2• Breast and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 3. The cervix is visualized , and the vaginal mucosa is hypoestrogenized . Serum studies show a luteinizing hormone concentration of 22 mlU/mL , follicle-stimulating hormone concentration of 33 mlU/mL , and prolactin concentration of 9 ng/ml. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Turner syndrome is a common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is secondary to gonadal (ovarian) dysgenesis in the setting of a 45,XO genotype. Other signs of Turner syndrome include a short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands and feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, fused kidney, and infertility. Additionally, as a result of decreased estrogen concentrations, patients fail to develop mature secondary sexual characteristics of breast and pubic hair development. As well, patients may develop vaginal atrophy or dryness related to low estrogen concentrations, like postmenopausal patients. Vital signs will be within normal limits, and diagnosis is made through a karyotype analysis. Other labs that may aid in diagnosis are increased concentrations of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle­ stimulating hormone (FSH) as a result of the lack of negative feedback from estrogen, but these findings are nonspecific.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Anorexia nervosa (Choice A) presents with extremely low body weight, fear of weight gain, and dysphoria, as well as bradycardia and lanugo on physical examination. While it can present with amenorrhea as a result of suppression of the hypothalamic-ovarian-pituitary axis, it is unlikely in this patient with an overweight BMI. Congenital absence of the uterus (Choice B) is because of an error in the normal development of the Mullerian system that results in complete absence of the uterus and, occasionally, the upper vagina. However, these patients will have functional ovaries and therefore adequate maturation of secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast and pubic hair development. Hyperprolactinemia (Choice D) presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea, most commonly to the result of a pituitary gland adenoma. High concentrations of prolactin inhibit gonadotropin-releasing hormone and subsequently cause decreased concentrations of FSH and LH. This patient's prolactin concentration is within reference ranges. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Choice E) leads to amenorrhea as caused by the decreased release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, FSH, and LH, which results in impaired follicle maturation and ovulation, as well as a lack of development of secondary sexual characteristics. This patient's FSH and LH are within reference ranges, making this an unlikely diagnosis. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (Choice F) most commonly presents with hirsutism, increased body weight, and irregular menses because of anovulation secondary to increased androgen concentrations. The LH to FSH ratio is typically increased, and ultrasonography of the pelvis will show numerous ovarian follicular cysts. It is more commonly associated with secondary oligomenorrhea than primary amenorrhea. Pregnancy (Choice G) causes amenorrhea as the endometrial lining is maintained to support the developing embryo. However, it typically causes secondary amenorrhea in a sexually active patient, rather than primary amenorrhea. Educational Objective: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is because of ovarian dysgenesis. Other signs include the absence of secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands and feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, fused kidney, and infertility. LH and FSH concentrations are typically increased because of the absence of negative feedback from estrogen, and diagnosis is made with a karyotype analysis.

questionStem: A 24-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 14 weeks' gestation comes for her first prenatal visit. She has a history of multiple sexually transmitted diseases . Her last tetanus toxoid injection was 5 years ago. Her 4-year-old daughter developed a low-grade fever, respiratory symptoms , and a rash 24 hours ago. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 14-week gestation . Fetal heart tones are heard . Hepatitis B surface antigen assay is negative , and rubella titer is less than 1 :8. Which of the following is the most appropriate vaccination for this patient?
correctExplanation: Maternal immunization is important for both maternal and fetal health. Ideally, vaccinations are given prior to conception, but some vaccinations are safe to administer during pregnancy. Live attenuated vaccines are made of viable viral pathogens whose virulence has been reduced. However, if a mutation were to occur in the viral genome to revert the attenuation, the infection could be contracted. Live attenuated vaccines include those to measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR), yellow fever, intranasal influenza, smallpox, varicella-zoster, rotavirus, and the oral poliovirus vaccines. As a rule, live vaccinations should be avoided during pregnancy because of the risk, although low, of contracting the disease. In contrast, inactivated vaccines are made by killing the virus, which makes it safe to administer to pregnant patients. Vaccinations considered to be safe in pregnancy that are routinely given to all pregnant patients include the tetanus toxoid, diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) and influenza vaccines. Additional vaccinations may be warranted depending on the patient's immunization status and degree of risk for contracting preventable infections. In this case, the patient is not immunized against hepatitis B or rubella infection. The hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant vaccine with no known potential for causing harm in the mother or fetus and is safe to administer during pregnancy. However, as the rubella vaccine is part of the MMR live attenuated vaccine, it is not administered during pregnancy. The patient will likely also need a Tdap vaccine later in her pregnancy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Inactivated poliovirus (Choice B), or the Salk poliovirus vaccine, is not necessary in this patient as there is no indication that she was not previously immunized to poliovirus, as is standard. The Sabin poliovirus is an oral, live attenuated virus, which would be contraindicated during pregnancy. Measles (Choice C), mumps (Choice D), and rubella (Choice E) are given together in the MMR vaccine. This is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. However, this vaccine should be administered to the patient following her pregnancy. Tetanus vaccination is recommended during pregnancy but with the Tdap vaccine, not the tetanus toxoid (Choice E) vaccine. The Tdap vaccine also immunizes against Bordetella pertussis, the causative pathogen of whooping cough. This allows maternal antibodies to develop and cross the placenta, providing some protection to the fetus and infant until they can receive their own pertussis vaccination at the age of 2 months. Administration of the Tdap vaccine to all pregnant women is an important preventative strategy against pertussis. Educational Objective: Maternal immunization is important for both maternal and fetal health. Live attenuated vaccines, such as MMR, should be avoided during pregnancy and given following pregnancy, if necessary. Tdap and inactivated influenza vaccines are given routinely to all pregnant patients and additional immunizations, including hepatitis B, may be given on a case-by-case basis.

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of heavy vaginal bleeding for the past 3 days. She has no history of serious illness. Menopause occurred 6 years ago. A Pap smear 1 year ago showed no abnormalities . Physical examination today shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows an irregularly shaped uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation . Her hemoglobin concentration is 9 g/dl , and hematocrit is 27%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration
choices.C: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

correctExplanation: Abnormal uterine bleeding should be suspected when bleeding is irregular, unpredictable, or not associated with usual premenstrual signs and symptoms (eg, bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps). It may be caused by structural abnormalities such as cervical or endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia, malignancy, inflammation or infection of the genital tract, coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endocrine dysfunction (eg, thyroid disorders, prolactin, androgens), iatrogenic, or idiopathic. In postmenopausal patients and patients over the age of 45, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy. The most appropriate next step in evaluation would be an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer. If a patient cannot tolerate an outpatient procedure or if the outpatient sampling is nondiagnostic, a dilation and curettage or hysteroscopy can be performed. A hysteroscopy with sampling allows for a more complete evaluation of the endometrium (eg, polyps, myomas, structural abnormalities).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) concentration (Choice A) would not disclose the cause of abnormal uterine bleeding in this patient. FSH is increased in postmenopausal patients but is not useful in the evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding. In endometrial carcinoma, the measurement of cancer antigen 125 can be used for the surveillance of patients' disease progression. MRI of the pelvis (Choice B) may be used to evaluate myometrial, cervical, or lymph node invasion and metastasis of endometrial carcinoma but is infrequently used. MRI would not be the next step in the evaluation for endometrial carcinoma, which is more definitively evaluated by tissue sampling. Transfusion of packed red blood cells (Choice C) is generally not necessary in a stable patient with a hemoglobin concentration greater than 7 g/dl. The patient in the question has a hemoglobin of 9 g/dl and does not meet criteria to receive a transfusion at this time. Hysterectomy (Choice E) may be indicated if endometrial carcinoma is diagnosed. However, in a patient with abnormal uterine bleeding, prior steps need to be taken to diagnose the cause of the abnormal uterine bleeding. Educational Objective: Abnormal uterine bleeding refers to irregular menstrual bleeding that may be abnormal in quality, duration, or timing. In postmenopausal patients and patients over the age of 45, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy. The next appropriate step in evaluation would be an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer.

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of nausea, urinary frequency , and fatigue for 2 months . She has never had a menstrual period. Breast development is Tanner stage 4. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m 2• Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.C: Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone concentrations

correctExplanation: Clinicians should maintain a low threshold of suspicion for pregnancy in adolescent and teenage patients who are at high risk for unintended pregnancy. Pregnancy should always be considered as a potential cause of presumed primary amenorrhea and should be excluded before considering other causes. Early symptoms of pregnancy include fatigue, nausea, urinary frequency, and irregular menstruation. A careful history should be taken, including of the patient's menstrual history, sexual activity, contraceptive usage, and the possibility of pregnancy. A urine pregnancy test should be obtained if it is possible that the patient may be pregnant.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complete blood count (Choice A) is useful in the diagnosis of anemia, which may be caused by iron deficiency in menstruating females. Anemia also presents with symptoms of lightheadedness, diaphoresis, and pallor. Measurement of serum estrogen concentration (Choice B) may reflect abnormalities in the ovarian production of estrogen and may disclose the cause of primary amenorrhea, such as gonadal dysgenesis 45,X (Turner syndrome). This patient presents with Tanner stage 4 secondary sexual characteristics, suggesting normal estrogen concentrations. Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone concentrations (Choice C) may disclose hypothalamic or pituitary disorders that lead to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and primary amenorrhea. Patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism will usually not present with Tanner stage 4 secondary sexual characteristics. A progesterone challenge test (Choice E) is useful for distinguishing outflow tract disorders from hormonal etiologies of amenorrhea. Educational Objective: Pregnancy should always be considered as a potential etiology of presumed primary amenorrhea and should be excluded before considering other causes. Early symptoms of pregnancy include fatigue, nausea, urinary frequency, and irregular menstruation.

questionStem: A healthy 22-year-old primigravid woman at 33 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of heavy, painless vaginal bleeding for 30 minutes . Pregnancy had been uncomplicated . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Examination shows a nontender uterus consistent in size with a 33-week gestation . The vertex is not engaged in the pelvis . Speculum examination shows vaginal bleeding from a closed cervix . The fetal heart rate is 140/min. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
correctExplanation: Causes of vaginal bleeding in the third trimester include, but are not limited to, trauma to the vagina or cervix from intercourse, cervical ectropion, cervicitis, uterine rupture, placental abruption, placenta accreta, increta, or percreta, vasa previa, and placenta previa. Placenta previa is an abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or completely overlies the internal cervical os. Placenta previa is usually detected on routine prenatal ultrasonography. Its most common presenting symptom is painless vaginal bleeding during the third trimester. The incidence of placenta previa is higher earlier in pregnancy and decreases with increasing gestational age as the placenta often migrates cephalad. If mild, bleeding from placenta previa may self-terminate within several hours. However, severe bleeding from placenta previa may lead to hemorrhagic shock, which is associated with maternal tachycardia, hypotension, decreased organ perfusion, and eventual organ failure. Fetal distress will generally also be present. Treatment of hemorrhagic shock from placenta previa involves cesarean delivery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Amniotic fluid embolism (Choice A) is a rare complication of childbirth and occurs during delivery or immediately postpartum as a result of amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation. It presents with shortness of breath, altered mental status, hypoxia, and hypotension. Complications include disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, cardiovascular collapse, and maternal and/or fetal death. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (Choice B) can be a complication of amniotic fluid embolism and occurs because of a pathologic activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to microthrombi, consumption of platelets, and coagulopathy that is characterized by both thrombosis and hemorrhage. Sepsis (Choice D) occurs from severe infections and is characterized by an inflammatory and organ-dysfunctional state. Pregnant patients are susceptible to several types of infections, including urinary tract infections which may present with fever and dysuria, and chorioamnionitis which typically presents with fever, tachycardia, and uterine tenderness. Uterine rupture (Choice E) is a dangerous complication of pregnancy wherein the muscular wall of the uterus tears. Severe pain is a common initial finding. Hemodynamic instability can manifest in the mother with tachycardia and hypotension, and in the fetus with late decelerations, tachycardia, bradycardia, or loss of beat-to-beat variability. Risk factors for uterine rupture include vaginal birth after cesarean delivery, multiparity, and induction of labor with prostaglandin analogues or oxytocin. Educational Objective: Placenta previa is an abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or entirely overlies the internal cervical os. It can spontaneously resolve, but if it persists into the third trimester, may result in painless vaginal bleeding. Severe bleeding from placenta previa may lead to hemorrhagic shock, and treatment involves cesarean delivery.

questionStem: A 32-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician with her partner because she has been unable to conceive for 18 months . She also has had moderate dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia . Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 days. Examination of the patient and her partner, including physical examination , semen analysis , testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae , serial urinalyses to document luteinizing hormone surge , in-phase endometrial biopsy, and hysterosalpingography , shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is most likely associated with this patient's infertility?
correctExplanation: Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside of the uterus, and classically presents with symptoms of abdominal and pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Local inflammatory responses to ectopic endometrial cells cause abdominal and pelvic pain, which may be severe. The pain is often cyclic in response to fluctuating hormone concentrations during the menstrual cycle. The standard for diagnosis is a diagnostic laparoscopy, which evaluates for visual evidence of ectopic endometriotic implant lesions and permits obtaining samples for histology. Chronic inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes leads to infertility in many women with endometriosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hyperprolactinemia (Choice B) causes growth of glandular breast tissue and presents with unexpected lactation (galactorrhea). Inappropriate elevation of prolactin often arises from a hyperfunctioning anterior pituitary microadenoma. Dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia are not typical symptoms of hyperprolactinemia. Hypothyroidism (Choice C) presents with weight gain, lethargy, fatigue, constipation, hair loss, and cold intolerance. It may also result in amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea. Inadequate cervical mucus (Choice D) is a cause of infertility but is not associated with symptoms such as dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia, which are more suggestive of endometriosis. Pelvic adhesions (Choice E) are a delayed result of surgery, infection (eg, pelvic inflammatory disease), or chronic inflammation from severe endometriosis. While pelvic adhesions may be present and cause abdominal pain in some patients with endometriosis, infertility in most cases is directly related to ectopic endometrial tissue and associated inflammation and scarring within the fallopian tubes, rather than pelvic adhesions. Educational Objective: Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside of the uterus, and classically presents with symptoms of abdominal and pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Many patients experience infertility as a result of inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes.

questionStem: A 69-year-old nulliparous white woman has the sudden onset of severe pain in the upper back after sitting down. She has hypertension treated with a ~-adrenergic blocking agent. She drinks one alcoholic beverage with dinner each night. An x-ray of the spine shows a compression fracture of the 10th thoracic vertebra . Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for this condition?
correctExplanation: Osteoporosis is a common condition that is characterized by the progressive loss of bone mineral density leading to decreased bone strength. This decreased bone mineral density often leads to fragility fractures, such as in this patient, who experienced a thoracic compression fracture with a minimal axial load when sitting. Osteoporosis and resultant fractures can greatly decrease mobility, even leading to death in elderly individuals. The disease classically affects postmenopausal women with inflammatory disorders, and individuals with metabolic or endocrine disorders, such as hypercortisolism or hyperparathyroidism. Osteoporosis can be induced by long-term treatment with medications that cause an increase in bone resorption, such as corticosteroids. Osteoporosis tends to affect females at a higher rate than males, especially those of Caucasian ethnicity. Males generally develop higher peak bone mass during the first 30 years of life. Given the chronic and generally linear rate of bone mineral loss, males will therefore retain higher bone mineral density for a longer period given the higher bone mineral density starting point than females. As testosterone and estrogen both stimulate osteoblasts and increase or maintain bone mineral density, the loss of estrogen leads to an accelerated loss of bone mass in post-menopausal women.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alcohol use (Choice A) has a negative effect on bone mineral density; however, this effect is mostly seen with heavy drinking over many years. Alcohol is a diuretic and can cause loss of electrolytes, including calcium. Hypertension (Choice B) is associated with low bone mineral density; however, it is not as significant of a risk factor as genetic predisposition by race. The use of antihypertensive medications may also be a protective factor. Nulliparity (Choice C) may be associated with low bone mineral density but to a lesser extent than conditions that shorten or reduce the amount or duration of estrogen stimulus on bone, such as early menopause, smoking, low BMI, and late menarche. Use of a ~-adrenergic blocking agent (Choice E) is not generally a significant risk factor for the development of osteoporosis. The use of ~-adrenergic blockers has been associated with increased bone mineral density and decreased fracture risk. Educational Objective: Osteoporosis is a progressive loss of bone mineral density that occurs with aging and can lead to fragility fractures. Risk factors include female gender, Caucasian ethnicity, chronic inflammatory disease, use of corticosteroids, adrenal, thyroid, or parathyroid disease, sedentary lifestyle, and low estrogen states.

questionStem: A 2-week-old newborn is brought for an initial examination . She was born at home to a 25-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy . Her parents say that it takes a long time to feed the newborn , and she usually does not finish her bottle. They are also concerned that she may be constipated . She is at the 50th percentile for length and weight and 90th percentile for head circumference . She has a hoarse cry. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows large anterior and posterior fontanelles , a large protruding tongue , and a small umbilical hernia. The skin is dry and slightly mottled . There is mild hypotonia . Which of the following is most likely to have predicted these findings?
correctExplanation: Congenital hypothyroidism can be caused by maternal hypothyroidism, thyroid agenesis, thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, or iodine deficiency. Characteristics of newborns with congenital hypothyroidism include lethargy, hoarse cry, hypotonia, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, large fontanelles, dry skin, hypothermia, constipation, poor feeding, and failure to thrive. Routine newborn screening has been developed to detect congenital hypothyroidism by measuring thyroxine (T 4) or thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH). If untreated, it can result in neurocognitive deficits and intellectual disability. Treatment involves levothyroxine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Fetal monitoring (Choice B) can be performed with a non-stress test (NST) that measures fetal heart rate and heart rate patterns such as accelerations and decelerations for 20 minutes. This can be combined with evaluation of fetal breathing, fetal movement, fetal tone, and amniotic fluid volume to perform a biophysical profile (BPP) for fetal assessment. NST and BPP are done for fetal monitoring in the setting of underlying medical conditions, post-term pregnancy, intrauterine growth restriction, or pregnancy complications. Paternal karyotype analysis (Choice C) is completed in the evaluation of infertility for individuals who have experienced recurrent pregnancy loss or in patients from high risk populations undergoing prenatal genetic counseling (eg, Ashkenazi Jewish heritage). It is not done in the evaluation of an uncomplicated pregnancy; chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis can be performed for karyotypic analysis of the fetus. Prenatal ultrasonography (Choice D) is completed in the first trimester to confirm the presence of an intrauterine pregnancy, estimate gestational age, and evaluate for uterine abnormalities. Measurement of nuchal translucency is done to evaluate the risk for trisomy. In the second trimester, ultrasonography can evaluate fetal anatomy and biometry, amniotic fluid volume, and placental position. Maternal glucose tolerance testing (Choice E) is typically performed between 24 and 28 weeks' gestation to evaluate for gestational diabetes. Gestational diabetes can lead to an increased risk for congenital anomalies, spontaneous abortion and stillbirth, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Neonatal effects of gestational diabetes can include hypoglycemia because of a sudden change in the maternal-fetal glucose balance, hyperbilirubinemia, polycythemia, and an increased risk for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Educational Objective: Signs and symptoms of congenital hypothyroidism include lethargy, hoarse cry, hypotonia, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, large fontanelles, dry skin, hypothermia, constipation, poor feeding, and failure to thrive. Routine newborn screening has been developed to detect congenital hypothyroidism by measuring T 4 or TSH.

questionStem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a third episode of a Bartholin gland abscess over the past 5 years . Culture of the abscess cavity is most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: A Bartholin gland abscess can occur when a Barthol in gland becomes obstructed and infected. A Bartholin gland is located on each side of the introitus and provides secretions that lubricate the vagina. Occasionally, the ducts of these glands become obstructed, leading to a Barthol in cyst. This presents as a small area of painful, fluctuant swelling over the posterior aspect of the labium majus. With ongoing obstruction and inflammation, infection can develop, leading to a Bartholin gland abscess, marked by erythema and tenderness to palpation of the cyst. Abscesses are commonly polymicrobial and organisms may come from both the skin and enteric flora. If a single organism is identified, it is usually Neisseria gonorrhoeae, but this is not as common as a polymicrobial source. Bartholin gland abscesses are treated with incision and drainage, often with placement of a catheter to promote complete evacuation, followed by antibiotic administration.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Bacteroides fragilis (Choice A) is an anaerobic, Gram-negative bacillus and a normal component of the gastrointestinal microbiota. It only results in infections when displaced from the colon such as following surgery, rupture, or trauma, where it has the potential to cause bacteremia, intra-abdominal infections, peritonitis, and subcutaneous abscesses. Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice B) classically presents with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral or vaginal discharge. However, it can also be asymptomatic. Complications include cervicitis, epididymitis, reactive arthritis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. It is not a cause of a Bartholin duct abscess. 13-Hemolytic streptococcus (Choice C) includes Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) and Streptococcus agalactiae (group B). S. pyogenes is a common organism responsible for superficial skin infections such as cellulitis. S. agalactiae can colonize the vagina and cause neonatal sepsis after vaginal delivery. Both can contribute to a polymicrobial cause of a Bartholin duct abscess, but neither would be likely to result in a monobacterial abscess. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice D) is a possible cause of a Bartholin gland abscess but it is not the most common culture result. Educational Objective: Bartholin gland abscesses are commonly polymicrobial and organisms may originate from both the skin and enteric flora. If a single causative organism is identified, it is often Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a foul-smelling vaginal discharge for 10 days. She is sexually active with one partner. She had a bilateral tubal ligation 7 years ago. Examination shows a watery vaginal discharge with vu Ivar irritation . Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.B: DNA probe for Chlamydia trachomatis of the cervix

correctExplanation: Bacterial vaginosis is a common gynecologic condition characterized by a shift of vaginal flora and overgrowth of particular bacterial species, most commonly Gardnerella vagina/is. G. vagina/is is a Gram-variable, facultative anaerobe. Bacterial vaginosis presents with gray, thin, malodorous vaginal discharge. Vaginal pH is increased over 4.5, and a fish-like odor is detected upon KOH testing. The identification of clue cells on wet mount preparation is the most appropriate confirmatory test. Metronidazole is the first-line therapy. Bacterial vaginosis is not considered a sexually transmitted infection and treatment of asymptomatic sexual partners is not recommended.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Culture for Candida albicans (Choice A) is useful for evaluation of Candida vulvovaginitis. Vaginal candidiasis results from the overgrowth of Candida species. Symptoms include vaginal pruritus, vu Ivar erythema, and white, thick discharge. DNA probe for Chlamydia trachomatis of the cervix (Choice B) is indicated for the evaluation of cervicitis. C. trachomatis cervicitis manifests with thin, watery discharge and cervical motion tenderness, although patients may also be asymptomatic. Absence of cervicitis on this patient's examination renders this diagnosis less likely. Serologic testing for syphilis (Choice C) can detect the presence of antibodies against Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis. Syphilis presents in multiple stages with varying symptoms, including primary with a painless chancre, secondary with fever, diffuse maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata, and tertiary with tabes dorsalis, aortitis, and gummas. Vaginal culture for Gardnerella vagina/is (Choice D) is not diagnostic of bacterial vaginosis, as G. vagina/is forms part of the normal vaginal flora and is found in many healthy females . Wet mount with the presence of clue cells is more diagnostically useful. Wet mount is also useful for excluding the presence of motile trichomonads, which may be suggestive of trichomoniasis as an alternate diagnosis. Educational Objective: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by the vaginal overgrowth of Gardnerella vagina/is, a Gram-variable, facultative anaerobe. It presents with gray, thin, malodorous vaginal discharge, a vaginal pH greater than 4.5, and a fish-like odor upon KOH testing. Identification of clue cells on wet mount microscopy is a useful confirmatory test.

questionStem: A 25-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of almost continuous vaginal bleeding since delivery 5 days ago. She underwent a cesarean delivery because of a breech presentation at 40 weeks' gestation . She has had no difficulty breast-feeding . She is afebrile . Approximately 5 ml of old blood is visible in the vagina . The cervix is closed , and the uterus is firm and approximately 10 cm in length . Her hematocrit is 37%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Vaginal discharge (lochia) following delivery may last during the period of the puerperium for 4 to 6 weeks. The early discharge, termed lochia rubra, contains blood and may last for up to 10 days. Lochia slowly becomes less bloody and more serous, termed lochia serosa, before finally becoming white to yellow in color, termed lochia alba. This patient's stable hemodynamics, normal hematocrit, and the small amount of blood identified on examination are suggestive of normal lochia rubra. More significant bleeding may suggest delayed or prolonged postpartum hemorrhage and should prompt an immediate evaluation. Common causes of postpartum hemorrhage include uterine atony, lacerations or trauma to the uterus, cervix, vagina, or introitus, retained products of conception, and coagulopathy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Coagulation profile (Choice B) is useful for the evaluation of delayed postpartum hemorrhage secondary to coagulopathies such as von Willebrand disease. Coagulation profile is not necessary for normal lochia. Administration of methylergonovine (Choice C), an ergot alkaloid, may be useful for the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage secondary to uterine atony. Postpartum hemorrhage secondary to uterine atony presents with significant bleeding and potential hemodynamic instability. Administration of oxytocin (Choice D) is frequently used for the same indication. Both medications increase uterine smooth muscle contraction and muscular tone, providing a tamponade effect on any sites of uterine bleeding. Dilation and curettage (Choice E) is useful for managing postpartum hemorrhage secondary to retained placental fragments. Retained placental fragments present with significant postpartum bleeding, pelvic pain, fever, and malodorous discharge. Educational Objective: Vaginal discharge following delivery is termed lochia and may last during the period of the puerperium for 4 to 6 weeks. Lochia progresses through three stages termed rubra, serosa, and alba, which are characterized by vaginal discharge that is bloody, serous, and white to yellow, respectively. The normal bleeding of lochia is not significant; significant bleeding should raise suspicion for delayed postpartum hemorrhage and should prompt an immediate evaluation.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman at 7 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital for an appendectomy for a ruptured appendix . During the operation , one ovary is inadvertently removed due to extensive adhesions from previous operative procedures . Pathologic examination of an ovary specimen shows a corpus luteum cyst. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone therapy until 10 weeks' gestation

correctExplanation: The corpus luteum develops from the follicle following ovulation. Its primary role is secretion of progesterone from luteal cells. The progesterone maintains the endometrial lining, prepares it for embryo implantation, and decreases uterine contractility in support of the developing embryo. Following implantation, the corpus luteum continues to secrete progesterone for the first 7 to 10 weeks' gestation to maintain the pregnancy. After this time, the primary secretion of progesterone comes from the placenta. The corpus luteum is maintained by human chorionic gonadotropin from the placenta. After the placenta begins secreting progesterone, the corpus luteum degrades; however, without the corpus luteum to secrete progesterone, as in this patient, spontaneous abortion would occur. Therefore, in this patient, supplementation of progesterone until 10 weeks' gestation is appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Estrogen supplementation until 10 weeks' gestation (Choice A) is not necessary. Although the corpus luteum also secretes estrogen, which helps to maintain the pregnancy, estrogen is not as necessary for the viability of an implanted embryo as progesterone. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) therapy until 10 weeks' gestation (Choice B) is not necessary to maintain the pregnancy. FSH is responsible for the development of mature ovarian follicles prior to ovulation. It does not play a significant role following fertilization, as increased concentrations of estrogen and progesterone provide negative feedback on its production. Termination of pregnancy (Choice D) is a highly individualized choice. However, with supplementation of the progesterone lost from the corpus luteum, this patient's pregnancy will likely progress normally with no harmful effects on the fetus. No treatment is indicated (Choice E) is incorrect, as failure to supplement progesterone that would have otherwise been generated by the corpus luteum can lead to spontaneous abortion. Educational Objective: Progesterone is secreted from the corpus luteum through 7 to 10 weeks' gestation, with the progesterone being responsible for maintaining an appropriate endometrial lining and quiescent uterus for embryo development. The placenta later takes over progesterone production.

questionStem: A previously healthy 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of vulvar pain. She is sexually active with three male partners , and they use condoms inconsistently . Examination shows a tender, nonindurated ulcer on the right labium majus that bleeds easily when touched . Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: A variety of sexually transmitted infections may cause formation of a tender genital ulcer. These include genital herpes and chancroid, caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) and Haemophilus ducreyi, respectively. In contrast, lymphogranuloma venereum caused by Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes L 1, L2, and L3, a syphilitic chancre caused by Treponema pallidum, and granuloma inguinale caused by Klebsiel/a (or Calymmatobacterium) granulomatis are nontender. The causative organisms of painful genital ulcers can be distinguished clinically on the basis of the ulcer appearance. For example, the ulcer of chancroid is exudative and accompanied by significant inguinal lymphadenopathy. The ulcers of genital herpes are round and shallow, and some vesicles may be intact.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Calymmatobacterium granulomatis (Choice A) is the causative organism of granuloma inguinale, or donovanosis. The ulcer of granuloma inguinale (also called Donovanosis) is red, friable, and induces additional ulcers on oppositional skin. It is painless, not painful. Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice B) classically presents with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral or vaginal discharge. However, it can also be asymptomatic. Complications include cervicitis, epididymitis, reactive arthritis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. It is not a cause of genital ulcers. Human papillomavirus (Choice D) is a sexually transmitted viral infection that can cause cervical/vulvar and penile/anal carcinoma, as well as condylomata acuminata. It would not be expected to cause genital ulcers. Treponema pallidum (Choice E) is the causative spirochete of syphilis. Untreated syphilis demonstrates multiple stages with varying symptoms, including primary syphilis, which is characterized by a painless chancre. The chancre of primary syphilis is shallow with a clean base. Educational Objective: HSV (genital herpes) and Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) both cause painful genital ulcers. In contrast, nontender genital ulcers may be caused by Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes L 1, L2, and L3 (lymphogranuloma venereum), Treponema pallidum (primary syphilitic chancre), and Klebsiel/a granulomatis (granuloma inguinale). The ulcer of chancroid is typically exudative and accompanied by significant inguinal lymphadenopathy.

questionStem: A previously healthy 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after the sudden onset of loss of consciousness . She has a 1-day history of temperatures to 39.4°C (103°F), vomiting , watery diarrhea , and a rash over her face , trunk, and arms . Her last menstrual period started 5 days ago; she routinely uses tampons . Her temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 30/min , and her palpable systolic blood pressure is 70 mm Hg. Examination shows erythema of the conjunctivae and pharynx . Pelvic examination shows 10 to 15, 0.5-cm ulcers over the vaginal mucosa . Culture of a lesion scraping grows Staphylococcus aureus . This patient is at greatest risk for mortality from which of the following complications?
correctExplanation: Staphylococcus aureus produces an exotoxin called toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1 ). TSST-1 is a superantigen that triggers the massive production and release of cytokines including IL-1, IL-2, IFN-y, and TN F­ a, leading to toxic shock syndrome (TSS). TSS is associated with the prolonged, continuous use of tampons or nasal packing. TSS presents with fever, a diffuse erythematous macular rash, and distributive shock caused by endothelial dysfunction causing leakage of fluid from the vascular space to the interstitial space along with diffuse vasodilation. The resultant shock and inflammatory state lead to multiorgan failure. Manifestations from the gastrointestinal system include abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and liver failure. Cutaneous involvement may present as a mucous membrane rash in addition to diffuse erythroderma and sloughing. Renal failure manifests with increased creatinine concentration, electrolyte derangements, and low urine output. Acute anemia and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy may occur. Neurologic manifestations may include encephalopathy, confusion, or seizures. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is serious complication. ARDS is characterized by diffuse inflammatory lung injury and results in dyspnea and hypoxic respiratory failure, which may require mechanical ventilation. Patients with ARDS are critically ill and mortality is increased.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hemorrhage (Choice B) is an unlikely complication of TSS. The resultant hypotension from TSS is not because of hemorrhage or hypovolemia, rather, it is to the result of cytokine and toxin-mediated endothelial dysfunction leading to a distributive shock. Hepatic failure (Choice C) and renal failure (Choice E) are potential consequences from TSS secondary to hypotension and hypoperfusion resulting in end-organ damage. However, the risk of death from hepatic or renal failure would be less than from ARDS. Pulmonary embolism (Choice D) is not a known complication ofTSS. Educational Objective: Toxic shock syndrome secondary to Staphylococcus aureus exotoxin production can cause a fever, diffuse erythematous macular rash, hypotension/distributive shock, and multiorgan system failure. ARDS is a complication of TSS and carries an increased rate of mortality.

questionStem: A 42-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for the past year. She also says she has had hot flashes daily and vaginal dryness . Two years ago, she was diagnosed with cancer of the right breast ; she underwent lumpectomy , sentinel node biopsy, and four cycles of chemotherapy followed by radiation therapy. There has been no evidence of recurrence . She has not had a menstrual period since beginning the second cycle of chemotherapy 18 months ago . She is in a monogamous relationship with a male partner and has frequent unprotected sexual intercourse . She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m 2• Her pulse is 80/min , respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Examination of the right breast shows a well-healed lumpectomy scar. Examination of the left breast shows no abnormalities . The abdomen is soft and nontender . Pelvic examination shows vaginal atrophy with no vulvar, vaginal , or cervical lesions. The uterus is normal sized , and there are no adnexal masses . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's infertility?
correctExplanation: Anovulation can be caused by pregnancy, polycystic ovarian syndrome, abnormalities or immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, menopause, premature ovarian failure, inadequate nutrition, chromosomal abnormalities, and thyroid disorders. Other causes of infertility include fallopian tube blockage, sperm hypo- or immotility, inability of sperm to penetrate the corona radiata of the ovum, structural abnormalities of the uterus, and thyroid disorders. Chemotherapy and radiation therapy can be toxic to the ovaries and cause premature ovarian failure. Premature ovarian failure is defined as the depletion or dysfunction of ovarian follicles with the associated cessation of menses in women under the age of 40 years. While this patient is above the age for this definition, she likely is experiencing earlier-onset menopause secondary to chemotherapy-induced damage to her ovaries, resulting in ovarian follicle loss or dysfunction. Menopause is characterized by the lack of ovarian estrogen production, resulting in manifestations such as vaginal atrophy, hot flashes, and infertility.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adrenal insufficiency (Choice A), in its primary form, is commonly caused by autoimmune destruction or tuberculosis. It presents with hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, acid-base and metabolic derangements, and skin hyperpigmentation secondary to a deficiency of aldosterone and cortisol. It does not describe this patient's clinical condition. A prolactin-secreting tumor, most commonly in the pituitary gland, can result in hyperprolactinemia (Choice B) which inhibits gonadotropin-releasing hormone, as well as FSH and LH. It can present with amenorrhea but is often associated with galactorrhea. Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (Choice D) can also lead to anovulation and amenorrhea by virtue of decreased gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which subsequently leads to decreased FSH and LH. It is a common cause of amenorrhea or anovulation in young athletes. This patient is more likely to suffer from primary ovarian dysfunction related to chemotherapy. Hypothyroidism (Choice E) presents with weight gain, fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, and irregular or heavy menses. Physical examination typically discloses bradycardia, dry edematous skin, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. This patient does not show any additional signs to suggest hypothyroidism. Educational Objective: Chemotherapy and radiation therapy can be toxic to ovaries and cause early-onset ovarian follicle loss and dysfunction. Premature ovarian failure is defined as the depletion or dysfunction of ovarian follicles with the associated cessation of menses in women under the age of 40 years. It is characterized by the lack of ovarian estrogen production, which can present with the typical symptoms of menopause such as vaginal atrophy, hot flashes, and infertility.

questionStem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 36 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. Her blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a fundus of 37 cm. Fetal Heart Rate (beats/min) Fetal heart tones are heard in the midabdomen , and the rate is 144/min. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk, and there is no pedal edema . The cervix is 50% effaced and 1 cm dilated ; the vertex is at -1 station. During pelvic examination , the patient feels a sudden , dramatic fetal movement , and her membranes rupture . A large gush of clear fluid is seen. A fetal heart rate of 144/min is heard on auscultation . Cervical examination now shows no change in dilation or effacement. She begins to have painful contractions every 6 to 8 minutes that last 45 to 60 seconds . An electronic fetal monitor with an internal pressure catheter is applied . A fetal heart tracing is shown . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? --r--.--..-, ,-,--,- 210 ~~~--,---.--.---,-~,-.
correctExplanation: Normal labor and delivery typically occur after 37 weeks' gestation with the onset of contractions associated with cervical dilation and the rupture of membranes. Labor that begins prior to 37 weeks' gestation is referred to as preterm labor, and rupture of membranes prior to onset of labor is referred to as premature rupture of membranes. Following the onset of labor and rupture of membranes, labor continues through three stages. The first stage encompasses the start of labor (contractions and cervical change) until the completion of cervical dilation and effacement. The second stage includes the time from complete cervical dilation to the baby's birth, and the third stage consists of the delivery of the placenta. The first stage of labor is divided into a latent stage and active stage, based on the degree of cervical dilation, with the active stage beginning after 4 cm of cervical dilation is achieved. During labor, it is pertinent to monitor the fetal heart rate, which provides insight into the fetal wellbeing. A healthy fetal heart rate is between 110/min and 160/min with 6/min to 25/min of variability and spontaneous accelerations. Intermittent early and variable decelerations can also occur during the normal process of labor as a result of head compression and umbilical cord compression, respectively. Tachycardia, bradycardia, undetectable variability, and late decelerations indicate fetal distress, none of which are exhibited in this fetal heart tracing. Therefore, as this patient has begun labor, experienced rupture of membranes, and demonstrates no sign of fetal distress, observation and continued monitoring are appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Fetal scalp blood pH sampling (Choice B) is useful in detecting metabolic abnormalities of the fetus, including acidemia, when there are signs of fetal distress. However, this fetal heart tracing is reassuring. Administration of oxytocin (Choice C) is often used to augment or induce labor. It can be utilized in the setting of hypotonic contractions during protraction of labor but would not yet be necessary in this patient in early labor. Amnioinfusion (Choice D) is the infusion of fluid into the amniotic sac, which is typically done in the setting of persistent and severe variable decelerations. Immediate cesarean delivery (Choice E) is indicated, for example, in cases of fetal distress, failure to progress, placenta previa, uterine rupture, critical maternal illness, and impending maternal demise. Educational Objective: Normal labor and delivery occurs with the onset of contractions, cervical change, and rupture of membranes. It is associated with the typical fetal heart rate tracing, which consists of a heart rate between 110/min and 160/min with variability of 6/min to 25/min and spontaneous accelerations.

questionStem: Four weeks after a total vaginal hysterectomy for cervical dysplasia , a 57-year-old woman comes for a follow-up visit. A pathology report confirms the presence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3 with all surgical margins clear of disease . Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for future screening for recurrent squamous cell intraepithelial neoplasia in this patient?

choices.C: Colposcopy of the vagina in 1 yea
choices.E: No further testing for this condition is necessary

correctExplanation: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3 is a high-grade cervical lesion with an increased risk for progression to cervical cancer. Cervical carcinoma is classically associated with infection from human papilloma virus (HPV) high-risk strains 16, 18, 31, and 33. Risk factors include multiple sexual partners, smoking, and immunosuppression. Screening Pap smears are recommended every 3 years in women aged 21 to 29 years and every 5 years in conjunction with HPV co-testing (every 3 years if co-testing is not performed) in women aged 30 to 65 years. Abnormal Pap smear cytology results are most commonly evaluated by colposcopy, which allows for the visual assessment and biopsy of abnormal lesions. CIN 3 disease requires excision via either a loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) or a cone biopsy of the cervix (also known as cold knife conization). Hysterectomy is performed for recurrent or persistent cervical dysplasia. This patient remains at risk for the development of cancer given the presence of CIN 3 on her uterine pathology and requires yearly follow up with Pap smears of the vaginal cuff to screen for the recurrence of dysplasia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Human papillomavirus testing in 3 months (Choice A) would not identify recurrence of dysplasia, although it may provide some insight into the likelihood of its development, as someone who is positive for human papillomavirus is more likely to develop dysplasia. Colposcopy of the vagina in 1 year (Choice C) is not necessary without evidence of dysplasia on annual Pap smear or obvious lesions seen on pelvic examination. Random vaginal biopsy in 1 year (Choice D) would not be appropriate, as this should not be performed unless there is evidence of dysplasia at her vaginal cuff on future Pap smears. As well, random vaginal biopsy is haphazard, and would be insensitive to detect recurrent dysplasia. No further testing for this condition (Choice E) is incorrect, as this patient remains at high risk for recurrence of dysplasia given her high-grade lesion on pathology. She should continue to receive annual Pap smears, with further evaluation pending their results. Educational Objective: Evidence of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia on post-hysterectomy uterine pathology warrants continued annual Pap smears to monitor for the recurrence of dysplasia .

questionStem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 10-month history of breast tenderness that is worse just prior to the onset of menses . Her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals , and she is currently on day 26 of her menstrual cycle. Examination shows multiple , bilateral , firm cystic areas of the breasts. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Fibrocystic changes of the breast occur most commonly in premenopausal women. Patients may present with various sites of breast pain and lumps, which may be bilateral. The condition is characterized by the presence of cysts, stromal fibrosis, and apocrine metaplasia on histology, and is believed to occur in response to hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle. Reexamination after menses may be helpful for diagnosis because the size of fibrocystic changes should subside after menses, distinguishing it from other causes. On examination, the cysts may appear blue. Fibrocystic change is a benign disease and does not generally convey an increased risk for cancer except for certain subtypes, however, it can result in recurrent mastalgia. If there is associated discomfort, aspiration can be performed which may relieve symptoms. Cyst aspiration can yield fluid that is clear, milky, yellow, green, or brown, which are all benign. Supportive care is also appropriate, using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, and a well-fitting brassiere. Oral contraceptive therapy has not generally been shown to relieve symptoms of fibrocystic breast disease or cyclic breast pain.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cytology of expressed nipple discharge (Choice B) may be useful in some patients for the evaluation of ductal carcinoma. However, mammography or fine needle biopsy are preferred methods over nipple fluid cytology. This patient's presentation of bilateral, cyclic mastalgia is more suggestive of fibrocystic disease. Mammography (Choice C) is the preferred screening method for breast carcinoma. The United States Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening for all women beginning at age 50. This patient's findings are not suggestive of malignancy and mammography subjects the patient to an uncomfortable test that may lead to an unnecessary biopsy. Aspiration of the cysts (Choice D) may be helpful for alleviating mastalgia in patients with fibrocystic disease. However, reexamination after menses may be helpful for confirming the diagnosis prior to more invasive treatments, such as needle aspiration, and is a more reasonable next step. Biopsy of the cysts (Choice E) is not usually necessary for patients with fibrocystic changes. If re-examination after menses does not demonstrate a reduction in size of the fibrocystic changes, a biopsy may be performed to evaluate for other possible causes. Educational Objective: Fibrocystic change of the breast is a benign condition occurring in menstruating women that presents with multiple, bilateral, painful breast cysts. Reexamination after menses should demonstrate a reduction in size of the fibrocystic changes, which distinguishes the diagnosis from other causes.

questionStem: A previously healthy 47-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of excessive vaginal bleeding with the passage of clots. During this time , she has had to change her sanitary pad every 2 hours. She has had occasional hot flashes during the past 6 months . Her menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals until 1 year ago. She now has 2 weeks of bleeding every 2 months. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . Six months ago, a Pap smear showed no abnormalities . She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m 2• Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone concentration

correctExplanation: Abnormal uterine bleeding should be suspected when bleeding is irregular, unpredictable, or not associated with usual premenstrual signs and symptoms (eg, bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps). It may be caused by structural abnormalities such as cervical or endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia, malignancy, inflammation or infection of the genital tract, coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endocrine dysfunction (eg, thyroid disorders, prolactin, androgens), and may be iatrogenic or idiopathic. The patient in the question has no stigmata or history of thyroid disorder, coagulopathy, polycystic ovarian syndrome, or ovulatory dysfunction. In patients over the age of 45, who are perimenopausal or postmenopausal, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy. The next appropriate step in evaluation would be an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer. If a patient cannot tolerate an outpatient procedure or if the outpatient sampling is nondiagnostic, a dilation and curettage or hysteroscopy can be performed. A hysteroscopy with sampling allows for a more complete evaluation of the endometrium (eg, polyps, myomas, structural abnormalities).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. A Pap smear (Choice A) would not be the appropriate next step as a recent Pap smear 6 months ago showed no abnormalities. Repeat Pap smear and cytology would be the next step in management for women with atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), although this should occur 12 months after the previous Pap smear. Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone (LH) concentration (Choice B) or serum testosterone concentration (Choice C) would not be the next best step. LH is increased in postmenopausal patients and testosterone concentrations are decreased, but neither is useful in the evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding. In endometrial carcinoma, the measurement of cancer antigen 125 (CA 125) may sometimes be useful for the surveillance of disease progression or response. CT scan of the pelvis (Choice D) would not be helpful in the initial evaluation of uterine bleeding as it does not adequately evaluate the endometrium. Ultrasonography would be a helpful initial imaging modality to evaluate for the presence of polyps, adenomyosis, and endometrial hyperplasia. Educational Objective: Abnormal uterine bleeding may be caused by structural, neoplastic, coagulopathic, infectious, endocrine, or iatrogenic sources. In patients over the age of 45, who are perimenopausal or postmenopausal, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy. The next appropriate step in evaluation would be an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer.

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the onset of severe abdominal pain and nausea and vomiting . During a routine visit 2 weeks ago, pelvic examination showed an 8-cm right adnexal mass. Ultrasonography showed an 8-cm, mature cystic teratoma on the right ovary. Abdominal examination today shows severe rebound tenderness with guarding in the right lower quadrant. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
correctExplanation: Ovarian teratomas are typically unilateral and can rapidly grow, leading to complications such as pain, hemorrhage, necrosis, and ovarian torsion. Ovarian torsion describes a condition in which the ovary twists on its ligamentous support. The suspensory ligament of the ovary contains the ovarian artery and vein; if twisted, it can lead to impaired blood supply resulting in ovarian infarction. Ovarian torsion may occur in patients with normal ovaries; however this is less common, and an ovarian mass or cyst increases the risk for torsion. As the size of an ovarian mass increases, the risk for torsion also increases. Malignant masses that adhere to the pelvis may be at lower risk for torsion. Signs and symptoms of ovarian torsion include acute, severe unilateral pelvic pain, abdominopelvic tenderness and guarding, an adnexal mass, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis relies on the clinical presentation, but Doppler ultrasonography evaluation of the ovary can be used to confirm torsion. Treatment involves emergent surgery for detorsion of the ovary in an attempt to conserve it.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute appendicitis (Choice A) typically presents with periumbilical abdominal pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant of the abdomen, along with nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation. It is typically a gradually worsening course over hours to days, whereas the acute, severe abdominal pain in this patient with a known large ovarian cyst is more likely because of ovarian torsion. Ectopic pregnancy (Choice B) refers to the abnormal implantation of the embryo outside of the uterine endometrium (eg, in the fallopian tube, cervix, myometrium, ovary, or peritoneum) in an anatomic location that cannot support a pregnancy. It should be suspected in a patient with a positive urine pregnancy test that presents with vaginal bleeding and acute abdominopelvic pain in the first trimester. Pelvic inflammatory disease (Choice D) typically presents with fever, mucopurulent cervical discharge, and cervical or adnexal tenderness. Adnexal tenderness may be present in cases of tuba-ovarian abscess. Renal calculi (Choice E) may present with unilateral flank pain that is colicky and sometimes radiates to the groin with associated hematuria. It would typically not cause abdominal tenderness on physical examination. On urinalysis, there are typically red blood cells without casts. Educational Objective: Ovarian torsion describes a condition in which the ovary twists on its ligamentous support, leading to impaired blood supply. Ovarian torsion may occur in patients with normal ovaries; however, an ovarian mass or cyst increases the risk for torsion.

questionStem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 31 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of shortness of breath at rest. She has gestational diabetes treated with diet. She measures her blood glucose concentrations four times daily ; her 1-hour postprandial concentrations have averaged 144 mg/dl . Ultrasonography at 18 weeks' gestation showed a fetus who had normal anatomy and was consistent in size with gestational age. The patient is Rh-negative and received Rh0(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks' gestation ; antibody screening was negative . Her pulse is 88/min , and respirations are 22/min . The lungs are clear to auscultation and percussion . Examination shows a fundal height of 44 cm. The cervix is 4 cm dilated and 50% effaced ; the vertex is at -2 station. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Polyhydramnios refers to an excess of amniotic fluid. Polyhydramnios is associated with fetal developmental defects that result in impaired swallowing, such as anencephaly, esophageal atresia, or duodenal atresia. Risk factors for polyhydramnios also include maternal diabetes mellitus, as in this case, maternofetal Rh incompatibility, and congenital infections. As in this patient, the size of the gravid uterus may greatly exceed that which is expected for gestational age, leading to maternal symptoms of dyspnea through prevention of diaphragmatic excursion. Diagnosis is facilitated with ultrasonography, which will show an enlarged pool of amniotic fluid, and may be used to assess the amniotic fluid index. Polyhydramnios is defined sonographically as an amniotic fluid index greater than 25. Treatment is supportive, although patients with severe symptoms may be treated with amniocentesis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Anencephaly (Choice A) is a frequent cause of polyhydramnios because it impairs fetal swallowing through the lack of neural control of the swallow reflex. While it could be an indirect cause of the symptoms of dyspnea, which are directly caused by polyhydramnios, the patient's ultrasonography at 18 weeks' gestation did not show anencephaly. Incorrect gestational age (Choice B) is a cause of discrepancy between the size of the gravid uterus and estimated gestational age. However, it is less likely to lead to such a large discrepancy and is less likely given this patient's risk factors for polyhydramnios. Rh isoimmunization (Choice D) occurs when the maternal immune system (when Rh-negative) becomes sensitized to the presence of Rh-positive fetal blood. Hemolytic disease of the newborn leading to hydrops fetalis may result, though it does not commonly cause polyhydramnios or uterine enlargement. Twin gestation (Choice E) is unlikely given that it was not detected on previous ultrasonography at 18 weeks' gestation. Educational Objective: Polyhydramnios refers to an excess of amniotic fluid that is associated with fetal developmental defects that result in impaired swallowing, such as anencephaly, esophageal atresia, or duodenal atresia. Additional risk factors include maternal diabetes mellitus, maternofetal Rh incompatibility, and congenital infections. Polyhydramnios is defined sonographically as an amniotic fluid index greater than 25.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. Her last menstrual period was 12 weeks ago. Her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated . Examination shows a closed cervix and a uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation . Her blood group is AB, Rh-negative . Ultrasonography detects a fetal heart rate. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: Determination oft:,. OD 450 in amniotic fluid

correctExplanation: Rh-negative mothers are at a high-risk for developing anti-Rh antibodies if exposed to blood from a Rh-positive fetus, which most commonly occurs during delivery. If Rh antigens from the fetal circulation enter the maternal circulation, it is possible that the mother's immune system will form antibodies against the Rh antigen. While this carries no significant complication with the initial exposure, a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus can result in severe hemolytic anemia of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) as maternal antibodies cause hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes when they cross the placenta. Rho(D) immune globulin acts by binding to Rh-positive cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the immune system from developing antibodies to the Rh antigen, but it is not always effective. Therefore, the best way to determine whether the mother has been exposed to Rh-positive blood and subsequently formed anti-Rh antibodies is the indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test, which is conducted by combining red blood cells (RBCs) that contain the antigen of choice with the patient's serum. If the patient's serum contains antibodies against the antigen, in this case the blood antigen Rh, the antibodies will bind to the RBCs. When Coombs reagent, or antiglobulin antibody, is added, erythrocytes will agglutinate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Glucose tolerance tests (Choice A) are typically completed at 24 to 28 weeks' gestation to screen for gestational diabetes, so care can be taken to avoid the complications associated with uncontrolled hyperglycemia during pregnancy. This patient is only at 12 weeks' gestation which makes a glucose tolerance test unnecessary. Measurement of hemoglobin A 1c (Choice C) would allow screening for pre-gestational diabetes at 12 weeks' gestation. However, this patient has no symptoms of diabetes (eg, polyuria, thirst, weight gain), making a screen for pre-gestational diabetes unnecessary. Determination oft:,. OD 450 in amniotic fluid (Choice D) can accurately diagnose severe fetal hemolytic anemia in the setting of Rh alloimmunization because of the presence of increased bilirubin in the amniotic fluid. However, it will remain unknown if this patient is at risk for developing fetal hemolytic anemia in the absence of an indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test. Administration of Rh0(D) immune globulin (Choice E) is typically performed for an Rh-negative mother at 28 weeks' gestation, and following the delivery of an Rh-positive newborn, any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and any episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. However, Rh0 (D) immune globulin is ineffective in a patient that has already developed Rh antibodies, making an indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test a more important initial diagnostic study. Educational Objective: An indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test can be used to determine whether an Rh-negative patient has developed anti-Rh antibodies and is an important component of early prenatal care, especially in patients with previous pregnancies.

questionStem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician for counseling prior to conception . She feels well. She is recently married , and she and her husband wish to start a family immediately . She has a 10-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with an insulin pump. During the past 3 years , she has been hospitalized twice for ketoacidosis . She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m 2. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Her serum glucose concentration is 180 mg/dl in the physician's office. Which of the following measures will have the greatest impact on the success of this patient's pregnancy?

choices.A: Adding an oral hypoglycemic to the regimen

correctExplanation: Tight glucose control during conception and pregnancy in a patient with pre-gestational diabetes mellitus (type 1 or 2) is important in minimizing the effects of hyperglycemia on the fetus. Human placental lactogen produced by the placenta increases maternal insulin resistance, especially in a patient that is already insulin dependent. This leads to increased concentrations of glucose in the maternal circulation, and subsequently the fetal circulation. Fetal hyperglycemia in turn causes the fetus to produce excess insulin, as well as decrease the rate of gluconeogenesis. The insulin acts as a growth factor, leading to macrosomia, and inhibits the production of surfactant, which leads to respiratory distress syndrome. After birth, the fetus still synthesizes excess insulin but is no longer exposed to the maternal blood glucose concentration, which leads to hypoglycemia. Other complications associated with diabetes during pregnancy include congenital malformations (eg, cardiac, caudal regression), fetal demise, preeclampsia, preterm labor, intrauterine growth restriction caused by uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal mortality.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adding an oral hypoglycemic to the regimen (Choice A), while being an option for management of type 2 diabetes mellitus, would be ineffective in treating hyperglycemia caused by type 1 diabetes mellitus. Further, oral hypoglycemics are not frequently utilized during pregnancy given an absence of fetal safety data and sufficient management with insulin supplementation. Adding an exercise program (Choice B) to this patient's daily routine would be one mechanism to help better control blood glucose. However, it alone is unlikely to be effective in the absence of insulin dose adjustments in this patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus and an absence of endogenous insulin production. Prenatal vitamin supplementation (Choice C) should be recommended to minimize the risk for congenital malformations, such as neural tube defects. However, this patient would still be at risk for the complications of poor glucose control during pregnancy. Excess weight gain (Choice E) during pregnancy increases the risk for macrosomia, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and gestational diabetes, whereas inadequate weight gain increases the risk for fetal growth restriction and preterm birth. Weight gain in this patient is less important than tight blood glucose control. Educational Objective: Tight maternal blood glucose control in a patient with pre-gestational diabetes mellitus decreases the risk for macrosomia, respiratory distress syndrome, postnatal hypoglycemia, congenital malformations, preeclampsia, preterm labor, and maternal and fetal mortality.

questionStem: A 4 ?-year-old woman comes for a routine health maintenance examination . She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years , but she quit 1 year ago. She has had one lifetime sexual partner and has not been sexually active for 3 years . Pap smear and mammography showed normal findings 8 months ago. Her mother died of breast cancer at the age of 60 years . Physical and pelvic examinations show no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test for this patient?
correctExplanation: Screening tests are used to identify potentially treatable conditions early in their course to prevent long-term morbidity or mortality. Cancer screenings are an important item of discussion at health maintenance examinations. The decision to perform screening tests for malignancy is based on the age of the patient and whether they have an increased risk for any specific cancers. Screening tests also decrease in value the more often they are performed. For example, this asymptomatic patient will not benefit from repeated Pap smear or mammography since they were both normal 8 months ago. Screening for colorectal carcinoma should begin at age 50 in this patient and lung cancer at age 55 based on guidelines from the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Screening Pap smears (Choice A) are recommended every 3 years in women ages 21 to 29 years and every 5 years in conjunction with HPV co-testing (every 3 years if co-testing is not performed) in women ages 30 to 65 years. As this patient had a Pap smear 8 months ago that showed no abnormalities, there is no need to complete another at this time. X-ray of the chest (Choice B) is not used as screening for lung cancer. The USPSTF recommends performing low-dose CT scans as the screening test in adults who have a 30-pack-year smoking history, are between the ages of 55 and 80 years, and are either currently smoking or have quit during the past 15 years. This patient does not warrant lung cancer screening yet given her age, but with her smoking history she will need a low-dose CT scan after reaching the age of 55 years. Mammography (Choice C) is used as a screening technique for breast cancer and is recommended by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (AGOG) for women of average breast cancer risk to occur every 1 to 2 years after the age of 40 years. The decision to screen for breast cancer before the age of 40 years is made on a case-by-case basis. The incidence of breast cancer is lower in this age group, mammography is less sensitive, and potential harms of false positives include unnecessary procedures or emotional stress. As this patient had a mammography 8 months ago that showed no abnormalities, there is no need to complete another at this time. Colonoscopy (Choice D) is useful in the diagnosis and management of colorectal pathology such as malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, arteriovenous malformation, and strictures. In patients with no family history of colorectal carcinoma, screening colonoscopies should begin at the age of 50 years and occur every 10 years or sooner if polyps are identified. This patient does not have an indication for a colonoscopy at this time. Educational Objective: Screening tests are used to identify potentially treatable conditions early in their course to prevent long-term morbidity or mortality.
