In a 47-year-old woman the only screening test for malignancy necessary by AGOG recommendations is a Pap smear (every 5 years in conjunction with HPV testing) and mammography (every 1 to 2 years).

questionStem: A 30-year-old multigravid woman at 37 weeks' gestation is admitted in labor 6 hours after the onset of regular uterine contractions . Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . By abdominal palpation , her fetus is thought to be in breech presentation . Her amniotic membranes are intact. Her cervix is 2 cm long and 1 cm dilated; the presenting part is at -3 station but is difficult to palpate . Ultrasonography shows a double footling breech presentation . During labor, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?

choices.D: Prolapse of the fetal umbilical cord

correctExplanation: Fetal malpresentation occurs when any portion of the fetus besides the occiput presents at the cervical os. This malpresentation prevents the head from properly engaging in the pelvis for descent. This can similarly occur in polyhydramnios, as the excess amniotic fluid can prevent any body part from presenting at the cervical os until the rupture of membranes occurs. A serious complication that can occur in fetal malpresentation is umbilical cord prolapse. Because of the lack of occiput engagement at the cervical os, the cord can protrude through the cervix following the rupture of membranes before the fetus descends into the pelvic opening. Further contractions can then cause cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Given the high risk associated with vaginal deliveries in the setting of fetal malpresentation, delivery is usually completed via an elective cesarean delivery when the condition is known. Cord prolapse, however, is an obstetric emergency, requiring immediate cesarean delivery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chorioamnionitis (Choice A) is a bacterial infection of the fetal membranes and commonly occurs in premature or prolonged rupture of membranes. Maternal fever and leukocytosis are characteristic, and the uterus may be tender to palpation. However, it is not a common complication of fetal malpresentation. Fetal shoulder dystocia (Choice B) occurs when, after delivery of the fetal head, the fetal shoulders are impacted behind the pubic symphysis or sacral promontory. This can lead to brachia! nerve injury, asphyxia, and death. It is associated with macrosomia, post-term pregnancy, and maternal obesity. Breech presentation does not increase the risk for shoulder dystocia. Postpartum hemorrhage (Choice C) is most commonly caused by uterine atony in the setting of macrosomia, multiple gestations, prolonged labor, or uterine infection. It can also be caused by cervical or vaginal tract laceration and retained products of conception. Uterine rupture (Choice E) occurs when the muscular wall of the uterus tears and presents with severe abdominal pain, hemodynamic instability, and loss of fetal station. Risk factors include previous cesarean deliveries and induction of labor, not a breech presentation. Educational Objective: Rupture of membranes when there is no palpable presenting fetal body part or there is fetal malpresentation carries a high risk for umbilical cord prolapse, which can lead to cord compression and fetal hypoxia.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She feels well, and pregnancy has been uncomplicated . Amniocentesis for fetal karyotype at 16 weeks' gestation showed no abnormalities , and she received Rho{D) immune globulin . She has gained 8.2 kg (18 lb) during her pregnancy . Her blood pressure is 135/78 mm Hg. Fundal height is 29 cm. The fetus is in a longitudinal lie with a cephalic presentation . The fetal heart rate is 160/min. The patient's blood group is A, Rh-negative . Two days ago, serum anti-D antibody titer was negative . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Repeat serum anti-D antibody titer in 2 to 4 weeks
choices.D: Amniocentesis for measurement of bilirubin concentration
choices.E: Cordocentesis for measurement of fetal hemoglobin concentration

correctExplanation: Rh-negative mothers are at a high-risk for developing anti-Rh antibodies if exposed to blood from a Rh-positive fetus, which most commonly occurs during delivery. If Rh antigens from the fetal circulation enter the maternal circulation, it is possible that the mother's immune system will form antibodies against the Rh antigen. While this carries no significant complication with the initial exposure, a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus can result in severe hemolytic anemia of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) as maternal antibodies cause hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes when they cross the placenta. Rho(D) immune globulin acts by binding to Rh-positive cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the immune system from developing antibodies to the Rh antigen. Administration of Rho(D) immune globulin is typically performed for Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks' gestation and following the delivery of an Rh-positive newborn, any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and any episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. Rh0(D) immune globulin is ineffective in a patient that has already developed Rh antibodies.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Repeat serum anti-D antibody titer in 2 to 4 weeks (Choice A) would determine if the patient had developed alloimmunization in that time period. However, it is more important to prevent the development of anti-D antibodies with the administration of Rho{D) immune globulin now, as the patient is at 28 weeks' gestation. Kleihauer-Betke (acid elution) test (Choice B) is used to quantify the amount of fetal blood to which the maternal circulation has been exposed in order to determine adequacy of Rh immune globulin dosing. It is frequently used when an Rh-negative mother gives birth to an Rh-positive child. Amniocentesis for measurement of bilirubin concentration (Choice D) and cordocentesis for measurement of fetal hemoglobin concentration (Choice E) can be used to determine whether the fetus is experiencing hemolysis and anemia. However, as this patient has a negative anti-Rh antibody screen, it is unlikely that the patient has developed severe fetal hemolytic anemia. It is pertinent at 28 weeks' gestation to administer Rh0(D) immune globulin to prevent this from occurring. Educational Objective: Rh-negative mothers are at a high-risk for Rh alloimmunization when exposed to Rh antigens from the fetal circulation. Alloimmunization can be prevented by the administration of Rho{D) immune globulin at 28 weeks' gestation and following the delivery of an Rh-positive newborn, any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and any episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. r O

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman at 22 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital because of fractures of right ribs 4-10 sustained in a motor vehicle collision . She is intubated . Her blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, and urine output is 50 ml/h . Fetal monitoring shows no fetal heart tones . Laboratory studies show : Hematocrit Leukocyte count Platelet count Prothrombin time Partial thromboplastin time Plasma fibrinogen 30% 9500/mm3 70,000/mm 3 16 sec >100 sec 50 mg/dL (N=200-400) Fibrin split products are present in the serum at a 1 :160 dilutional titer. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows free fluid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.D: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

correctExplanation: Antepartum intrauterine fetal demise commonly presents with decreased fetal movement and lack of fetal heart tones on exam. Ultrasonography confirms the lack of cardiac activity and intrauterine fetal demise. In high-income countries, stillbirth is most commonly caused by chromosomal abnormalities, uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal medical disease, whereas it is more commonly to the result of maternal infection, preeclampsia, or obstructed labor in low-income countries. It can also be caused by significant blunt abdominal trauma, leading to probable placental abruption or uterine rupture, as in this patient. Delivery for antepartum intrauterine fetal demise is based on the mother's wishes, with immediate induction or delayed natural delivery both feasible options in the absence of any complicating medical issues. Labor typically begins 1 to 2 weeks after fetal demise. Coagulation abnormalities can occur with delayed delivery because of the release of tissue factor {thromboplastin) from the placenta. This can lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation {DIC), which presents with thrombocytopenia, prolongation of partial thromboplastin and prothrombin times, increased □-dimer levels, and decreased fibrinogen. As this patient has developed DIC based on her laboratory abnormalities, urgent delivery of the fetus is warranted. However, as she is intubated and not in active labor, cesarean delivery is the most appropriate next step.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. CT scan of the abdomen {Choice A) could be utilized to evaluate for any signs of damage to the abdominal organs in the setting of trauma. However, it would offer no additional information about the fetus that could not be assessed by ultrasonography. Given the development of coagulation abnormalities and fetal demise, delivery is the most pertinent next step. Exchange transfusion {Choice B) is used in sickle cell disease and, occasionally, in severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia of the newborn to reduce the concentrations of hemoglobin Sand bilirubin, respectively. It does not play a role in the management of DIC. Platelet transfusion {Choice C) is indicated when a patient's platelet concentration falls below 1 0,000/mm 3 without evidence of bleeding or 50,000/mm 3 when the patient is actively bleeding or requires a surgical procedure. This patient does not require a platelet transfusion at this time. Transfusion of packed red blood cells {Choice D) is most commonly indicated when the hematocrit falls below 21 %, although more liberal transfusion protocols are used in patients with evidence of end organ damage or hypotension. This patient's hematocrit is 30%, indicating that transfusion is unnecessary at this time. Educational Objective: Retention of the fetus following intrauterine demise can lead to acute disseminated intravascular coagulation {DIC) with thrombocytopenia, prolongation of partial thromboplastin and prothrombin times, increased □-dimer concentration, and decreased fibrinogen concentration. Development of DIC requires urgent delivery of the fetus, via vaginal or cesarean delivery.

questionStem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 26 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of an 8-hour history of moderate abdominal pain and cramping . She has no history of serious illness or operative procedures . Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated . Vital signs are within normal limits. On pelvic examination , the cervix is 6 cm dilated and 100% effaced; the presenting part is at +1 station . Ultrasonography shows a fetus in a breech presentation and consistent in size with a 26-week gestation . The patient undergoes an emergent cesarean delivery. Twenty-four hours after delivery, the patient's temperature is 41 °C (105.8°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 30/min , and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . Abdominal examination shows moderate tenderness to palpation over the uterus. Urinalysis shows 2+ RBCs and trace leukocyte esterase . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: In an immediately postpartum patient with fever and uterine tenderness, puerperal sepsis should be suspected. Puerperal sepsis refers to sepsis presenting immediately after delivery and is typically characterized by the presence of fever and abdominal pain, mucopurulent vaginal discharge, uterine tenderness, or septic shock. Septic shock is a term used to refer to the decreased organ perfusion that occurs from an overwhelming infection. Septic shock is a form of distributive shock, and is classically diagnosed with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and signs of infection on examination, as well as leukocytosis and lactic acidosis. Risk factors for puerperal sepsis include cesarean delivery, premature rupture of membranes, prolonged labor, and manual removal of the placenta. Because of the risk for puerperal sepsis following cesarean delivery, women typically receive a prophylactic dose of antibiotics at the time of surgery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Pneumonia (Choice A) is characterized by fever, a cough productive of sputum, malaise, and chest discomfort. On physical examination, there may be abnormal lung sounds such as crackles or rhonchi, along with increased tactile fremitus. Pyelonephritis (Choice C) typically presents with fevers, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain with associated costovertebral angle tenderness on physical examination. This most commonly occurs from ascending urinary tract infections. Urinalysis in pyelonephritis often exhibits >10 WBC/hpf, may show red blood cells as evidence of mucosal inflammation, and white blood cell casts. Bacteria are generally seen on microscopy, with gram-negative rods being the most common pathogen. A urinalysis without white blood cells would effectively rule out pyelonephritis in this patient. Retained placental fragments (Choice D), also called retained products of conception, are a potential cause of postpartum hemorrhage. If causing severe bleeding, the retained placental fragments need to be urgently manually removed. Removal of the entire placenta promotes uterine contraction and decreases postpartum hemorrhage. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (Choice E) is a rare sequela of endometritis that can lead to local invasion and infection of the pelvic vein walls, which causes intimal damage and thrombosis. This condition typically presents with pelvic pain and fever, which is often widely variable in course, ranging from normal temperature to febrile temperatures. Diagnosis typically occurs through blood cultures. If this patient were persistently febrile despite appropriate antibiotic treatment for endometritis and puerperal sepsis, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis should be considered. Educational Objective: Puerperal sepsis refers to sepsis presenting immediately after delivery and is typically characterized by the presence of fever and abdominal pain, mucopurulent vaginal discharge, uterine tenderness, or septic shock. Risk factors for puerperal sepsis include cesarean delivery, premature rupture of membranes, prolonged labor, and manual removal of the placenta.

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of urinary incontinence for 4 weeks . Sometimes she is unable to reach a bathroom quickly enough after feeling the need to void. She recalls falling on wet grass 3 weeks ago but did not notice any injuries . She has gastroesophageal reflux disease and hypertension . Her medications include hydrochlorothiazide and famotidine . She stopped taking hydrochlorothiazide 7 days ago because she thought it was causing the incontinence , but the symptoms have continued . She takes no other medications . Her blood pressure is 137/92 mm Hg. Examination , including pelvic examination , shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her incontinence?

choices.B: Loss of progesterone effect on the bladder mucosa

correctExplanation: Urge incontinence most commonly occurs as a result of detrusor hyperreflexia or overactivity, leading to uninhibited bladder contractions. It typically presents with the urge to urinate followed by the leakage of a variable amount of urine. It is most associated with neurologic disorders (eg, multiple sclerosis, spinal stenosis, or spinal cord injuries) but may also be idiopathic. Although this patient experienced a fall, her symptoms began 1 week prior to this incident, making a traumatic neurologic cause less likely. Physical examination and laboratory studies disclose no abnormalities. Post-void urinary bladder residual volume will generally be within reference range. When evaluating urinary incontinence, however, it is important to rule out an associated urinary tract infection, especially when the urinary incontinence is new in onset. Treatment of urge incontinence includes strengthening the pelvic floor, weight loss, minimizing caffeine and alcohol intake, bladder training or timed voiding, and antimuscarinic agents (eg, oxybutynin).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adverse effect of medication (Choice A) is a possible cause of urinary incontinence, especially in the case of diuretics. However, this patient stopped taking hydrochlorothiazide 7 days ago and her symptoms have persisted, making this an unlikely cause of her incontinence. Loss of progesterone effect on the bladder mucosa (Choice B) does not typically cause incontinence. However, estrogen deficiency in the setting of menopause can cause atrophy and inflammation of the vagina and urethra, which can lead to overactive bladder or pelvic floor laxity with stress incontinence. Obstruction of the bladder outlet (Choice C) causes overflow incontinence, which presents with the leakage of urine when the hydrostatic pressure of urine within the bladder overwhelms the closing pressure of the urethral sphincters or obstructing lesions. Causes include benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatic carcinoma, urethral injury, or urinary bladder cancer obstructing the urethral orifice. This patient has urge incontinence but does not have overflow incontinence. Spinal cord injury (Choice D) can lead to urge incontinence but more commonly leads to overflow incontinence caused by a neurogenic bladder. Spinal cord injury leading to urinary retention is unlikely in the absence of neurologic deficits, such as lower extremity weakness or perinea! anesthesia. Educational Objective: Urge incontinence presents with urinary urgency and leakage of variable amounts of urine as a result of detrusor hyperreflexia, most commonly in neurologic disorders, although it can be idiopathic.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman , gravida 4, para 1, aborta 3, comes to the physician with her 31-year-old husband because of three first-trimester spontaneous abortions during the past 15 months. The patient received the diagnosis of each pregnancy by serum 13-hCG testing and ultrasonography . After diagnosis , there was no evidence of embryonic viability on ultrasonography , and spontaneous abortion occurred at 7 weeks' gestation . Seven years ago, she had deep venous thrombosis of the left lower extremity while taking an oral contraceptive and was treated with anticoagulation therapy for 6 months . Physical examination of the patient and her husband shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is most likely to establish the cause of recurrent spontaneous abortion in this patient?

choices.A: Karyotype analysis of the patient and her husband
choices.B: Karyotype analysis of subsequent abortus material
choices.E: Endometrial biopsy during the luteal phase

correctExplanation: Spontaneous abortion (SAB) is the demise of a fetus before 20 weeks' gestation. SAB typically presents with acute vaginal bleeding and cramping. There are various stages of SAB depending on the presence or absence of a fetal heartbeat, whether the cervical os is open or closed, and the extent of fetal passage through the cervix. Early pregnancy loss occurs in the first trimester, and risk factors include an age greater than 35 years, prior fetal demise, uterine anatomic distortion, diabetes, thyroid disorders, coagulopathies or hypercoagulability, and substance use. The most common underlying cause of fetal death is a chromosomal abnormality, often associated with advanced maternal age. SAB that occurs after the first trimester is more commonly related to uterine cavity abnormalities (eg, fibroids), cervical insufficiency, congenital malformations, and placental abruption or premature labor. Recurrent pregnancy loss is typically evaluated with karyotype analysis, hysterosalpingography, serum antiphospholipid antibody assay, and evaluation of thyroid function. In this patient with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss and deep venous thrombosis, the most likely cause is antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Karyotype analysis of the patient and her husband (Choice A) could determine the presence of gonadal mosaicism or Robertsonian translocations that could predispose the fetus to chromosomal abnormalities. However, it is typically used when other evaluations are normal given the relatively low prevalence of abnormal parental karyotypes, and in this patient, karyotype abnormality is less likely than hypercoagulability. Karyotype analysis of subsequent abortus material (Choice B) could determine whether the patient had a chromosomal abnormality that could potentially explain her previous SABs. However, this would require her to become pregnant again without an explanation for the recurrent losses, which would likely result in another SAB. Hysterosalpingography (Choice D) is an x-ray technique used to determine the structure of the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes, including tube patency. It is useful in the evaluation of recurrent pregnancy loss, but an anatomic issue with the uterus or fallopian tubes is less likely than antiphospholipid antibody syndrome in this patient with a history of deep venous thrombosis. Endometrial biopsy during the luteal phase (Choice E) can be used to evaluate for a luteal phase defect, which is typically caused by inadequate progesterone secretion to prepare the endometrium for embryo implantation. It is a less common independent cause of recurrent pregnancy loss and more frequently causes infertility. Educational Objective: Recurrent early pregnancy loss is caused by chromosomal abnormalities, uterine anatomic anomalies, antiphospholipid syndrome, coagulopathies, thyroid disorders, diabetes, and substance use. Typical evaluation involves hysterosalpingography, serum antiphospholipid antibody assay, evaluation of thyroid function, and karyotype analysis. In this patient with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss and deep venous thrombosis, the most likely cause is antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, is brought to the emergency department because of headaches for 4 days and slurred speech for 3 hours. She also has had fatigue and intermittent vaginal bleeding since delivering a healthy newborn at term 4 months ago; the bleeding has been heavy at times . Her blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a closed cervical os. Ultrasonography shows a slightly enlarged uterus with a small clot in the endometrial cavity. There are bilateral , 8-cm, cystic, ovarian masses . Neurologic examination shows right-sided weakness . Her hematocrit is 28%, and serum 13-hCG concentration is 530,000 mlU/mL . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Choriocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm of trophoblastic tissue that can develop after pregnancy, including both molar pregnancies and full-term or preterm pregnancies. It is highly aggressive and typically presents with distant metastases, with a predilection for the lung, vagina, brain, and liver. Symptoms are secondary to bleeding from the primary tumor or metastases, and thus include vaginal bleeding, hemoptysis, dyspnea, headache, seizures, stroke-like symptoms, jaundice, and abdominal pain. Physical examination may disclose an enlarged uterus and bilateral adnexal masses (eg, theca lutein cysts). Laboratory studies will show markedly increased 13-hCG concentration, as in this patient. Pelvic ultrasonography is useful in diagnosis, with choriocarcinoma appearing as a hypervascular uterine mass. Chest x-ray is used to evaluate for lung metastases, and further imaging, such as CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis or MRI of the brain, is warranted based on clinical symptoms. It is treated with chemotherapy and surgical resection, and 13-hCG concentration is serially measured to monitor for progression or recurrence.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Ectopic pregnancy (Choice B) refers to an abnormal extrauterine pregnancy occurring in an anatomic location that cannot support a pregnancy. It commonly presents with vaginal bleeding, abdominopelvic pain, abnormal ultrasonography without an intrauterine fetal pole, and abnormally low serum 13-hCG concentration, which in a normal pregnancy should double every 48 hours. Germ cell ovarian tumors (Choice C) include teratomas, dysgerminomas, yolk sac tumors, and mixed germ cell tumors. Broadly, they present with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, bloating, a unilateral pelvic mass on physical examination, and increased concentrations of hormones such as 13-hCG, a-fetoprotein, and lactate dehydrogenase. They would not be expected to cause neurologic symptoms. Hydatidiform moles (Choice D) commonly present with persistent nausea and vomiting, first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size out of proportion to expected gestational age as a result of an abnormal fertilization of an ovum. Pelvic ultrasonography will show diffuse echogenic structures in the uterus and bilateral ovarian theca-lutein cysts. They are precursors to malignant trophoblastic disease, such as choriocarcinoma. Threatened abortion (Choice E) presents with vaginal bleeding that occurs before 20 weeks' gestation. However, fetal cardiac activity is present and the cervical os remains closed. This is unlikely in the setting of a recent pregnancy with ongoing vaginal bleeding and would not explain her neurologic symptoms. Educational Objective: Choriocarcinoma is a malignancy of trophoblastic tissue, and presents with vaginal bleeding, hemoptysis, dyspnea, headache, seizures, stroke-like symptoms, jaundice, and abdominal pain because of its aggressive and early metastases to the vagina, lungs, brain, and liver. It is associated with markedly increased 13-hCG and bilateral theca lutein cysts. Choriocarcinoma is treated with chemotherapy and, occasionally, surgical resection.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman with a 2-week history of urinary frequency , urgency, and burning comes to the physician for a follow-up examination . One week ago, urinalysis showed 20-50 WBC/hpfwith no protein , glucose , bacteria , ketones , or crystals . Urine dipstick showed trace blood . Her symptoms have not improved with 1 week of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy. Pelvic examination shows urethral tenderness . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Urinalysis remains unchanged . In addition to urine culture , which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Cytologic examination of suprapubic urine aspirate
choices.B: Gram stain of the cervical mucus

correctExplanation: A patient with persistent symptoms of urethritis (eg, urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria) despite adequate treatment for a urinary tract infection with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole raises concern for other causes of urethritis such as sexually transmitted infections secondary to Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Both of these organisms can cause symptoms of urethritis, and if left untreated, can progress to cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and tuba-ovarian abscess. Urinalysis for typical urinary tract infections show greater than 10 WBC/hpf, may show red cells as evidence of mucosal inflammation. Bacteria are generally seen on microscopy. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular pathogen and does not appear on urinalysis or Gram stain, resulting in absence of visualized bacteria on urinalysis. Diagnosing chlamydia! urethritis involves urethral culture and/or nucleic acid amplification tests to evaluate the presence of Chlamydia species. Treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering a potential Neisseria gonorrhoeae coinfection.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cytologic examination of suprapubic urine aspirate (Choice A) would not be appropriate in a patient who is able to give a clean urine sample. Suprapubic aspiration is an invasive method of urine sampling that can be used in children that are unable to urinate and are unable to have a transurethral bladder catheterization. Gram stain of the cervical mucus (Choice B) can be helpful in diagnosing cervicitis. Chlamydia species can cause cervicitis, but would typically present with mucopurulent discharge, a friable, inflamed cervix, and cervical motion tenderness on pelvic examination. In a patient with isolated urethritis, endocervical sampling would not disclose a diagnosis. PPD skin test (Choice C) is used in the evaluation of tuberculosis. A positive PPD skin test may be because of a latent tuberculosis infection or active tuberculosis. Symptoms of tuberculosis include fever, cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, and weight loss. It does not typically cause urethritis. Chlamydia can result in pharyngitis, but in a patient without symptoms of pharyngitis, a throat culture (Choice D) would not be the next best step. Educational Objective: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen and does not appear on urinalysis or Gram stain, resulting in the absence of bacteria on urinalysis. Diagnosing chlamydia! urethritis involves urethral culture and/or nucleic acid amplification tests to evaluate the presence of Chlamydia species. Treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering a potential Neisseria gonorrhoeae coinfection.

questionStem: A 30-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, has had fever and lower abdominal pain for 24 hours. Two days ago , she underwent a low transverse cesarean delivery because of failure to progress in labor after 18 hours. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). The lungs are clear to auscultation . The incision is mildly tender and pink. The fundus is near the umbilicus and extremely tender. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this infection ?
correctExplanation: A recent postpartum patient with fever and severe uterine tenderness raises suspicion for endometritis. Postpartum endometritis is an acute, typically polymicrobial infection of the uterine endometrium involving a mixture of aerobes and anaerobes from the genital tract. During labor and delivery, microbes from the genital tract can enter the uterine cavity and result in postpartum infection. Patients typically present with fever, severe tenderness of the uterine fund us, and mucopurulent vaginal discharge. Risk factors for endometritis include premature or prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labor, cesarean delivery (as in this patient), bacterial vaginosis, Streptococcus aga/actiae (group B) colonization, and manual removal of the placenta. Treatment requires broad-spectrum antibiotics such as clindamycin and gentamicin for appropriate anti-microbial coverage.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Gram-negative aerobes (Choice A) including Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause endometritis, but more often cause cervicitis and endometritis unrelated to pregnancy and are unlikely to be the cause of postpartum endometritis. Gram-negative anaerobes (Choice B) such as Bacteroides species, Fusobacterium species, and gram-positive anaerobes (Choice D) such as C/ostridium species are rare and unlikely causes of endometritis. Endometritis is typically a polymicrobial infection. Gram-positive aerobes (Choice C) can cause endometritis such as in streptococcal or staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome but are typically secondary to the prolonged use of tampons. They would be unlikely in the postpartum setting. Educational Objective: Postpartum endometritis is an acute, typically polymicrobial, infection of the uterine endometrium involving a mixture of aerobes and anaerobes from the genital tract. Patients typically present with fever, severe tenderness of the uterine fund us, and mucopurulent vaginal discharge.

questionStem: A 37-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She conceived 17 weeks ago by in vitro fertilization . Pregnancy has been uncomplicated . Physical examination shows no abnormalities . The uterus is consistent in size with a 17-week gestation . Her maternal serum a-fetoprotein concentration is 7.3 multiples of the median. Which of the following is the most likely fetal abnormality?
correctExplanation: Myelomeningocele is a condition where the neural crest arch fails to fully form posteriorly. As a result, the dura and spinal cord protrude posteriorly out of the spinal canal. This condition is associated with an abnormality in folate metabolism or a lack of adequate folic acid concentrations to support neural crest cell differentiation and neural tube development. Maternal diabetes is an additional risk factor. It results in nerve dysfunction and paralysis distal to the lesion. It is commonly diagnosed prenatally with an increased a-fetoprotein on prenatal maternal serum screening, evidence of the malformation on fetal ultrasonography, and the presence of acetylcholinesterase in the amniotic fluid.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cystic fibrosis (Choice A) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by failure to pass meconium in infancy, recurrent sinus and pulmonary infections, digital clubbing, bronchiectasis, and pancreatic insufficiency caused by deficient trafficking of a membrane chloride channel. Screening for cystic fibrosis is included in most newborn screens. Down syndrome (Choice B) is caused by trisomy of chromosome 21 and presents with characteristic facies, intellectual disability, single palmar creases, atrioventricular septal defects, duodenal atresia, and an increased risk for acute lymphoblastic leukemia and Alzheimer disease. It is associated with increased human chorionic gonadotropin and inhibin A, as well as decreased a-fetoprotein and estriol concentrations on second trimester quadruple screening. Tay-Sachs disease (Choice D) is a lysosomal storage disorder that presents with developmental delay, neurologic deficits, and a cherry red spot on the macula caused by a deficiency of hexosaminidase A. It is not associated with increased concentrations of serum a-fetoprotein. Ventricular septal defect (Choice E) is a non-cyanotic congenital heart lesion that is commonly asymptomatic. Physical examination will disclose a loud, harsh holosystolic murmur over the precordium. It has no relation to a-fetoprotein concentration. Educational Objective: a-Fetoprotein concentration is increased in maternal serum in the setting of neural tube defects, such as meningocele and myelomeningocele.

questionStem: Immediately after cesarean delivery because of abruptio placentae , a 25-year-old woman loses consciousness . She had an estimated blood loss of 1200 ml. Her pregnancy was uncomplicated . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 26/min , and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. Examination shows frothy pink sputum . Bilateral wheezes are heard on auscultation . The fundus is firm. Laboratory studies show : Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Platelet count Bleeding time Prothrombin time Partial thromboplastin time Thrombin time Plasma fibrinogen Fibrin split products 7 g/dl 8000/mm 3 60,000/mm 3 9 min 20 sec (INR=2) 55 sec 5 sec 100 mg/dl (N=200-400) 80 µg/ml (N<10) An x-ray of the chest shows pulmonary edema . An ECG shows tachycardia . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A
correctExplanation: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare and potentially fatal complication of childbirth caused by amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation. It most commonly occurs during delivery or in the immediate postpartum period. It typically presents with acute onset of shortness of breath, altered mental status or unconsciousness, and bilateral wheezing. Signs of fetal distress can also occur if the fetus remains in utero at the time of occurrence. Vital signs will show tachycardia, hypoxia, and severe hypotension. The patient can quickly decompensate into cardiovascular collapse and cardiopulmonary arrest. Chest x-ray may show pulmonary edema, as in this patient. Treatment is generally supportive, with patients often requiring fluids or blood products and mechanical ventilation. Complications include diffuse bleeding from venipuncture sites, the vagina, or the cesarean delivery incision caused by disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), in addition to increased rates of fetal and maternal mortality. Acute DIC presents with thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, prolongation of the prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT), and decreased fibrinogen as a result of the consumptive coagulopathy with rapid fibrinolysis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Eclampsia (Choice B) presents with hypertension, proteinuria, headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, and seizures in a pregnant patient after 20 weeks' gestation, although it can also occur postpartum. It would not be expected to present with wheezing and frothy pink sputum unless flash pulmonary edema had occurred. Hypovolemic shock (Choice C) occurs secondary to significant reductions in a patient's intravascular volume, most commonly related to hemorrhage, dehydration, or gastrointestinal losses, which results in decreased stroke volume and cardiac output. Although this patient had a significant amount of blood loss with her cesarean delivery, her hemoglobin concentration remains above the typical transfusion threshold and hypovolemia would not explain her pulmonary edema or coagulation abnormalities. Pulmonary embolism (Choice D) presents with shortness of breath, tachycardia, and hypoxia, as well as hypotension if the pulmonary embolism is massive and hemoptysis if infarction has occurred. The embolism commonly originates from a deep venous thrombosis of the lower extremities. It would not be expected to cause coagulation abnormalities. Septic shock (Choice E) refers to the decreased organ perfusion from an overwhelming infection and resultant hypotension. It is a form of distributive shock and is clinically diagnosed with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and signs of infection on examination, as well as leukocytosis and lactic acidosis. The presentation is typically less abrupt (hours to days) in comparison to amniotic fluid embolism (minutes to hours).

questionStem: A 39-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, comes for a routine health maintenance examination . Menses have occurred at irregular intervals since menarche at the age of 14 years . Her last menstrual period occurred 6 months ago and was extremely heavy. She has declined to take hormones to regulate menses because she does not want to have a monthly menstrual period. Her only child was conceived 8 years ago after she was treated with clomiphene . She has had mild hirsutism since adolescence . Which of the following serum concentrations is most likely to be increased?
correctExplanation: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) presents with irregular menses, infertility, and hirsutism, often in patients with an increased body weight. It requires two of the following for diagnosis: oligo/anovulation, polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography, and clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism. It is associated with signs of insulin resistance, such as acanthosis nigricans and increased blood glucose levels. PCOS is associated with an abnormal hypothalamic hormonal feedback response, which leads to increased luteinizing hormone (LH) in comparison to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), as well as markedly increased androgen production from the theca lutein cells. This results in an increased serum concentration of testosterone. Treatment includes weight loss, combined oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, and spironolactone or ketoconazole for hirsutism. Clomiphene stimulates ovulation and can also be utilized for individuals desiring pregnancy. If the patient is diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, oral medications (eg, metformin) or insulin may also be necessary. A potential complication of long-standing PCOS is endometrial cancer caused by the chronic anovulation resulting in prolonged exposure of the endometrium to unopposed estrogen.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Follicle-stimulating hormone (Choice A) is increased in menopause and premature ovarian failure, which present with irregular menstruation or amenorrhea, hot flashes, and night sweats caused by anovulation and a low estrogen state. This is less likely than PCOS in this woman of reproductive age with signs of hyperinsulinemia, hyperandrogenism, and obesity. Progesterone (Choice B) is increased at various times during the menstrual cycle, particularly during the luteal phase as it acts to maintain the secretory endometrium. Increased concentrations of progesterone would more likely present with amenorrhea because of endometrial atrophy (mechanism of progestin-based contraceptives) than irregular menstruation. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (Choice D) is increased in primary hypothyroidism, which most frequently presents with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and menstrual abnormalities. Physical signs include bradycardia, dry and edematous skin, as well as the delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. It is less likely to be the cause of this patient's chronic oligo/anovulation and hirsutism. Thyroxine (T 4) (Choice E) is increased in hyperthyroidism, which presents with heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss, diaphoresis, diarrhea, and amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea. It is not associated with hyperandrogenism. Educational Objective: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) presents with chronic anovulation, signs of androgen excess, obesity, insulin resistance, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography. Treatment includes weight loss and combined oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, along with antihyperglycemic medications or insulin for the management of concomitant diabetes mellitus, if diagnosed.

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of an 18-month history of increasingly severe menstrual cramps associated with diarrhea and vomiting . The symptoms cause her to miss 2 days of school each month , and her school performance is beginning to decline . Menarche was at the age of 13 years . Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals . She is not sexually active . She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows normal-appearing external genitalia , vagina , and cervix . The uterus is small, mobile , and nontender . There are no adnexal masses or nodularity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Primary dysmenorrhea is defined as menstrual pain that accompanies each menstrual cycle but is not associated with any underlying pathology. In order to diagnose primary dysmenorrhea, causes of secondary dysmenorrhea must be ruled out. These may include endometriosis, leiomyomata uteri (fibroids), adhesions, pelvic inflammatory disease, or adenomyosis. Many of these can be reasonably assessed on pelvic examination, which in this case did not show any abnormalities. Primary dysmenorrhea typically presents with pain in the lower abdomen and pelvis, which may radiate to the lower back or thighs. It is often accompanied by nausea, diarrhea, headaches, and flushing. It can be attributed to uterine vasoconstriction in response to an excess of prostaglandin. Thus, treatment targets this pathway with medications including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and topical heat therapy. Combined oral contraceptives or a progestin intrauterine device (IUD) may also be utilized to regulate these symptoms if persistent.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adenomyosis (Choice A) is the presence of glandular endometrial tissue in the myometrium, and generally presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain. It commonly occurs in a multigravid woman, often between the ages of 40 and 50 years. On examination, a large, globular uterus may be palpated. These findings are not present in this patient. Endometrial polyps (Choice B) may cause uterine bleeding that is irregular, unpredictable, or not associated with usual premenstrual signs and symptoms (eg, bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps). It does not typically cause dysmenorrhea. This patient also has regular menses without menometrorrhagia, which is a common feature of endometrial polyps. Endometriosis (Choice C) denotes the presence of endometrial tissue outside of the uterus, and classically presents with symptoms of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. The standard for diagnosis is a diagnostic laparoscopy, which evaluates for endometriotic implant lesions on the peritoneum. Pelvic examination often discloses tenderness of the uterine wall and surrounding structures with possible uterine immobility secondary to pelvic adhesions. Leiomyomata uteri (Choice D), also known as uterine fibroids, are benign neoplasms of the uterine myometrium. They are a potential cause of abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain and are typically visible on ultrasonography. They may also be palpated on examination, if large. They are a common indication for hysterectomy. Educational Objective: Primary dysmenorrhea is defined as menstrual pain that accompanies each menstrual cycle but is not associated with any underlying pathology. Causes of secondary dysmenorrhea include endometriosis, leiomyomata uteri (fibroids), adhesions, pelvic inflammatory disease, or adenomyosis, the majority of which can be evaluated on physical examination. Treatment of primary dysmenorrhea involves the administration of NSAIDs and topical heat therapy, with combined oral contraceptives and progestin intrauterine device as options for persistent symptoms.

questionStem: A previously healthy 23-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks' gestation has had nausea and vomiting for 4 weeks . She can tolerate small amounts of food intermittently but usually vomits 3 to 4 times daily. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall; she has lost 1.8 kg (4 lb) and currently weighs 54 kg (119 lb). Ultrasonography shows a viable fetus consistent with a 10-week gestation . Which of the following is the most likely effect of her condition on the fetus?
correctExplanation: Severe nausea with inability to maintain adequate oral intake is a common presenting symptom of hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) and can lead to clinically significant levels of dehydration and starvation ketosis. HG is usually associated with weight loss in early pregnancy and extends past the first trimester, when typical morning sickness resolves. Tachycardia, mild hypotension, and signs of dehydration (eg, dry mucous membranes) would be expected on vital signs and physical examination. Laboratory studies disclose ketones in the blood and urine, as well as hypoosmolar hyponatremia, and hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis caused by dehydration and volume contraction; ketosis can also contribute to a secondary metabolic acidosis. As HG is associated with molar pregnancy, it is important to exclude this condition with pelvic ultrasonography and assessment of the concentration of ~-human chorionic gonadotropin. Treatment of HG includes vitamin B6, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and in severe cases, total parenteral nutrition. When treated appropriately, there are generally no long-term adverse effects on the developing fetus.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Developmental delay (Choice A) is associated with a variety of conditions, including chromosomal abnormalities, lysosomal storage disorders, sex chromosome disorders, neurologic disorders, endocrine abnormalities, and vitamin deficiencies. However, it is not a suspected consequence of hyperemesis gravidarum. Premature birth (Choice B) is birth that occurs before 37 weeks' gestation, and its risk is increased by maternal diabetes, extremes of age, placenta previa or abruption, cervical insufficiency, multiple gestations, and maternal tobacco use. If insufficiently treated and unable to gain weight, this patient may be at risk for preterm labor, but this is less likely than no adverse effect if treated appropriately. Pulmonary hypoplasia (Choice C) typically occurs secondary to oligohydramnios in the setting of fetal urogenital tract defects. In such cases, the fetal thorax is compressed and there is insufficient amniotic fluid for the fetus to inspire into the lungs, which causes inadequate lung development. It is not caused by maternal HG. Spontaneous abortion (Choice D) most commonly occurs in the first trimester because of chromosomal abnormalities of the fetus, though can occur as a result of intrauterine infection, uterine structural abnormalities, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, and maternal endocrinopathy. It is less likely to be caused by maternal HG if treated appropriately. Educational Objective: Hyperemesis gravidarum presents with severe, often intractable nausea and vomiting, preventing adequate oral intake in a pregnant patient with consequent dehydration and starvation ketosis. Associated findings include ketonuria and ketonemia, hyponatremia, and hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Treatment consists of vitamin Bs, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and total parenteral nutrition, if necessary. With appropriate treatment, there are rarely any adverse fetal effects.

questionStem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of a migraine . She has a history of migraines treated with sumatriptan . She reports that she has not taken any pain relief medication for her headache because of concern regarding possible harm to her fetus . Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation . Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Migraine headache is a frequent occurrence during pregnancy. Acetaminophen is considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding and is useful for treating acute pain associated with migrainous headache. Acetaminophen selectively inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes in the central nervous system, resulting in analgesia. Adverse effects include hepatotoxicity if taken in excess. Importantly, migrainous or tension headaches must be distinguished from other types of headache that may indicate serious conditions such as preeclampsia, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, or pituitary apoplexy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Butalbital (Choice B) is a barbiturate. In addition to their addictive properties, barbiturates have been shown to cause a variety of fetal birth defects, including neural tube defects, tetralogy of Fallo!, and cardiac septal defects. The fetus is most susceptible to these teratogenic effects during the first trimester, as in this patient. Ergotamine (Choice C) is an ergot alkaloid. Ergot alkaloids are contraindicated in all trimesters of pregnancy because of their uterotonic and vasoconstrictive properties that can cause fetal distress, birth defects, and miscarriage. Meperidine (Choice D) is a synthetic opioid and should not be used in pregnancy as a result of the risk for dependence and addiction, and because of the risk for neonatal opioid withdrawal. Sumatriptan (Choice E) is useful for the treatment of migraine. However, there is evidence that it may lead to an increased incidence of behavioral problems when used in the first trimester. There is no conclusive evidence that sumatriptan exposure causes birth defects, however, acetaminophen is well-evidenced as safe in pregnancy without teratogenic effects. Educational Objective: Migraine headache is a frequent occurrence during pregnancy. The selection of an analgesic during pregnancy should account for the susceptibility of the fetus to teratogens during the first trimester and to the addictive properties of analgesics for both the mother and fetus. Acetaminophen is generally considered to be safe for the treatment of acute pain during pregnancy and breastfeeding. r O

questionStem: A 17-year-old primigravid patient has been in labor for 15 hours; she has made no progress for the past 3 hours. The cervix is 5 cm dilated and 80% effaced; the vertex is at +2 station . Contractions occur every 5 minutes . Assuming a normal-sized full-term fetus and a clinically adequate pelvis , which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.B: Cesarean delivery for failure to progress
choices.C: Intramuscular sedation for 2 hours of rest

correctExplanation: Labor consists of three defined stages. The first stage encompasses the start of labor (contractions and cervical change) until the completion of cervical dilation and effacement. The second stage includes the time from complete cervical dilation to birth, and the third stage consists of the delivery of the placenta. The first stage of labor is divided into a latent stage and active stage, based on the degree of cervical dilation, with the active stage beginning after 4-cm cervical dilation is achieved. The active stage of labor can be protracted, which occurs when the cervix is dilating at less than 1 to 2 cm/hour, or arrested, in which case there is no cervical change for greater than 4 hours with adequate contractions or no cervical change for greater than 6 hours with inadequate contractions, as in this patient. Abnormal progression of the active stage of labor can be caused by hypotonic contractions, cephalopelvic distortion, and a non-occiput anterior fetal presentation. Inadequate contractions are defined as occurring less than three or four times in a ten-minute period with a strength less than 200 Montevideo units. Montevideo units are calculated by summing the strength of each uterine contraction (uterine peak pressure minus baseline pressure) over a 10-minute interval. This patient demonstrates contractions every 5 minute, which raises the concern for inadequate, hypotonic contractions. Protraction and arrest of the active phase of labor can be managed with oxytocin to augment uterine contractions and prostaglandins to assist in cervical ripening, with cesarean delivery utilized if oxytocin augmentation is ineffective.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cesarean delivery (Choice B) may be necessary if the oxytocin augmentation fails to increase the frequency and strength of uterine contractions. However, as cesarean delivery is more invasive than vaginal delivery, this patient warrants a trial of oxytocin augmentation prior to proceeding to cesarean delivery. Intramuscular sedation for 2 hours of rest (Choice C) is not recommended, as this patient is in active labor. Sedation with rest will only prolong the labor further, which adds risks for complications such as chorioamnionitis to the patient and her fetus. Intravenous hydration (Choice D) is used to replace fluids lost because of gastrointestinal losses, bleeding, or insensible losses. It does not play a role in the augmentation of labor. X-ray pelvimetry (Choice E) is a radiographic technique used to evaluate maternal pelvis and fetal size in the setting of suspected cephalopelvic disproportion. It may be useful in determining fetal lie but is generally not recommended when it can be avoided, given the risk for radiation exposure to the fetus. Educational Objective: Active labor can be protracted, when cervical dilation proceeds at a rate less than 1 to 2 cm/hour, or arrested, when cervical dilation does not change in 4 hours with adequate contractions or 6 hours with inadequate contractions. An initial trial of oxytocin augmentation may be appropriate in cases of inadequate, hypotonic contractions, before proceeding to operative delivery.

questionStem: A 23-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of increasingly severe pain of the left breast over the past 3 days. She now describes the pain as excruciating. Five days ago , she delivered a 3700-g (8-lb 3-oz) newborn vaginally after an uncomplicated labor. Her pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios , and labor was induced at 39 weeks' gestation . Her postpartum course has been uncomplicated . She is breast-feeding . Her temperature is 37 .5°C (99.5°F). Examination shows a tender, edematous area on the lateral aspect of the left breast that is not erythematous or warm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: A~lication of heat to the area

correctExplanation: This patient presents with a painful breast lump whose appearance coincided with breastfeeding, consistent with the diagnosis of a galactocele. Galactoceles are retention cysts that form as a result of obstruction of a lactiferous duct. They may be painful or painless and tend to appear during lactation or shortly after cessation of lactation. Patients may develop a secondary infection with formation of a breast abscess, which presents with fever and localized erythema and calor overlying the abscess. Diagnosis of a galactocele is facilitated with mammography and ultrasonography. Treatment is primarily supportive with massage and application of heat, although patients with refractory symptoms may benefit from therapeutic fine needle aspiration.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aminoglycoside therapy (Choice B) is useful for the treatment of bacterial infections. This patient's lack of fever and absence of erythema or calor overlying her breast lump suggest against an infectious process. Aminoglycosides are associated with risk for significant adverse effects, including sensorineural hearing loss and nephrotoxicity, and are not first line for the treatment of mastitis or breast abscess. Dicloxacillin therapy (Choice C) is an appropriate first line agent for the treatment of mastitis and breast abscess. However, this patient's lack of fever and absence of erythema or calor overlying her breast lump suggest against an infectious process. Needle aspiration and culture (Choice D) is not indicated. Needle aspiration may be helpful for patients with a galactocele who have failed conservative therapy. Culture of the fluid is not usually necessary. Incision and drainage (Choice E) is not preferred over fine needle aspiration for the management of a refractory galactocele or breast abscess, as it is more invasive and has an increased rate of scarring and unfavorable cosmetic outcomes. Educational Objective: Galactoceles are retention cysts that form as a result of obstruction of a lactiferous duct that appear during lactation or shortly after cessation of lactation. Diagnosis of a galactocele is facilitated with mammography and ultrasonography. Treatment is primarily supportive with massage and application of heat, although patients with refractory symptoms may benefit from therapeutic fine needle aspiration.

questionStem: A previously healthy 47-year-old woman comes to the physician 3 weeks after she noted a lump in her right breast during self-examination . Physical examination shows a 3-cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Mammography shows no abnormalities . Ultrasonography shows a cystic component ; fine-needle aspiration biopsy yields cloudy straw-colored fluid. The mass is still present after aspiration . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Breast cancer encompasses many types of breast carcinoma, including invasive ductal and lobular carcinoma, medullary carcinoma, inflammatory breast carcinoma, and cystosarcoma phylloides. The most common type is invasive ductal carcinoma, which typically presents as a palpable, immobile breast mass, which may demonstrate features such as spiculated margins and microcalcifications on mammography. They can be associated with pathologic nipple discharge. Evaluation of a breast mass first involves imaging with either mammography, if over the age of 35 years, or ultrasonography, if under the age of 35 years to evaluate whether the palpable mass has features concerning for breast cancer. This is because younger women's breasts are denser and more challenging to evaluate with mammography than the breasts of older women. Mammography may be followed by ultrasonography. In this case, the mass persisted after ultrasonography-guided aspiration of fluid, indicating it is likely not a simple cyst. Therefore, it should be biopsied to rule out a breast malignancy. Biopsy is invasive and reserved for cases of moderate to increased clinical suspicion after investigation with diagnostic imaging takes place.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Indefinite observation (Choice A), observation for 6 weeks (Choice B), or observation for 1 year (Choice C) are not appropriate management strategies. This mass has concerning features, namely the presence in a female over the age of 35 years and the persistence of the mass after aspiration, warranting urgent biopsy to rule out a breast carcinoma. Repeat mammography (Choice D) will not provide any new information about the diagnosis. Instead, biopsy is needed to definitively diagnose the pathology. Thermography (Choice E) is a screening test utilized in breast cancer that uses the body temperature of the skin and underlying soft tissues to identify the presence of a breast cancer. It is not used routinely as it has a false positive rate of 25% and a false negative rate of over 60%. Educational Objective: A breast mass with suspicious imaging features that demonstrates persistence after attempted aspiration is concerning for an underlying breast carcinoma. The next appropriate step in management is to conduct a core-needle or excisional biopsy to sample the lesion. This will allow a definitive diagnosis to be made.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 4, para 3, at 38 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital 8 hours after premature rupture of membranes . Pregnancy had been uncomplicated . Previous pregnancies were uncomplicated with spontaneous vaginal delivery of 3430-g (7-lb 9-oz), 3629-g (8-lb), and 3770-g (8-lb 5-oz) newborns at 37 to 39 weeks' gestation . She has no history of serious illness . Her only medication is a prenatal vitamin . Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 80/min , respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/65 mm Hg. The cervix is 1 cm dilated and 80% effaced . Labor augmentation with oxytocin is begun and results in contractions 2 to 3 minutes apart . The cervix is now 8 cm dilated and 100% effaced ; the vertex is at +2 station . Her temperature now is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min , and blood pressure is 105/58 mm Hg. The baseline fetal heart rate is 175/min with mild variable decelerations . The uterus is tender. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Chorioamnionitis is a polymicrobial bacterial infection of the fetal membranes and commonly occurs in premature or prolonged rupture of membranes because of the migration of vaginal flora into the uterus . Other risk factors include repeated digital vaginal examinations, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, and genital tract infections. Maternal fever and leukocytosis are characteristic, and the uterus may be tender to palpation with the presence of purulent amniotic fluid. Further evaluation of the amniotic fluid may disclose a positive Gram stain with culture, numerous leukocytes, and low glucose concentration. A fetal heart tracing would likely show tachycardia secondary to the maternal fever. Complications include uterine atony, wound infections, pelvic abscess, and sepsis. Treatment consists of delivery and intravenous antibiotics. As this patient is in active labor, with signs of appropriate cervical change, the addition of intravenous antibiotics and careful monitoring of labor progression are warranted.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Increased oxytocin therapy (Choice B) is not necessary, as this patient has demonstrated adequate progression of labor on her current dose of oxytocin with contractions every 2 to 3 minutes and significant cervical change. Forceps delivery (Choice C) and vacuum extraction (Choice D) are often utilized for a prolonged second stage of labor or in the setting of fetal distress . They require a dilated and effaced cervix, ruptured membranes, and engaged occiput. As this patient is progressing appropriately through labor, assisted vaginal delivery is not necessary at this time. Immediate cesarean delivery (Choice E) is occasionally required in the setting of chorioamnionitis if there is evidence of fetal or maternal instability. However, this patient is progressing appropriately through the active stage of labor with no signs of fetal distress. Educational Objective: Chorioamnionitis is a polymicrobial infection of the fetal membranes that presents with fever, tender uterus, purulent amniotic fluid, and leukocytosis. Risk factors include prolonged or premature rupture of membranes. Treatment requires the administration of intravenous antibiotics and delivery.

questionStem: A 67-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of a rapidly increasing lower abdominal mass. Twenty years ago, she underwent radiation therapy of the pelvis for early cervical cancer; the uterus was not removed . She has been receiving estrogen and progesterone replacement therapy since then. She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years . Examination shows a normal-appearing vulva, vagina , and cervix . The uterus measures 16 cm. She undergoes exploratory laparotomy , total abdominal hysterectomy , and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy . Pathologic evaluation shows a uterine sarcoma . Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this pathologic finding?
correctExplanation: Uterine sarcoma is a rare malignant proliferation of the myometrium or the stroma of the uterus that most commonly occurs in postmenopausal women and typically presents with postmenopausal bleeding, abdominal pain, bloating, and a rapidly enlarging pelvic mass. Physical examination will disclose an enlarged uterus, and ultrasonography will show a heterogeneous mass with possible foci of internal necrosis. Typical evaluation includes an endometrial biopsy, as well as a biopsy of the mass itself, while treatment involves a total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, as well as lymph node dissection, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy depending on the extent of disease. Risk factors for the development of uterine sarcoma include pelvic radiation therapy, a history of retinoblastoma, and long-term use of tamoxifen.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cigarette smoking (Choice A) increases the risk for lung, urothelial, pancreatic, and squamous cell cancers (eg, skin, cervical, anal). It does not increase the risk for uterine sarcoma. Excessive estrogen (Choice B) plays a role in the development of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma because of its proliferative effect on the endometrium. This risk is decreased when used concomitantly with progesterone. Genetic predisposition (Choice C) can increase the risk for uterine sarcoma in the case of childhood retinoblastoma and the rare syndrome of hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer. This patient is otherwise healthy with the exception of her history of cervical cancer. Human papillomavirus infection (Choice D) is a sexually transmitted viral infection that can cause cervical, vulvar, penile, or anal carcinoma, as well as condylomata acuminata. It does not increase the risk for uterine sarcoma. Educational Objective: Uterine sarcoma presents with a rapidly enlarging pelvic mass, abdominal pain, postmenopausal bleeding, and an enlarged uterus. Risk factors include a history of pelvic radiation, retinoblastoma, and long-term use of tamoxifen. r O

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman , gravida 7, para 5, aborta 2, comes to the physician because of a mass protruding from the vagina for 1 week ; she feels something moving within the mass. She has also had severe low back pain for 6 months. Eight years ago, she underwent a vaginal hysterectomy and anterior and posterior colporrhaphy for treatment of uterovaginal prolapse . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) occurs secondary to pelvic floor dysfunction and weakness, resulting in the herniation of abdominopelvic organs which cause mass effect and protrusion along the vaginal wall. POP may occur secondary to prolapse of any one of several visceral organs. It is more common in individuals who have had multiple childbirths, advancing age, and obesity, which are all risk factors for pelvic floor dysfunction. Even though this patient has had her uterus removed, along with an anterior and posterior colporrhaphy for prior uterovaginal prolapse, additional viscera may still prolapse into the vaginal wall through other portions of the pelvic floor. These herniations impair urinary, defecatory, and sexual function. When the intestines herniate through the pelvic floor and impress upon the vaginal canal, it is referred to as an enterocele. The small bowel usually prolapses into the superior wall of the vagina, with a visible bulge usually present on physical examination. The patient may feel a sensation of peristalsis, causing the feeling of something moving within the mass. POP tends to be slowly progressive if not treated.
incorrectExplanation: nd F Cystocele (Choice A) is common in multiparous women as a result of weakness of the pelvic floor, which causes the bladder to prolapse into the anterior vaginal wall. It is associated with stress urinary incontinence but can also cause urinary retention or incomplete bladder emptying. Physical examination most commonly discloses a bulge on the anterior vaginal wall, and urethral hypermobility is absent. Femoral hernias (Choice C) occur when a portion of intestine or omentum protrudes through the femoral ring below the inguinal ligament, presenting as a painful mass along the anterior thigh. They are more common in women and are more likely to cause strangulation than other herniations of the bowel. An indirect inguinal hernia (Choice D) occurs when a loop of bowel or omentum exits the abdomen through the internal inguinal ring. They are more common in males and do not cause a mass to protrude from the vagina. Sigmoid intussusception (Choice E) occurs when an intestinal lead point causes the sigmoid colon to telescope on itself. The lead point may be a tumor or lymphoid hyperplasia but results in a segment of bowel transposing and telescoping into an adjacent segment as peristalsis occurs. It is more common in children, and may present with symptoms of bowel obstruction. Urethrocele (Choice F) is caused by prolapse of the urethra into the anterior wall of the vagina, and is a common cause of stress urinary incontinence, especially in multiparous women. Educational Objective: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) occurs secondary to pelvic floor dysfunction and weakness, resulting in the herniation of pelvic viscera into the wall of the vagina. Urethrocele (prolapse of the urethra), cystocele (prolapse of the bladder), enterocele (prolapse of the small bowel), and rectocele (prolapse of the rectum) are the primary subtypes of POP.

questionStem: A healthy 27-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She says that she feels well and has not had any uterine contractions . She reports that the baby has been very active . The patient has had a 1-kg (2-lb) weight gain since her last visit 2 weeks ago. She does not drink alcohol and quit smoking after she learned she was pregnant. She works as a bartender . Her blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a fundal height of 28 cm. Fetal heart tones are 150/min. Leopold maneuvers confirm a cephalic presentation . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Fundal height is often used to estimate gestational age. The distance in centimeters between the pubic symphysis and top of the uterine fundus approximates the gestational age in weeks. Typically, gestational age is calculated from the last menstrual period. When there is a discrepancy between these two measurements, the most appropriate next step in management is ultrasonography to assess the fetus through objective parameters for accurate dating or to assess for discrepancies in fetal size. Measurements of the fetal crown-rump length, biparietal diameter, femur length, and abdominal circumference can be used to accurately date a pregnancy. Ultrasonography-guided gestational age measurements are the most accurate during the first trimester. Ultrasonography can also determine other causes for a fundal height smaller than expected, such as intrauterine growth restriction, or larger than expected, including multiple gestations, hydatidiform moles, and fetal macrosomia. In this case, the patient is likely experiencing intrauterine growth restriction, which can be secondary to uteroplacental insufficiency, congenital infections, or maternal substance use.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Follow-up visit in 2 weeks (Choice A) would be appropriate if this patient had a healthy gestation at 36 weeks. However, as this fetus is potentially experiencing intrauterine growth restriction, performing ultrasonography is pertinent to confirm the diagnosis. Induction of labor (Choice C) is typically done with oxytocin in the setting of post-term pregnancy, medical complications of pregnancy (eg, eclampsia, chorioamnionitis), and fetal growth restriction. However, prior to inducing labor, it is important to confirm the diagnosis of intrauterine growth restriction. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (Choice D) is useful in the confirmation of severe fetal anemia and can offer additional diagnostic information on chromosomal or other fetal abnormalities if amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling are nondiagnostic. However, it is invasive and carries the risk for fetal bleeding, fetomaternal bleeding, infection, and fetal loss. Amniocentesis (Choice E) is an invasive sampling of amniotic fluid through the abdominal wall, usually performed at 15 to 20 weeks' gestation, to evaluate for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities. While it may be useful in determining the cause of intrauterine growth restriction, the diagnosis should first be confirmed with ultrasonography. Cesarean delivery (Choice F) is the operative delivery of the fetus through the abdominal wall and is typically done in the setting of fetal malpresentation, macrosomia, placenta previa, and arrest of the active stage of labor. It plays less of a role in the management of intrauterine growth restriction. Educational Objective: Fundal height and gestational age discrepancies should be evaluated with fetal ultrasonography. Measurements of the fetal crown-rump length, biparietal diameter, femur length, and abdominal circumference can be used to accurately date a pregnancy.

questionStem: The basal body temperature graph shown was obtained from a 22-year-old nulligravid woman who has been unable to conceive for 18 months. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals . Which of the following hormones is the most likely cause of the increase in basal body temperature on the 15th day?
correctExplanation: The first half of the menstrual cycle is referred to as the follicular phase, which begins with menses and is variable in length. During menses, follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone (FSH and LH, respectively) concentrations increase and stimulate the developing follicle. The follicle produces estrogen, which leads to proliferation of the endometrium in preparation for implantation of a fertilized ovum. As estrogen rises, a surge occurs, which in turn stimulates a surge in LH that causes ovulation. Immediately following ovulation, the luteal phase begins as the corpus luteum forms. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrial lining, but it is also known to increase basal body temperature. Deficiency of progesterone can lead to a luteal phase defect and infertility. If no implantation occurs, the corpus luteum degrades to the corpus albicans and estrogen and progesterone concentrations decrease, causing menstruation.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Estrogen (Choice A) concentrations are increased immediately after ovulation, although it briefly decreases prior to its synthesis by the corpus luteum. It leads to proliferation and maintenance of the endometrium thickness, but it does not cause increases in basal body temperature. Follicle-stimulating hormone (Choice B) is responsible for follicular maturation and is increased in menopause and premature ovarian insufficiency, which present with irregular menstruation or amenorrhea, hot flashes, and night sweats because of anovulation and a low estrogen concentration. It is decreased following ovulation. Human chorionic gonadotropin (Choice C) is secreted by the placenta in order to maintain the corpus luteum and its production of progesterone. It would not be present immediately following ovulation prior to fertilization and embryo implantation. Luteinizing hormone (Choice D) triggers ovulation and increases the production of androgens in the ovary. It peaks just before ovulation and decreases thereafter. It does not directly cause an increase in basal body temperature.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination 4 months after beginning a trial of oral contraceptive therapy for menometrorrhagia . Her symptoms have improved . Menses now occur at regular 28- to 30-day intervals and last 3 days . Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She is otherwise healthy and takes no other medications . Physical examination , including pelvic examination , shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the improvement in this patient's bleeding?

choices.A: Enhanced progesterone secretion by the corpus luteum

correctExplanation: Menometrorrhagia can be caused by a variety of structural abnormalities, systemic disorders, and endocrine dysfunction, such as leiomyomas or polyps, coagulopathies, and anovulatory cycles. It is defined by abnormally heavy menstrual periods that occur irregularly. Evaluation involves pelvic examination and ultrasonography. It can be treated with combined oral contraceptives, a progesterone intrauterine device, high­ dose oral progesterone therapy, or surgical resection depending on the underlying pathology. In this case, the combined oral contraceptives minimized the patient's bleeding as they resynchronized the endometrium into a typical hormonal cycle. During menses, follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone (FSH and LH, respectively) concentrations increase and stimulate the developing follicle. The follicle produces estrogen, which leads to proliferation of the endometrium in preparation for implantation of a fertilized ovum. Following ovulation, the corpus luteum forms.
