Cricothyroidotomy (Choice E) is a type of invasive airway access. It may be indicated in cases of airway compromise in which endotracheal intubation is unsuccessful. Educational Objective: Tension pneumothorax occurs when air is able to enter the pleural space but is prevented from exiting. This leads to an increasing amount of air trapped in the pleural space with subsequent collapse of the lung parenchyma and mass effect on the mediastinum. It is characterized by respiratory distress, tracheal deviation, hypotension, decreased breath sounds, and hyperresonance to percussion on physical examination. Management requires emergent needle decompression followed by placement of a chest tube.

questionStem: After undergoing a tonsillectomy , a 2-year-old boy develops seizures in the recovery room. During the 45-minute operation , he received 1 L of 5% dextrose in water. Measurement of which of the following serum concentrations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The patient is likely suffering from acute hyponatremia complicated by seizures after receiving hypotonic fluids for his procedure. Measurement of the sodium concentration will confirm the diagnosis. Sodium is the most prevalent extracellular cation, and maintaining a normal serum concentration is essential for the proper functioning of tissue and movement of water between the intracellular and extracellular spaces. Derangements of sodium concentration are mostly caused by imbalances in water content of the extracellular fluid (as regulated by antidiuretic hormone activity) as opposed to actual changes in total body sodium content. Administration of hypotonic fluids such as 5% dextrose in water dilutes the serum, resulting in osmotic pressure that drives water molecules into the intracellular space. The primary acute symptoms are because of an acute cerebral edema, which can progress to altered mental status, gait disturbances, seizures, coma, and death. Management requires the careful return of sodium to normal serum concentrations.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Creatinine (Choice A) is used as a marker for the glomerular filtration rate. Increased serum creatinine concentrations can indicate acute kidney injury, which can be a complication of surgery as a result of transient hypotension. Administration of intravenous fluids during procedures reduces this risk. Glucose (Choice B) concentrations are likely increased in this patient receiving dextrose. Decreased glucose concentration can present with altered mental status and seizures. In the absence of insulin resistance, temporarily increased glucose concentrations are unlikely to cause symptoms. Potassium (Choice C) concentration is unlikely to be altered in this otherwise healthy patient. Hypo- and hyperkalemia increase the risk for cardiac dysrhythmias. Urea nitrogen (Choice E) concentration may be increased in acute kidney injury or because of increased gut absorption of urea nitrogen products in a gastrointestinal bleed. Increased urea nitrogen concentrations may cause uremic syndrome, which presents with fatigue, nausea, and altered mental status. Educational Objective: Hyponatremia is a potential complication of the administration of hypotonic intravenous fluids. Acute hyponatremia results in cerebral edema caused by the movement of water from the extracellular space to the intracellular space, and it may present with altered mental status, ataxia, seizures, coma, and/or death.

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by police because of a 5-hour history of hallucinations , profuse sweating , and intermittent yelling and flailing . He is striking out at those near him and requires leather restraints . His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor, profuse diaphoresis , and recent bruising . Mental status examination shows incoherent speech , episodic screaming, and agitation . He is disoriented to person , place, and time . The most appropriate next step in management is administration of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Phencyclidine (PCP) is an illicit substance that acts on the central nervous system in a variety of ways. It antagonizes NMDA receptors leading to excitatory neurotransmitter release, inhibits reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, and stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors. Acute PCP intoxication can lead to psychosis, bizarre behavior, agitation, aggression, rotatory nystagmus, and ataxia. Patients may be diaphoretic, tachycardic, and hypertensive because of sympathomimetic effects. Chronic PCP use can lead to major depressive disorder, psychotic symptoms, memory loss, and dysarthria. Control of psychomotor agitation is the first step in management of patients with PCP intoxication for the safety of the patient and medical staff. Chemical sedation with benzodiazepines such as intramuscular lorazepam or midazolam can be administered to control symptoms. Once a patient is adequately sedated, further evaluation can be completed to assess for traumatic injuries or complications of PCP intoxication such as rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, hypertension, seizures, encephalopathy, or a comatose state.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intramuscular naloxone (Choice B) is indicated for cases of opioid overdose. Opioid overdoses are characterized by respiratory depression presenting as a decreased respiratory rate, apnea, and hypoxia. This patient is severely agitated, making PCP intoxication more likely. Intravenous 50% dextrose (Choice C) is indicated in hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia can cause confusion, altered mental status, lightheadedness, and syncope. Hypoglycemia would be unlikely to cause hypertension and psychomotor agitation as seen in this patient. Intravenous flumazenil (Choice D) is indicated for benzodiazepine overdose. It is a competitive inhibitor of the GABA receptor at the benzodiazepine binding site. Benzodiazepine overdose is characterized by sedation and potential respiratory depression, not psychomotor agitation as seen in this patient. Intravenous 5% glucose and 0.9% saline (Choice E) are typically administered as maintenance fluids in patients who are unable to tolerate oral nutrition or for patients who are fasting prior to a surgical procedure. It would not help in sedating this patient. Educational Objective: Acute PCP intoxication can lead to psychosis, bizarre behavior, agitation, aggression, rotatory nystagmus, and ataxia. Control of psychomotor agitation is the first step in management of patients with PCP intoxication for the safety of the patient and medical staff. Chemical sedation with benzodiazepines such as intramuscular lorazepam or midazolam can be administered to control symptoms.

questionStem: An asymptomatic 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a health maintenance examination . He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . His parents both have essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia . He has an active lifestyle and plays several sports . He consumes a wide variety of foods, including meat, fruit, and vegetables , and drinks two to three glasses each of whole milk and fruit juice daily. He is currently at the 90th percentile for height and above the 97th percentile for weight and BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate dietary recommendation at this time?

choices.B: Begin dietary supplementation with a multivitamin
choices.D: Decrease his intake of milk and fruit juice
choices.E: Increase his intake of fruit and vegetables

correctExplanation: This 10-year-old boy displays signs concerning for obesity given his BMI over the 971h percentile. Pediatric obesity causes health consequences in nearly every organ system including cardiovascular (hypertension, dyslipidemia), endocrine (diabetes mellitus, hyperandrogenism, early menarche), gastrointestinal (nonalcoholic fatty liver disease), musculoskeletal (slipped capital femoral epiphysis), and pulmonary (obesity hypoventilation syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea). This patient is at further increased risk given his family history of hypertension and dyslipidemia. The first step in weight management in this patient is to decrease his caloric intake. His dietary history discloses that he is drinking an excessive amount of highly caloric beverages including whole milk and fruit juice. While milk contains beneficial nutrients such as calcium and vitamin D, whole milk contains approximately 100 calories per 8 oz serving. In contrast, fruit juice has little nutritional value and also contains approximately 100 calories per 8 oz serving. This simple dietary intervention is the most appropriate first step in managing this patient's weight.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Avoid low-fat diets (Choice A) will encourage continued weight gain in this patient rather than help to decrease his weight. By simply decreasing whole milk and fruit juice intake, this patient may not need to pursue any specific diet. There is no evidence that this patient does not have adequate vitamins and minerals in his diet, so there is not an indication to begin dietary supplementation with a multivitamin (Choice B). Furthermore, beginning a multivitamin would not affect the patient's weight, which is the primary concern in this otherwise well child. Continuing his current diet (Choice C) will continue to perpetuate weight gain. It will also promote eating habits which will impact his adolescent and adult years. By improving his eating habits, he will be better prepared to manage his weight in the future. While increasing his intake of fruits and vegetables (Choice E) would be a healthy dietary intervention, it will not improve his weight. However, replacing high calorie, processed snacks with fruits and vegetables is another healthy habit to encourage in children and adolescents. Educational Objective: Childhood and adolescent obesity is becoming increasingly present in resource-rich countries. Obesity in this age group is associated with numerous health detriments. Patients and their parents should be taught healthy eating habits early in life.

questionStem: A previously healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of intermittent fever. During the past 3 days , he has had decreased activity and joint pain. Yesterday he developed a red rash on his chest. He attends day care. He appears pale and is not in acute distress . His temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 24/min . Examination shows a petechial rash over the chest. The conjunctivae are pale. There is diffuse adenopathy in the cervical chain. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard . The spleen is palpated 1 cm below the left costal margin . There is no swelling or redness of the joints . Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 6.4 g/dL, leukocyte count of 50,000/mm 3, and platelet count of 1 0,000/mm 3.

choices.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia G) Lead poisoning
choices.B: Anemia of chronic disease H) Red blood cell aplasia (acquired)
choices.C: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia I) Sickle cell disease
choices.E: Hemolytic uremic syndrome K) Uremia of chronic renal failure

correctExplanation: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia and is likely the result of diffuse bone marrow infiltration by malignant blast cells with subsequent displacement of normal erythroid progenitor cells. The diagnosis of leukemia is supported by the presence of fever, petechial rash, diffuse adenopathy, splenomegaly, and leukocytosis to 50,000/mm 3• Evaluation of the peripheral blood smear would most likely show malignant circulating blasts of the lymphoid lineage. B-lymphocyte malignancies are more common than T-lymphocyte malignancies, and evaluation with flow cytometry is necessary to determine the specific type of malignant cell, followed by mutational analyses. Treatment typically entails chemotherapy and many patients with ALL will enter remission. Bone marrow transplant can be curative in many cases.
incorrectExplanation: Anemia of chronic disease (Choice B) is a common finding in autoimmune and inflammatory disease, chronic infections, and malignancy. Increased hepcidin concentrations decrease iron absorption and increase iron storage in the reticuloendothelial system (RES), which prevents the use of iron by erythrocyte precursors, thereby resulting in anemia. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Choice C) results from the binding of an autoantibody to RBC surface antigens, leading to removal by the RES or to intravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis is made by a positive antiglobulin (Coombs) test, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, low haptoglobin, and the presence of spherocytes and reticulocytes on the peripheral smear. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (Choice D) results in oxidative stress and hemolysis upon exposure to certain medications such as sulfa medications. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (Choice E) is classically associated with infection from Escherichia coli O157:H7, a Gram-negative rod. It often presents in children with bloody diarrhea, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure. Hereditary spherocytosis (Choice F) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins. Peripheral smear shows spherocytes. Definitive treatment is with splenectomy. Lead poisoning (Choice G) inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and ~-ALA dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. Clinical manifestations of lead poisoning include encephalopathy, cognitive dysfunction, peripheral nephropathy, hearing loss, renal tubular dysfunction, interstitial nephritis, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, and anemia. Red blood cell aplasia (acquired) (Choice H) is often an autoimmune process that results in the destruction of erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow leading to anemia with a low reticulocyte count. All other cell lines are unaffected.

questionStem: A 7-year-old girl with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis is brought to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive fatigue . She has had occasional fever and swelling and pain of the knees during the past month . She appears ill. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102 °F), pulse is 104/min , and respirations are 20/min . Examination shows pale conjunctivae . The spleen is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin . The right knee is warm , erythematous , and mildly swollen ; range of motion is limited . Laboratory studies show :

choices.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia G) Lead poisoning
choices.B: Anemia of chronic disease H) Red blood cell aplasia (acquired)
choices.C: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia I) Sickle cell disease
choices.E: Hemolytic uremic syndrome K) Uremia of chronic renal failure

correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Mean corpuscular volume Leukocyte count Reticulocyte count Platelet count 9.5 g/dL 75 µm 3 11 ,000/mm 3 0.5% 400 ,000/mm 3 This patient with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (ie, juvenile idiopathic arthritis) with fevers, fatigue, right knee effusion, and splenomegaly most likely has anemia of chronic disease (ACD). ACD is found in many autoimmune, infectious, and malignant disease states. Chronic inflammation results in increased hepcidin production, which consequently leads to a decreased responsiveness of the bone marrow to erythropoietin and retention of iron within the reticuloendothelial system (RES). This confluence offactors leads to a state of functional iron deficiency despite adequate iron stores. Patients present with either normocytic (early) or microcytic (late) anemia and reduced numbers of reticulocytes, indicating inadequate bone marrow response to anemia. Other laboratory findings include a normal to slightly high ferritin concentration with decreased serum iron concentration and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC).
incorrectExplanation: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Choice A) is a common pediatric malignancy of B or T lymphocytes that may present with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, with circulating leukemic blasts on peripheral blood smear. The mechanism of anemia in this disease is secondary to bone marrow infiltration by malignant cells with obliteration of erythroid precursors. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Choice C) results from the binding of an autoantibody to RBC surface antigens, leading to removal via the RES or to intravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis is made by a positive Coombs test, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, decreased haptoglobin, and the presence of spherocytes and reticulocytes on the peripheral smear. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (Choice D) results in oxidative stress and hemolysis upon exposure to certain medications such as sulfa medications. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (Choice E) is classically associated with infection from Escherichia coli O157:H?, a Gram-negative rod. It often presents in children with bloody diarrhea, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Hereditary spherocytosis (Choice F) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins. Peripheral smear shows spherocytes. Definitive treatment is with splenectomy. Lead poisoning (Choice G) inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and ~-ALA dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. Clinical manifestations of lead poisoning include encephalopathy, cognitive dysfunction, peripheral nephropathy, hearing loss, renal tubular dysfunction, interstitial nephritis, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, and anemia.

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of lower abdominal cramps and intermittent pain in her knees and hips for 6 weeks . The cramps are relieved by bowel movements . During this period , she has had 6 to 10 urgent, bloody bowel movements daily. Examination shows a swollen , mildly tender left knee joint. Her hemoglobin concentration is 14.5 g/dl , leukocyte count is 16,000/mm 3, and platelet count is 790,000/mm 3. Analysis of knee joint aspirate shows straw-colored , slightly turbid fluid with a leukocyte count of 2000/mm 3 (40% segmented neutrophils) . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ulcerative colitis is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa and submucosa, typically beginning in the rectum and advancing proximally in a continuous distribution. Symptoms include chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and tenesmus. Imaging typically demonstrates loss of haustral markings. Diagnosis of ulcerative colitis is by colonoscopy and biopsy, which demonstrates characteristic crypt abscesses. Potential complications of ulcerative colitis are fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, and perforation. Inflammatory bowel disease can also be associated with extraintestinal manifestations including uveitis, arthritis, aphthous stomatitis, and pyoderma gangrenosum. Treatment includes immunomodulators, biologics, and steroids, although total colectomy is generally curative and would eliminate the patient's risk for colorectal carcinoma.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adenovirus gastroenteritis (Choice A) is a cause of self-limited viral gastroenteritis with acute nausea, vomiting, and non-bloody diarrhea. It would be unlikely to cause bloody diarrhea and 6 weeks of symptoms. Chronic nonspecific diarrhea of childhood (Choice B) is an idiopathic condition characterized by diarrhea in otherwise healthy children. It does not cause weight loss, abdominal pain, or bloody stools. Giardiasis (Choice C) presents with foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea, and bloating, typically in campers who ingest cysts from freshwater. It does not typically cause bloody stools. Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Choice D) is a small-vessel vasculitis that occurs in children and typically presents with gravity-dependent purpura (eg, buttocks, legs, and feet), arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain (eg, intussusception). Pseudomembranous colitis (Choice E) is caused by C/ostridium difficile, which produces toxins that result in dysfunction of the brush border and a subsequent secretory diarrhea. C. difficile infections are associated with the presence of pseudomembranes that appear as patchy regions of white mucosa on colonoscopy. C. difficile infection is an opportunistic and often hospital-acquired infection that commonly occurs after the use of antibiotics, especially ampicillin and clindamycin, as a result of the loss of native colonic microbiota. Educational Objective: Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa and submucosa. Symptoms include chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and tenesmus.

questionStem: A previously healthy 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressively worsening headaches and difficulty walking over the past 6 weeks . Examination shows bilateral papilledema , right abducens palsy, and gait ataxia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The peak incidence is between ages 5 and 9 years of age, and they are frequently located in the cerebellum. The position of a medulloblastoma in the cerebellum typically leads to occlusion of ventricular drainage, which causes increases in intracranial pressure. Thus, patients typically present with headaches or nausea (from increased intracranial pressure), as well as gait ataxia or incoordination (caused by cerebellar disruption), as in this patient. Physical examination will often demonstrate nystagmus, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria, cranial nerve palsies, and papilledema. Diagnosis is made with MRI and biopsy, with the specimen for the latter most commonly taken during surgical resection. Lumbar punctures are also performed to evaluate for metastatic spread through the cerebrospinal fluid and spinal leptomeninges. In addition to surgery, treatment includes radiation and chemotherapy. Complications include neurologic abnormalities, such as developmental delay and hearing loss, and endocrine abnormalities.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acoustic neuroma (Choice A) is a benign tumor of Schwann cells that arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve. It presents with ipsilateral hearing loss and vertigo, as well as ipsilateral dysmetria if compressing the cerebral peduncles. This patient does not have hearing loss. Dandy-Walker syndrome (Choice B) is a condition in which the cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle are malformed, resulting in cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle and posterior fossa with consequent hydrocephalus. It presents early in life with developmental delay, hydrocephalus, and cerebellar or cranial nerve dysfunction. It would be less likely in this previously healthy 7-year-old. Optic nerve glioma (Choice D) is a neoplasm of the optic nerve that is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, although it can occur independently. It is most frequently an astrocytoma that occurs in childhood. It presents with a gradual onset of proptosis, vision loss, and less frequently, hydrocephalus and endocrinopathies because of spread. This patient has had relatively acute onset of symptoms of ataxia and cranial nerve palsies without evidence of vision loss. Pinealoma (Choice E) classically presents with a paralysis of upward gaze, diplopia, and signs of increased intracranial pressure. While this patient does have increased intracranial pressure and right abducens palsy, he does not have a paralysis of upward gaze. Educational Objective: Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor in children, often presenting in patients aged five to nine years with signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, headache, nausea, vomiting) and gait ataxia or incoordination. Treatment requires surgical resection, radiation, and chemotherapy.

questionStem: A previously healthy 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of right scrotal pain and swelling for 3 hours. There is no history of trauma . He was sexually active 3 months ago , and he did not use a condom . Examination shows tenderness and edema in the region of the right testicle . The cremasteric reflex is absent on the right side. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

choices.C: Persistent patency of the processus vaginal is

correctExplanation: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac. The resultant twisting of the spermatic cord, which contains the gonadal artery, pampiniform plexus, and gonadal vein, results in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow to the testis. Patients typically present with acute, severe testicular pain with diffuse tenderness and swelling. Patients may also exhibit nausea, vomiting, and lower abdominal pain. There is typically a negative cremasteric reflex with a high-riding, transverse lie of the testicle on physical examination. If not properly and expeditiously managed with surgical detorsion and orchiopexy, testicular torsion can result in testicular infarction as well as infertility.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Leukemic infiltration of the testis (Choice A) is seen in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Because of the blood-testis barrier, chemotherapy is less able to reach the testis. Testicular leukemia presents as painless testicular enlargement. Malignant infiltration of the testis (Choice B) can occur in testicular tumors such as seminoma, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, or yolk sac tumor. Presentation is variable depending on the type of tumor. Seminoma is the most common testicular tumor and presents as painless testicular enlargement. Persistent patency of the processus vaginalis (Choice C) can lead to the formation of a hydrocele if filled by peritoneal fluid, or hematocele if complicated by blood accumulation. It also increases the risk for an indirect inguinal hernia. Persistent patency of the urachus (Choice D) contributes to a persistent connection between the bladder and the umbilicus. Patients with a patent urachus can present with clear urine leaking out of the umbilicus. It can also be asymptomatic or potentially complicated by infection. Educational Objective: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac. The resultant twisting of the spermatic cord, which contains the gonadal artery, pampiniform plexus, and gonadal vein, results in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow.

questionStem: A healthy 9-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for a well-child examination . Her parents are concerned that she is not gaining enough weight. She is breast-feeding six times daily and taking small amounts of baby food from a spoon. She is at the 5th percentile for weight and 25th percentile for length and head circumference . Review of the growth chart shows that this growth pattern has been consistent since birth. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassurance that this growth i:>attern is within normal limits
choices.B: Increasing caloric intake by adding more baby food
choices.D: Supplementing breast-feeding with whole cow milk

correctExplanation: Growth charts show the percentile curves of body measurements such as head circumference, body weight, and length for children. They are used to evaluate for normal growth, short stature, growth delay, failure to thrive, nutritional deficiencies, malabsorption, endocrinopathy, and other disorders. Clinicians use the growth chart provided by the World Health Organization (WHO), which is an international standard for infant growth. For infants less than 2 years of age, infants are classified as low weight or short stature if they are less than 2nd percentile for weight or length, respectively. This patient is the 5th percentile for weight, which, while low, is not yet of concern. In addition, her growth pattern has been consistent since birth. Further assessment to investigate growth or nutritional problems should be performed if infants are less than the 2nd percentile or if there are major changes in growth pattern.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Increasing caloric intake by adding more baby food (Choice B) would not be an appropriate recommendation, as the patient's weight and length are within normal limits on the growth chart. This may be an appropriate recommendation if the patient's weight was less than the 2nd percentile and the reason for growth delay was inadequate caloric intake. Replacing breast-feeding with soy-based formula (Choice C) would not be appropriate. Breastfeeding is a standard source of nutrition for the growth and healthy development of infants. Supplementing breast-feeding with whole cow milk (Choice D) would be harmful to the infant. Early introduction of whole cow's milk prior to one year of age has been associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus, increased risk for developing cow's milk allergy, constipation, and iron deficiency anemia. Educational Objective: Growth charts show the percentile curves of body measurements such as head circumference, body weight, and length for children. Patients less than 2 years of age are classified as low weight or short stature if they are less than the 2nd percentile for weight or length, respectively.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 6-month history of increasingly severe pain with menses . Her mother reports that during this time , her daughter has missed 2 days of school during each menstrual period because of severe pelvic cramps associated with vomiting . Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 4 to 5 days. Her last menstrual period was 7 days ago . She currently takes acetaminophen , which provides minimal relief of her symptoms . She has had three lifetime sexual partners , and they use condoms inconsistently . The patient is an honor roll student despite frequent absences from school. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows a tender, normal-sized uterus and no masses . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy females and occurs in the absence of secondary causes, such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis, or uterine fibroids. Symptoms often begin during adolescence and commonly interfere with quality of life and with essential activities such as school or work. Patients describe crampy lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses, which persists for several days, along with fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pre-syncopal symptoms, and headache. Endometrial sloughing is accompanied by the production of prostaglandins, which stimulate painful uterine contractions. Patients are typically treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, thereby limiting prostaglandin synthesis, or with oral hormonal contraceptives.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A pregnancy test (Choice A) can be used to evaluate for pregnancy, particularly ectopic pregnancy in the setting of severe abdominal pain. However, this patient's most recent period was 7 days ago, making pregnancy unlikely. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice B) can be used to evaluate for structural abnormalities of the uterus or adnexa, such as fibroids or ovarian cysts that can cause recurrent abdominopelvic pain. However, there was no evidence of structural abnormalities during this patient's pelvic examination. Narcotic therapy (Choice C) carries a high risk for physical dependence and opioid use disorder. It would be inappropriate to start narcotic therapy for pain control in this patient before trying other options, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy. Selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor therapy (Choice E) is used in the treatment of major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. It does not play a role in the management of primary dysmenorrhea. Educational Objective: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy females and occurs in the absence of secondary causes. Symptoms include crampy lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses and persists for several days, as well as fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pre-syncopal symptoms, and headache. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.

questionStem: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician 2 months after his parents noticed that he seemed to be ignoring them. On questioning , they note that he does not appear to be startled by loud noises. Growth and development have been otherwise normal. He was born at term to a 28-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1. His mother's blood group is A, Rh-negative , and his blood group is A, Rh-positive . He had a serum total bilirubin concentration of 25 mg/dL at the age of 2 days and received phototherapy for 2 days. He continued to be mildly jaundiced until the age of 1 month. Serum studies since then have shown no abnormalities . Examination today shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's current condition?
correctExplanation: Kernicterus occurs as a result of the deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in a newborn's brain, usually in the basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum. It typically presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures. If untreated, it can cause long-term neurologic abnormalities, such as gaze palsies or sensorineural hearing loss. Unconjugated or indirect bilirubin is circulating insoluble bilirubin that is largely bound to albumin. It has not yet undergone conjugation in the liver. Causes of increased unconjugated bilirubin include hemolysis, breast milk jaundice, Crigler-Najjar syndrome, Gilbert syndrome, and physiologic jaundice. In newborns, causes also include maternal exposure to sulfonamide antibiotics, which displace bilirubin from albumin in the neonate, thereby increasing the free plasma concentrations of unconjugated bilirubin. Kernicterus typically occurs when the bilirubin concentration exceeds 25-30 mg/dL, which is commonly caused by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency or Rh-hemolytic disease of the newborn, the latter of which was likely present in this patient given the discordant Rh status of him and his mother. Risk factors include prematurity, cephalohematoma or significant bruising, poor breastfeeding, and East Asian ethnicity. Treatment to prevent severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and subsequent kernicterus is phototherapy or exchange transfusion. Exchange transfusions are particularly useful in hyperbilirubinemia that is caused by anti-Rh(D) antibodies, as they allow removal of the antibodies as well as the bilirubin.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Avoidance of breast-feeding (Choice A) could be considered in breast milk jaundice or breastfeeding jaundice, although it is usually not required as the increased bilirubin concentrations seen are typically benign. Breast milk jaundice is hypothesized to occur because of the presence of beta-glucuronidase in breast milk, which deconjugates bilirubin and allows it to be reabsorbed. Breastfeeding jaundice occurs as a result of relative hypovolemia secondary to inadequate intake, which results in hyperbilirubinemia. Water supplementation (Choice B) is generally not advised in infants, as their kidneys are incapable of properly reabsorbing sodium, which results in hyponatremia. This can cause altered mental status and seizures. Water supplementation is not used to treat hyperbilirubinemia. Longer course of phototherapy (Choice C) could have decreased the overall amount of unconjugated bilirubin, as phototherapy converts indirect bilirubin into a water-soluble form that can be excreted. However, it would have been less effective in this patient with severe hyperbilirubinemia likely secondary to anti-Rh(D) antibody-mediated hemolysis. Antibiotic therapy (Choice D) is used in the treatment of neonatal infections, such as Escherichia coli or Streptococcus aga/actiae meningitis. Bacterial meningitis is associated with a high mortality if untreated, as well as prolonged neurologic complications, such as hearing loss, even when treated. A missed diagnosis of bacterial meningitis would have certainly led to neonatal demise or significant morbidity. Educational Objective: Kernicterus is caused by high concentrations of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, commonly in hemolysis because of Rh alloimmunization or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. It is associated with poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures as a result of deposition of bilirubin in the basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum. If untreated, it can lead to long-term neurologic sequelae, such as hearing loss.

questionStem: A 4-year-old boy has had fatigue , decreased appetite , and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss over the past 2 months. He appears listless . His pulse is 80/min while supine and 105/min while standing , and his blood pressure is 85/60 mm Hg while supine and 75/45 mm Hg while standing . Serum glucose concentration is 465 mg/dl . Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones , 4+ glucose , and 1 to 2 WBC/hpf . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: A pediatric patient presenting with fatigue, decreased appetite, weight loss, and hyperglycemia raises suspicion for type 1 diabetes mellitus. Type 1 diabetes mellitus can also be complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and patients can present with DKA as their initial manifestation. DKA can also result from increased insulin requirements during times of physiologic stress (eg, infection) or insulin nonadherence. DKA occurs as a result of the accumulation of serum ketones such as beta-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs because of the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Type 1 diabetes mellitus can also result in dehydration caused by hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and osmotic diuresis. This diuresis can result in dehydration, ketonuria, and orthostasis. Orthostatic vital signs are significant pulse increases greater than 20/min, systolic pressure decreases over 20 mm Hg, or diastolic pressure decreases over 10 mm Hg with changes in position from supine to seated to standing. Because of the patient's osmotic diuresis, orthostatic hypotension, and dehydration, the first step in care requires the administration of 0.9% saline intravenously for fluid resuscitation.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Urine culture {Choice A) would not be the next appropriate step for this patient. Urinary tract infection is unlikely in a patient without symptoms of dysuria, urinary urgency, or frequency, and less than 5-10 WBC/hpf on urinalysis. Urinalysis discloses ketones and glucose, consistent with DKA, and the patient would benefit from fluid resuscitation. Oral glucose tolerance test {Choice B) is typically performed to evaluate for type 2 diabetes mellitus or for maternal gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks' gestation. Gestational diabetes can lead to an increased risk for congenital anomalies, spontaneous abortion and stillbirth, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. In a patient with a random glucose greater than 200 mg/dl and associated symptoms, the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus can be made. Measurement of hemoglobin A 1c {Choice C) is useful for the diagnosis and long-term management of diabetes mellitus. It would be less helpful in the acute management of a new diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and DKA. Administration of subcutaneous insulin {Choice D) can be helpful in this patient, although insulin should be administered intravenously for the management of DKA once the patient is appropriately resuscitated with intravenous fluid. In a patient with signs of dehydration and orthostasis, intravenous fluid resuscitation should be the first step in management. Educational Objective: Type 1 diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis can result in significant dehydration caused by hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and osmotic diuresis. The first step in care requires fluid resuscitation with intravenous isotonic fluids.

questionStem: A 1-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of low-grade fever and watery diarrhea . She has had 8 to 10 watery stools daily that contain mucus but no blood ; she has had fewer wet diapers than usual. She has not had vomiting or symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection , but her father reports that she became very fussy earlier today. She has been drinking juice and children's electrolyte supplement but not eating much food . Her older brother had a mild upper respiratory tract infection and diarrhea last week . On arrival , she appears lethargic . She is at the 25th percentile for length and weight. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 160/min , respirations are 30/min , and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. The mucous membranes are dry. The lungs are clear to auscultation . Cardiac examination shows a grade 1/6, systolic ejection murmur with no rub or gallop . The abdomen is soft, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly . The extremities are cool, and capillary refill time is 3 to 4 seconds . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show : Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Celiac disease (Choice A), or gluten-sensitive enteropathy, presents with diarrhea and malabsorption caused by gliadin hypersensitivity. It does not present with an acute onset and rarely leads to significant volume depletion. Diabetic ketoacidosis (Choice B) may present with volume depletion and metabolic acidosis. However, in an infant this is most commonly caused by type 1 diabetes mellitus, which presents with polyuria and

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of watery diarrhea and vomiting . During this period , he has not had an appetite for food but has been drinking sugar-free soda. There has not been any change in urinary output. On arrival , he is alert and interactive . His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 24/min , and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Examination shows a soft, nontender abdomen and no organomegaly . Bowel sounds are normal. Serum studies show: Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Na• K+ cI ­ HC0 3- Glucose 140 mEq/L 4.5 mEq/L 110 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 45 mg/dl Prolonged vomiting with inability to maintain adequate oral intake and diarrhea can lead to clinically significant levels of dehydration and starvation ketosis. In this case, the child has adequate fluid intake and does not demonstrate signs of dehydration but has had inadequate caloric intake. Starvation ketosis occurs when glycogen stores in the liver have been exhausted, typically after one day of fasting. Following this, blood glucose is maintained primarily through the breakdown of muscle and fat to provide substrates for hepatic gluconeogenesis. After approximately 3 days of fasting, adipose cells and their stored fatty acids become the primary source for energy through the production of ketone bodies. This patient's laboratory values, including profound hypoglycemia, decreased bicarbonate, and increased anion gap are suggestive of starvation ketoacidosis in acute illness, prolonged fasting from persistent vomiting and diarrhea, and inadequate caloric intake. Starvation ketoacidosis is a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. If serum or urine ketones were measured, they would be increased. Production of ketone bodies will continue to provide the brain with an energy source during prolonged fasting.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adrenal insufficiency {Choice A) may occur in a patient taking chronic glucocorticoids who becomes ill and does not receive any additional glucocorticoid to compensate for the state of acute illness. Insufficient adrenal production of glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids would cause hypotension, hyperkalemia, and hypernatremia, none of which are present in this patient. Fatty acid oxidation defect {Choice B) would prevent formation of ketones. Instead, this patient is successfully producing ketones in response to a starvation state caused by an acute illness. His alert and interactive state supports that he is generating enough fuel for his brain in the form of ketones and thus must have functional fatty acid oxidation. Fructose 1-phosphate aldolase deficiency {Choice C) causes hereditary fructose intolerance. This typically presents when fructose-containing foods such as fruit and fruit juice is introduced into the diet. Affected children develop hypoglycemia and vomiting after fructose ingestion. This child's illness is acute and he has not been ingesting fructose. Insulin deficiency {Choice E) is the cause of diabetic ketoacidosis (OKA). Like starvation ketosis, OKA shows decreased bicarbonate, increased anion gap, and presence of ketones. However, unlike starvation ketosis which demonstrates hypoglycemia, OKA is associated with hyperglycemia. Educational Objective: Decreased caloric intake secondary to prolonged vomiting and diarrhea can lead to hypoglycemia and starvation ketosis. This can cause a metabolic acidosis characterized by decreased bicarbonate and an increased anion gap. Serum and urine ketones will be increased.

questionStem: A 10-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department because of poor feeding and drowsiness for the past day. He also has had two episodes of vomiting today. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery and weighed 3600 g (7 lb 15 oz). On arrival , he is lethargic . His skin color is a shade darker than his parents' skin color. His temperature is 36.1 °C (97°F), pulse is 180/min, respirations are 70/min , and blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg. The anterior fontanel is sunken , and the scalp has sparse fine blond hairs. The nipples and scrotum are darkly pigmented. The pupils are equal , round , and reactive to light and accommodation . There is no scleral icterus . The lungs are clear to auscultation . Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm and no murmurs . S 1 and S2 are normal. The abdomen is soft with no masses or organomegaly . Genital development is Tanner stage 1; the penis is 4 cm long. Testes are descended . Serum studies are most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis, particularly of cortisol, with variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. Because of decreased production of hormones, the adrenal gland is stimulated by the pituitary in an attempt to increase hormone production, leading to adrenal hyperplasia, the namesake of this condition. The most common form of CAH and the cause of this patient's manifestations is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents with salt wasting in a newborn or precocious puberty in a child, as well as virilization of infants with an XX karyotype (eg, clitoral hypertrophy, labial fusion), caused by increased concentrations of androgens. Because of the enzyme deficiency, concentrations of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, and testosterone are increased, while aldosterone and cortisol are decreased, leading to hypotension, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia (caused by inadequate cortisol). Diffuse hyperpigmentation of the skin, as seen in this newborn, is characteristic. Melanin production is regulated in part by melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH). MSH is a byproduct of proopiomelanocortin (POMC) which also produces adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In adrenal insufficiency, stimulation of ACTH production by POMC simultaneously produces MSH, leading to diffuse hyperpigmentation in affected patients. Treatment of CAH consists of exogenous glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid supplementation.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. When present, aldosterone binds to receptors in the collecting tubule of the nephron and leads to placement of sodium and potassium channels on the luminal cell membrane. Potassium exits the cell through the channel and into the lumen. Without aldosterone, potassium does not leave the cell and instead accumulates in the interstitium and blood, causing increased serum potassium, not decreased serum potassium (Choices A, C, and E). Without elimination of potassium, there is no gradient by which sodium reenters the cell. Instead, sodium remains in the lumen and is lost in the urine. This is called salt wasting and is accompanied by a decreased serum sodium, not normal (Choice F) or increased sodium (Choice D). Educational Objective: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia results from a defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis. Its most common form, 21-hydroxylase deficiency, presents with salt wasting in infants or precocious puberty in children. It also causes the virilization of XX infants, increased concentrations of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. Treatment includes the exogenous administration of mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids.

questionStem: A 2½-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because she is concerned about his language development. He uses fewer words than his two older siblings did at the same age. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . He began walking at the age of 11 months. He feeds himself , plays well with his siblings , and does well in day care. Motor development is appropriate for age. He knows 100 words but does not use them in phrases . Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this child's language development?

choices.E: No further evaluation is indicated at this time

correctExplanation: Children with developmental delay should undergo audiometry to evaluate for hearing loss. Failure to detect hearing loss can cause preventable delays in a child's language, social, and educational development. Hearing loss in children may occur because of either conductive or sensorineural etiologies. A careful history and general physical examination should be performed to evaluate for possible syndromic features. Weber and Rinne tests can distinguish conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends routine audiometry screening for all school-aged children.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intelligence testing (Choice A) is not an appropriate initial test for isolated delay in language development. This child's isolated delay in language development with otherwise normal developmental milestones is more concerning for hearing loss. Speech evaluation (Choice B) may be useful for identifying abnormalities of speech production. This child has a low-normal vocabulary for his age. While speech evaluation may be warranted, audiometry should be performed first. MRI of the inner ears (Choice D) may be indicated based on the results of audiometry and a careful physical examination but is not an appropriate initial test. No further evaluation is indicated at this time (Choice E) is incorrect. Failure to detect hearing loss can cause preventable delays in a child's language, social, and educational development. Educational Objective: Children with developmental delay should undergo audiometry to evaluate for hearing loss. Failure to detect hearing loss can cause preventable delays in a child's language, social, and educational development. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends routine audiometry screening for all school-aged children.

questionStem: A previously healthy 17-year-old girl comes to the physician 4 days after her sexual partner was diagnosed with gonorrhea . Examination shows no abnormalities . Tests for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are ordered . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: Oral azithromycin and intramuscular penicillin therapy
choices.E: No treatment indicated because the patient is asymptomatic

correctExplanation: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative diplococcus and can cause vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Vaginitis typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus. Cervicitis presents with similar discharge, but also with an erythematous, friable cervix and cervical motion tenderness on examination. When infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, PID with purulent cervical discharge, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and systemic symptoms such as fever can result. If left untreated, PID can become complicated by a tuba-ovarian abscess or intraabdominal abscess, presenting with focal tenderness and a fluctuant mass; it can cause consequent infertility. Gonorrhea can present with dissemination (tenosynovitis, dermatitis, polyarthralgia) or reactive arthritis. Risk factors for the development of gonorrhea include multiple sexual partners, new sexual partners, receptive anal intercourse, a young age, substance abuse, and inconsistent condom usage. Coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis is common, therefore treatment typically consists of ceftriaxone and doxycycline, with the latter covering a possible concurrent chlamydia! infection while confirmatory tests are pending. In a high-risk exposure to gonorrhea, empiric treatment to cover both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis is appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intramuscular ceftriaxone therapy only (Choice A) would treat gonorrhea. However, risk for coinfection with C. trachomatis is high, and this antibiotic regimen would not cover a chlamydia! infection. Oral azithromycin therapy only (Choice C) would treat a chlamydia! infection. However, this patient has been exposed to gonorrhea and requires additional treatment with ceftriaxone. Oral azithromycin and intramuscular penicillin therapy (Choice D) would cover a chlamydia! infection but would not cover gonorrhea, as N. gonorrhoeae has become increasingly resistant to penicillin. Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline would provide better coverage. No treatment indicated because the patient is asymptomatic (Choice E) is inappropriate, as failure to diagnose and treat this patient could lead to a multitude of complications, such as reactive arthritis, disseminated gonococcal infection, and pelvic inflammatory disease with consequent infertility. She has had a high-risk exposure to gonorrhea and empiric treatment is more appropriate. Educational Objective: N. gonorrhoeae can present with vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Following a high-risk exposure, empiric treatment with ceftriaxone and doxycycline, with the latter covering a possible concurrent C. trachomatis infection, is appropriate while confirmatory tests are pending.

questionStem: A previously healthy 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of moderate groin pain since he participated in a hockey game 24 hours ago. He recalls no trauma or injury to this area. He reports a decreased appetite today. He has not had fever. He appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows edema of the left aspect of the scrotum . There is marked tenderness to palpation of the superior aspect of the left testicle ; the pain does not improve with elevation of the testicle . A 3-mm area of bluish discoloration overlays the point of maximal tenderness ; there is no erythema . Cremasteric reflex is intact. Genital and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 2. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac, resulting in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow to the testis. Patients typically present with acute, severe testicular pain with diffuse tenderness and swelling and an absent cremasteric reflex. In contrast, patients with torsion of the appendix testis present with groin pain, a nontender testicle, a tender, palpable localized mass adjacent to one pole of the testicle, and an intact cremasteric reflex. The appendix testis is a vestigial structure, typically on the anterior and superior aspect of the testis and has a pedunculated shape that may predispose it to torsion. When torsed, the appendix testis may appear as a small blue or black mass in the scrotum. The diagnosis may be made clinically, or with ultrasound in cases where testicular torsion cannot be excluded. While patients with testicular torsion require surgical detorsion and orchiopexy to prevent infertility, management of torsion of the appendix testis is generally supportive, with analgesics and scrotal support.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Epididymitis (Choice A) is a common cause of painful scrotal swelling and refers to acute infection and inflammation of the epididymis. In younger males, this is commonly secondary to sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Patients with epididymitis may have moderate pain relief with elevation of the testis. Incarcerated hernia (Choice B) refers to the contents of a hernia becoming trapped in the hernia defect, unable to be reduced to native position. If this type of hernia contains bowel, an obstruction can result. An inguinal hernia can become incarcerated, but this would typically present with severe tenderness and a larger mass with swelling in the inguinal area. Orchitis (Choice C) is inflammation of the testes that results from an infection, sometimes from the paramyxovirus that causes mumps. Clinical manifestations include fever, myalgias, and fatigue. Especially when it occurs after puberty, it is a risk factor for infertility. Testicular hematoma (Choice D) can occur in blunt scrotal trauma and presents with testicular swelling, warmth, and pain. A 3-mm area of bluish discoloration is more likely caused by torsion of an appendix testis, not testicular hematoma, especially with no history of trauma. Educational Objective: The appendix testis is a vestigial structure, typically on the anterior and superior aspect of the testis and has a pedunculated shape that may predispose it to torsion. Patients with torsion of the appendix testis present with groin pain, a nontender testicle, a tender palpable localized mass adjacent to the testicle, and an intact cremasteric reflex.

questionStem: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination . He completed a 1-week course of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by a 5-day course of amoxicillin for pneumococcal pneumonia 2 weeks ago and has been asymptomatic since then. He has had six episodes of acute otitis media during the past 6 months. Immunizations are up-to-date . He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. Tympanic membranes are dull with clear effusions. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Segmented neutrophils Lymphocytes Monocytes Platelet count Serum lgA lgE lgG lgM Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment of this patient's underlying condition?
correctExplanation: 12 g/dL 8500/mm 3 40% 50% 10% 420,000/mm 3 10 mg/dL 10 IU/mL 100 mg/dL 20 mg/dL Monthly infusions of immune globulin should be given to this patient with a likely diagnosis of X-linked agammaglobulinemia. X-linked agammaglobulinemia is defined by defects in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, which is necessary for all stages of B lymphocyte development and proliferation. Deficiency of this enzyme results in failed B lymphocyte development. As B lymphocytes are responsible for secreting immunoglobulins once they differentiate into plasma cells, a defect in B lymphocyte maturation leads to a dearth of plasma cells and severely decreased immunoglobulin concentrations of every class, including lgM, lgG, lgE, and lgA. Patients present with recurrent infections caused by impaired humoral immunity, and treatment is with intravenous immunoglobulin concentrates.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Amoxicillin prophylaxis (Choice A) is given to patients with congenital heart disease or those with a history of endocarditis who are undergoing certain procedures. While amoxicillin would likely treat his recurrent episodes of otitis media, it would not correct the underlying problem. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor therapy (Choice B) is used to stimulate production of granulocytes in patients receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy; it is not the treatment for agammaglobulinemia. Oral prednisone therapy (Choice C) results in immunosuppression and an increased risk for infections. This would not be an appropriate therapeutic option for this patient. Splenectomy (Choice E) is employed occasionally for patients with refractory hereditary spherocytosis who develop debilitating anemia. Splenectomy generally increases the risk for infection with encapsulated organisms such as Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Educational Objective: Patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia have mutations in the BTK gene, which encodes a tyrosine kinase essential for all stages of B lymphocyte development and proliferation. They present with recurrent infections and decreased or absent concentrations of all immunoglobulin subclasses. Treatment is with intravenous immune globulin.

questionStem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was found in his grandmother's bedroom , surrounded by multiple open medication bottles . His grandmother states that her medications include imipramine , phenobarbital , iron supplements , aspirin , and oxycodone . On arrival , the patient is somnolent. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 70/min , respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. The pupils are 2 mm and nonreactive to light. The lungs are clear to auscultation . He is unresponsive to painful stimuli. Ingestion of which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient is intoxicated with oxycodone, an opioid medication. Opioids are central nervous system (CNS) depressants used as analgesics and recreational drugs. Opioids act throughout the CNS and peripheral nervous system and lead to euphoria (caused by interaction with dopamine), altered mental status, sedation, bradycardia (70/min is bradycardia in a 2-year-old patient), hypotension, depressed respiratory drive, and constricted pupils. Specifically, the µ 2 opioid receptor, located in the brainstem respiratory centers and on peripheral chemo- and baroreceptors, controls respiratory depression, which may be severe. Miosis is a distinctive finding that is less common in intoxication with other CNS depressants; it is caused by direct opioid receptor activity in the brain areas responsible for pupillary control. Opioids also act on receptors within the enteric nervous system, reducing gut motility and causing constipation. The treatment of opioid toxicity includes supportive care (eg, respiratory support) and naloxone, a short-acting opioid receptor antagonist.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aspirin overdose (Choice A) presents with respiratory alkalosis from salicylate stimulus of the medullary respiratory centers, along with high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Tinnitus may also be present. Though depressed mental status may be seen, respiratory depression, bradycardia, and pupillary constriction are more consistent with opioid intoxication. lmipramine overdose (Choice B) typically leads to cardiovascular toxicity (eg, QTc and QRS prolongation), CNS toxicity (eg, sedation, coma, seizures), and anticholinergic toxicity (eg, pupillary dilation, dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention). Pupillary constriction and bradycardia would be atypical. Iron toxicity (Choice C) may lead to free radical production and consequent gastrointestinal distress (eg, pain, nausea, diarrhea, and ultimately bowel obstruction), shock and metabolic acidosis, and hepatotoxicity. Pupillary constriction and bradycardia would be atypical. Phenobarbital (Choice E) is a barbiturate, a CNS depressant that has similar effects in toxicity to alcohol and benzodiazepines. The risk for dangerous respiratory depression is higher in barbiturates than benzodiazepines or alcohol. Pupils are typically a normal size. Educational Objective: Opioid intoxication causes symptoms of CNS depression including sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia, and hypotension. Miosis differentiates opioid intoxication from many other toxidromes.

questionStem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father because of a 36-hour history of fever and a 1-day history of pain and swelling of her joints . The pain and swelling began in her right knee, then increased to involve both knees, and has now migrated to her left ankle and left elbow. She is currently unable to walk because of the pain. Two weeks ago, she had a sore throat that resolved after 2 days without treatment. She has no known drug allergies . She appears uncomfortable when she moves . She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 136/min, respirations are 24/min , and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no rash. There is a grade 2/6, pansystolic , high-pitched murmur that is heard best at the apex and accentuated when she makes a fist. There is mild swelling of the left elbow and both knees; the left elbow and left knee are warm . Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 110 mm/h. An antistreptolysin O titer is 800 Todd/U (N<240) . Salicylate therapy is begun and results in marked improvement of the patient's symptoms . Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to prevent a recurrence of this patient's disorder?
correctExplanation: This girl presents with rheumatic fever, characterized by arthritis and mitral regurgitation, following an episode streptococcal pharyngitis. Rheumatic fever is a sequela of untreated group A Streptococcus infection, commonly pharyngitis, in which there is a type II hypersensitivity reaction to self-antigens having a similar structure to, and thus molecularly mimicking streptococcal M protein. Diagnosis is made by the Jones criteria, which describe many of the core clinical features of rheumatic fever. The major criteria include polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea; the minor criteria include fever, leukocytosis, arthralgia, and PR interval prolongation. Patients often have an increased antistreptolysin O titer. Biopsy of affected cardiac tissue discloses a granulomatous reaction with presence of Aschoff bodies. Complications of rheumatic fever include mitral valve inflammation leading to long-term sequelae of chronic mitral valve regurgitation, prolapse, or stenosis. Treatment of the initial streptococcal infection is effective for reducing the risk for developing rheumatic fever. Per American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines, once rheumatic fever has developed, treatment includes salicylates and a prolonged course of monthly penicillin treatments to reduce the risk for recurrence and further valvular damage.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Clindamycin (Choice A) and erythromycin (Choice B) are appropriate agents for the primary prevention of rheumatic fever in patients with penicillin allergies but are not most appropriate for secondary prevention of rheumatic fever recurrence in patients without penicillin allergies. Prednisone (Choice D), a corticosteroid, may be useful for reducing inflammation in rheumatic fever, but it does not help prevent disease recurrence. Salicylates reduce inflammation and pain associated with rheumatic fever. No pharmacotherapy is indicated (Choice E) is incorrect. Failure to treat with penicillin increases the patient's risk for recurrences of rheumatic fever with associated mitral valve damage. Educational Objective: Rheumatic fever is a sequela of untreated group A Streptococcus infection, commonly pharyngitis, in which there is a type II hypersensitivity reaction affecting the heart. Severe cardiac damage, including mitral valve regurgitation, prolapse, or stenosis may occur, especially if the rheumatic fever is untreated or recurrent. Penicillin is useful for preventing the development and recurrence of rheumatic fever.

questionStem: A 3977-g (8-lb 12-oz) male newborn is delivered at term to a 30-year-old primigravid woman . Apgar scores are 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . The mother's hepatitis B status is unknown because she received no prenatal care. Maternal hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) assay is ordered . Examination of the newborn shows no abnormalities . In addition to administration of hepatitis B vaccine (HBV) now, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment regimen for the newborn?

choices.B: Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) only now
choices.C: HBIG at 2 and 6 months of age
choices.D: HBV at 2 and 6 months of age
choices.E: HBIG only if maternal HBsAg is positive and HBV at 2 and 6 months of age

correctExplanation: The recommended schedule of hepatitis B immunization and immunoprophylaxis in newborns is dependent on the maternal HBsAg status. HBsAg assay is an important component of prenatal care and is typically checked at the first prenatal visit. If HBsAg is positive or if there are signs of active maternal hepatitis B infection, the newborn should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine (HBV) intramuscularly and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) as early as possible, with additional doses of HBV at 2 and 6 months of age. In a HBsAg negative mother, only HBV is needed and doses are given at birth, 2 months, and 6 months. As in this case, if the mother's HBsAg status is unknown but there is no evidence of active infection, the newborn should receive HBV within 12 hours and HBIG can be delayed until the maternal serologies have returned. If the serology returns positive for HBsAg, the infant should receive HBIG within 1 week. If the serology returns negative for HBsAg, the newborn does not require HBIG. In either case, the newborn will still require the second and third doses of HBV at 2 and 6 months, respectively.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Observation only (Choice A) without follow-up of the maternal HBsAg titer is not appropriate. If the titer returns positive or unknown, HBIG should be given. HBIG only now (Choice B) is not necessary. Administration of HBIG to a neonate born to a hepatitis B infected mother may occur within the first week of life, which provides adequate time for the maternal HBsAg assay to return. Even if the maternal HBsAg assay is positive, HBIG at 2 and 6 months of age (Choice C) is not necessary. HBV should be given at these time points but HBIG is only needed at birth. HBV at 2 and 6 months of age (Choice D) will be inadequate if the maternal HBsAg titer is positive. Educational Objective: In a mother without prenatal care and an unknown HBsAg status, the newborn should be given the first dose of HBV. HBIG should be given if the maternal HBsAg assay returns positive or remains unknown, but not if it returns negative. In either case, the newborn should receive the full HBV series, which includes additional doses at ages 2 and 6 months.

questionStem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 5-day history of increased thirst and urination and a 2-day history of decreased activity. Although she had been previously toilet trained and dry at night, she has had several episodes of nocturnal wetting over the past week. She has not had fever, vomiting , or diarrhea. Two weeks ago, she fell off her tricycle , but no injuries were apparent. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Examination shows sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Serum Na + Cl· K+ HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Glucose Creatinine Urine pH Specific gravity Blood Glucose Protein Osmolality 159 mEq/L 125 mEq/L 4.5 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 43 mg/dl 122 mg/dl 1.0 mg/dl 6 1.001 negative negative negative 125 mOsmol/kg Central diabetes insipidus may result from head trauma and is characterized by the inadequate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also known as vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary. ADH binds V 2 receptors of the late distal convoluted tubule and the collecting tubule principal cells, which results in the insertion of aquaporin channels in the luminal surface. This results in increased free water absorption and maintains tight regulation of serum osmolality. Inadequate production of ADH by the posterior pituitary gland may occur in various pathologies, such as pituitary tumors, trauma, tuberculosis, or intracranial surgery. This results in a decreased concentration of aquaporin channels inserted within the principal cells of the collecting tubule, leading to an inability to absorb adequate amounts of free water, which causes dilute urine, decreased urine osmolality, hypernatremia, and increased serum osmolality. The hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect this increased serum osmolality, which causes the patient to report extreme thirst. Patients typically also present with production of large volumes of dilute urine, dehydration, and altered mental status. Treatment is with desmopressin, an analog of vasopressin, which results in recovery of free water via aquaporin insertion in the collecting tubule.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Chronic renal failure (Choice A) can have variable etiology, and in children it may be caused by intrinsic renal disease such as polycystic kidney disease, chronic nephritic or nephrotic glomerular disease, or congenital urinary tract abnormalities leading to postrenal obstructive disease. It would be unlikely in this patient with normal creatinine and no history of kidney impairment.

questionStem: A 1-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of increasing irritability and difficulty breathing over the past 6 hours. She has a 3-day history of nasal congestion , cough , and rectal temperatures to 37.5°C (99.5°F). Over the past 2 days, she has been given an over-the-counter cough and cold preparation every 4 hours without improvement , and her parents have been suctioning her nose after applying saline nose drops . She has only breast-fed once in the past 6 hours. Her rectal temperature is 37.3°C (99.1 °F), pulse is 260/min , respirations are 65/min , and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation . The liver edge is palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin , and the spleen is not palpable . An ECG is shown . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) refers to an abnormally rapid heart rate and rhythm originating from above the ventricles, typically with a regular rhythm and a narrow QRS complex on ECG. Patients with SVT can manifest with acute symptoms of lightheadedness, palpitations, diaphoresis, and syncope. In infants, signs and symptoms can include pallor, irritability, poor feeding, and cyanosis. Infants who present with SVT typically have a pulse between 220 and 280/min. SVT may be caused by structural defects in the His-Purkinje system (eg, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome), or it may be provoked by alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, or psychological stress. In this patient, it may have been provoked by infection or use of an over-the-counter cough and cold preparation, which can contain pseudoephedrine, a sympathomimetic drug that can be used as a nasal decongestant. Because of its sympathomimetic effects, it can cause adverse reactions of tachycardia, anxiety, and palpitations. In patients who are hemodynamically unstable, cardioversion is indicated in the management of SVT. For patients who are hemodynamically stable, attempts can be made to terminate the tachyarrhythmia by vagal maneuvers (eg, ice or cold water over the face) or with adenosine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Atrial fibrillation (Choice A) can occur with a rapid ventricular rate but typically presents with irregular tachycardia. Atrial fibrillation also occurs more often in patients with structural heart disease, and supraventricular tachycardia is more likely in a previously healthy patient with regular tachycardia. Long QT interval syndrome (Choice B) is a disorder of prolonged ventricular depolarization and repolarization. It appears on ECG with a prolonged QT interval. It can be complicated by polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or torsades de pointes. Sinus tachycardia (Choice C) would be unlikely to have a pulse of 260/min. The maximal pulse from the sinus node is typically lower than 220/min and on ECG, there are P waves prior to every QRS complex. Pulse resulting from supraventricular tachycardia can be higher because of a reentrant rhythm that bypasses the atrioventricular node. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) (Choice E) shows a wide QRS complex tachycardia on ECG. VT occurs when an abnormal electrical focus or a reentry circuit causes rapid contraction of the ventricles. There are many criteria for defining VT on the rhythm strip, but the general morphology will show wide QRS complex tachycardia. There are monomorphic and polymorphic forms of VT. Treatment depends on the duration, type, and symptomatology. Educational Objective: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) refers to an abnormally rapid pulse and rhythm originating from above the ventricles, typically with a narrow QRS complex on ECG. II

questionStem: A previously healthy 14-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 2-month history of the left eye wandering . She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Examination of the eye shows left eye wandering . A photograph of the eyes is shown . The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This child presents with leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex) and a sensory exotropia, which is suggestive of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of retinal neuroendocrine cells and is the most common ophthalmic malignancy in children. Retinoblastoma results from inactivating mutations of both copies of the RB1 gene, which functions as a tumor suppressor by halting cell cycle progression at the G1 checkpoint.
