questionStem: An otherwise healthy 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of decreased libido and delayed ejaculation. He says that his symptoms are having a detrimental effect on his relationship. He has not had similar problems in the past. Four months ago, he was evaluated for low mood and loss of interest and productivity; his symptoms have been well controlled with sertraline since that time. He takes no other medications. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following neurotrans mitters is most likely responsible for this patient's current symptoms?
correctExplanation: Increased serotonin likely explains this patient's sexual dysfunction. Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that increases synaptic serotonin activity and improves mood in patients with major depressive disorder. SSRls common ly cause sexual dysfunction within all three phases of sexual response (libido, sexual arousal, and orgasm). If the sexual dysfunction is persistent and distressing, management commonly involves lowering the SSRI dose, switching to an antidepressant with a lower risk for sexual dysfunction (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine), or adding bupropion or a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil. Libido is typically enhanced by dopamine and gonadal hormones and may be inhibited by medications such as antipsychotics and SSRls. Arousal is promoted by acetylcholine, which leads to vasodilation of the helicine/vaginal arteries and consequent penile/clitora l tumescence. Medications with anticholinergic activity and SSRls inhibit arousal. Norepinephrine enhances orgasm (and ejaculation), and beta­ blockers and SSRls inhibit orgasm.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acetylcholine (Choice A) mediates arousal via the vasodilation of the helicine or vaginal arteries. Medications with anticholinergic activity, which include paroxetine but not sertraline within the SSRI class, may inhibit arousal but would not likely affect libido or ejaculation. y-Aminobutyric acid (Choice B), or GABA, is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. GABA is not known to be involved in sexual response. Dopamine (Choice C), which may be increased by methylphenidate, amphetamines, and cocaine, increases libido and may play a role in ejaculation. However, antidepressants do not affect dopamine signaling.

questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 27-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of pain in his neck and left shou lder radiating through the latera l surface of his left arm to his thumb and index finger. Exam ination shows a decreased biceps reflex on the left. Muscle strength is 4/5 on extension of the left wrist. Sensat ion to light touch is decreased over the left thumb and index finger. The remainder of the examination, including neurologic examination, shows no abnormal ities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: C6 radiculopathy is the most likely diagnosis. The C6 dermatome is located on the lateral aspect of the forearm and extends to the latera l two digits of the hand. Injury to the C6 nerve roots will cause decreased sensation, pain, and/or paresthesia in these distributions along with motor dysfunction of elbow flexion and wrist extension. The C6 nerve root carries efferent information for the biceps reflex. Dermatomes and myotomes are components of the embryonic somite, a paired segment of paraxial mesoderm. When fully developed, the dermatome is an area of skin whose afferent fibers trave l within a single spinal nerve, and myotome is a group of muscles innervated by efferent fibers from a single spinal nerve. Radiculopathy refers to patho logy of a spinal nerve root and may be caused by spondylosis (degenerative changes of the spine), disc herniation, infection, tumor, demyelination, or infarction. Disc herniation and spondylosis are the most common causes and lead to compression of the nerve root as it exits the spinal cord. Sensory deficits, motor dysfunction, and pain typica lly occur in the dermatomal and myotomal distribution that corre lates to the affected nerve root.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. C4 radiculopathy (Choice A) would lead to sensory and motor dysfunction in the neck and shoulders around the acromioclavicu lar joint. Sensory and motor dysfunction in the distal upper extremity and an absent biceps reflex are more consistent with C6 radicu lopathy. C5 radiculopathy (Choice B) would lead to sensory and motor dysfunction in the latera l aspect of the shoulder and upper arm. C5 radiculopathy typica lly results in an absent biceps reflex, as the C5 nerve root carries afferent information for this reflex. However, C5 radiculopathy would not cause decreased sensation in the digits. - -- - -- - . - - - - - -- - -- .. - - - - -- - -- -- - - .. -- - - .. --- - -- ..

questionStem: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of a ?-day history of increas ingly severe pain around the waist. He says that it feels like a burning belt from the left midback to the umbilicus. He has a history of chron ic low back pain. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glyburide and asthma treated with beclome thasone and albuterol inhalers. He comple ted a 10-day course of corticostero ids for asthma 3 weeks ago. Examination shows numbness in the left T12 distribution. The remainder of the exam ination shows no abnor malities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient's history of diabetes and presenting signs and symptoms of burning pain in a dermatomal distribution are, in the absence of other findings, consistent with a diagnosis of diabetic radiculopathy. Formation of advanced glycation end products in chronic diabetics leads to microvascular ischemic damage to various tissues, including to the vasa nervorum. This mechanism underlies the pathogenesis of both diabetic polyneuropathy, as well as diabetic radiculopathy. Diabetic thoracic radiculopathy presents with unilatera l burning and electric-like pain extending from the back to the anterior abdomina l midline in a dermatomal distribution that may involve one or several spinal levels. Patients often experience numbness and muscular weakness of the affected nerve distribution. Most patients experience improvement in their symptoms over several months with conservative treatment.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Ankylosing spondylitis (Choice A) is an autoimmune disorder affecting the axial joints, especial ly the intervertebral and sacroi liac joints. Patients present with slowly progressive, dull, lower back pain and stiffness that characteristically improves with activity. Patients usually present in the third decade of life and rarely experience burning pain. Atherosclerotic vascular disease (Choice B) may cause claudication, which presents with pain of the lower extremity that occurs in the setting of exercise and resolves with rest. Patients may experience coolness, pallor, hair loss, and poor wound healing of the affected limb. - - - - -- - .

questionStem: A 12-year-old girl with systemic lupus erythematosus is brought to the emergency department by her parents after they had difficulty awakening her this morning. She has needed constant stimulation to stay awake. Over the past 2 days, she has had a flu-like illness and vomiting. She has been unable to take her corticosteroid and antihypertensive medications. Her temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 60/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 180/130 mm Hg. She is obtunded but moves all extremities to painful stimuli. Funduscopic exam ination shows bilatera l papilledema with flame hemorrhages. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk and symmetric. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 12 mm/h. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy is a known complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and results from acute and severe increases in blood pressure. It may manifest with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizure, and can progress to obtundation and coma. Visual symptoms may result from cortical hypertension or from hypertensive retinopathy, manifesting as papilledema and flame hemorrhages on fundoscopic examination. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessively rapid drops, which can cause cerebral or cardiac ischemia. In genera l, a decrease in the mean arterial pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with gradual correction over the next day or more. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodi lator and is a preferred agent because of its short half-life, allowing it to be titrated via intravenous infusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Brain neoplasm (Choice A) can cause altered mental status in a subacute or chronic time course. It would be less likely in this patient who is presenting with acute hypertensive encephalopathy. Cerebral vasculitis (Choice B) as a manifestation of SLE is rare. Cerebral vasculitis can present with neurologic deficits, headache, seizures, or coma. Hypertensive encephalopathy is more likely in this patient. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice D) presents common ly in younger, overweight fema les taking vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazol. It is usually associated with a holocephalic headache and blurry vision.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 3-day history of increased drowsiness. During this period, she also has been feeding poorly and "spitting up" after each feeding. She has not had fever. She was born at term following an uncompl icated pregnancy and delivery. On arrival, she is respons ive to tactile stimuli. She is at the 25th percenti le for length and weight and 90th percenti le for head circumference. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a bulging anterior fontanel. There is a hyperpigmented macule with hair growth on the upper lumbar spine; her parents report that this finding was noted at birth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Chiari malformations are rare congenita l malformations that typical ly present in infancy with feeding and breathing problems, spina bifida (classically manifesting as myelomeningocele), and obstructive hydrocephalus (presenting as large head circumference and bulging anterior fontane l in this patient) as a result of the downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis and tonsils. This patient's hyperpigmented macule with hair growth on the upper lumbar spine likely represents spina bifida occulta (a small defect in the vertebrae). Some patients also demonstrate eye movement abnormalities. Some Chiari malformations present in adolescence with bilateral cranial nerve palsies, weakness, and cerebellar dysfunction as a result of the downward displacement of the cerebel lar tonsils and consequent brainstem compression. Imaging typically demonstrates downward displacement of the cerebe llar vermis and tonsils, along with ventriculomegaly from hydrocephalus. Treatment involves surgical intervention for neural tube defects, shunting for hydrocephalus, and medical management of feeding and respiratory difficulties.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bacterial meningitis (Choice A) typica lly presents with fever and signs of meningeal irritation (nausea, irritability, confusion, anorexia, headache, and nuchal rigidity). Spina bifida occulta is not associated with acute bacterial meningitis. Hydrocephalus may result from bacterial meningitis. Idiopathic increased intracrania l pressure (Choice C) would present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (nausea, vomiting, positional headache) without hydrocephalus or other central nervous system pathology. Spina bifida occulta would be atypical. - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - .

questionStem: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of headac hes accompanied by nausea and vomiting over the past 2 weeks; they are located behind the left eye and improve after sleep. The headaches started during final examinat ions, and she now is missing 2 to 3 days of school weekly because of the pain. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 95/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Migraine is a common condition that presents with recurrent primary headaches. Migraine headaches are typically severe, unilateral, throbbing, and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. The pain is usually located behind or adjacent to the eye. Some patients additiona lly experience an aura before or during the headache, which may present with vision loss followed by the perception of scintillating shapes or lines or paresthesia. Migraine triggers include stress, menstruation, weather changes, fasting, and alcoholic beverages. Sleep may improve migraines. Migraines are postulated to arise from deficient serotonin inhibition of descending pain pathways. Acute migraine treatment includes triptans and/or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For patients with disabling or frequent migraines, prophylactic treatment is also recommended and includes ~-adrenergic blockers, antidepressants such as tricyclic antidepressants and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and anticonvulsants.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Brain tumor (Choice A) may cause generalized headaches associated with vomiting that typically occur while patients are lying supine as a result of increased intracranial pressure and may be accompanied by papilledema and blurred vision. This patient's headache improved in the supine position. Cluster headaches (Choice B) are primary headaches that typically present with short-lived, unilateral, severe pain in the orbital, supraorbital, or temporal region of the head and are accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, miosis, ptosis, lacrimation, nasal congestion). This patient did not demonstrate autonomic symptoms. Sinusitis (Choice D) may be associated with bilateral, pressure-like, periorbital headaches and nasal congestion. Headaches are not typically associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia. This patient's unilatera l headaches that started during a stressful period are more consistent with migraine.

questionStem: Over the past year, a 72-year-old man has had progressive aching in his lower extremities when he walks in the shopp ing mall. Initial ly, the pain began after 15 minutes of walking and resolved after he stopped; now, it starts after 5 or 10 minutes of walking, and it occas ionally occurs when he stands up after sleeping all night. The pain radiates from his buttocks to his feet. He desc ribes it as a "terrib le" pain. He has mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease but cont inues to smoke one pack of cigarettes daily. He has cervical arthritis and often has neck and arm pain. Exam ination shows decreased breath sounds bilatera lly. Strength and sensation are normal in the extremities. Babinski's sign is absent bilatera lly. Deep tendo n reflexes are 1 + in both knees and ankles and 2+ in the upper extremities. Dorsalis ped is pulses are norma l. Wh ich of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Alcoholic rhabdomyolysis J) Hypoka lemic periodic paralysis
choices.B: Amyotrophic latera l scleros is K) Hypothyroid myopathy
choices.C: Becke r muscu lar dystrophy L) Lumbar spinal stenosis
choices.G: Epidura l metastatic carc inoma P) Sensorimotor periphera l neuropathy
choices.H: Epste in-Barr virus infection Q) Spinal cord compression

correctExplanation: Lumbar spinal stenosis refers to the narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal, which results in compression of the lumbar nerve roots or spinal cord. Patients may present with symptoms of radicu lopathy, including back pain that radiates to the buttocks and legs, leg numbness, paresthesia, or weakness. Hip extension increases pressure on the nerve roots, while flexion of the hips relieves pressure. Consequently, patients may demonstrate neurogenic claudication, in which extension of the hips (eg, standing or walking) leads to symptoms. The most common cause of lumbar spinal stenosis is degenerative joint disease and osteophytosis, which often occurs with age. The diagnosis is confirmed by MRI. Treatment involves nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, physical therapy, and surgery.
incorrectExplanation: , M, N, 0, P, and Q. Alcohol rhabdomyolysis (Choice A) refers to muscle necrosis from long-term alcohol use. Alcohol rhabdomyolysis wou ld present with diffuse pain. Amyotrophic latera l sclerosis (Choice B) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder featuring a combination of upper and lower motor neuron weakness patterns.

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 4-mo nth histo ry of increas ing low back pain that is most severe on awakening in the morning. His pain is relieved by stretching. There is no history of trauma. He is otherwise healthy except for occasional dysuria. Exam ination shows decreased forward flexion of the spine and tenderness over the lumbosac ral area and at the insertion site of the Achilles tendon. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Abdomina l aortic aneurysm G) Metastatic cance
choices.C: Herniated disc at L4-L5 I) Pyelonephritis
choices.D: lnterverteb ral discitis J) Rheumatoid arthritis
choices.F: Lumbar spinal stenosis L) Systemic lupus erythematos us

correctExplanation: Ankylosing spondyl itis (AS) refers to an inflammatory arthritis of the spine and other joints (eg, the sacroiliac joints) along with extra-articu lar inflammation. Patients typically present at younger than age 40 years with insidious chronic low back pain that worsens at night and improves with activity (caused by the mobilization of inflammatory materia l from joints). This pattern of pain is known as inflammatory back pain. Sacroi liac arthritis and enthesitis (inflammation of the attachments of tendons and ligaments to bone) are other common joint manifestations. Extra-articular manifestations commonly include anterior uveitis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowe l disease. AS is associated with reactive arthritis, which classical ly presents with post-infectious conjunctivitis, arthritis, and urethritis. Over time, patients with AS can develop decreased spine mobility, hyperkyphosis, osteopenia, and an increased risk for vertebra l fragility fractures. Laboratory studies demonstrate increased acute phase reactant concentrations (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate) along with a positive HLA-B27 test in many patients. Plain x-rays may illustrate fused vertebrae and sacroiliac joints. Treatment typica lly begins with nonsteroida l anti-inf lammatory drugs and escalates to disease-modifying immunomodulating medication in refractory cases.
incorrectExplanation: nd L. questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency depart ment 1 hour after a 25-m inute episode of right facia l droop, weakness of the right arm and hand, and an inability to talk. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, chron ic atrial fibr illation, and gout. Her medications include metoprolol, fosinopril, glyburide, and allopurinol. Her pulse is 80/min and irregular ly irregular, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg. Cardiac examinat ion shows no murmurs . Sensat ion is decreased to pinprick in the distal lower extremities. Achilles tendon reflexes are decreased. The remainder of the neurolo gic examination shows no abnormalities. A CT scan of the head shows no areas of infarction or hemorrhage . Echocardiography shows dilation of the left atrium with thrombus in the left atrial appendage, left ventricular hypertrophy, and mild mitral regurgitation. Carotid ultrasonography shows mild stenos is of both the right and left internal carot id arteries without thromb us or ulceration. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to prevent similar episodes in the future?
correctExplanation: Transient ischemic attack is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without evidence of infarction. This patient has multiple risk factors for ischemic stroke including hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, atherosclerotic disease, and atrial fibrillation. An embolic ischemic stroke involves an event in which a clot breaks off and travels to the brain, occluding blood flow at a cerebral artery. Emboli can come from proximal vessels, such as the internal carotid artery, or from an atrial thrombus. This patient has an atrial thrombus, which can embolize and cause an ischemic stroke. After a transient ischemic attack, measures for prevention of an ischemic stroke should be enacted. In this patient with atrial fibrillation and a known atrial thrombus, an anticoagulant would be the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to help prevent ischemic stroke. Warfarin is an anticoagulant that interferes with the carboxylation of coagulation factors. This occurs through the inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is necessary for recycling vitamin K, an essentia l cofactor in the synthesis of coagulation factors in the liver.

Ticlopidine (Choice D) is also an antiplatelet agent that inhibits platelet aggregation. It is not commonly used because of adverse effects of neutropenia and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. He has fractured his arm and has bruised himself many times . Bysta nders say that he suddenly becomes pale and sweaty and then slumps to the floor like a rag doll. Jerking or twitching movements of the trunk and extremities occur for severa l seconds during episodes. He recovers comp letely and is not confused at the end of the episode. He has had two myocardia l infarctions.

correctExplanation: Syncope is characterized by abrupt, transient loss of consciousness (LOC) with loss of postural tone. Syncope is genera lly caused by interruption of blood flow to the brain. Many causes of syncope are identifiable based on the history, and the patient's age and comorbidities. For example, vasovagal syncope is associated with a brief prodrome of lightheadedness, nausea, and diaphoresis, often in association with a fear-inducing event (eg, a patient loses consciousness when seeing a needle or blood). It occurs due to a sudden increase in vagal tone, leading to vasodilation and bradycardia (resulting in low cardiac output). In this case, the patient experienced a brief prodrome of pallor and diaphoresis, followed by LOC, in the setting of advanced age and a cardiac comorbidity. His age and cardiac history increase the likelihood of cardiogenic syncope (eg, a transient non-perfusing arrhythmia such as ventricu lar tachycardia); thus, investigation shou ld occur to determine the cause and prevent future episodes. Syncope is often accompanied by micturition, tongue biting, jerking, or twitching - these events are not exclusive ly associated with seizures. Syncope is generally not accompanied by a postictal period; patients usually return to their menta l base line within minutes of the event.

Complex partial seizure (Choice B) may involve a preceding aura, motor symptoms (especially motor automatisms such as lip-smacking or fidgeting), autonomic dysfunction, and/or confusion. They do not necessari ly involve loss of postura l tone.

He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within norma l limits. Exam ination shows mild ataxic dysarthria. Muscle strength is 5/5 throughout. questionStem: A 47-yea r-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of gradual hearing loss in the left ear. She also has had difficulty maintaining her balance over the past 3 months. Six months ago, she had an episode of nephrolithiasis complicated by a severe urinary tract infection requiring intravenous antibiotic therapy. Examination shows a decrease of the left nasolab ial fold and a slight perioral droop when she smiles. The forehead movements are intact bilaterally. Her gait is normal, but she has difficulty with tandem walking. Audiomet ry shows moderate high-frequency hearing loss on the left with impaired speech discrimination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient most likely has an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) compressing the vestibulocochlear nerve and the upper motor neurons that synapse on the facial nerve. Acoustic neuromas are benign tumors consisting of Schwann cells that arise from the vestibu locochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII). Lesions of the vestibulocochlear nerve typically disrupt ipsilateral hearing and the sensation of head and body position, which leads to difficulty with balance and tandem (heel-to-toe) gait as in this patient. Mass effect from progressive ly enlarging acoustic neuromas can compress the neighboring facial nerve or the upper motor neurons synapsing on the facial nerve, leading to a flattened nasolabial fold and perioral droop. If the upper motor neurons are affected, the forehead is spared, as the facial nerve nucleus that controls forehead musculature is dually innervated by upper motor neurons from bilateral precentral gyri. Because of this, the patient would be expected to symmetrically raise her eyebrows. Alternatively, lesions involving the lower motor neurons of facial expression (eg, facial nerve inflammation in Bell palsy) affect the forehead and lower face together. Depending on patient age, tumor size, and symptom burden, acoustic neuromas can be managed with observation, radiation, or surgery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aminoglycoside ototoxicity (Choice B) can damage the cochlea or the vestibular organs. However, facial nerve palsy and the onset of vestibular symptoms months after aminoglycoside exposure would be atypical. Brain stem infarction (Choice C) could lead to variable cranial nerve dysfunction. However, the onset would be acute and the cranial nerve deficits would occur simultaneously. This patient instead ,experienced slowly progressive cranial nerve dysfunction over months. Mastoiditis (Choice D) refers to an infection of the mastoid air cells in the mastoid bone, typically resulting from middle ear infection in children and presenting with acute ear pain and postauricular tenderness. questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 4 ?-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of progressively severe bifrontal headac he. He has a scant beard and a sallow, waxy comp lexion. Exam ination shows bilateral tem poral hemia nopia. Visua l acuity is norma l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Cluster headac hes G) Pituitary adenoma
choices.E: Occipital neuralgia K) Temporoma ndibular joint syndrome

correctExplanation: This patient's findings of headache and bitemporal hemianopsia are consistent with a diagnosis of pituitary adenoma. Benign adenomas are the most common neoplasms identified in the pituitary gland, and may secrete hormones, such as prolactin or growth hormone, causing symptoms of hyperpituitarism. More common ly, pituitary mass lesions do not cause hyperpituitarism but instead cause compression of normal pituitary neurons, leading to hypopituitarism and dysfunction of multiple endocrine axes. The pituitary gland rests in the bony sella turcica, just inferior to the optic chiasm. Retinal gang lion cell fibers from the nasal retina, which supply the temporal visual fields, decussate at the chiasm, and are vulnerable to compression by pituitary mass lesions. Since the decussating nasal retinal fibers carry information from the temporal visual fields, the resultant visual field deficit is most commonly a bitemporal hemianopsia, a finding suggestive of a pituitary mass.
incorrectExplanation: nd K. Cluster headaches (Choice A) present with severe, stabbing unilateral periorbital or fronta l pain, and are typica lly accompanied by signs and symptoms of ipsilateral dysautonomia, including lacrimation, conjunctiva! injection, and rhinorrhea. Cluster headaches do not typical ly produce visua l field deficits. Craniopharyngioma (Choice B) is a rare pituitary mass derived from remnants of the Rathke pouch that may present with bitemporal hemianopsia. However, it is more common in children. Pituitary adenoma is a more likely diagnosis in a previous ly healthy adult. Medulloblastoma (Choice C) is a common malignancy of the brain in children. It is an aggressive malignancy and produces signs and symptoms of headache, nausea and vomiting, and ocular symptoms of bilatera l abducens nerve palsy and papil ledema secondary to increased intracranial pressure. ~~. - ·- .. -. - - - ....... - - . ··-•- ·- . -• •- -· ·- ••- . - -· . . - - - . . - .. . ·••-. . - ..

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of worsening excess ive daytime sleepiness, even during important events such as meetings at work. She says she has trouble sustain ing her attention and that her symptoms are beginning to impair her work productivity. She also reports occasional episodes in which her muscles go limp and she falls sudden ly. She has injured herself during two of these episodes. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Her pulse is 85/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
correctExplanation: Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep disorder characterized by daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis that responds to modafinil therapy. Narcolepsy arises from deficient production of orexins in the hypothalamus, which may result from genetic or autoimmune causes. Orexins typica lly induce the secretion of monoamines such as norepinephrine throughout the brain to promote wakefulness. As a result, patients suddenly and inappropriate ly transition into sleep during the day. Further, rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep features (eg, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis) occur during wakefulness. Cataplexy refers to a sudden loss of muscle tone and usually occurs in response to positive emotion. The clinical diagnosis should be confirmed by a polysomnography (to confirm the rapid transition into REM sleep and rule out other causes of daytime sleepiness) and a multiple sleep latency test (to confirm decreased sleep latency). Treatment includes a regular sleep schedule, avoidance of daytime naps, and, in patients with severe daytime sleepiness, modafinil. Modafinil has an unclear mechanism of action that involves increasing orexin and monoamine availability.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Weight loss program (Choice A), continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) (Choice B), and uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (Choice F) all target obstructive sleep apnea. Obstructive sleep apnea features repetitive obstruction of the pharyngeal airway during sleep and typica lly occurs in older, male patients with obesity as a result of a combination of structura l, vascular, and neuromuscular factors. Patients become hypoxemic several times nightly and experience fragmented sleep, leading to daytime sleepiness. REM sleep phenomena during wakefulness is instead consistent with narco lepsy. In patients with suspected narcolepsy, comorbid obstructive slee a nea should be ruled out with ol somno ra h .

questionStem: A 68-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of a spinning sensation. She reports feeling as though the room is spinning particular ly when she tries to turn over in bed; the feeling usually resolves within 1 minute. She has no vomiting with an episode but does feel a little queasy. Examination shows normal hearing . Ocular movemen ts are full when the patient is sitting, but when her head is allowed to hang off the examination table, she develops a coarse, rotatory nystagmus beating to one side. The remainder of the exam ination shows no abnorma lities. The most likely cause of this patient's condition is an abnormality at which of the following sites?
correctExplanation: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is a common cause of vertigo that occurs as a result of a calcium carbonate particle (otoconium) that gets displaced from the otolith organs into the adjacent semicircu lar canals. The otolith organs and semicircu lar canals are located in the inner ear and sense movement of the head. Normally, otoconia are contained within the matrix of the otolith organs, adding weight to the organs so that the organs shift in position when head position changes. When otoconia become dislodged, they cause abnormal movement of the endolymph within the semicircular canals and the subsequent sensation of head movement. Consequently, patients present with minutes-long, abrupt episodes of vertigo that may be accompanied by nausea, which resolve when holding still. The cochlear apparatus is intact, resulting in norma l hearing. Symptom resolution with particle repositioning maneuvers such as the Epley maneuver serves to both diagnose and treat BPPV. Vertigo is the sensation that the surroundings are moving and is associated with lesions of the peripheral or central vestibular system. Peripheral vertigo is typically short- lived and sudden in onset, whereas central vertigo is insidious in onset and may cause constant and sustained vertigo. Peripheral causes of vertigo such as BPPV may also present with uni- or multidirectional nystagmus and may decrease as patients focus their gaze, while central causes of vertigo such as brainstem tumors or strokes typically lead to purely unidirectional nystagmus that does not improve with primary gaze.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Lesions of the auditory cortex (Choice A), located in the temporal lobe, result in impairment of the conscious perception of auditory sensations. The vestibular cortices are instead distributed across the parietal and temporal cortices. A brain stem (Choice B) mass of the cerebellopontine angle (eg, acoustic neuroma, meningioma, glioma) typically affects the vestibulocochlear nerve and may also affect other cranial nerves (eg, trigeminal, abducens, facial nerves). The resulting vertigo would likely be insidious in onset and constan t (rather than episodic); also likely to be accompanied by hearing loss. Additionally, sensory and

questionStem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents after the Thanksgiving holiday break because of a 4-day history of rapid, irregular involuntary movements of her face, trunk, and extremities. Her parents say that during this period, she has been anxious and irritable and has had headaches. She seems to be worry ing obsessive ly about things that formerly would not have worried her. She has no history of serious illness except for migratory joint pain that occurred in the early fall. Examination shows restless-appearing, genera lized involuntary movements of the face, trunk, and extremities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

choices.A: Autoimmune disorder of the basal ganglia

correctExplanation: This patient likely has Sydenham chorea, which is a manifestation of an autoimmune disorder of the basal ganglia. The combination of choreiform movements and migratory joint pain suggest a diagnosis of rheumatic fever, a complication of Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) infection. Though arthritis is typically an early manifestation of acute rheumatic fever, Sydenham chorea is a latent manifestation and may occur months after the initial streptococcal infection. In acute rheumatic fever, streptococca l infection causes immune cross-reactivity with neurona l and cardiac cell membrane proteins and the deposition of immune complexes in the joints and soft tissues. The binding of antibodies to basal ganglia neurons results in choreiform movements (involuntary, random, irregular movements) of the face, trunk, and extremities that may be more prominent on one side of the body. Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as emotional !ability and obsessive-compulsive disorder (a disorder associated with basal ganglia pathology) may also occur. Sydenham chorea may occur as an isolated manifestation of acute rheumatic fever or in conjunction with arthritis, carditis, erythema marginatum, and/or subcutaneous nodules. As such, patients with Sydenham chorea should receive an echocardiography to evaluate for carditis. The treatment of acute rheumatic fever involves nonsteroida l anti-inf lammatory drugs and penicillin to ensure the eradication of Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). Sydenham chorea is typical ly self-limited, but severe and impairing neuropsychiatric symptoms may be managed with antipsychotic or anticonvulsant medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Conversion disorder (Choice B), or functional neurologic disorder, involves acute neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not fully explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. This patient's symptoms and physical examination findings are instead consistent with a known disease.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman with breast cancer metastatic to bone is brought to the emergency department because of a 12-hour history of severe pelvic pain and numbness. She has not urinated for more than 24 hours. Her only medication is hydrocodo ne. On arrival, her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 152/70 mm Hg. Rectal examination shows decreased rectal sphincter tone. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the lower extremities. Sensation to light touch is decreased in a saddle distribution. Abdomina l examination shows suprapubic fullness. Placement of a urinary catheter yields 800 ml of clear yellow urine and resolves the pelvic pain but not the numbness. An MRI of the spine shows a tumor pushing into the L4-S 1 intrathecal space. Which of the following is the most appropr iate immediate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome occurs because of compression of the spinal nerve roots comprising the cauda equina. Often, such compression occurs as a result of malignancy, trauma (eg, compression fractures with fragment retropulsion), disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spinal epidural abscess, or spinal epidura l or subdural hematoma. Symptoms include lower extremity numbness, weakness, paralysis, hyporeflexia, perinea! anesthesia, fecal incontinence with poor rectal tone, and overflow incontinence marked by inability to void and urinary retention. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to investigate the cause of cauda equina syndrome, and to determine the necessity of surgical decompression. Initial treatment for patients with epidural spinal cord compression and neurologic deficits include symptomatic treatment, pain control, and glucocorticoid therapy prior to operative therapy. High-dose glucocorticoid therapy (eg, dexamethasone) is helpful as a bridge to definitive therapy, can help control pain, and may transient ly improve neurologic function secondary to decreasing edema at the site of cord compression.

In a patient who takes hydrocodone and is opiate-tolerant, pain control will likely require opioid analgesics. Intravenous or intrathecal administration of chemotherapy (Choices C and D) or radiation therapy (Choice E) may all be helpful for definitive treatment of the tumor, but glucocorticoids are the next immediate step in management. Radiation therapy can help with expeditious local control of spinal metastases. Chemotherapy can be helpful for tumors causing cauda equina, however, systemic chemotherapy may take days to weeks to take effect. questionStem: A 42-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband after he found her in a confused state when he returned home from a 3-day fishing trip. She has a long-standing relapsing psychiatric condition controlled with lithium carbonate, haloperidol, and clonazepam. She does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. She appears drowsy. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. The pupils are 2 mm and reactive. There is a coarse tremor of the upper extrem ities. Deep tendon reflexes are increased throughout. She responds only to vigorous stimulation. On mental status examinat ion, her speech is slow and slurred. She appears perplexed and sleepy and does not respond to questions. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 14,000/mm3 Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine Lithium 60 mg/dL 2.5 mg/dL 3.5 mEq/dL (therapeutic range=0.6-1.2) In addition to discont inuing lithium carbonate, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The patient presents with signs and symptoms of lithium toxicity including confusion, neuromuscular excitabi lity, coarse tremors, and myoclonic jerks. Severe lithium toxicity can cause seizures, status epilepticus, and encepha lopathy. Lithium is also associated with kidney toxicity and end-stage kidney disease. Lithium is filtered in the glomeru lus and is reabsorbed in the proximal tubules. Increased lithium reabsorption can occur in states of volume depletion and decreased lithium clearance can occur in kidney impairment. Management of lithium toxicity includes intravenous fluid resuscitation to maximize lithium clearance. Hemodialysis may be necessary in patients with severe lithium toxicity, seizures, altered mental status, or end-stage kidney disease resulting in impaired ability to excrete lithium.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Observation only (Choice A) would be inappropriate in this patient with severe lithium toxicity. Lithium is primarily excreted in the urine, which would be impaired in this patient with acute kidney injury. Therefore, in this case, lithium should be cleared by hemodialysis.

questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 62-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of intermittent drooping of his left eyelid and episodes of double vision. Neurologic examinat ion shows bilatera l ptosis, more prominent on the left. There is weakness of left eye abduction and adduction and weakness of right eye abduction. Pupillary reflexes are normal. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?
correctExplanation: This patient's presenting findings of intermittent ptosis, diplopia, and reduction of extraocular movements are suggestive of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis is a B lymphocyte-driven autoimmune disorder characterized by the formation of inhibitory anti-acetylcholine receptor autoantibodies. Patients typically experience muscular weakness and fatigue that worsens toward the end of the day, as well as ocular symptoms of drooping eyelids and diplopia. Many patients present with ocular findings and later develop generalized symptoms involving the proximal muscles. In severe exacerbations (myasthenic crises), patients may deve lop weakness of the muscles of the throat, diaphragm, and chest wall, leading to dysphagia and acute respiratory failure. Myasthenia gravis is diagnosed with the detection of serum autoantibodies. A chest x-ray is useful for detecting the presence of thymoma, which frequently produces myasthenia gravis as a paraneoplastic phenomenon. Some patients experience resolution of symptoms after surgical resection of a thymoma, although most patients require treatment with corticosteroids and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (eg, pyridostigmine). Myasthenic crisis is treated with intravenous immune globulin, plasmapheresis, intubation, and mechanical ventilation.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Colon cancer (Choice A) is common in elderly patients, but rarely produces orbital metastases. Colon cancer more frequent ly metastasizes to the liver. While colon cancer may produce paraneoplastic findings, such as the Leser-Trelat sign, characterized by the sudden appearance of numerous seborrheic keratosis on the back and trunk, it does not typically cause myasthenia gravis. Lymphoma (Choice B) may occur in the orbit, typically involving the conjunctiva or the orbital adnexal tissues such as the lacrimal gland, extraocular muscles, and eyelids. Patients typica lly present with unilateral proptosis and may present with ptosis or diplopia. However, these symptoms would be progressive and unremitting, rather than intermittent. questionStem: Over the past 3 months, a 60-year-o ld woman has had 2-minute episodes characterized by a rising sensation in the abdomen followed by loss of awareness. During an episode, she stares, makes chewing movements, and makes fumb ling moveme nts with her hands; afterwards, she is confused for a few minutes. Visual fields are shown. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities. The most likely diagnosis is a lesion at which of the following locations?
correctExplanation: This patient's visual fields demonstrate a left superior field quadrantanopia. In conjunction with her symptoms of seizures, characterized by staring, chewing movements, automatisms of the hands, and postictal confusion, a left superior field quadrantanopia raises concern for a lesion of the right tempora l lobe, such as an astrocytoma. After decussating at the optic chiasm, retinal gang lion cell axons carrying information from the left visual field traverse the optic radiations and synapse at the lateral geniculate nucleus. Neurons from the latera l geniculate nucleus travel to the primary visual cortex via the optic radiations, which divide into superior and inferior divisions. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous Next Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause .... https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 33 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Clinical Neurology Self-Assessment Please Walt • • • C) Optic nerve D) Parietal lobe E) Temporal lobe Correct Answer: E. This patient's visual fields demonstrate a left superior field quadrantanopia. In conjunction with her symptoms of seizures, characterized by staring, chewing movements, automatisms of the hands, and postictal confusion, a left superior field quadrantanopia raises concern for a lesion of the right tempora l lobe, such as an astrocytoma. After decussating at the optic chiasm, retinal ganglion cell axons carrying information from the left visual field traverse the optic radiations and synapse at the lateral geniculate nucleus. Neurons from the lateral geniculate nucleus travel to the primary visual cortex via the optic radiations, which divide into superior and inferior divisions. The right superior division travels through the right parietal lobe and carries information from the right inferior visual fields. In contrast, the right inferior division travels through the right temporal lobe by looping around the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, forming the Meyer loop, and carries information from the right superior visua l fields. Lesions of the tempora l lobe that interrupt the Meyer loop produce a characteristic contralatera l superior quadrantanopia, a visua l defect described as a wedge-shaped loss of vision.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. The frontal lobe (Choice A) contains the frontal eye fields, which are important in the generation of eye movements. Lesions affecting the frontal eye fields can produce an ipsilateral conjugate gaze preference but do not produce visua l field deficits. The occipital lobe (Choice B) is the location of the primary visual cortex. Lesions of the occipital lobe produce homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. The optic nerve (Choice C) carries all the visual information from the retina of its respective eye. A lesion of the optic nerve, such as in the setting of glioma, demye linating optic neuritis, or trauma, produces a complete visual field defect of one eye. The parietal lobe (Choice D) contains the superior division of the optic radiation, which carries information from the inferior visua l fields. A unilateral lesion of the parietal lobe may produce a contralateral inferior visual field quadrantanopia. Educational Objective: Temporal lobe lesions that interrupt the Meyer loop of the inferior division of the optic radiation produce a characteristic contralateral superior visua l field quadrantanopia. Superior visual field quadrantanopia in conjunction with symptoms of seizures should raise suspicion for a mass of the tempora l lobe, such as an astrocytoma.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 57-year-o ld man comes for a follow-up examination because of progress ive weakness of his arms and legs. Six months ago, examination showed no abnorma lities except for 4/5 muscle strength in all extrem ities. Current examinat ion shows fascicu lations in the hands and right lower extremity and pseudobu lbar palsy. Sensat ion is normal and cranial nerves are intact. He is oriented, and affect is appropriate. An MRI of the brain shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's disease?

choices.D: Neoplastic infiltration of the central nervous system
choices.F: Neuronal loss in the substantia nigra

correctExplanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder arising in midlife that affects both lower motor neurons arising from the anterior horn and upper motor neurons of the lateral corticospinal tract within the brain and spinal cord. Neurons degenerate because of an unknown etiology that may involve RNA processing and/or excitotoxicity, and gliosis results. Patient presentations are variable, though typically feature a combination of upper motor neuron (eg, increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) and lower motor neuron findings (eg, decreased muscle tone, hyporeflexia, early muscle atrophy) in an asymmetric distribution that may include the bulbar muscles. Some patients may experience cognitive or behavioral changes, though other patients are cognitively normal. The diagnosis is primarily clinical but may be supported by electromyographic findings of acute and chronic denervation and reinnervation. MRI of the brain and spine should be performed to rule out other diseases. Treatment should include riluzole, which may modestly improve survival but does not cure the disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Amyloid deposition (Choice A) occurs in Alzheimer disease. Alzheimer disease may feature apraxia (potentially related to parietal cortex damage) but does not typically lead to upper neuron or lower motor neuron dysfunction. Demyelination (Choice B) occurs in acute conditions such as pontine myelinolysis and chronic autoimmune disorders such as multiple sclerosis. Demyelination can affect the white matter of the corticospinal tract but would not affect the anterior horns (gray matter). Neoplastic infiltration of the central nervous system (Choice D) may lead to localized upper motor neuron dysfunction because of mass effect. However, generalized dysfunction in both an upper and lower motor neuron pattern is more consistent with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

questionStem: A 62-year-o ld man is brought to the physician by his wife because of a 3-year history of progressive forgetfulness. He has difficulty remembering names, especia lly of people he has recently met. He retired from his profession as a retail clerk 12 weeks ago because he had been forgetting the names of customers and new products and could no longer effectively perform his job. He also has had progressive difficulty with activities of daily living; his wife now chooses his clothes for him. He has no history o1f head trauma. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Physical examination shows no abnorma lities. On mental status examination, he has an indifferent mood and affect. He is oriented to person, place, and time but takes a few minutes before he correctly names the date. His Mini-Menta l State Examination score is 22/30. There is no evidence of auditory or visua l hallucinations. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Administration of a drug from which of the following classes is most appropriate for this patient?
correctExplanation: Alzheimer dementia (AD) results from decreased cholinergic signaling and is treated with acetylcho linesterase inhibitors. Cholinergic neurons-which primarily originate from the locus coeruleus and basal forebrain and project widely to areas including the cortex­ mediate attention, learning, and memory. AD is the most prevalent dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive decline that begins with short-term memory impairment and decline in visuospatial abilities and progresses to apraxia, language abnormalities, and dysexecutive syndrome (resulting in the inability to pick out clothes in this patient). The disease culminates in behaviora l and personality changes that prevent the patient from performing basic activities of daily living, such as bathing. Acetylcholinesterase normally hydrolyzes acetylcholine in synaptic clefts. Donepezil and other cholinesterase inhibitors non-competitively and reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase activity and thereby increase the amount of synaptic acetylcholine available for neurotransmission. Though donepezil may slow the rate of cognitive decline and modestly improve functiona lity, donepezil and the other cholinesterase inhibitors are not curative.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dopamine agonists (Choice B) increase dopamine signaling and therefore relieve parkinsonism. This patient does not demonstrate motor findings typical of Parkinson disease such as tremor, bradykinesia, or postural instability. NMDA receptor agonists (Choice C), such as endogenous glutamate, mediate activity-dependent synaptic changes of learning and memory. Howeve r, NMDA agonism is not a known drug mechanism because of the risk for excitotoxicity.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 20 minutes after he was found by a janito r on the floor of a restroom at a bus station. At the scene, he was having continuous, genera lized tonic-clon ic seizures. An endotracheal tube was placed, and supplementa l oxygen was administered. On arrival to the emergency department, he is flushed and diaphoret ic. There are no external signs of trauma. His temperatu re is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg. The pupils are 4 mm and reactive to light. Examination shows tonic stiffening of the trunk and synchronous clonic jerking of the extrem ities. In addition to intravenous administration of dextrose, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatme nt?
correctExplanation: Status epilepticus is defined as continuous epileptic activity for at least five minutes, or at least two discrete seizures with incomp lete interval recovery of consciousness. Status epilepticus is a neurologic emergency that portends increased morbidity and requires prompt evaluation and treatment. The first-line treatment for convulsive status epilepticus involves benzodiazepines (eg, lorazepam, midazolam, or diazepam), which have been shown to control seizures rapidly. Benzodiazepines bind the GABAA receptor, a chloride channel, and increase the frequency of its opening. y-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that counterbalances neuronal excitation, making benzodiazepines an effective treatment for seizure cessation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Fosphenytoin (Choice A) blocks sodium channels and is typically a second-line choice in the treatment of status epilepticus. Benzodiazepines are the first-line treatment of convulsive status epilepticus. Naloxone (Choice C) is an opioid receptor antagonist used in the treatment of opiate or opioid overdoses, which classica lly present with bradypnea and pinpoint pupils. Naloxone has also been used to treat clonidine overdose. Phenobarbital (Choice D) can be effective for controlling seizures, however it is not the first-line pharmacotherapy as a result of slow administration and adverse effects of prolonged sedation and hypotension. Valproic acid (Choice E) increases sodium channel inactivation and increases GABA concentration. It is typically second- line in the treatment of status epilepticus.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 37-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of a 10-day history of increasingly severe headaches. The pain has been unremitt ing for the past 18 hours; he describes it as severe and pounding. His pulse is 70/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg. Examination of the face and neck shows mild swelling and a dusky reddish-purple skin color with venous distention over the head and neck; the skin color below the neck is normal. Examinat ion of the optic fundi shows papilledema. Neurologic examinat ion shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's increased intracrania l pressure?

choices.C: Obstruct ion of cerebrospina l fluid flow
choices.D: Obstruction of venous return to the heart

correctExplanation: Obstruction of venous return to the heart through the superior vena cava (SVC) leads to superior vena cava syndrome, which presents with facial swelling, headaches, and occasional ly altered mental status or respiratory distress. Superior vena cava syndrome is most common ly caused by extrinsic compression of the SVC by an intrathoracic malignancy, such as lung cancer or lymphoma. Physical examination typically shows facial plethora, venous distension over the head and neck, and papilledema, as in this patient. While a chest x-ray may be abnormal, CT venography is typically diagnostic. Stent placement and radiation therapy are used to treat symptoms, but superior vena cava syndrome is classically associated with a poor prognosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dilation of cerebral arteries (Choice A) is associated with the development of migraine headaches, which present with unilateral, pounding-type headaches that are associated with photophobia and phonophobia. They typically last for less than 48 to 72 hours and may have a preceding aura. They do not cause facial plethora and venous distension. An intracrania l mass lesion (Choice B) classically presents with focal neurologic deficits, such as hemiplegia, altered mental status, and signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as headache and nausea. Physical examination may demonstrate papilledema. However, it would not be expected to cause discoloration of the face or venous distension of the head and neck. Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow (Choice C) and overproduction of cerebrospinal fluid (Choice E) can both lead to hydrocephalus. Hydrocephalus commonly presents with headache, altered mental status or behavior, and nausea or vomiting because of increased intracranial pressure. While papilledema may be present, venous distension would not be.

questionStem: Five days after a left hemicolectomy for colon cancer, a 62-year-old man is transferred to the intensive care unit because of temperatures to 40.6°C (105°F), lethargy, diaphores is, and labile blood pressure for 3 hours. His postoperative course had been complicated by temperatures to 37.8°C (100°F) and nocturnal agitation since day 2; he has required haloperidol therapy (2 mg nightly). He has a history of bipolar disorde r. Medications include morphine by patient-controlled analgesia pump, lithium carbonate, and clonazepam. He is lying expression less in a pool of sweat and is drooling. His temperature is 40.6°C (105°F), pulse is 140/min, and blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. Examination shows wet skin and dry mucosa. There is a herpetic lesion on his lower lip. The neck is supple and the intraveno us catheter insertion site is nontender with no erythema. Bowel sounds are hyperactive; there is no organomega ly. The wound is clean and dry with no erythema. Neurologic examination shows a masked facies and a marked intention tremor. Deep tendon reflexes are hyperactive and symmetric. Babinski sign is absent. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglob in Leukocyte count Segmented neutrophils Bands Lymphocytes Monocytes Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine Creatine kinase 15 g/dL 20,000/mm 3 80% 5% 10% 5% 38 mg/dL 1.6 mg/dL 1000 U/L Urinalys is and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is most likely in this patient who has received high-potency antipsychotic medication. NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity or tremor, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especia lly high-potency antipsychotics r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous Next Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause .... https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 38 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Clinical Neurology Self-Assessment Correct Answer: E. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is most likely in this patient who has received high-potency antipsychotic medication. NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity or tremor, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especia lly high-potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol) and antidopaminergic nausea medications. Rigidity and tremor result from dopamine antagonism in the nigrostriatal pathway, while autonomic dysfunction and hyperthermia may result from dopamine antagonism in the hypothalamus. Characteristic laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis along with increased serum concentration of creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and alkaline phosphatase (as a result of prolonged muscle rigidity and consequent myolysis). Treatment is supportive and includes discontinuation of the offending medication, hydration, cooling blankets, and benzodiazepines if needed for agitation. Dantrolene is potentially beneficial.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Antibiotic-related fever (Choice A) is unlikely in this patient. While some antibiotics can cause mild increases in body temperature, marked hyperthermia is not a common side effect of antibiotic therapy. Furthermore, this patient is not current ly taking antibiotics. Herpes encepha litis (Choice B) presents with fever, altered mental status, and neurologic abnorma lities, such as seizure, aphasia, hemiparesis, or cranial nerve deficits. Neuroimaging will typically demonstrate changes in the tempora l lobe. Encephalitis is commonly associated with nuchal rigidity, which this patient does not demonstrate, making herpes encephalitis a less likely cause of his presentation. Additiona lly, an increased creatine kinase concentration is not consistent with herpes encephalitis. Lithium toxicity (Choice C) presents with nausea, vomiting, dysrhythmias, altered mental status, and neuromuscu lar excitability, such as tremors in acute toxicity. Chronic toxicity has more prominent neuro logic symptoms and can also cause nephrogenic diabetes insipid us. Malignant hyperthermia (Choice D) is caused by a genetic defect in the ryanodine receptor and presents with muscle rigidity, tachycardia, fever, lactic acidosis, and hypercarbia when the patient is exposed to succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics. While the presentation is similar to NMS, this patient has not been exposed to agents that trigger malignant hyperthermia since his surgery, making this a less likely cause of his illness. Postoperative sepsis (Choice F) presents with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and leukocytosis, as well as hypotension and lactic acidosis if the patient is in septic shock, in the setting of a known or suspected infection. It is rarely associated with hypertension. Furthermore, this patient has no signs of infection on physical examination. Educational Objective: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Characteristic laboratory abnorma lities include leukocytosis along with increased concentrations of creatine kinase, alkaline phosphatase, and lactate dehydrogenase.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency depart ment because of progress ive visual dimming in her right eye since awakening 8 hours ago. Her symptoms began with a mild headache over her right eye before going to bed last night. She says this headac he is different than her usual migraines that have improved since she started treatment with propranolol. Fundusco pic exam ination shows no abnorma lities of the right eye, but the patient cannot read and can barely count fingers with the right eye. Visua l acuity in the left eye is norma l. A CT scan of the head shows normal findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Optic neuritis results from autoimmune demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve and presents in young, often female, patients with unilatera l vision loss and pain that is exacerbated with extraocular movements. Ocular examination demonstrates reduced visua l acuity and color vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and may demonstrate optic disc edema. Diagnosis is confirmed with MRI demonstrating hyperintensity of the optic nerve. Patients with optic neuritis are at increased risk for multiple sclerosis (MS), and optic neuritis is a common initial finding in patients with MS. Recently, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) have been identified as causative of some cases of optic neuritis. Patients who develop optic neuritis as a result of antibodies against MOG and AQP4 often have severe presentations but also have decreased risk for subsequent MS compared to patients with optic neuritis who lack these autoantibodies. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial demonstrated that a short course of treatment with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone speeds the rate of visual recovery and delays the onset of MS, although it does not impact final visual acuity, and demonstrated that the presence and quantity of periventricular white matter lesions on MRI is the most important prognostic risk factor for the subsequent development of MS.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Diabetic retinopathy (Choice A) results from microvascular damage to retinal capillaries and is characterized by the presence of microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhages, and retinal nerve fiber layer infarctions. Diabetic retinopathy is usually symmetric between both eyes and is not painful.

questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 4 ?-year-o ld man is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of progressive weakness. He says that during this period, his feet "flop" while walking, and he trips when walking up stairs. During the past week , he has had difficulty standing up from low chairs and open ing jars. He has not had pain or tingling. He has had constipation but no changes in bladder or sexual functio n. He has not had any recent infections or vaccinations. He takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He drinks three to four beers daily; for the past 6 weeks he has been drinking home-d istilled whiskey. Examination shows atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the hands and feet. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the wrist and finger extensors, interosseous, iliopsoas, and hamstring muscles and 3/5 in the anterior tibialis, peronei, and posterior tibial is muscles. Deep te ndon reflexes are 1 + diffuse ly. Babinski sign is absent. Sensory examination shows no abnorma lities. Laboratory studies show microcytic anemia and hyperuricemia . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's neurologic symptoms?
correctExplanation: Symptoms of acute lead poisoning occur within days or weeks of exposure and include abdominal pain, constipation, arthra lgia, myalgias, muscle weakness, excessive fatigue, headache, and difficulty concent rating. With prolonged exposure, chronic neurologic symptoms such as decline in cognition, depression, distal motor neuropathy, decreased hearing, tremor, and decreased brain volume on imaging may be present. The distal motor neuropathy causes lower motor neuron signs such as atrophy of muscles and hyporeflexia, as shown in this patient. Microcytic anemia is also common, since lead inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and o-ALA dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. In adults, exposure to lead primarily comes through occupation and/or hobbies. Individuals working with batteries, mining, construction , or ammunition are at higher risk. Illegally distilling alcohol has a risk for lead toxicity because of the leaching of lead from solder in the still, which is likely where this patient received exposure. Diagnosis is suspected based on exposure and symptoms and confirmed with increased serum lead concentration. Management of lead poisoning depends on the blood lead concen tration and presence of symptoms, and includes chelation with dimercaprol, ethylene diamine tetraacetate, or succimer. Sources of lead should be investigated and eliminated.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acute intermittent porphyria (Choice A) is an autosoma l dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase, resulting in deficient synthesis of heme and accumulation of porphobilinogen. Patients typically present during an acute attack with psychosis, abdominal pain, muscle weakness, neuropathy, and burgundy-colored urine. This patient's subacute presentation in the context of alcohol distillation is more consistent with lead poisoning.

questionStem: An 18-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he fell 25 feet. On examination, he is paraplegic and has urinary incontinence . Examination of the lower extremities shows absent reflexes and flaccid tone. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. X-rays of the spine show a fracture dislocat ion of T10. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's urinary incontinence?

choices.B: Compression of the S3-4 nerve roots
choices.C: Compression of the T10- 11 nerve roots
choices.D: Compression of the thoracic spinal cord

correctExplanation: An injury at the level of the thoracic spinal cord would affect the thoracic cord and may also affect segments distal to the level of the injury, including the lumbosacral segments that innervate lower extremity musculature and sensation. An injury at the level of T10 can affect sympathetic efferent fibers that provide inhibitory input to the bladder and urethra via the hypogastric nerve. Sympathetic stimulation through these fibers usually causes relaxation of bladder musculature and contraction of urethra l sphincter, resulting in urinary retention. Injury to these fibers will cause urinary incontinence as a result of impaired inhibition of bladder contraction. Spina l cord pathologies that result in urinary incontinence result in complex interactions between signals from the parasympathetic, sympathetic, and somatic nervous systems and may present with urge or overflow incontinence, altogether termed neurogenic bladder.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Compression of the conus medullaris (Choice A) often occurs at the level of L2. It can also present with sphincter dysfunction, spastic or flaccid paralysis, as well as saddle anesthesia. An injury at T10 would be unlikely to affect the conus medullaris. Compression of the S3-4 nerve roots (Choice B) describes cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina syndrome presents with low back pain, weakness of lower extremities, bladder and rectal sphincter paralysis leading to urinary retention, and sensory deficits. Compression of the T10-11 nerve roots (Choice C) would result in a thoracic radiculopathy in a dermatomal distribution resulting in pain and numbness around the umbilicus. Rupture of the bladder neck (Choice E) would present with hematuria, pelvic pain, lower abdominal pain, and difficulty voiding. It would be unlikely to be the cause of the patient's urinary incontinence and would not present with lower extremity neurologic symptoms.
