Bacterial meningitis presents acutely with fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status in a toxic-appearing patient. While immunosuppressed patients are at risk for bacterial meningitis, this patient's subacute history of mild symptoms is more consistent with cryptococca l meningitis. Additionally, CSF analysis in bacterial meningitis would show a neutrophi lic predominance. Intravenous methylprednisolone (Choice D) is used in the treatment of allergic or autoimmune reactions, multiple sclerosis exacerbations, and a variety of other conditions. Multiple sclerosis presents with various neurologic lesions occurring over varying periods of time, with an acute exacerbation defined as a new neurologic impairment associated with a new brain or spinal cord lesion on MRI. It does not typically present with signs of meningeal irritation. Additionally, CSF in multiple sclerosis consists of a lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal protein concentration, and the presence of oligoclonal bands. questionStem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-wee k history of moderate pain, numbness , and tingling in her right hand. She states that the pain is worse at night and is not relieved with acetam inophen or ibuprofen. She has a 10-year history of chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis treated with thyroid hormone therapy. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examina tion, tapping the palmar surface of the right wrist elicits a tingling sensation in the thumb and index fingers. Her serum thyroid-stim ulating hormone concentratio n is 2 µU/ml. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's symptoms?

choices.A: Immunolog ic damage to the brachia! nerve
choices.B: Immunolog ic damage to the median nerve
choices.C: Immunolog ic damage to the radial nerve
choices.D: Immunolog ic damage to the ulnar nerve
choices.E: Mechanical entrapment of the brachia I nerve
choices.F: Mechanical entrapment of the median nerve
choices.G: Mechanical entrapment of the radial nerve
choices.H: Mechanical entrapment of the ulnar nerve

correctExplanation: Mechanica l entrapment of the median nerve leading to carpal tunnel syndrome is the most likely mechanism of this patient's symptoms. The carpal tunnel describes a conduit in the wrist that is formed by the flexor retinaculum anteriorly and the carpal bones posteriorly. Both the median nerve and the flexor tendons of the fingers trave l through this canal. Increased pressure in this canal can lead to compression of the median nerve, resulting in paresthesias of the first three digits, primarily on the palmar surface. When severe, weakness of the thumb with atrophy of the thenar eminence may occur. The Tinel test involves tapping the volar surface of the wrist in the midline. A positive test, as in this case, leads to tingling in the first two digits and occasionally the third digit, which corresponds with the distribution of the median nerve. This condition occurs common ly in those with jobs that involve repetitive wrist movement such as typing, but it can be idiopathic. It commonly develops in obese patients and is more common in women. Nighttime symptoms are frequently encountered, and the initial treatment requires wrist splints worn at night. Refractory or severe symptoms may be referred for surgical intervention.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Immunologic damage to the brachia! (Choice A), median (Choice B), radial (Choice C), or ulnar (Choice D) nerves may occur in neuralgic amyotrophy, also called Parsonage-Turner syndrome, which is thought to be related to immune-mediated damage of the nerves of the brachia! plexus. It most commonly involves the nerves of the upper or middle brachia! plexus but can involve more distal, singular nerves. Patients develop debilitating pain and weakness that gradually improve over months.

questionStem: After falling from a horse during a steeplechase, a 42-year-old man has immediate paralysis in all four extremities and has loss of sensation below the clavicles bilaterally. On examination by paramedics , he is alert, dyspneic, and unable to move his extrem ities or trunk. His pulse is 98/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. After transport to a trauma center, his sensory examination returns to normal, and he regains normal strength of the arms and forearms, although the hands and lower extremities remain weak. Examination shows bladder distention. An MRI of the cervical spine shows contusion with edema of the spinal cord at C3 and C4. Plain x-rays of the cervical spine show a nondisplaced fracture of the vertebral body of C3. Which of the following is the most appropr iate next step in management?

choices.F: Surgical exploration of the cervical spine

correctExplanation: ~ Next Spinal cord compression can occur in the setting of trauma, malignancy with vertebral metastases, and infections (eg, epidural abscess). Its presentation depends on the level of the lesion and the degree of spinal cord compression. Traumatic spinal cord injury is typica lly caused by fracture or dislocation of the vertebrae. Acute traumatic spinal cord injuries typica lly cause immediate compression or shearing of the spinal cord, with a secondary injury of the spina l cord occurring after the initial injury because of consequent inflammation, edema, and ischemia. Symptoms include back or neck pain, flaccid paralysis, numbness, bowel and bladder incontinence or retention, and hyporeflexia. Patients may also deve lop neurogenic shock, depending on the level of injury, with bradycardia and hypotension secondary to injury to the sympathetic outflow tract, as well as respiratory failure caused by diaphragmatic paralysis. Diagnosis is classically made using MRI of the spine, as well as spinal x-rays or CT to visualize skeleta l abnormalities. Management includes clinical stabilization, and the use of intravenous glucocorticoid therapy to decrease spinal cord edema. Patients may also require intubation and mechanical ventilation, vasopressor support, cardiac pacing, and/or surgical spine stabilization.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Intravenous ceftriaxone therapy (Choice A) is used in the treatment of bacteria l meningitis, along with vancomycin and, depending on patient age, ampicillin. Bacteria l meningitis presents acutely with fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status in a toxic-appearing patient, although it can also cause focal neurologic deficits. - • . . - .. - •• • - • •• •• - . - • - - . - • • • • • • • . • . . • - • . • • ••• • - -. -. . :1 • • • • • •• . . - . . • ••

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by police after he was found in a state of confusion outside a convenience store. He says he feels anxious. He has not had fever, headac he, abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. He has a 3-year history of uncontrolled hypertension. He has no allergies and takes no medications. He does not smoke. He usually drinks 12 to 14 beers daily. He says he has never used illicit drugs. He is disheveled and agitated and picks at imaginary things in the air. He is disoriented to person, place, and time. His temperatu re is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 160/105 mm Hg. Examination shows diaphoresis and trem ulousness. There is seborrhea and rosacea of the face. There are no signs of head trauma. The neck is supple. There is diffuse hyperreflex ia. Babinski sign is absent bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: This patient has developed delirium tremens, a serious complication of alcohol withdrawal. Alcohol increases the central nervous system activity of y-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol therefore leads to sympathetic overdrive. Uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal typically presents with tremors , anxiety, restlessness, diffuse hyperreflexia, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis, which can occur hours after the cessation of alcohol use. Delirium tremens, the most concerning and life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal, involves severe confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visual hallucinations, and autonomic instability (variab le heart rate and blood pressure with hyperthermia). Delirium tremens typically begins 2 to 5 days after the patient's last alcoholic drink. Delirium tremens is managed supportively with benzodiazepines (GABAA receptor agonists) to address the psychomotor agitation associated with withdrawal and prevent the worsening of withdrawal manifestations. Management also includes fluid resuscitation, nutritional supplementation, and frequent assessment including vital sign checks.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Acute subdural hematoma (Choice A) refers to bleeding between the dura and arachnoid membranes, most common ly caused by head trauma in elderly patients and persons with alcohol use disorder. Patients typically present with a declining neurologic status or coma.

questionStem: A 6-month-o ld boy is adm itted to the hospital for evaluation of spasms. The child's father and a paternal aunt are mildly retarde d and have seizures. The father has acneiform lesions on his cheeks, but without comedones. Examination of the patient shows five 1- to 2-cm depigmented areas on the chest and flexor surfaces of the upper and lower extremities. A CT scan of the head shows a subependyma l calcification near the foramen of Monro on the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Tuberous sclerosis is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder characterized by benign tumors in severa l organ systems. Hamartomas can form in the soft tissue (leading to Shagreen patches, or subcutaneous oval nodules) or brain (leading to epilepsy and intellectua l disability). Cardiac rhabdomyomas (leading to mitral regurgitation) and renal angiomyolipomas are also common. Other typical dermatologic findings include ash leaf spots (hypomelanotic macules) and angiofibromas, which are acneiform lesions without comedones (clogged hair follicles). Subependymal giant cell tumors are common, which typically demonstrate calcifica tion and may increase the likelihood of developing seizures. Though these tumors are benign, patients are at risk for developing malignancies in the soft tissues, brain, or kidney. Diagnosis is typically clinical but may be confirmed by genetic testing indicating a mutated TSC gene. Management requires anticonvulsant medication for seizures and surgica l resection of rapidly growing or symptomatic tumors.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Idiopathic hypercalcemia (Choice A) is a rare condition that typically presents in infancy with developmenta l delay, constipation, polyuria, vomiting, feeding problems, and weight loss. Adults can rarely demonstrate an idiopathic increase in vitamin D and consequen tly become hyperca lcemic. Neither variant is hereditary nor associated with dermatologic findings. Neurofibromatosis (Choice B) is a hereditary neurocutaneous disorder. Type 1 presents with cutaneous neurofibromas (benign neoplasms derived from neural crest cells), cafe au lait spots, pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), optic gliomas, and pheochromocytomas. Type 2 presents with cutaneou s neurofib romas, bilateral vestibular schwannomas, additional schwannomas of the cranial nerves or in the spinal cord, intracranial meningiomas, and neuropathy. Subependymal brain lesions are atypical, and the dermatologic findings differ between tuberous sclerosis and neurofibromatosis. Sturge-Weber syndrome (Choice C) is a neurocutaneous disorder that presents with the proliferation of capil lary-size blood vessels

questionStem: A 62-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of progress ive difficulty climbing stairs, generalized muscle pain, and dry mouth. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia . Current medications include atorvastatin, atenolol, and glybur ide. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. At his last visit 6 weeks ago, an x-ray of the chest showed a solitary lung nodule. Today, his pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg. Examination of the lower extremities shows bilateral proximal weakness and hyporeflexia. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies show an incremental increase in the amplitude of evoked motor response. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented these symptoms?

choices.E: More aggressive treatme nt of high blood pressure

correctExplanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an uncommon neurologic condition that affects neuromuscu lar junction transmission. Normally, action potentials lead to depolarization in the termina l bouton of the axon. Voltage-gated calcium channels consequently open and allow calcium influx, which triggers the exocytosis of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles into the synaptic cleft. Patients with LEMS possess antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels on presynaptic lower motoneurons, which decreases calcium influx and the subsequent release of acetylcholine. This patient with a smoking history and proximal muscle weakness, with a known lung nodule, likely has paraneoplastic autoantibody production against voltage-gated calcium channels, causing LEMS in the setting of small cell lung cancer. Patients may also have depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes. The muscle weakness typica lly improves with exercise as small amounts of acetylcholine accumulate in the synaptic cleft over time, increasing the frequency of postsynaptic action potentials in skeletal muscle cells. This can be seen on nerve conduction studies, as well. Autonomic symptoms such as decreased salivation (and consequent dry mouth) may also occur. The diagnosis may be confirmed with nerve conduction studies and electromyography with exercise testing. In this patient, smoking cessation would have prevented the development of lung cancer and consequent LEMS.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Daily aspirin therapy (Choice B) is used in the prophylaxis and treatment of cardiovascu lar disease, such as coronary artery disease and stroke. It does not play a role in the prevention of lung cancer development. Discontinuing atenolol therapy (Choice C) or atorvastatin therapy (Choice D) would not have prevented this patient from developing lung cancer and subsequent LEMS. While ~-adrenergic blocker therapy can cause fatigue and statin therapy can cause myopathy, neither causes hyporeflexia.

questionStem: A 30-year-old construction worker comes to the physician because of constant midlower back pain for 1 month. He has no leg pain. Straight-leg raising causes discomfort only in the low back. Sensor imotor examination is normal. Which of the following is the most approp riate next step in management?

choices.A: Restriction of heavy lifting until the pain resolves and instruction in proper body mechanics
choices.C: Vocational rehabilitation and change in occupat ion
choices.D: Epidural injection of corticosteroids and nonsteroida l anti-inflammatory drugs
choices.E: lnterverteb ral disc excisio n and fusion

correctExplanation: Low back pain is a common condition that is self-limited for many individuals. There are many causes of low back pain, and it rarely can be caused by a serious illness that requires medica l treatment or surgica l intervention. Risk factors for low back pain include strenuous work, heavy lifting, trauma, obesity, and age. Most patients present with a lumbosacral strain caused by heavy lifting or extended periods of sitting. In patients with a history of trauma or osteoporosis, vertebra l compression fractures or other vertebral fractures are a consideration. Signs and symptoms that increase the risk for an urgent medica l or surgical cause of low back pain include fever, focal midline spinal tenderness, weight loss, pain increased at night, focal neurologic symptoms, and urinary incontinence or urinary retention. In this patient with no sensorimotor abnormalities, the most likely cause of his low back pain is a lumbosacral strain from heavy lifting and construction work. Most patients with lumbosacral pain will improve within 4 weeks with short-term symptomatic therapy, including pain control, restriction of heavy lifting, physical therapy, and instructions on proper body mechanics, allowing for an early return to activity. Prolonged periods of inactivity and bed rest are to be avoided.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bed rest and oral analgesics (Choice B) would not be the most appropriate management. While oral analgesics can help with pain, early movement and physical therapy has been shown to decrease pain and expedite return of function. Bed rest will increase pain and prolong time to recovery. Vocational rehabilitation and change in occupation (Choice C) wou ld not be appropriate before a trial of physical therapy. The patient is young and will likely recover after a period of restricting heavy lifting and physical therapy to prevent further injuries. Epidural injection of corticosteroids and nonsteroida l anti-inflammatory drugs (Choice D) would also be inappropriate prior to a period of physical therapy and restriction of heavy lifting. Typically, physical therapy and rehabilitation are sufficient to treat lumbosacral strain in a majority of patients.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of deep aching neck and shoulder pain, progressive weakness of his hands, and poor coordination. Two years ago, he had a whiplash injury that resolved without treatment over a 3-month period. Neurologic examination shows hyporeflexia of the upper extremities. He has atrophy of intrinsic hand muscles bilaterally. There is asymmetr ic decreased strength of grip and finger abduct ion and extension. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the upper torso and shoulders. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Syringomyelia refers to a progressive ly expanding cystic lesion involving midline spinal cord structures, most commonly in the cervical or thoracic spinal cord. Syringomyelia may be associated with congenita l malformations such as Chiari malformation type I, spinal cord infections, autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis, neoplasms, or spinal cord trauma. Syringomyelia typical ly compresses spinothalamic fibers decussating in the anterior white commissure. Consequent ly, patients present with deficits in pain and temperature sensation in the bilateral upper extremities and/or torso. (Since the ascending spinothalamic tracts in the lateral spinal cord are unaffected, sensation in the lower body is intact.) Neuropathic pain in the upper extremities may occur. The lesion can expand to compress the bilateral anterior horns (the location of the cell bodies of lower motoneurons). Therefore, patients may present with a lower motoneuron pattern of dysfunction in the bilateral upper extremities (eg, decreased muscle tone, hyporeflexia, early muscle atrophy). The cyst may progressively expand to compress the lateral corticospinal tract in severe cases, leading to an upper motoneuron pattern of dysfunction in the lower body.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Choice A) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects the anterior horns and the lateral corticospinal tract. Subsequent ly, patients demonstrate a combination of upper and lower motoneuron findings in an asymmetric distribution. Sensory impairment is atypical, and a pattern of dysfunction that can be localized to a single lesion within the cervical or thoracic spinal cord is more consistent with a syringomye lia. Anterior spinal cord syndrome (Choice B) results from ischemia of the anterior spinal artery (eg, by thrombosis or trauma), leading to dama e to the cortices inal, s inothalamic, and autonomic tracts. The s ndrome manifests with loss of ain and tern erature sensation

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 13-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after a genera lized tonic-clonic seizure that occurred at school. Her teacher noted that the seizure was preceded by jerking of the right arm. She had a similar episode 8 months ago. Examination at that time showed no abnormalities, and no treatment was begun. She was born in Mexico, and she and her parents have made occasional trips to rural Mexico; their last visit was 2 years ago. She was lethargic on arrival to the emergency department, but she is now awake and alert. Her temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F). The neck is supple. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Her leukocyte count is 6400/mm3. A CT scan of the head is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test for family members of this patient?

choices.A: Examination of the stool for ova and parasites

correctExplanation: Neurocysticercosis is a central nervous system (CNS) infection caused by the pork tapeworm Taenia so/ium that occurs most common ly in endemic rural regions of Latin America, Asia, and Africa. Symptoms include headache, seizures, signs of increased intracranial pressure, and, rarely, altered vision. Some patients are asymptomatic, while other patients may present with muscle or subcutaneous nodules. Typical manifestations on CT or MRI include cystic, ring-enhancing, calcified lesions in the brain parenchyma, meninges, ventricles, spinal cord, and/or orbit. A scolex (larval head) may also be demons trated on imaging. Treatment includes symptomatic management of increased intracrania l pressure and seizures, antiparasitic therapy, and/or steroids. questionStem: A 6-year-o ld girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of progressive weakness and numbness of the legs. This morning, she had urinary incontinence. One year ago, she underwent resectio n of a medulloblastoma and placeme nt of a ventric uloperitoneal shunt for residual hydrocep halus; her postopera tive course had been uncomplicated. Currently, she is drowsy and irritable. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 126/54 mm Hg. Funduscopic examina tion shows no abnormalities. Examination of the lower extremities shows weakness and diffuse sensory loss; deep tendon reflexes are decreased. Which of the following is the most likely underly ing mechanism for these symptoms?

choices.B: Metastatic spread of the cancer hematogenously
choices.C: Metastatic spread of the cancer through cerebrospinal fluid pathways
choices.D: Radiation necrosis of the brain stem
choices.E: Thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery
choices.F: Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus

correctExplanation: Metastatic spread of cancer through cerebrospina l fluid pathways is the mechanism behind this patient's development of cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina syndrome occurs as a result of compression of the spinal nerve roots comprising the cauda equina. Often, such compression occurs because of malignancy (as in this case), trauma, disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spinal epidura l abscess, or spinal epidural or subdura l hematoma. Symptoms include lower extremity numbness, weakness, paralysis, hyporeflexia, perinea! anesthesia, fecal incontinence with poor rectal tone, and overflow incontinence marked by an inability to void with associated urinary retention. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to investigate the cause of cauda equina syndrome and to determine the necessity of surgical decompression. Initial treatment for patients with epidural spinal cord compression and neurologic deficits include symptomatic treatment, pain control, and glucocorticoid therapy prior to operative therapy. High-dose glucocorticoid therapy is helpful as a bridge to definitive therapy and may transiently improve neurologic function by decreasing edema at the site of cord compression.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Local recurrence of the medulloblastoma (Choice A) would cause neurologic deficits specific to the region of the brain being affected by the tumor. While, depending on the location, this could cause lower extremity weakness, it would cause hyperreflexia rather than hyporeflexia because of the involvement of the upper motoneuron. This patient's lower extremity hyporeflexia indicates a peripheral cause affecting the lower motoneuron. Metastatic spread of the cancer hematogenous ly (Choice B) would be more likely to cause foci of malignancy to develop in other or ans includin the bones, liver, or lun s. questionStem: A 45-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 1 minute. She had a headac he 6 hours ago and nausea and vomiting 2 hours ago. She has no history of seizures and has had no medical problems other than hypertension treated with enalapril and hydroch lorothiazide. Her temperatu re is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 100/min and regular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 230/140 mm Hg. She appears drowsy but is responsive to commands. Examination shows no abnormalities other than the funduscopic findings shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: This patient's presenting signs and symptoms of hypertension, tachycardia, altered mental status, tonic-clonic seizures, and optic disc edema are consistent with a diagnosis of hypertensive encephalopathy. Hypertensive encepha lopathy may result from acute and severe increases in blood pressure and may manifest with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizures. It may progress to obtundation and coma. Visual symptoms may result from cortical hypertension or from hypertensive retinopathy. Retinal findings may include optic disc edema and nerve fiber layer infarction or hemorrhage. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessive ly rapid drops in blood pressure, which can cause cerebral or cardiac ischemia. In general, a decrease in the mean arterial pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with gradua l correction over the next day or more following. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodi lator and is a preferred agent because of its very short half-life, allowing it to be titrated via intravenous infusion. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous Next Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause .... https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 49 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Clinical Neurology Self-Assessment include optic disc edema and nerve fiber layer infarction or hemorrhage. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessively rapid drops in blood pressure, which can cause cerebral or cardiac ischemia. In general, a decrease in the mean arterial pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with gradual correction over the next day or more following. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodilator and is a preferred agent because of its very short half-life, allowing it to be titrated via intravenous infusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Clonidine (Choice A) is an oral or intravenous antihypertensive agent that stimulates a 2-adrenergic receptors. It is commonly used as an adjunct oral agent for the management of hypertensive emergency but is less appropriate as initial pharmacotherapy. Furosemide (Choice B) is an oral or intravenous loop diuretic. Diuretics are not typically used in the treatment of hypertensive emergency because of their comparative ly long half-life and duration of action. Lisinopril (Choice C) is an oral angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Oral agents are not preferred in the initial management of hypertensive emergency. Proprano lol (Choice E) is an oral or intravenous nonselective ~­ adrenergic blocker. It is not typically used as a primary agent in the treatment of hypertensive emergency because of its comparatively long half-life and duration of action. It may progress to obtundation and coma. Retinal findings may include optic disc edema and nerve fiber layer infarction or hemorrhage. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodilator and is a preferred agent because of its very short half-life, allowing it to be titrated via intravenous infusion.

questionStem: A 42-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of progressive weakness and numbness in her legs and blurred vision and discomfort in both eyes. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Visual acuity is 20/80 bilateral ly. Examination shows bilatera l optic disc edema. Muscle strength is 5/5 in the upper extremities and 4/5 in the lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ in the upper extremities and 4+ in the lower extremities. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. A lumbar puncture is performed. Analysis of the cerebrosp inal fluid shows: Glucose Total protein WBC RBC Oligoclonal bands 80 mg/dl 105 mg/dl 50/mm 3 5/mm 3 0 bands An MRI of the brain shows multiple periventricu lar white matter lesions. An MRI of the thoracic spine shows an abnorma l T2 signal and mild enhancement within the thoracic cord spanning T3 to T6. Which of the following abnormalities is most likely to be noted on further testing in this patient?

choices.C: Aquaporin-4 autoantibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid

correctExplanation: Aquaporin-4 autoantibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are diagnostic of neuromyelitis optica (NMO), a disease characterized by intense inflammation and demyelination of both the optic nerves and various spinal cord segments, with involvement of both grey and white matter. Common manifestations include episodes of optic neuritis, which manifests as vision loss and pain, and transverse myelitis, which can affect any level of the spinal cord. Other unique findings include episodes of hiccups with associated nausea and vomiting. The disease course is often described as relapsing and remitting, with some patients experiencing few symptoms between episodes. Treatment is with high-dose intravenous steroids and, occasionally, plasma exchange for acute attacks. Prophylaxis with eculizumab or other biologic agents is warranted at the time of diagnosis.

questionStem: A//-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of headache, confusion, and blurred vision. He has not had any recent trauma to the head or eyes. He has chronic hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, irritable bowel syndrome, and bilateral hearing loss. Current medications are hydrochlorothiazide, glipizide, amlodipine, losartan, and chlordiazepoxide. On arrival, he is holding his head in his hands. He is oriented to name and place but not to date of birth, month, year, or the current president. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 64/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 230/130 mm Hg. Visual acuity is 20/30 in both eyes. Visual fields are full. Funduscopic examination shows blurred optic disc margins and several slit-like hemorrhages in both fundi. ACT scan of the head shows a hypoattenuated area in both occipital lobes and an old lacunar infarct in the basal ganglia and thalami. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy results from acute and/or severe increases in blood pressure. It potentially manifests with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizure, and may progress to obtundation and coma. Visual symptoms may result from cortical dysfunction or from hypertensive retinopathy, including retinal hemorrhages and exudates. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessively rapid drops in blood pressure, which can cause end-organ ischemia. In general, a decrease in the mean arterial pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with gradual correction over the next day or more following. Intravenous agents such as labetalol, esmolol, nicardipine, and nitroprusside are preferred for initial management.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Oral 81-mg aspirin (Choice A) can be used as secondary prevention of ischemic stroke. While this patient does have evidence of prior strokes on CT scan, his acute encephalopathy is secondary to his increased blood pressure, and primary management should be focused on lowering his blood pressure. Intravenous alteplase (Choice B) is a fibrinolytic medication used for ischemic strokes that binds to fibrin clots and converts plasminogen to plasmin, which lyses clots. If given early (generally within 3 to 4.5 hours), alteplase may promote neurologic recovery. This patient has evidence of prior strokes on CT scan, likely secondary to his uncontrolled hypertension, but is well outside of the window for receiving alteplase. Additionally, blood pressure greater than 180/110 mm Hg is a contraindication to receiving alteplase as there is increased risk for hemorrhagic conversion. Intravenous dexamethasone (Choice C) is sometimes used in cases of spinal cord compression or cerebral edema secondary to brain tumors. Corticosteroids are not a part of the management of hypertensive encephalopathy. Intravenous heparin (Choice D) may be indicated in the event of a thromboembolic ischemic stroke caused by underlying atrial fibrillation. This patient has no evidence of an underlying cardiac arrhythmia, and his strokes are likely caused by his underlying poorly controlled hypertension. Educational Objective: Hypertensive encephalopathy results from acute and/or severe increases in blood pressure. It potentially manifests with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizures, and may progress to obtundation and coma. Treatment should be focused on carefully lowering the blood pressure. Intravenous agents such as labetalol, esmolol, nicardipine, and nitroprusside are preferred for initial management. r 4 CA ws - Previous Score Report ——EEEEEEEEEEEe)) V a! LCS Calculator

questionStem: A5/-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after he was found walking unsteadily and speaking in a confused and incoherent manner. Neurologic examination shows bilateral abducens nerve palsies, coarse nystagmus in all directions of gaze, and severe truncal ataxia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vitamin B,, or thiamine, plays a complex role in neuronal physiology including in axon conduction, glucose utilization, and neurotransmitter synthesis. Thiamine deficiency results in neuronal damage through a mechanism that likely involves oxidative toxicity. Thiamine deficiency causes two potential syndromes: Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome. The classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy demonstrates encephalopathy, ataxia, and oculomotor dysfunction caused by neuronal damage in the cerebellum, midbrain, and pons. Common ocular manifestations include nystagmus and horizontal gaze palsy as a result of damage to the abducens nuclei. Thiamine deficiency is most encountered in the setting of alcohol use disorder due to poor nutritional intake, thiamine malabsorption, and impaired cellular utilization of thiamine. Over time, thiamine deficiency can result in damage and atrophy of the mammillary bodies, visible on MRI of the brain, which manifests as Wernicke encephalopathy. The symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy are reversible but increase the risk for developing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome in chronic alcohol users if not immediately treated with high-dose parenteral thiamine. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is an irreversible condition that features psychosis, anterograde and retrograde amnesia, and the consequent tendency to confabulate, or verbalize false stories or memories to compensate for the inability to remember.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Diabetic polyneuropathy (Choice A) commonly results in sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Findings of ataxia and nystagmus would be atypical. Huntington disease (Choice B) is a hereditary, progressive neurodegenerative disorder associated with atrophy of the caudate nuclei in the basal ganglia. The disease usually presents with an insidious onset of psychiatric and cognitive symptoms, followed by motor symptoms (eg, chorea, hypotonia, dystonia, loss of voluntary control of movements). Lead encephalopathy (Choice C) presents with cognitive dysfunction, encephalopathy, hearing loss, and peripheral neuropathy. Distal motor neuropathy causes lower motor neuron signs, including weakness, atrophy, hypotonia, and hyporeflexia. Non-neurologic manifestations of lead poisoning include renal tubular dysfunction, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, and anemia. Multiple sclerosis (Choice D) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease that presents with focal neurologic deficits separated in space and time. Ataxia and nystagmus are atypical. r 4 CA ws - Previous Score Report ——EEEEEEEEEEEe)) V a! LCS Calculator

questionStem: A24-year-old man comes to the physician 1 day after he had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at work. His symptoms began with a rising sensation in the upper middle abdomen. His coworker told him that he started to stare, licked his lips, and then fell to the floor. He had generalized shaking of his arms and legs. After he awakened, he was confused for several minutes and smelled an odor of burnt rubber that his coworkers did not notice. He has noticed a similar odor three times in the past 2 months. He was hit by a baseball bat at the age of 12 years and had a brief loss of consciousness. He has been otherwise healthy. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely location of the abnormality?
correctExplanation: Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures are also called complex partial seizures. As this name suggests, these seizures affect a specific (focal) region of the brain and therefore produce motor or sensory symptoms that are localized to one or a few areas of the body. Patients will be unresponsive during the seizure (impaired awareness). Focal seizures can spread to the bilateral hemispheres, evolving into generalized tonic-clonic seizures, as in this patient. Tonic-clonic seizures are characterized by the sudden onset of muscle contractions followed by rhythmic jerking of the extremities. Oral automatisms and autonomic disturbances such as an epigastric rising sensation, as in this patient, are suggestive of a temporal lobe lesion, the most common origin of seizures. Manual automatisms and upper limb dystonia can also occur in temporal lobe seizures. Patients may experience visual, auditory, or sensory auras preceding the seizure. Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures are often accompanied by a brief postictal state marked by confusion and fatigue. These seizures will demonstrate localized rhythmic activity with generalized slowing on EEG. Treatment requires antiepileptic medication. For patients with refractory temporal lobe epilepsy, surgical excision of the lesion can be considered.

Brain stem (Choice A) lesions involving the medulla, midbrain, or pons may result in focal seizure activity characterized by convulsive movements; however, brainstem involvement more typically occurs in the setting of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Cerebellum (Choice B) lesions can result in focal seizure activity characterized by focal motor or hemifacial seizures, but these seizures are extremely rare. Cerebellar involvement more typically occurs in the setting of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Frontal lobe (Choice C) lesions can also present with focal seizures with impaired awareness. Disturbance of the higher cognitive functions of the frontal lobe can lead to features such as speech disturbances, complex automatisms, and strong emotional expressions such as crying or laughing. Focal seizures with intact awareness with motor symptoms may also occur as a result of involvement of the primary motor cortex. Occipital lobe (Choice D) lesions are uncommon causes of focal seizure activity, but typically present with visual manifestations such as visual hallucinations, cortical blindness, and deviated gaze. Parietal lobe (Choice E) lesions can result in focal seizure activity involving the primary somatosensory cortex, resulting in sensory disturbances such as numbness, tingling, warmth, or pain. questionStem: A6/-year-old man has had four acute episodes of aphasia over the past year. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 142/82 mm Hg. Serum studies show a glucose concentration of 150 mg/dL, total cholesterol concentration of 296 mg/dL, and HDL-cholesterol concentration of 28 mg/dL. Carotid ultrasonography shows 90% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to decrease this patient's risk for a stroke?

choices.A: Control of blood pressure with diet and medication
choices.B: Control of serum LDL-cholesterol concentration with diet and medication
choices.C: Control of serum glucose concentration with diet, oral agents, or insulin
choices.D: Control of ventricular rate with digoxin

correctExplanation: This patient with four separate episodes of acute aphasia that self-resolved has a presentation concerning for multiple transient ischemic attacks (TIAs). TIA is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without evidence of infarction. The symptoms last less than 24 hours by definition and may last as little as a few minutes. Patients with TIAs are at increased risk for having an ischemic stroke; therefore, management of patients with a TIA should focus on identification and treatment of modifiable risk factors. Such risk factors include large vessel atherosclerosis, arrhythmias, known cardiac thrombus, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypercoagulable states. Patients who have been diagnosed with TIA should undergo MRI, Doppler ultrasonography of the carotid arteries, echocardiography, and cardiac monitoring. Patients with 70% to 99% stenosis of the carotid arteries should undergo carotid endarterectomy or carotid stenting to decrease their subsequent risk for stroke.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Control of blood pressure and control of serum LDL-cholesterol concentration with diet and medication (Choices A and B) and control of serum glucose concentration with diet, oral agents, or insulin (Choice C) are all important measures that should be taken to decrease the risk for stroke in this patient. Aspirin therapy (Choice E) is also indicated as secondary stroke prevention in this patient. However, carotid endarterectomy should take precedence for this patient with known significant carotid artery atherosclerosis, as this was likely the direct embolic source for his ischemic event and would lead to the greatest reduction in risk for subsequent stroke. Control of ventricular rate with digoxin (Choice D) would not be appropriate for this patient with a normal heart rate. Digoxin may be used to achieve rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation who do not have an adequate response to more conventional therapies such as beta blockers and calcium channel blockers. While atrial fibrillation is a known risk factor for thromboembolic strokes, controlling the heart rate does not decrease that risk. Therefore, patients with atrial fibrillation and increased stroke risk should be on warfarin therapy (Choice F) or another anticoagulant medication such as rivaroxaban or dabigatran. Educational Objective: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without evidence of infarction. The symptoms last less than 24 hours by definition and may last as little as a few minutes. Patients with TIAs are at increased risk for having an ischemic stroke, and therefore management of patients with a TIA should focus on identification and treatment of modifiable risk factors. Patients with 70% to 99% stenosis of the carotid arteries should undergo carotid endarterectomy or carotid stenting to decrease their subsequent risk for stroke. r 4 e 18 - Previous Score Report et) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: A60-year-old woman is brought to the office by her husband because of a 6-week history of progressive unsteadiness, incoordination, and slurred speech. During the past 6 months, she also has had a nonproductive cough, fatigue, and a 7-kg (15-Ib) unintentional weight loss despite no change in appetite. She has not seen a physician in more than 10 years and does not take any medications. She has smoked fifteen cigarettes daily for the past 40 years. She drinks alcoholic beverages only on social occasions. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dysarthria, but no aphasia is noted. Cranial nerves are intact except for bilateral horizontal nystagmus. She has no focal muscle weakness or sensory deficit. Finger-nose testing and heel-shin testing discloses bilateral dysmetria. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+. The patient is unable to tandem walk. MRI of the brain discloses multiple T-2 hyperintensities in both cerebral hemispheres and mild cerebellar atrophy with enhancement of the cerebellar folia. MR angiography of the circle of Willis shows no abnormalities. Carotid Doppler ultrasonography discloses minimal stenosis in the common carotid arteries bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: A variety of paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes may occur following an abnormal immune response to the presence of an underlying malignancy. The most implicated tumors are small cell lung carcinoma, breast and ovarian carcinoma, and Hodgkin lymphoma. In many cases, the onset of a paraneoplastic disorder may precede detection of the primary malignancy; therefore, patients may present without a known cancer history and a high index of suspicion for an occult tumor must be maintained. Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (PCD) is a rare disorder characterized by dysfunction of the cerebellar vermis with signs and symptoms of ataxia, intention tremor, vertigo, nystagmus, dysarthria, and eventual loss of ambulation. A variety of autoantibodies may be detected in association with PCD, most commonly anti-Yo antibodies, which target an antigen specific to cerebellar Purkinje cells. MRI often shows cerebellar atrophy. Further diagnostic evaluation should be performed to identify the primary malignancy in a patient with suspected PCD.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Choice A) is a human prion disease that presents with rapidly progressing dementia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, cerebellar dysfunction, corticospinal tract dysfunction, basal ganglia dysfunction, and stimulus-induced myoclonus. While Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease may cause a rapidly progressive dementia, this patient’s history of smoking, cough, and unintentional weight loss are suggestive of malignancy and a paraneoplastic disorder. Miller-Fisher syndrome (Choice B) is a subset of Guillain-Barré syndrome, an autoimmune demyelinating disorder. Miller-Fisher syndrome is characterized by the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia. This contrasts with Guillain-Barré syndrome, which presents with acute-onset, ascending, bilateral muscle weakness. This patient has normal deep tendon reflexes, suggesting against the diagnosis. Multisystem atrophy (Choice C) is a parkinsonian, neurodegenerative disorder characterized by parkinsonism, autonomic dysfunction, and ataxia. Autonomic symptoms may include orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, anhidrosis, urinary incontinence, and erectile dysfunction. Progressive supranuclear palsy (Choice E) is a parkinsonian, neurodegenerative disorder characterized by gait instability, oculomotor deficits (classically vertical gaze palsy), frontal lobe deficits, bradykinesia, and muscle rigidity. Wernicke encephalopathy (Choice F) results from vitamin B, (thiamine) deficiency and presents with the triad of encephalopathy, ataxia, and oculomotor dysfunction (typically nystagmus and horizontal gaze palsy). It most commonly affects patients with a history of alcohol use disorder. 4 gf a (is - eS las Previous

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 16-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 6-hour history of temperatures to 38.9°C (102°F), fussiness, and decreased feeding. He was born at 39 weeks’ gestation to a 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, and weighed 3090 g (6 Ib 13 oz) at birth. The mother received routine prenatal care. Pregnancy was complicated by group B streptococcal infection at 37 weeks’ gestation; no other abnormalities were noted on screening. The mother received three doses of intrapartum ampicillin. The patient was discharged on the second day of life. Well-child examinations on days 3 and 14 of life showed no abnormalities. At 2 weeks of age, he weighed 3232 g (7 lb 2 oz). He is currently breast-feeding. He has not had sick contacts. Today, he weighs 3260 g (7 Ib 3 oz). Head circumference is at the 50th percentile. His rectal temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 142/min and regular, respirations are 48/min, and blood pressure is 58/40 mm Hg. Examination shows no cyanosis or rash. The head is normocephalic with no signs of trauma. The anterior and posterior fontanels are open and ballotable; the anterior fontanel is not bulging. There is mild scleral icterus. The liver edge is palpated 1.5 cm below the right costal margin. The spleen is not palpable. The umbilical cord has detached; the site is dry and nonerythematous. A lumbar puncture is performed. Results of urinalysis and blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Discharge after administration of a single dose of ceftriaxone

correctExplanation: Neonatal sepsis is often categorized on the basis of time from parturition, as the period of time in which symptoms begin may indicate which pathogen is likely involved, thereby guiding therapy. Early-onset neonatal sepsis occurs within 72 hours of birth, generally as a result of exposure to pathogens acquired from the mother, either through hematogenous or transplacental spread or, commonly, contact acquisition in the birth canal. Late-onset neonatal sepsis presents 72 hours or more after birth and is most likely acquired by contact with environmental pathogens, although those acquired from the mother are still possible. Neonatal sepsis often presents with symptoms of lethargy, fever, poor feeding, weak cry, and respiratory distress. The most common pathogens associated with late-onset neonatal sepsis include group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli. Infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units are also at risk for other gram-negative bacteria, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and Staphylococcus aureus. Syndromes of serious bacterial infection include bacteremia, meningitis, and pneumonia. Workup for a suspected case of sepsis in a child younger than 30 days of age may include blood cultures, lumbar puncture, chest x-ray, complete blood count, and urinalysis, depending on the timing and nature of the patient’s symptoms. Treatment includes intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover the common pathogens. The combination of ampicillin and gentamicin is preferred due to effective coverage against the most common causative agents of neonatal sepsis.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Discharge after administration of a single dose of ceftriaxone (Choice A) and admission to the hospital for observation only (Choice B) are incorrect, as this septic and hypotensive newborn requires intravenous antibiotics and further workup. Intramuscular ampicillin and gentamicin therapy (Choice C) could be an appropriate choice if the newborn required only one dose of antibiotics. This patient will require several days of antibiotics, and therefore intravenous administration is more appropriate as it avoids the need to re-stick the newborn multiple times. Intramuscular ceftriaxone therapy (Choice D) and intravenous ceftriaxone therapy (Choice F) are incorrect. Ceftriaxone should be avoided in newborns at risk for hyperbilirubinemia as it displaces bilirubin from albumin, increasing the free plasma concentrations of unconjugated bilirubin, and thereby increasing the risk for kernicterus. questionStem: An 18-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-month history of increasingly severe left knee pain. The pain was originally mild and intermittent but has progressed to be severe and constant. He has noticed fullness in the area above the left knee during the past month; during the past 2 weeks, there has been increased difficulty walking and bearing weight on the affected leg. There is no recent history of trauma to the knee. He says that he "has not been feeling well overall" during the past month and that he has had a 2-kg (4.5-lb) unintentional weight loss because of decreased appetite. He has no other history of serious illness, and his only medication is ibuprofen as needed for partial pain relief. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows erythema and tenderness of the left distal thigh and above the knee; there is limited flexion of the knee. An x-ray of the knee shows an area of medullary and cortical bone destruction with periosteal new bone formation at the diaphysial end of the lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's underlying condition?

choices.C: Knee brace placement and physical therapy
choices.D: F ) Oral vitamin D supplementation and bisphosphonate therapy

correctExplanation: Osteosarcoma is a rare, primary malignant tumor of the bone that affects the metaphysis of long bones. Osteosarcoma has a bimodal distribution, most frequently affecting adolescents and patients over age 60 years. Presenting symptoms include localized pain, pathologic fractures at the areas of involvement, and associated weight loss. Physical examination may show a large, tender, palpable soft tissue mass. Imaging, including x-ray and MRI, may be used to evaluate the extent of involvement. Standard of care for otherwise healthy patients with osteosarcoma includes surgical resection and chemotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Intramuscular corticosteroid injection (Choice A) may be used in the treatment of systemic inflammatory conditions. These injections are generally administered in the superior lateral buttocks to avoid injection into the sciatic nerve region. Intramuscular steroid injections are not used in the treatment of osteosarcoma. Intravenous antibiotic therapy (Choice B) is used in the treatment of septic arthritis and many infectious conditions. The most common causative microorganism in septic arthritis is Staphylococcus aureus. Antibiotics targeting S. aureus are often used as empiric antibiotic therapy. Knee brace placement and physical therapy (Choice C) are commonly used in the treatment of acute knee injuries and osteoarthritis. Knee braces provide added stability to the joint, while physical therapy aims to increase muscle strength and flexibility as well as prevent recurrent injury to the affected area. Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy (Choice E) such as naproxen is commonly used in the treatment of acute pain and osteoarthritis. These medications inhibit the COX enzyme. Adverse effects include gastritis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and nephropathy. They may be suitable adjuncts in cases of osteosarcoma but are not the primary treatment. Oral vitamin D supplementation and bisphosphonate therapy (Choice F) may be used in the treatment of osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is diagnosed by DEXA scan and is most common in postmenopausal female patients. Educational Objective: Osteosarcoma is a primary malignant tumor of the bone most frequently affecting adolescent and elderly patients. Patients may present with localized pain, pathologic fracture, and a palpable, tender mass on physical examination. Patients are evaluated with imaging studies and treated with surgical resection and chemotherapy. 4 a Previous Score Report Calculator

questionStem: A6/-year-old man with a 15-year history of emphysema comes to the office because of right-sided shoulder pain for 6 months. He has not had chest pain, palpitations, or headache. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. He has worked as a coal miner for 45 years. He appears older than his age. He is not in distress. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. The left pupil is 3 mm, the right pupil is 2 mm; they both react to light. There is ptosis on the right. Examination shows decreased diaphragmatic excursion on the right and a prolonged expiratory phase. There is moderate clubbing of the fingers. Intrinsic muscles of the right hand are atrophic; muscle strength is 4/5 in the right upper extremity. X-ray of the chest shows a 3 x 4-cm right apical mass. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's shoulder pain?

choices.A: Extrinsic compression of the spinal cord

correctExplanation: Bronchogenic carcinoma commonly presents with cough, weight loss, hemoptysis, and potential signs of bronchial obstruction such as wheezing or prolonged expiratory phase. If the carcinoma is located within the lung apex, referred to as a Pancoast tumor, it can infiltrate multiple adjacent structures such as the superior vena cava, subclavian vessels, sympathetic chain, recurrent laryngeal nerve, or brachial plexus. This can result in presenting features of Horner syndrome (unilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis of the face), ipsilateral shoulder and upper extremity pain, and hoarseness. If the Pancoast tumor involves the right lung apex, superior vena cava syndrome may occur, which manifests with bilateral upper extremity and facial swelling, erythema, and vascular congestion caused by insufficient venous drainage from mass effect or vessel invasion. A Pancoast tumor typically presents as a consolidative, rounded mass in the lung apex on chest x-rays and CT scans.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Extrinsic compression of the spinal cord (Choice A) can occur with metastatic cancers to the spine or with an infection such as an epidural abscess, which can present with weakness and numbness in a dermatomal or myotomal distribution. It would be unlikely to cause Horner syndrome. Small cell carcinoma of the lung is a neoplasm of neuroendocrine cells and is associated with numerous paraneoplastic syndromes, including Cushing syndrome caused by increased production of ACTH (Choice B). ACTH produced by small cell carcinoma stimulates the adrenal gland zona fasciculata to increase the production of cortisol. Hypercortisolism, or Cushing syndrome, ensues with its many manifestations, including proximal muscle weakness, osteoporosis, hypertension, hyperglycemia, truncal obesity, moon facies, striae, amenorrhea, and/or immunosuppression. Squamous cell carcinoma is associated with hypercalcemia due to production of parathyroid-like hormone (also known as parathyroid hormone-related peptide) (Choice D). Hypercalcemia can present with nephrolithiasis, chronic bone pain, abdominal discomfort, and psychiatric disturbances. Jugular vein thrombosis (Choice E) would not compress adjacent structures and would be unlikely to cause Horner syndrome. Educational Objective: Pancoast tumors can infiltrate adjacent structures such as the superior vena cava, subclavian vessels, sympathetic chain, recurrent laryngeal nerve, or brachial plexus and can lead to Horner syndrome, ipsilateral shoulder and upper extremity pain, and hoarseness. questionStem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive difficulty walking and a 2-month history of urinary incontinence. His wife reports that he is extremely slow to answer questions. Neurologic examination shows bilateral grasp reflexes and increased muscle tone in all extremities. When he tries to walk, he appears "glued" to the floor and cannot take steps without assistance. He is oriented to person, place, and time but speaks very little. Which of the following is most likely to be increased in this patient?
correctExplanation: This patient presents with findings suggesting normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), with the characteristic combination of dementia, gait instability, and urinary incontinence. NPH refers to a type of communicating (nonobstructive) hydrocephalus in which the ventricles are enlarged, leading to damage of the white matter tracts connecting the frontal lobes and basal ganglia. Patients commonly present with frontal cognitive deficits (eg, frontal release signs such as the reemergence of the grasp reflex) and subcortical cognitive deficits (eg, psychomotor slowing, inattention, executive dysfunction). Signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, papilledema, postural headaches) are typically absent. Many cases of NPH are idiopathic though some are secondary to a defect in cerebrospinal fluid drainage from the ventricles due to scarring or obstruction of the ventricular lining from prior hemorrhage or meningitis. The diagnosis is primarily clinical, although ventriculomegaly on brain imaging is suggestive. The most appropriate next step in management is a lumbar puncture to assess the opening pressure and clinical response to removing cerebrospinal fluid. Placement of a ventricular shunt may be needed for long-term management.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cerebrospinal fluid leukocyte count (Choice A) may be increased in meningitis and encephalitis, which commonly present acutely or subacutely with fever, headache, and altered mental status. This patient does not have a fever or headache, and his symptom onset was chronic and insidious. Cerebrospinal fluid pressure (Choice B) is likely to be normal in this patient as denoted by the name “normal-pressure hydrocephalus.” Excess cerebrospinal fluid collects in the ventricles but does not increase opening pressure. Opening pressure is often increased in meningitis and in idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Cortical sulci (Choice C) are increased in patients with neurodegenerative brain diseases such as dementia, Alzheimer type. In NPH, cortical sulci are not significantly increased. Striatal dopamine (Choice D) is increased by certain Parkinson disease medications. Dopamine dysregulation is not present in NPH. Educational Objective: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus refers to a type of communicating (nonobstructive) hydrocephalus in which the ventricles are enlarged, leading to damage of the white matter tracts connecting the frontal lobes and basal ganglia. Patients commonly present with the characteristic combination of dementia, gait instability, and urinary incontinence. r 4 “ rs. - Previous Score Report et) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic with her husband because she has had six episodes of severe abdominal pain during the past 4 months. She says when the episodes occur, the pain is continuous and located "all over my belly." During initial episodes, the pain persisted for 3 to 4 hours, but during more recent episodes, the pain has lasted 2 to 3 days. She rates the pain at its worst as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The episodes are accompanied by nausea, bloating, numbness in her hands and feet, severe burning pain in her thighs and calves, and severe constipation; these associated symptoms subside with the resolution of the abdominal pain. She also passed red urine after her most recent episode. Her husband says she often sweats during these episodes and he once measured her pulse rate at 100/min. The patient has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has a family history of similar episodes in multiple relatives. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the color of this patient's urine?
correctExplanation: Acute intermittent porphyria is the most likely diagnosis for this patient with episodic abdominal pain and peripheral neuropathy in a “stocking-glove’” distribution, which is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in the porphobilinogen deaminase gene HMBS. This enzyme catalyzes the third step in heme synthesis, which combines four porphobilinogen (PBG) molecules into hydroxymethylbilane, which is subsequently converted to uroporphyrinogen III. Loss of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of PBG, which is toxic to the nervous system. Additionally, increased activity of the upstream enzyme, delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS1) leads to accumulation of aminolevulinic acid, which is also toxic. PBG accumulation in urine produces a reddish tinge and is also diagnostic when detected by urinalysis. The mutation affects both erythroid cells and hepatocytes. The disease’s manifestations are primarily neurologic and include peripheral neuropathy, bladder dysfunction, and autonomic dysfunction. Abdominal pain is classic and results often from ileus. The penetrance is low, so a family history is not often present, which can delay the diagnosis. Disease flares can occur after exposure to certain triggers, such as medications, tobacco, alcohol, stress, and starvation.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Carotene (Choice A) is a naturally occurring pigment that is converted into vitamin A. It is found in many plants, such as carrots, pumpkins, and sweet potatoes, and in many vitamin supplements. It may cause a harmless, orange urinary discoloration when consumed in excess, but does not produce neurologic or gastrointestinal symptoms. Hemoglobin (Choice B) may impart a reddish discoloration to urine in association with a variety of autoimmune, infectious, inflammatory, and coagulation disorders (eg, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura). However, this patient's presentation is most suggestive of acute intermittent porphyria, which does not cause hemoglobinuria. Hydroxocobalamin (Choice C) is a vitamin used for the treatment of cyanide poisoning. It may impart a harmless, red discoloration to urine following administration. Myoglobin (Choice D) may impart a red discoloration to urine in the setting of myoglobinuria, which may occur in the setting of rhabdomyolysis, polymyositis, or a variety of metabolic disorders, such as McArdle disease. Educational Objective: Acute intermittent porphyria is an autosomal dominant disease with low penetrance caused by deficiencies in the porphobilinogen deaminase gene HMBS leading to the accumulation of hepatically synthesized heme intermediates such as porphobilinogen (PBG), which are toxic to the nervous system. questionStem: A previously healthy 24-year-old man is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of progressive loss of vision in the right eye and pain behind the eye with movement. He has no history of similar symptoms. Funduscopic examination shows no abnormalities. Visual acuity is 20/100 on the right. Visual field testing shows a right central scotoma. There is a right afferent pupillary defect. Over the next 10 years, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following conditions?
correctExplanation: Optic neuritis results from autoimmune demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve and presents in young, often female patients with unilateral vision loss and pain that is exacerbated with extraocular movements. Ocular examination discloses decreased visual acuity and color vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and possible optic disc edema. Diagnosis is confirmed with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI sequences showing hyperintensity of the optic nerve. Patients with optic neuritis are at increased risk for multiple sclerosis (MS), and optic neuritis is a common initial finding in patients with MS. Recently, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) have been identified as causative of some cases of optic neuritis. Patients who develop optic neuritis due to antibodies against MOG and AQP4 often have severe presentations but also have decreased risk for subsequent MS compared with patients with optic neuritis who lack these autoantibodies. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial demonstrated that a short course of treatment with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone speeds up the rate of visual recovery and delays the onset of MS, although it does not impact final visual acuity. It also demonstrated that the presence and quantity of periventricular white matter lesions on MRI is the most important prognostic risk factor for the subsequent development of MS.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Glaucoma (Choice A) occurs as a result of increases in pressure within the anterior chamber of the eye and may present as acute, painful or chronic, painless vision loss. Diabetes mellitus, anticholinergic medications, and Sturge-Weber syndrome have all been associated with increased risk for glaucoma. Graves ophthalmopathy (Choice B) may present with exophthalmos, eyelid retraction, and lid lag, and is associated with Graves disease. Herpes encephalitis (Choice C) may present with headache, confusion, fever, and seizures. It is most commonly caused by herpes simplex virus 1. Macular degeneration (Choice D) may present with insidious blurring of central vision and metamorphopsia. Advanced age is the biggest risk factor associated with developing macular degeneration. Myotonic dystrophy (Choice F) typically presents with muscle weakness, myotonia, cataracts, frontal balding, cardiac arrhythmias, and hypogonadism. The most frequently affected muscles include the facial muscles, sternocleidomastoid, distal forearm muscles, intrinsic hand muscles, and ankle dorsiflexors. It is a genetic condition caused by a trinucleotide repeat. Temporal arteritis (Choice G) is a vasculitis of medium and large vessels in elderly patients that commonly presents with headache, jaw claudication, and proximal muscle stiffness. Patients typically experience amaurosis fugax prior to the onset of abrupt, irreversible vision loss. It has been associated with polymyalgia rneumatica but not optic neuritis. . . . .
