questionStem: A56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 1 hour after he was found by his neighbor sitting in the hallway of his apartment building and speaking unintelligibly. On admission, the patient is confused and somnolent; he is unable to provide a medical history. He has alcohol-related cirrhosis complicated by bleeding from esophageal varices, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. His medications are spironolactone, furosemide, nadolol, and ursodiol. During his last clinic visit 2 weeks ago, the patient stated that he has remained abstinent from alcohol use. His examination at that time showed mild confusion. Today, the patient appears somnolent but is easily aroused. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 56 kg (123 Ib); BMI is 18 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows palmar erythema and gynecomastia. The abdomen is protuberant with caput medusae radiating from the umbilicus. When asked to outstretch his arms with wrists extended, the patient's hands transiently drop forward in a nonrhythmic manner. Mental status examination shows a reduced attention span. He is oriented to person but not to place, time, or situation. Results of laboratory studies are shown: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL Hematocrit 34% Leukocyte count 7800/mm3 Serum Nat 133 mEq/L K* 3.2 MEq/L Urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL Ammonia 54 yg/dL Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?
correctExplanation: Hepatic encephalopathy is commonly associated with decompensated liver cirrhosis. Signs of hepatic encephalopathy include confusion, stupor, asterixis, tremor, and myoclonus on physical examination. Hepatic encephalopathy results from accumulation of ammonia produced by colonic bacteria. Serum ammonia concentrations in patients with hepatic encephalopathy may be increased, though this is not necessary for the diagnosis. Treatments for hepatic encephalopathy include rifaximin and lactulose. Rifaximin is a gut-selective, nonabsorbable antibiotic with activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. It acts on the beta subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase to inhibit bacterial synthesis and is bactericidal. Lactulose is degraded by colonic bacteria to create an acidic environment, thereby converting ammonia to ammonium, which cannot be readily absorbed across the gut wall. It is then excreted with feces, lowering total body levels.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Branched-chain amino acid supplementation (Choice A) may be used for supplementation in patients with decompensated liver failure who require protein restriction. Branched-chain amino acids are not used as a treatment for hepatic encephalopathy. a & oe (fs - l ar Previous Score Report et) V al LCS Calculator Help Pause

questionStem: A46-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 18 hours after the sudden onset of severe, intermittent, left-sided facial pain. She describes the pain as "an electric jolt that turns on and off every minute." The pain started while she was brushing her teeth the previous evening and is localized to the left premolar area of the upper dental arch. She reports that ibuprofen relieved the pain for 3 hours, but the pain recurred this morning when she rinsed her mouth with cold water. She has hypertension and multiple sclerosis. Her medications are metoprolol, lisinopril, and fingolimod. Her maternal aunt also has multiple sclerosis. The patient appears anxious and occasionally winces in pain. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 64/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following reflexes should be tested in order to determine if further diagnostic studies are indicated at this time?
correctExplanation: Trigeminal neuralgia is a neuropathic pain disorder that presents with severe shooting or burning pain within the innervated regions of the sensory branches of the trigeminal nerve. The trigeminal nerve divides into three sensory branches, V1 to V3, which innervate the forehead (V1) and the skin overlying the zygomatic and maxillary bone (V2) and the mandible (V3). The pathophysiology of the pain is believed to be related to compression of the trigeminal nerve by adjacent blood vessels or bone as it exits the skull base. Symptoms may be triggered by light touch, shaving, or swallowing, or may occur without any precipitant. The pain is generally described as severe. The trigeminal nerve also mediates the corneal reflex, which involves blinking of the eyelids caused by stimulation of the cornea. Trigeminal neuralgia is associated with loss of the corneal reflex. Treatment includes carbamazepine or surgical decompression.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. The gag reflex (Choice B) is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve as well as the vagus nerve. The palmomental reflex (Choice C) is a primitive reflex present in neonates and infants that involves an involuntary contraction of the mentalis muscle of the mandible elicited by stimulation of the thenar eminence. The pupillary light reflex (Choice D) involves the optic nerve and the oculomotor nerve and causes constriction of the pupils in response to light. Loss of the pupillary light reflex can occur in the setting of an optic nerve injury, brainstem lesion, or oculomotor nerve injury. The visual threat reflex (Choice E) involves involuntary blinking in response to a visual threat and is associated with the optic nerve. Educational Objective: Trigeminal neuralgia is a neuropathic pain disorder that presents with severe shooting or burning pain within the innervated regions of the sensory branches of the trigeminal nerve. The trigeminal nerve mediates the corneal reflex, which is lost in trigeminal neuralgia. 4 oe (ts y — Previous Score Report et) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: A33-year-old woman comes to the physician 24 hours after a fainting episode. Menses have occurred at irregular intervals over the past 6 months. She has had numbing and tingling of her left hand for 2 years. She has had intermittent episodes of sharp, stabbing lower abdominal pain over the past 5 years; she has had no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation. Treatment with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and codeine has been ineffective. Three exploratory laparoscopies did not disclose the cause of the pain, and surgical treatment for uterine adhesions did not provide any significant relief. She has a history of multiple sexual partners but has abstained for the past 3 years because of dyspareunia. Her blood pressure is 140/84 mm Hg. The abdomen is moderately tender to light and deep palpation with no rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are active. Pelvic examination is difficult to perform because of increased cervical pain. There is bilateral tenderness on palpation of the ovaries. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient with numerous non-specific symptoms with no medical explanation after extensive workup has a presentation concerning for somatization disorder. In somatization disorder, or somatic symptom disorder, the patient is excessively preoccupied with one or more somatic symptoms such that these symptoms disrupt the patient's daily life. These symptoms may or may not originate from an underlying disease, though they are typically unconsciously produced or exacerbated by psychological factors such as stress. Patients persistently devote excessive time and energy to these symptoms or related health concerns (eg, repeatedly going to the doctor). Patients often undergo extensive diagnostic testing that is unrevealing. Management of somatic symptom disorder centers around regular primary care follow-up that targets coping skills, provides reassurance, and avoids unnecessary tests.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Conversion disorder (Choice A), also known as functional neurologic symptom disorder, involves neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not fully explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. Functional neurologic symptom disorder is postulated to represent the subconscious conversion of intolerable emotional distress into physical symptoms. Crohn disease (Choice B) is characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract and presents with abdominal pain, bloody or watery diarrhea, low-grade fever, and weight loss. Pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and numbness are not consistent with a diagnosis of Crohn disease. Endometriosis (Choice C) is caused by ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus and presents with chronic dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and infertility. Symptoms are typically cyclical. The gold standard for diagnosis is diagnostic laparoscopy, which evaluates for endometriotic implant lesions on the peritoneum. This patient has had three laparoscopies that did not show ectopic endometrial tissue. Illness anxiety disorder (Choice D) is characterized by persistent excessive anxiety about having or acquiring a serious illness despite negative diagnostic testing. These patients often experience minimal symptoms and have normal physical examinations. This patient has a preoccupation with her symptoms rather than a specific diagnosis. Educational Objective: Somatization disorder is characterized by excessive preoccupation with one or more somatic symptoms such that these symptoms disrupt the patient's daily life. Patients persistently devote excessive time and energy to these symptoms or related health concerns (eg, repeatedly going to the doctor). 4 e Previous Score Report Calculator

questionStem: A5/-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive hearing loss in his left ear. He initially only had difficulty hearing while talking on the telephone, but now he has difficulty hearing most of the time. During this period, he occasionally has had a 30-second episode of unsteadiness and a spinning sensation. He has been otherwise healthy. Examination shows flattening of the left nasolabial fold and decreased wrinkling of the forehead on the left side. There is rotatory nystagmus on right lateral gaze and profound sensorineural hearing loss on the left. Mental status examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely location of the lesion?
correctExplanation: Acoustic neuromas are tumors derived from Schwann cells involving the vestibulocochlear nerve. The vestibulocochlear nerve originates between the pons and medulla oblongata and exits the brainstem near the cerebellopontine angle. Symptoms associated with the development of an acoustic neuroma include hearing loss and tinnitus associated with the cochlear nerve as well as gait instability and vertigo associated with the vestibular nerve. As tumors enlarge there may be involvement of the trigeminal nerve or facial nerve. Patients with neurofibromatosis 2 may present with bilateral acoustic neuromas. Imaging studies, including CT scan or MRI, can be used to make the diagnosis. Treatment options include surgical resection or radiation therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Brain stem tegmentum (Choice A) is the portion of the brainstem ventral to the cerebral aqueduct and fourth ventricle. This area would not be affected by an acoustic neuroma. Cochlea (Choice C) is a component of the inner ear and plays a role in the sensation of hearing and transducing auditory signals to the brain. Patients with damage to the cochlea experience sensorineural hearing loss. Mastoid bone (Choice D) is located posterior to the ear and contains mastoid air cells. This area is a potential space for infection in patients with fever of unknown origin or following prolonged or spreading otitis media. Mastoiditis, or inflammation of the mastoid bone, would not cause this patient's symptoms. Temporal lobe (Choice E) contributes to the cerebral cortex and is associated with auditory perception, language recognition, comprehension, and speech. A lesion involving the Wernicke area of the temporal lobe results in Wernicke aphasia where patients can produce speech though it is often garbled and inappropriate. Educational Objective: Acoustic neuromas are caused by overgrowth of Schwann cells of the vestibulocochlear nerve. The vestibulocochlear nerve originates between the pons and medulla oblongata and exits the brainstem near the cerebellopontine angle. Patients with acoustic neuromas may present with hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, and gait abnormalities. Bilateral acoustic neuromas are associated with neurofibromatosis 2. questionStem: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the physician because of a 3-month history of brief memory loss two to three times weekly. She also has had difficulty maintaining her balance. She has glaucoma, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension. Her medications are pilocarpine eyedrops, losartan, and atorvastatin. Her pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. Examination shows arcus senilis and slight restriction of upward gaze. Deep tendon reflexes are decreased at the ankles compared with the knees. On gait testing, she walks flexed at the waist and is unable to tandem walk. On mental status examination, she is fully oriented. She performs serial sevens without difficulty. Her immediate, recent, and remote memory is intact. She displays normal abstract thinking. Which of the following best explains this patient's neurologic findings?
correctExplanation: This patient with brief episodic memory loss, arcus senilis, decreased Achilles reflexes, and flexed posture is showing signs of psychomotor slowing consistent with normal aging. Normal aging includes a slow decline of executive functioning, attention span, and problem-solving after age 70 years. Other findings consistent with aging include decreased or absent Achilles reflex, arcus senilis (grey or white arch visible around the outer edge of the cornea), decreased vision and hearing, decreased immune response, and increased suicide rate. Despite these common changes, an individual experiencing normal aging should still be able to function in society.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cerebellar degeneration (Choice A) may present with truncal and limb ataxia, broad-based gait, and intention tremor. Multiple lacunar infarctions (Choice B) may present with purely motor symptoms, purely sensory symptoms, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria. Infarcts in these deep penetrating vessels are secondary to hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and/or hypercholesterolemia. Parkinson disease (Choice C) is caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and is characterized by resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability. Peripheral neuropathy (Choice D) has many causes, including metabolic, toxic, autoimmune, and/or hereditary neuropathy. Symptoms include paresthesia or pain, and extremity weakness in a “stocking-glove’” distribution. Educational Objective: Normal aging includes a slow decline of executive functioning, attention span, and problem-solving after age 70 years. Other findings consistent with normal aging include decreased or absent Achilles reflex, arcus senilis, decreased vision and hearing, decreased immune response, and increased suicide rate. 4 ry (is ~- e a Previous Score Report et) V al Lc S Calculator Help Pause

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 37-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 3-day history of weakness of her arms and legs. Her symptoms began 6 days ago with backache and a prickling sensation in her legs. She is alert and oriented. Vital signs are within normal limits. Cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the distal upper and lower extremities and 4/5 in the proximal upper and lower extremities. She is unable to walk without assistance. Sensation to pinprick is decreased below the knees. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in the Achilles and patellar tendons bilaterally. Babinski sign is absent bilaterally. Laboratory studies show: Serum glucose 102 mg/dL Cerebrospinal fluid Glucose 66 mg/dL Protein 90 mg/dL WBC 0-—2/mm° Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Compression of the cervical spinal cord

correctExplanation: This patient most likely has Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) leading to an ascending polyneuropathy. In GBS, a preceding infection (eg, Campylobacter jejuni, influenza-like illnesses) leads to autoimmune cross-reactivity with the myelin of the nerve roots exiting the spinal cord. The ventral nerve roots, containing motor and sympathetic efferents, are most commonly involved, though the dorsal nerve roots (controlling sensation) may also be affected. As such, patients typically present with acute symmetric muscle weakness with depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes (reflecting a lower motor neuron pattern of dysfunction) that begins in the lower extremities and may rapidly ascend to involve the upper extremities, bulbar muscles, and/or respiratory muscles. Autonomic dysfunction (eg, blood pressure fluctuations, cardiac irregularities) is common. Sensory deficits and pain can also occur, though these symptoms are typically mild compared with motor dysfunction. The diagnosis is confirmed by increased cerebrospinal fluid protein with normal cell counts on lumbar puncture, termed albuminocytologic dissociation, thought to reflect generalized inflammation. Management includes respiratory support and, for severe cases, plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin therapy. Intravenous immunoglobulin therapy may work by neutralizing the cross-reactive antibodies that cause GBS.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Compression of the cervical spinal cord (Choice A), such as with a herniated cervical disc, leads to cervical myelopathy. This can present with varying degrees of sensory and motor neurologic deficits, along with the potential for autonomic dysfunction, including bowel and bladder function. Multiple sclerosis (Choice C) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease that presents with focal neurologic deficits separated in space and time. Patients with multiple sclerosis may present initially with optic neuritis or transverse myelitis, which may demonstrate a sensory level and a band-like sensation, along with possible autonomic and motor symptoms. Myasthenia gravis (Choice D) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by the formation of inhibitory antiacetylcholine receptor autoantibodies. Common symptoms include muscular weakness, fatigue, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens toward the end of the day, dysphagia, and respiratory distress. Patients may present with an associated thymoma. 4 r ly (is - i a Previous Score Report etd) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: A5/-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after his wife was unable to arouse him from sleep. He has hypertension but is currently taking no medications. His blood pressure is 190/100 mm Hg. Examination shows both eyes deviated to the left. He does not withdraw his right upper and lower extremities to painful stimuli. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient with uncontrolled hypertension, left eye deviation, right-sided weakness, and depressed mental status has a presentation concerning for intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). ICH can occur in patients with chronic hypertension, typically due to hemorrhage from small penetrating arteries in the pons, midbrain, thalamus, putamen, caudate, or cerebellum. Risk factors for hypertensive ICH include uncontrolled hypertension and antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, such as with aspirin or warfarin. Patients can present with headache, vomiting, confusion, altered mental status, stupor, or coma. Focal neurologic deficits depend on the site of the ICH and can include hemiparesis, hemisensory symptoms, gaze palsy, dysarthria, aphasia, or if in the cerebellum, ataxia, vomiting, and disequilibrium. Patients may manifest upper motor neuron examination findings such as spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar reflex (Babinski sign). Diagnosis is made with noncontrast CT scan of the head, which will show hyperdense intraparenchymal acute blood products.

Horizontal deviation of both eyes toward the affected ear indicates an intact reflex. This test is often performed as a part of the cranial nerve examination in a patient with suspected brain death. EEG (Choice B) would be appropriate in the setting of suspected seizure. Patients with seizures often have eye deviation, but this patient lacks other common features consistent with seizures, including focal or generalized shaking, incontinence, and tongue biting. MRI of the spine (Choice D) would be appropriate if spinal cord injury or compression was suspected. Patients with spinal cord compression often present with back or neck pain in addition to weakness or numbness corresponding with the area of spinal involvement. Lumbar puncture (Choice E) should be performed if the diagnosis of meningitis is suspected. Patients with meningitis often present with fever, headache, neck pain and rigidity, and confusion. Gaze deviation and unilateral upper motor neuron signs are not consistent with meningitis. questionStem: A63-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of double vision. She also has a 1-week history of moderate pain and numbness around her right eye. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Examination shows exophthalmos of the right eye. When asked to look to the right, the patient reports double vision; the right eye does not fully abduct. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the right forehead and below the right eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Cavernous sinus thrombosis classically follows an infection or injury involving a structure drained by the cavernous sinus and results in cranial nerve deficits involving those that traverse the cavernous sinus (Ill, IV, V1, V2, or VI). Causes include sinusitis, orbital cellulitis, dental infections, pharyngitis, and cellulitis or abscess, especially within the danger triangle of the face (formed by the apex of the nose and the corners of the mouth). Features include fever, orbit pain, exophthalmos, periorbital edema, impaired pupil reactivity, and impaired extraocular movement, causing diplopia. Impaired corneal reflex and sensation in the V1 and/or V2 distribution can also occur. When the cause is orbital cellulitis, patients may additionally present with pain with extraocular movements and optic nerve dysfunction, which can be suggested by the presence of decreased color perception, a relative afferent pupillary defect, or optic disc edema. Patients in whom cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected should undergo urgent CT venography or contrast-enhanced MR venography. Treatment involves anticoagulation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and antifungals. Even with prompt recognition and appropriate treatment, the burden of long-term complications, including visual impairment and stroke, remains high.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Graves disease (Choice B) can present with weight loss, insomnia, palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, diaphoresis, thyromegaly, and exophthalmos. Laboratory studies show increased thyroxine and triiodothyronine, decreased TSH, and the presence of TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies. While this patient has exophthalmos, she lacks other systemic signs of Graves disease. Mitochondrial myopathy (Choice C) is a hereditary condition that can present with ophthalmoplegia, seizures, myoclonus, peripheral neuropathy, proximal muscle weakness, and fatigue. Diagnosis can be confirmed by ragged red fibers on muscle biopsy and mitochondrial crystalline inclusions on electron microscopy. This patient’s acute onset of ophthalmoplegia and lack of a compatible family history are not consistent with this diagnosis. Paramedian pontine infarction (Choice D) can affect the abducens and facial nerves, the medial longitudinal fasciculus, and the corticospinal tract, leading to impaired abduction of the ipsilateral eye, ipsilateral facial paresis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye and contralateral abduction saccade), and contralateral hemiparesis. Exophthalmos and a history of eye pain are not consistent with this diagnosis. Posterior communicating artery aneurysm (Choice E) may compress the ipsilateral oculomotor cranial nerve, resulting in ptosis, exotropia and hypotropia (lateral and inferior pupil position), diplopia, and mydriasis. The detection of a new oculomotor nerve palsy is a medical emergency, as aneurysmal rupture can lead to life-threatening subarachnoid hemorrhage. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (Choice F) causes microvascular damage to a variety of tissues, including nerves, and can cause cranial nerve palsy. Microvascular abducens nerve palsy presents with esotropia, unilateral abduction deficit, and horizontal gaze diplopia. Exophthalmos is not associated with microvascular nerve palsy. 4 ry. oO (5 = [ > a Previous

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 3-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of decreased feeding. He also has a 1-day history of cough that worsens when he attempts to feed. His mother reports that he seems hungry but "tires out" while feeding. He was born at 40 weeks' gestation to a 25-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He weighed 3600 g (7 Ib 15 oz) at birth. Until 1 week ago, he had been exclusively breast-fed; he now receives cow milk-based formula. The patient's father has been excavating the soil around the house to build a foundation for an additional room. On examination, the patient is alert and quiet and has a weak cry. He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 138/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 72/48 mm Hg. Examination of the skin shows no abnormalities. Facial expression is absent. The pupils are 5 mm and sluggishly reactive. The gag reflex is decreased. Transmitted upper airway noises are heard. No murmurs are heard. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Peripheral pulses are 2+ and symmetric. There is head lag and no spontaneous movement of the extremities. Muscle tone is decreased. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient with difficulty feeding, hypotonia, and facial muscle weakness has a presentation concerning for infantile botulism. Botulism is an acute disease of the neuromuscular junctio caused by exposure to the Clostridium botulinum toxin. C. botulinum is a gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic bacterium. It produces botulinum toxin, a potent neurotoxin tha is absorbed into the end-terminal of cholinergic motor neurons, where it cleaves SNARE proteins, thereby preventing the release of acetylcholine vesicles into the neuromuscular junction. Botulism is often encountered as a food-borne illness through contaminated food products. Historically, C. botulinum was responsible for outbreaks of “sausage poisoning” through contaminated ham products and acquired its name after the Latin for sausage, “botulus.” In the modern era, it is more often responsible for poisoning via the ingestion of raw honey or canned foods. In infants, infection most commonly occurs through inhalation of spores from contaminated soil or dust; however, a common route of exposure is the ingestion of spores in honey when a parent feeds it to a child. The infant gastrointestinal flora is not sufficiently mature to prevent infection. Botulism presents with rapidly progressive, symmetric hypotonia and hyporeflexia that begins with the cranial nerves, manifesting as ptosis, sluggish pupils, and a diminished gag reflex, and descends to the lower extremities, also causing constipation, poor feeding, and respiratory failure. Diagnosis is confirmed by identification of the botulinum toxin in the stool. Treatment requires hospitalization and administration of immune globulin, as well as supportive care, which often includes mechanical ventilation.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Measurement of serum cholinesterase activity (Choice B) can be performed in suspected cases of organophosphate toxicity. Patients classically present with diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, vomiting, lacrimation, and salivation. Measurement of negative inspiratory force (NIF) (Choice C) can be performed to assess respiratory muscle strength in patients with muscular weakness. A low NIF may indicate that a patient is at risk for respiratory muscle fatigue and decompensation and may necessitate respiratory support. Patients with botulism may develop diaphragmatic weakness and therefore may have a low NIF, but this is a nonspecific finding and is not diagnostic for any one disease. Additionally, measurement of NIF requires patient participation (patient is instructed to fully inhale), which would not be possible for this 3-month-old patient. Muscle biopsy (Choice D) is not a part of the workup for botulism. Biopsy should be normal in patients with botulism, as it is a disease of the neuromuscular junction, not the muscle itself Electromyography and nerve conduction studies (Choice E) and repetitive nerve stimulation study (Choice F) can be done to support the diagnosis of botulism, but the gold standard is the stool toxin assay. questionStem: A9-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. There is an open fracture of the tibial shaft, and the patient reports severe pain in the area surrounding the fracture. On examination, there is weakness of toe flexion, severe pain with passive extension of the toes, and plantar hyperesthesia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Compartment syndrome occurs when there is increased pressure in the intramuscular compartment that compromises circulation and neuromuscular and neurologic function. Compartment syndrome commonly occurs in the setting of trauma, including long bone fractures, and symptoms include pain out of proportion to the injury, paresthesia, and pain with passive stretching of the muscles. Late findings are pallor, pulselessness, and paralysis. Diagnosis is confirmed after clinical suspicion by measuring compartment pressures. Increased compartment pressure or minimal difference between compartment pressure and perfusing blood pressures confirm the diagnosis. Patients with compartment syndrome are treated with emergency fasciotomy to decompress involved compartments; delays may lead to poor outcomes.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complex regional pain syndrome (Choice B), or reflex sympathetic dystrophy, presents with regional pain that is out of proportion to the insult. Other symptoms include edema, abnormal sensation, swelling, and erythema. The most common inciting event for complex regional pain syndrome is a soft tissue injury. Deep venous thrombosis (Choice C) causes extremity swelling, pain, and discoloration. Symptoms may be acute or subacute in nature, and patients are treated with anticoagulants. This patient's clinical presentation is not consistent with deep venous thrombosis. Ruptured posterior tibial artery (Choice D) may result from posterior knee dislocation, direct trauma, or aneurysmal disease. This injury is usually the result of high-impact trauma, such as a motor vehicle collision. Patients may present with abnormal pulses and pain. Rapid identification of this injury, imaging with angiography, and repair of the injured vessel must be completed promptly to salvage the affected limb. Transection of the tibial nerve (Choice E) may occur in the case of high-impact trauma or during surgical procedures. Symptoms may differ depending on the level of injury. This patient's symptoms, including pain out of proportion to the injury, are more suggestive of compartment syndrome. Educational Objective: Compartment syndrome may arise in the setting of trauma and is associated with severe pain, paresthesia, and pain with passive movement. As vascular compromise worsens, patients may experience pallor, pulselessness, and paralysis. Diagnosis is made by measurement of compartment pressures, and patients are treated with emergent fasciotomy. 4 go (ic r — Previous Score Report et) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the office to request genetic testing. She was adopted at birth, and her adoptive parents were told that there was a strong maternal history of psychotic behavior and a movement disorder. The patient has been unable to obtain any further medical information. She has no history of serious illness. She takes no medications. She is planning to start college in the fall and has been an excellent student throughout high school. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. There is no evidence of abnormal movements. Mental status examination shows an anxious mood. She reports no hallucinations, and there is no evidence of delusions. After further counseling, the patient elects to proceed with genetic testing. Testing for which of the following is most appropriate at this time?
correctExplanation: Based on the reported maternal history of psychiatric and movement symptoms, this patient should be offered testing for Huntington disease (HD). HD is a hereditary, progressive neurodegenerative disorder typically arising in the 3rd to 6th decades of life associated with atrophy of the caudate nuclei in the basal ganglia, which can be seen on MRI of the brain. The disease usually presents with an insidious onset of psychiatric (irritability, depression, psychosis) and cognitive symptoms. Motor symptoms (chorea, hypotonia, dystonia, loss of voluntary control of movements) typically appear later in the disease course. Patients with HD typically die 10 to 40 years after disease onset. Chorea, a key HD symptom, can be initially experienced as restlessness. Treatment is symptomatic and can include tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine, which target chorea by depleting dopamine stores. HD is caused by expansion of a trinucleotide repeat (CAG) on chromosome four, which occurs when a series of three nucleotides in repetition are replicated incorrectly and too many repeats are included in the replicated product. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and also demonstrates anticipation, a genetic inheritance phenomenon in which future generations are affected at a younger age or with more severe symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Fragile X syndrome (Choice A) is an X-linked dominant cause of inherited intellectual disability that presents due to a CGG-trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR7 gene. It presents with clinical features including intellectual disability, an elongated face with a prominent jaw, a high-arched palate, large ears, hyperextensible joints, and postpubertal macroorchidism. These features are less consistent with this patient's reported family history. Hepatolenticular degeneration (Wilson disease) (Choice B) is caused by impaired metabolism of copper and deposition in the liver and brain. Most patients will have some degree of liver disease at the time of diagnosis. Neurologic and psychiatric manifestations are broad and can mimic other neurologic disorders, especially ones with movement-related symptoms. However, patients with neurologic abnormalities will almost always have Kayser-Fleischer rings. This, along with liver disease, can help distinguish Wilson disease from similar disorders. Initial testing involves measurement of serum ceruloplasmin concentrations. Parkinson disease (Choice D) is also characterized by movement-related, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. While having a first-degree relative with Parkinson disease increases the risk for developing it, the majority of cases are idiopathic. The largest risk factor is advanced age, and men are more likely than women to develop the disorder. Genetic testing can estimate risk but is likely to be lower yield than testing for HD in this patient. Porphyria (Choice E), particularly acute intermittent porphyria, refers to the abnormal accumulation of the red blood cell protein porphyrin and is characterized by episodic abdominal pain, polyneuropathy, psychological symptoms, and port wine-colored urine. The associated polyneuropathy typically presents as acute sensory and motor neuropathy of the extremities. Educational Objective: Huntington disease (HD) is a hereditary, progressive neurodegenerative disorder associated with atrophy of the caudate nuclei in the basal ganglia. questionStem: A2/-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of pain, weakness, and numbness in both arms and hands. Examination shows weakness and atrophy of the muscles of the arms and hands bilaterally. There is loss of sensation to pain and temperature over the neck, shoulders, and upper extremities but preservation of sensation to light touch. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in the upper extremities. He has thoracic kyphoscoliosis. Neurologic examination of the lower extremities and cranial nerves shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient presenting with a lower motor neuron pattern of dysfunction in the upper extremities likely has syringomyelia. Syringomyelia features a progressively expanding cystic lesion involving midline spinal cord structures. Syringomyelia may be associated with congenital malformations such as Chiari malformation type I, spinal cord infections, autoimmune diseases like multiple sclerosis, neoplasms, or spinal cord trauma. Syringomyelia typically damages spinothalamic fibers decussating in the anterior white commissure. Consequently, patients present with deficits in pain and temperature sensation in the bilateral upper extremities (because the ascending spinothalamic tracts in the lateral spinal cord are unaffected, sensation i the lower body is intact). The cystic lesion can expand to the bilateral anterior horns (the location of the cell bodies of lower motor neurons). Therefore, patients may also present with a lower motor neuron pattern of dysfunction in the bilateral upper extremities (eg, decreased muscle tone, hyporeflexia, early muscle atrophy). The cyst may also progressively expand to the lateral corticospinal tract in severe cases, leading to an upper motor neuron pattern of dysfunction (eg, spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign) in the lower body.
incorrectExplanation: nd J. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Choice A) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects the anterior horns along with the lateral corticospinal tract as it descends in the brain an spinal cord. Subsequently, patients demonstrate a combination of upper and lower motor neuron findings in an asymmetric distribution that may include the bulbar muscles. Sensory impairment would be atypical, and a pattern of dysfunction that can be localized to a single lesion within the cervical spine is more consistent with syringomyelia. Cerebellar degeneration (Choice B) can occur with chronic alcohol use, nutritional deficiency, or as a paraneoplastic disorder and presents with ataxia, gait instability, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Cervical spondylosis (Choice C) leading to narrowing of the cervical canal and compression of the cervical spinal cord often presents with neck or shoulder pain, numbness, and weakness of all extremities. Gait instability and weakness of the lower extremities with upper motor neuron characteristics are common early symptoms. Friedreich ataxia (Choice D) is a genetic condition that presents with ataxia, spasticity, and impaired speech typically in young children or adolescents. questionStem: An 85-year-old man with a 4-year history of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is evaluated in the intensive care unit (ICU) 3 weeks after admission for treatment of respiratory failure. Prior to admission, the patient had experienced progressive weakness since ALS was diagnosed, to the point where he was unable to swallow or speak. After admission to the ICU, he underwent tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation. Since admission, four attempts to wean the patient from the ventilator have failed. During today's evaluation, the patient is awake and remains unable to answer any questions correctly. He has little voluntary movement of the chest wall. Physical examination discloses diffuse atrophy, prominent fasciculations, marked weakness in all extremities, and diffuse hyperreflexia. Prior to admission, he told his family that he did not want extreme measures utilized to keep him alive. The patient does not have a living will, but his daughter has medical durable power of attorney for the patient. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for the physician to give this patient's family?

choices.B: Consider stem cell therapy for treatment of ALS
choices.C: Continue supportive care, administer antibiotic therapy, and attempt to wean the patient from the ventilator
choices.E: Request a consultation with the hospital ethics committee

correctExplanation: This patient has expressed a preference regarding end-of-life care prior to his current illness but is currently incapacitated and unable to express a preference regarding his care. Options for directing care in a state of incapacity include durable powers of attorney or advance directives, which enable patients to dictate their preferences for end-of-life care ahead of time or delegate these responsibilities to a designated person. A power of attorney grants a particular person authority to act on the patient’s behalf should the patient become incapacitated. This patient is currently incapacitated, and therefore legal authority for this patient's healthcare decision-making is held by the power of attorney. Given this patient’s previously stated wishes and poor prognosis for recovery, it is reasonable to consider discontinuing care. This decision must ultimately be made by the patient's designated power of attorney in this case.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Considering stem cell therapy for treatment of ALS (Choice B) is incorrect. Consideration of experimental treatments would be inappropriate given this patient's advanced state of disease and current respiratory failure. questionStem: A32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of daily generalized headaches. She occasionally has blurred vision in the right eye during a headache. Treatment with ibuprofen relieves the headaches. She has had a 23-kg (50-lb) weight gain and menstrual irregularity over the past year. Menses now occur at irregular 20- to 90-day intervals. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 Ib); BMI is 29 kg/m2. Examination shows a visual acuity of 20/20 in both eyes. The visual fields are normal. Optic discs are indistinct, and spontaneous venous pulsations are not observed. The remainder of the neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is primarily driven by impaired resorption of cerebrospinal fluid. Signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) include headache, nausea, vomiting, and tinnitus; transient visual obscuration or blurry vision secondary to pressure on the optic nerve can occur. Examination findings include papilledema and increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture without any underlying pathology to cause such findings on neuroimaging. It is primarily found in young women who are overweight. Although there is no malignant cause underlying the increased ICP, it may cause debilitating headaches and permanent vision loss. Headaches that are secondary to increased ICP often are worse when lying down and relieved by standing. The most common risk factors for the development of IIH include female sex and obesity. However, hypervitaminosis A is another potential cause of IIH. This can be from excessive dietary intake or from the use of retinoid medications such as isotretinoin or all-trans retinoic acid. Other medications associated with IIH include tetracyclines, oral contraceptives, danazol, and growth hormone.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Pituitary tumor (Choice B) can present with headache and either hypopituitarism or hyperpituitarism, depending on whether the tumor is nonfunctional or functional in nature. Compression of the adjacent optic chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopsia, not unilateral blurred vision. Status migrainosus (Choice C) is defined as a debilitating, refractory migraine attack persisting for over 72 hours. Treatment includes intravenous nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as ketorolac, as well as dopamine receptor blockers, such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine. Subdural hematoma (Choice D) may result from head trauma and hemorrhage from bridging veins in the subdural space. Evidence of increased ICP such as postural headache and papilledema are present, as in this patient, but progressive neurologic decline will also occur. On imaging, it appears as a crescent-shaped fluid collection abutting the internal surface of the skull, not bound by suture lines. Tension-type headache (Choice E) typically presents with bilateral dull, pressure-like or band-like pain across the frontal and temporal areas, often arising from stress. It does not present with postural headache, papilledema, visual deficits, or other neurologic signs. Educational Objective: Impaired resorption of cerebrospinal fluid is the mechanism behind idiopathic intracranial hypertension, which is characterized by headache, papilledema, and increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture without any underlying pathology to cause such findings on neuroimaging. It is primarily found in young women who are overweight. r 4 e ‘fg e C e Previous Score Report et) V al LCS Calculator Help Pause

questionStem: A/-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of dull, generalized headache for the past 2 days. During the past week, the patient has had difficulty walking and frequently has had loss of balance. She has no history of serious illness, and her growth and development have been appropriate for age. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 100/75 mm Hg. Physical examination shows tilting of the head to the left. There is marked horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze bilaterally. Visual field testing shows no abnormalities, and visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. Finger-nose testing shows past-pointing bilaterally. She has an ataxic gait, and there is in-toeing of the left foot. Romberg sign is present. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Tumor of the vestibulocochlear cranial nerve

correctExplanation: This patient with headache, ataxia, dysmetria, and nystagmus has a presentation concerning for a brain stem glioma. Gliomas are the most common pediatric brain tumor and are typically low-grade pilocytic astrocytomas. Pediatric gliomas commonly grow in the cerebellum but can occur in the brain stem. Patients typically present with focal neurologic deficits caused by mass effect that may progress over the course of months as a result of the tumor growing larger and affecting additional brain regions. Treatment centers around radiation and chemotherapy for brain stem gliomas.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Craniopharyngioma (Choice B) is a rare pituitary mass derived from remnants of the Rathke pouch. Due to its proximity to the optic chiasm, patients classically present with bitemporal hemianopsia, but a horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze as found in this patient would be very unusual. Great vein of Galen aneurysm (Choice C) is a rare form of arteriovenous malformation that affects one of the intracranial veins. This may be diagnosed on fetal ultrasonography or shortly after birth. Patients often present with signs and symptoms of heart failure. Meningitis (Choice D) may present with a headache, neck pain, and fever. This patient's lack of fever in addition to numerous focal neurologic deficits point to an alternative diagnosis. Tumor of the vestibulocochlear cranial nerve (Choice E), such as an acoustic neuroma, can cause ipsilateral hearing loss and vertigo, and if also compressing the trigeminal nerve, can lead to ipsilateral facial numbness and paresthesia. Educational Objective: Gliomas are the most common pediatric brain tumor and are typically low-grade pilocytic astrocytomas that may occur in the cerebellum or brain stem. Gliomas commonly present with focal neurologic deficits caused by mass effect that may progress over the course of months as a result of the tumor growing larger and affecting additional brain regions. 4 r. oe (is ~- > ri Previous

questionStem: A 71-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 2-month history of increasingly severe, aching pain in her shoulders, upper arms, and thighs. She says, "I can't roll over in bed any longer and my husband has to assist me in getting up from a chair." She also has had associated muscle stiffness that lasts 1 hour every morning upon awakening; the same stiffness sometimes occurs in the afternoon following periods of inactivity. She also reports awakening multiple times during the night, diffuse joint pain, and a 7.7-kg (17-lb) weight loss despite no change in appetite. Menopause occurred at age 56 years. She also has osteopenia and generalized anxiety disorder. Her medications are estradiol, escitalopram, and vitamin D and calcium supplementation. Her mother and aunt had rheumatoid arthritis, and her brother had sclerosing cholangitis. The patient appears to be in moderate discomfort. She is 174 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 64 kg (140 Ib); BMI is 21 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.3°C (97.3°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Muscle strength and tone are normal. She is unable to actively abduct the shoulders bilaterally past 90 degrees because of stiffness. Passive range of motion of the shoulders and hips is decreased. There is no pain on palpation of the temporalis muscles. Results of laboratory studies are shown: Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL Hematocrit 25% Leukocyte count 8200/mm? Platelet count 572,000/mm? Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 82 mm/h Serum C-reactive protein 15.3 mg/L Creatine kinase 112 U/L Electromyography and nerve conduction studies disclose no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

choices.B: Biopsy of the vastus medialis muscle
choices.E: Polymerase chain reaction testing for Rickettsia rickettsii

correctExplanation: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition characterized by proximal muscle and joint (eg, shoulder and hip girdle) pain, stiffness, and increased inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. If untreated, muscle weakness may occur from disuse atrophy. Systemic symptoms such as fatigue are commonly noted. It is most common in patients over age 60 years, and some patients have associated temporal arteritis. Signs of temporal arteritis such as throbbing temporal headache, vision changes, or jaw claudication should prompt temporal artery biopsy. The diagnosis of PMR is based on clinical features, and treatment is with prednisone for up to 1 year. It is common for patients to respond to prednisone almost immediately; thus, the absence of response should prompt consideration of a different diagnosis.

It commonly presents with headache and jaw claudication and is commonly associated with PMR. This patient does not display any symptoms suggestive of temporal arteritis. a ly és y — Previous Score Report et) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: A47-year-old man comes to the physician because of severe pain of the left eye and double vision that began after a motor vehicle collision 1 week ago. At the time of the collision, he hit his head but did not lose consciousness. He did not seek medical attention at that time. Examination shows exophthalmos, chemosis, and distention of the orbital and periorbital veins in the left eye. A bruit is heard over the left orbit. There is incomplete abduction of the left eye when looking to the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Carotid cavernous fistula (CCF) results from an inappropriate connection between the carotid artery and cavernous sinus, often caused by head trauma, aneurysmal rupture, inflammation, or vascular or connective tissue disease. Arterial pressure in the cavernous sinus results in cranial nerve deficits involving those that traverse the cavernous sinus (Ill, IV, V1, V2, or VI) as a result of extrinsic compression. Other findings can include vascular congestion of the ipsilateral eye and face, exophthalmos, chemosis, unilateral headache, eye pain, visual loss, and an audible bruit on auscultation of the eye. CCFs can be categorized as low-flow fistulas, which result from communication between the cavernous sinus and cavernous arterial branches, or as high-flow fistulas, which result from a direct communication between the cavernous sinus and the internal carotid artery. Cerebral angiography, the gold standard diagnostic modality, will show flow through the fistula. CT or MR angiography may also be used. First-line treatment is endovascular intervention with embolization or stenting.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acute cerebral infarction (Choice A) can present with a sudden change in mental status, upper motor neuron signs, and acute focal neurologic deficits, especially on one side of the body and may have speech difficulty, dysarthria, or aphasia, depending on the vascular territory involved. Exophthalmos and an ocular bruit are not consistent with an acute cerebral infarction Arteriovenous malformation (Choice B) describes an abnormal tangle of blood vessels located within the brain. A ruptured arteriovenous malformation may result in a subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). ICH appears as a hyperdense collection of blood within the brain parenchyma on CT scan. ICH often presents with focal neurologic deficits based on their location with an associated headache and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (eg, vomiting, altered mental status). Epidural hematomas (Choice D) are classically associated with trauma to the middle meningeal artery. They present on CT scan as a lens-shaped, biconvex hyperdense collection abutting the skull, often compressing adjacent brain, and are bound by dural sutures. Classic features include an initial lucid interval followed by deterioration of mental status caused by arterial bleeding and hematoma expansion, along with headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures, and coma. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Choice E) typically presents with an acute, severe headache along with neck stiffness, photophobia, and possible stupor or coma in severe cases. CT scan o the head typically shows hyperdense blood products in the cerebral sulci and basal cisterns. Intracranial aneurysms are the most common cause of nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage, followed by arteriovenous malformations. It is a neurosurgical emergency that may be fatal if progressive or untreated. Subdural hematomas (Choice F) may result from head trauma and hemorrhage from bridging veins in the subdural space. They present with subacute-onset headache, nausea, vomiting, and may present with focal neurologic deficits or seizures caused by mass effect. Subdural hematomas appear as a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection in parallel to the curvature of the skull and cross the dural sutures. r 4 @ oa = Previous Score Report eet) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: After renovating a new home, a 41-year-old woman has burning pain and tingling in her right index, long, and ring fingers, particularly at night. The thenar eminence becomes atrophied. Which of the following structures is most likely to be damaged?
correctExplanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel and presents with signs and symptoms including pain, weakness, and paresthesia of the first three digits and the lateral half of the fourth digit, along with positive provocative test maneuvers such as the Tinel or Phalen tests. The carpal tunnel is located anterior to the carpal bones and is bound by the flexor retinaculum. The flexor tendons of the fingers course through the tunnel, along with the median nerve. The space is rigid and does not generally permit compression; thus, any inflammatory, traumatic, or space-filling lesion may result in CTS. Patients generally present with pain and paresthesia in the median nerve distribution, along with weakness involving the muscles of the thenar eminence that eventually may atrophy. Symptoms are generally worse at night and relieved with shaking of the hands. CTS is frequently associated with pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, amyloidosis, ganglion cysts, obesity, and acute trauma to the wrist with impingement, or chronic remodeling and scar formation following a wrist injury. Patients with mild symptoms can be treated conservatively with wrist splinting. Wrist splints are typically worn at night but may also be used during the day. Splinting reduces the range of motion of the wrist and limits activities that increase pressure within the carpal tunnel. Patients who have persistent or severe symptoms or muscular weakness may require surgical decompression.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Injuries to the radial artery (Choice A) and ulnar artery (Choice B) would not result in chronic neurologic dysfunction or muscle atrophy. The radial nerve (Choice D) courses posterior to the humerus at the midshaft within the radial groove. It is often injured in displaced midshaft humerus fractures, with resulting wrist drop. The radial nerve supplies motor fibers to the triceps brachii and the extensor muscles within the posterior compartment of the forearm, and sensory fibers to the dorsum of the forearm, wrist, and hand. The ulnar nerve (Choice E) supplies motor fibers to the intrinsic muscles of the hand, and sensation over the anteromedial ring and small fingers and medial palm including hypothenar eminence. Damage to the roots or to the nerve along its course (eg, in the cubital tunnel) can result in motor dysfunction of the fingers, and numbness or paresthesia involving the medial aspect of the upper extremity. Educational Objective: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel and presents with signs and symptoms including pain, weakness, and paresthesia of the first three digits and the lateral half of the fourth digit, along with weakness and atrophy of the thenar eminence. om ly Previous Score Report

questionStem: A21-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her mother 1 hour after a 30-minute episode of generalized shaking. One week ago, the patient had a similar episode that began while she was at home watching television with her mother. At that time, the patient fell to the ground and had irregular jerking of her hands and legs. During the episode, her eyes were open and she was occasionally able to respond to her mother's commands. The episode lasted 10 minutes. The patient has had 15 similar episodes during the past week. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 6 years. She drinks three to four 12-0z beers weekly. She does not use illicit drugs. She works as a home health aide. She has been under great stress recently following her breakup with her fiance. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical, neurologic, and mental status examinations disclose no abnormalities. CT scan of the head discloses no abnormalities. During a video EEG, the patient has a typical seizure; there are no epileptiform EEG changes during the episode. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Conversion disorder, also Known as functional neurologic symptom disorder, involves neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not fully explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. This patient is presenting with episodes of generalized shaking and jerking during which she is able to respond to commands, and a negative EEG likely indicates psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, a form of conversion disorder. Functional neurologic symptom disorder is postulated to represent the subconscious conversion of intolerable emotional distress into physical symptoms. Psychiatric comorbidities such as depression are common but not present in all patients. Physicians should conduct a thorough history and physical examination and obtain laboratory and imaging studies to evaluate for medical or neurologic disease that may explain or partially explain the symptoms. Treatment of functional neurologic symptom disorder involves education about the diagnosis, physical therapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Long-term EEG monitoring (Choice B), often done for a 24-hour period, can be performed when titrating antiepileptic medications for patients with nonconvulsive status epilepticus. It can also be done if the diagnosis of epileptic seizures is still highly suspected after a negative short-term (30-minute) EEG. This patient's presentation is consistent with psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, which will not result in abnormal EEG activity. Measurement of serum prolactin concentration (Choice C) may be useful in helping to differentiate between epileptic and nonepileptic seizures. When measured within 20 minutes after an epileptic tonic-clonic seizure, serum prolactin concentrations are often two times the upper limit of normal. A normal prolactin concentration in this patient would be consistent with her psychogenic nonepileptic seizures but is unnecessary since she has already had a negative video EEG. MRI of the brain (Choice D) may be useful in the diagnosis of new-onset epileptic seizures with an unknown cause, but this patient’s presentation is consistent with conversion disorder, and an MRI is not necessary. Oxcarbazepine therapy (Choice E) is an appropriate option for some patients with epileptic seizures. Antiepileptic medications are not needed for patients with psychogenic nonepileptic seizures. Functional neurologic symptom disorder is postulated to represent the subconscious conversion of intolerable emotional distress into physical symptoms. questionStem: An 82-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of visual loss in the right eye. He has had no eye pain. He has had approximately five episodes of visual loss in the right eye over the past 3 weeks that lasted less than 1 hour. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Medications include captopril and simvastatin. His pulse is 85/min, and blood pressure is 135/90 mm Hg. Corrected visual acuity is 20/40 on the left and limited to hand motion on the right. There is a prominent afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Funduscopic findings of the right eye are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Age-related macular degeneration Central retinal artery occlusion
correctExplanation: This patient's presenting signs and symptoms of abrupt, painless vision loss and a pale fundus with normal foveal color are consistent with a diagnosis of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). CRAO commonly occurs as a result of embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery but may occur secondary to vasculitis, such as in the setting of temporal arteritis. Patients may have a history of preceding amaurosis fugax. Examination shows profound diminishment of visual acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and a pale fundus with preserved foveal color. CRAO is a medical emergency, as it is an ischemic stroke of the ophthalmic vasculature and indicates a high risk for associated ischemic stroke to the brain. Patients who present with CRAO should be admitted to a stroke center for emergent evaluation, including a search for a possible embolic source with echocardiography and duplex ultrasonography of the carotid arteries. A careful history and laboratory evaluation of ESR, serum C-reactive protein concentration, and platelet count should be performed to evaluate for possible temporal arteritis. There is no proven medical or surgical therapy for CRAO, and the visual prognosis is poor.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Age-related macular degeneration (Choice A) is an acquired retinal degeneration characterized by dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium and accumulation of macular drusen. Early stages of the disease may be asymptomatic or characterized by insidious blurring or metamorphopsia. In advanced stages, vision loss may result from retinal geographic atrophy or choroidal neovascularization with macular edema, exudation, or hemorrhage. Central retinal vein occlusion (Choice C) results in retinal ischemia and presents with acute vision loss, afferent pupillary defect, optic disc edema and hemorrhage, retinal vascular tortuosity, retinal hemorrhage, and often, subsequent retinal and iris neovascularization. Retinal hemorrhage is the predominant finding, rather than retinal pallor. Risk factors include age, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking, diabetes mellitus, coagulopathy or blood dyscrasia, and increased intraocular pressure. Hypertensive retinopathy (Choice D) manifests with optic disc edema, retinal nerve fiber layer infarctions, and retinal hemorrhages. Findings are typically bilateral. Previous

questionStem: A4/-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband 45 minutes after the sudden onset of a severe headache. She has a 25-year history of occasional throbbing headaches. The headaches occur once or twice annually, are associated with nausea and vomiting, and are relieved with sleep. She has hypertension treated with enalapril. On arrival, she can answer questions but is intermittently listless and agitated. Her temperature is 37.7°C (99.8°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 154/96 mm Hg. On examination, the left pupil is larger than the right. The left eye deviates slightly downward and outward. The patient resists flexion of the neck and exhibits pain when the neck is flexed. Muscle tone in the right upper and lower extremities is increased. Deep tendon reflexes on the right side are increased. Babinski sign is present on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: A ruptured intracerebral aneurysm is the most common cause of nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Saccular intracerebral aneurysms typically occur at bifurcations in the circle of Willis, most commonly at the site of the anterior communicating artery. Aneurysms can also be associated with hereditary diseases such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. This patient presents in a nontraumatic, altered mental state with findings concerning for increased intracranial pressure with herniation. This patient's focal neurologic findings and asymmetric pupils are concerning for possible transtentorial herniation. SAH results from bleeding into the subarachnoid space. Patients may present with an acute, severe headache, stupor, or coma in severe cases. Blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the meninges, leading to nuchal rigidity. CT scan of the head shows hyperdense blood products in the cerebral sulci and basal cisterns. As the blood products circulate within the subarachnoid space, complications include the development of communicating hydrocephalus in the acute stage, along with rebleeding and vasospasm in the week following the initial bleed.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Carotid artery dissection with embolization (Choice A) can lead to focal neurologic deficits such as with an acute ischemic stroke and upper motor neuron signs such as increased deep tendon reflexes and Babinski sign. However, it would be unlikely to cause nuchal rigidity. Uncontrolled hypertension can lead to intracranial hemorrhage (Choice B), which presents with a progressively worsening headache and focal neurologic deficits. Hypertension leads to intraparenchymal hemorrhages typically in the basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus, and/or pons. Nuchal rigidity would be unlikely, and this patient’s blood pressure discloses mild (not severe) hypertension. While patients with meningoencephalitis (Choice C) often present with acute headache and neck stiffness, the absence of fever makes it less likely. Pupil asymmetry is concerning for increased intracranial pressure and herniation, which would be unlikely with meningoencephalitis. Migraine headaches characteristically recur over time and may present with a pulsatile, unilateral or bilateral headache with associated photophobia or phonophobia. They are often triggered by foods, medications, noises, menses, or illness. Vertebrobasilar migraines (Choice E) can also be associated with diplopia, dysarthria, nausea, or vomiting. Educational Objective: The most common cause of nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage is a ruptured intracerebral aneurysm. Subarachnoid hemorrhages present with an acute, severe headache, neck stiffness, and can lead to altered mental status, stupor, and/or coma. r 4 . rs. - Previous Score Report et) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: A4/-year-old man has to quit his job as an automobile mechanic because of hand weakness and unsteadiness. He has bilateral wristdrop and upper limb ataxia. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 34% Mean corpuscular volume 76 ums Serum creatinine 2 mg/dL Chronic exposure to which of the following substances is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Symptoms of acute lead poisoning occur within days or weeks of exposure and include abdominal pain, constipation, arthralgia, myalgias, muscle weakness, excessive fatigue, headache, and difficulty concentrating. With prolonged exposure, chronic neurologic symptoms such as decline in cognition, depression, distal motor neuropathy, decreased hearing, tremor, and decreased brain volume on imaging may be present. The distal motor neuropathy causes lower motor neuron signs such as atrophy of muscles and hyporeflexia, as found in this patient. Microcytic anemia is also common, since lead inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and 5-aminolevulinic acid (6-ALA) dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. In adults, exposure to lead primarily comes through occupation and/or hobbies. Individuals working with batteries, mining, construction, or ammunition are at higher risk. Diagnosis is suspected based on exposure and symptoms and is confirmed with increased serum lead concentration. Management of lead poisoning depends on the blood lead concentration and presence of symptoms, and includes chelation with dimercaprol, ethylene diamine tetraacetate, or succimer. Sources of lead should be investigated and eliminated.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Arsenic (Choice A) poisoning is uncommon and can cause dermatitis, skin cancer, neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, and, in severe cases, systemic toxicity and death. Acute large exposure to arsenic can cause gastrointestinal distress, QT prolongation that may progress to torsades de pointes, cardiac arrhythmias, shock, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Cadmium (Choice B) poisoning may occur in the industrial setting among workers involved in electroplating, metallurgical industries, and battery production. Exposure typically occurs via inhalation and presents with fever, chills, myalgia, chest pain, cough, shortness of breath, pneumonitis, and pulmonary edema. Mercury (Choice D) poisoning may occur in an industrial setting among workers involved in the manufacture of thermometers, mirrors, fluorescent lighting, and gold. Patients present with headache, ataxia, tremor, hearing and vision loss, insomnia, peripheral neuropathy, and paresthesias. Thallium (Choice E) poisoning may occur through transcutaneous exposure or via inhalation or ingestion. Thallium was previously widely used as a rodenticide, but thallium poisoning is now rare in the developed world, although it is still used in the manufacture of semiconductors, electronics, and optics. Acute exposure presents with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, while chronic exposure presents with neurologic and psychiatric symptoms of headache, altered mental status, anxiety, psychosis, ataxia, tremor, and painful peripheral neuropathy and distal weakness. Educational Objective: Neurologic manifestations of lead poisoning include cognitive dysfunction, encephalopathy, hearing loss, and peripheral neuropathy. questionStem: A27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of difficulty speaking and moving. Seven days ago she began a course of mitoxantrone and high doses of cytarabine (ara-C) for a recurrence of acute myeloid leukemia. She has been lethargic and mildly confused for the past 24 hours. She is 140 cm (4 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 47 kg (103 Ib); BMI is 24 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows nystagmus and ataxic eye movements. Muscle strength is full, but there is marked ataxia in all extremities. She is unable to maintain her balance sitting or standing unsupported. She is somnolent but can respond appropriately to questions and instructions. Her speech is irregular in rate and volume. Language function and memory are normal. She can calculate well, and her abstract reasoning is intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Spread of leukemia to the central nervous system

correctExplanation: Acute-onset neurologic findings in the setting of recent chemotherapy are concerning for drug toxicity. Specifically, nystagmus, ataxia, impaired coordination, postural instability, and dysarthria or other speech abnormalities, in the setting of intact strength and higher cognitive functions are indicative of cerebellar dysfunction. Cytarabine, a pyrimidine analog, can cause loss of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum, leading to acute cerebellar syndrome. Risk factors include underlying neurologic dysfunction and impaired hepatic or renal function. Patients who present with acute cerebellar syndrome should discontinue cytarabine immediately. Some may experience permanent deficits, while others may experience spontaneous resolution.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cerebral infarction (Choice A) can present with a sudden change in mental status, upper motor neuron signs, and acute focal neurologic deficits, especially on one side of the body, and may have speech difficulty, dysarthria, or aphasia, depending on the territory involved. Cerebellar strokes, while less common, do occur. However, acute-onset cerebellar signs in the setting of a new course of cytarabine are more likely caused by drug toxicity. Encephalitis (Choice C) presents with fever, altered mental status, and neurologic abnormalities, such as seizure, aphasia, hemiparesis, or cranial nerve deficits. Neuroimaging will typically show changes in the temporal lobe. Encephalitis is commonly associated with nuchal rigidity or signs of central nervous system infection, which this patient does not demonstrate, making it a less likely cause of her presentation. Intracranial hemorrhage (Choice D) appears as a hyperdense collection of blood within the brain parenchyma on CT scan. Intracranial hemorrhage often presents with focal neurologic deficits based on its location with an associated headache and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (eg, vomiting, altered mental status). This patient does not demonstrate any signs of increased intracranial pressure. Spread of leukemia to the central nervous system (Choice E), also called leukemic meningitis, is usually asymptomatic. When it does occur, signs and symptoms vary widely depending on the location of spread, and can include headache, signs of increased intracranial pressure, behavioral changes, and focal weakness. Isolated cerebellar signs in the setting of recently started cytarabine is more consistent with drug toxicity. Educational Objective: Cytarabine, a pyrimidine analog, can cause loss of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum, leading to acute cerebellar syndrome. Features include nystagmus, ataxia, impaired coordination, postural instability, and dysarthria or other speech abnormalities. Strength, sensation, and higher cognitive functions are intact. Patients who present with acute cerebellar syndrome should discontinue cytarabine immediately. questionStem: A6/-year-old woman with a 15-year history of Parkinson disease comes to the office because of increasing involuntary movements over the past 2 years. She also has had nausea from her medication regimen of carbidopa-levodopa and ropinirole; attempts at medication adjustment have not been successful. She also has a long-standing history of cervical and lumbar stenosis treated with diclofenac and physical therapy. Her pulse is 70/min and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg while sitting; pulse is 75/min and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg while standing. Her speech is barely audible. Examination shows constant writhing movements of the mouth, neck, and limbs. She walks with her neck flexed and takes small steps with a decreased arm swing. Mental status examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical treatment?
correctExplanation: Parkinson disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by degradation of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Symptoms are associated with an imbalance of dopamine and acetylcholine, resulting in the characteristic findings of bradykinesia, resting tremor, muscle rigidity, and postural instability. Psychiatric disturbances, sleep disorders, and dementia are common complications in addition to prominent motor symptoms. Initial pharmacologic management of Parkinson disease consists of carbidopa-levodopa and/or other dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole. Patients who develop severe, disabling motor symptoms refractory to medications and physical therapy may be considered for device-assisted therapies or invasive lesioning procedures. Device-assisted therapies include deep brain stimulation. Invasive lesioning procedures are more common for patients who do not have access to device-assisted therapies or cannot afford them. Unilateral pallidotomy, which targets the internal globus pallidus to reduce inhibitory signaling, is an effective treatment for improving refractory tremor, bradykinesia, dyskinesia, chorea, and gait/balance instability. The thalamus and subthalamic nucleus are alternative targets for lesioning procedures.

It would not help with severe motor symptoms of Parkinson disease. Carotid endarterectomy (Choice B) is a treatment option for atherosclerotic disease of the carotid arteries. It is indicated for patients who have had a stroke or transient ischemic attack or are asymptomatic with hemodynamically significant stenosis.
