questionStem: Apreviously healthy 37-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife because of bizarre behavior for 2 days. He is very excitable and jumps when surprised. His wife says that he has been experiencing visual hallucinations. He refuses to drink liquids. For 3 days prior to this behavior, he had headache and sleepiness. Two months ago, he returned from a hunting trip in the mountains. His temperature is 40°C (104°F). Examination shows an inability to accurately answer questions and unusual behaviors such as picking at the air. He seems unable to swallow his secretions, and he is drooling. ACT scan of the brain shows no abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows: Glucose 70 mg/dL Protein 85 mg/dL Leukocyte count 150/mm3 Erythrocyte count none Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: This patient presents with headache and sleepiness that has progressed to hallucinations, hydrophobia, drooling, and fevers, which is suggestive of rabies. Rabies virus is a negative- sense, single-stranded, nonsegmented RNA virus belonging to the family of rhabdoviruses. The virus is transmitted through direct contact with saliva of an infected animal. In the United States, transmission occurs most often after a bite from a bat, raccoon, or skunk, but in third-world countries, transmission via dog bites is common. The virus has a long incubation period of weeks to months before symptom onset. It binds to acetylcholine receptors in peripheral nerves and travels up the axon in a retrograde fashion to the central nervous system. Initial symptoms include headache, fever, and malaise, but rapidly progress to agitation, photophobia, hydrophobia, and hypersalivation. Once symptoms are present, rabies is almost universally fatal. For this reason, persons who are bit by an animal at high risk for carrying rabies should seek care immediately. Copious irrigation of the wound followed by intramuscular administration of the killed vaccine is standard of care for all patients. If the patient has not been previously vaccinated, rabies immunoglobulin should be administered locally into the wound.

questionStem: A1/-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought to the clinic by his father because of a 4-week history of progressive right hip pain. Initially, the pain was intermittent and the patient rated it as a 5 on a 10-point scale; however, during the past 2 weeks it has become constant, and he now rates the pain as a 9 on a 10-point scale. The pain is not worsened by sneezing, coughing, or lifting objects. He was diagnosed with sickle cell disease at age 3 years; his disease course has been complicated by frequent bouts of dactylitis and pneumonia. He has had two blood transfusions done 9 and 6 years ago, respectively. He has been taking acetaminophen for the hip pain, but it has provided minimal relief. Family history is remarkable for sickle cell disease in his mother, brother, and two sisters, and for sickle cell trait in his father. The patient appears to be in moderate distress. Temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 114/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a decreased range of motion to hip flexion and abduction. There is no pain on palpation of the lateral aspect of the hip. Muscle strength is 5/5 throughout, and muscle tone is symmetric. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ in the lower extremities bilaterally. questionStem: A6/-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 24 hours after the onset of double vision, pain behind the right eye, and mild nausea. She describes her double vision as seeing objects side by side. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, and chronic renal insufficiency. Medications include fosinopril and glyburide. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, her double vision is most pronounced when she looks to the right. If she covers either eye, the double vision resolves. The pupils are 3 mm and minimally reactive to light. When the patient looks to the right, the right eye does not abduct. Achilles tendon reflexes are absent. Sensation to pinprick is decreased in a stocking distribution over the feet. An MRI of the brain is most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: The abducens nerve exits the brainstem ventrally at the pontomedullary junction and innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eye. The most common causes of acute abducens nerve palsy in adults include microvascular ischemia (secondary to diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease), idiopathic causes, and trauma. The abducens nerve is fragile and vulnerable to injury as it crosses the clivus by any mechanism causing downward traction. Abducens nerve palsy presents with binocular horizontal diplopia and ipsilateral abduction deficits of the affected eye. Diagnosis is made on clinical examination, and often there is no definitive finding on MRI. Treatment includes systemic workup for vasculopathic risk factors and patching to reduce diplopia. Abducens nerve palsy secondary to microvascular disease may resolve spontaneously over several months.

In addition, diplopia that is centrally mediated is typically bilateral, whereas diplopia that resolves when the patient covers one eye is likely due to an ocular cause. Enhancing meninges (Choice B) on MRI would be suggestive of an infectious or inflammatory process such as meningitis. While meningitis can present with focal neurologic deficits, patients typically have other signs or symptoms such as fever and nuchal rigidity. An infarct in the right medulla (Choice C) can lead to lateral medullary syndrome, which can present with ipsilateral ataxia of extremity movements, gait ataxia, Horner syndrome, and can be associated with nystagmus and dysarthria. An orbital tumor (Choice D) would be unlikely to result in abducens nerve palsy. It would more likely directly affect ipsilateral extraocular muscles through local mass effect. Educational Objective: The abducens nerve exits the brainstem ventrally at the pontomedullary junction and innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eye. questionStem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the onset of confusion. She appears agitated. She mistakes the attending physician for her brother and insists that he call their father. She admits to drinking regularly since the age of 22 years. Her last drink was 4 ounces of vodka 72 hours ago. Her pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 170/110 mm Hg. Physical examination shows ataxia and a three cycle/sec bilateral hand tremor. On mental status examination, she is oriented to person but not to place or time. After the examination, she yells, "| saw Dad here; why didn't you tell me he was coming to pay my bail? | could be out by now!" Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Alcohol increases the central nervous system activity of y-aminobutyric acid, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol therefore leads to sympathetic (excitatory) excess. Uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal typically presents with tremors, anxiety, restlessness, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis, which can occur hours after the cessation of alcohol use. If left untreated, alcohol withdrawal can be complicated by seizures and alcoholic hallucinosis (auditory or visual hallucinations). Delirium tremens, the most concerning and life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal, typically begins between 48 hours and 1 week after the patient's last drink. Presentation of delirium tremens includes severe confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visual or auditory hallucinations, and autonomic instability. Alcohol withdrawal is managed supportively with benzodiazepines (eg, lorazepam) to address agitation and prevent or treat the symptoms of withdrawal, along with fluids, nutritional supplementation, and frequent assessment including vital sign monitoring.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alcoholic hallucinosis (Choice A) is characterized by visual, tactile, or auditory hallucinations beginning 12 to 48 hours after the patient’s last drink. Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis typically have normal vital signs and remain oriented, unlike this patient. Idiosyncratic alcohol intoxication (Choice C) is a type of alcohol-induced psychosis in which ingestion of a small amount of alcohol results in aggression, belligerence, impaired consciousness, and hallucinations. Schizophrenia (Choice D) is a mental disorder characterized by psychosis, disorganized thoughts, and decline in functioning lasting longer than 6 months. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (Choice E) is an irreversible condition caused by vitamin B, (thiamine) deficiency, found most commonly in patients with alcohol use disorder. Patients may present initially with ataxia, confusion, and ophthalmoplegia that progresses to anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with the consequent tendency to confabulate, or verbalize false stories or memories, to compensate for the inability to remember. Educational Objective: Delirium tremens is a life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal that presents with confusion, agitation, visual hallucinations, and autonomic instability. questionStem: A24-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 4-month history of generalized weakness and moderate muscle aches. Initially, she had difficulty standing after she removed clothes from the dryer. Now, she has difficulty walking up stairs and rising from a chair. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her mother has rheumatoid arthritis. Examination of the patient shows periorbital purplish discoloration bilaterally. Cranial nerves are intact. Palpation of all muscles produces pain. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the deltoids, biceps, hip flexors, and quadriceps bilaterally; this result does not change with repeat testing. Muscle bulk and tone are normal. Bilaterally, deep tendon reflexes are 2+ in the brachioradialis muscles and ankles and 1+ in the biceps and quadriceps muscles. Sensation is intact throughout. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Dermatomyositis is an inflammatory condition that affects both skin and musculoskeletal systems. Cutaneous findings of dermatomyositis include a heliotrope rash involving the periocular area, Gottron papules overlying the joints of the dorsal hands, and a poikilodermatous rash distributed over the shoulders and chest/upper torso. Musculoskeletal symptoms include proximal muscle weakness, especially involving the deltoids, biceps, hip flexors, and quadriceps muscles, and patients may report difficulty rising to stand or lifting their arms over the shoulders. Diagnosis is made based on clinical findings and serologic testing, including antinuclear, anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP, and anti-Mi-2 antibodies along with serum creatine kinase assay. Patients diagnosed with dermatomyositis should undergo further workup including age-appropriate cancer screening to rule out an underlying occult malignancy, although malignancy is less common in younger patients.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Charcot-Marie- Tooth disease (Choice A) is a genetic disorder that presents with slowly progressive peripheral neuropathy, often in association with foot deformities such as hammertoes and pes cavus. It is commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Inclusion body myositis (Choice C) is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy that commonly affects older males. Symptoms include insidious onset of proximal or distal leg weakness and dysphagia. Characteristic muscle biopsy findings include infiltration of inflammatory cells, fibrosis, and inclusion bodies and/or vacuoles seen with staining. Unlike other inflammatory myopathies, inclusion body myositis is resistant to immunosuppressive therapies. Myasthenia gravis (Choice D) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by the formation of inhibitory antiacetylcholine receptor autoantibodies. Common symptoms include muscular weakness, fatigue, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens toward the end of the day, along with dysphagia and potential respiratory distress. A subset of patients with myasthenia gravis will have a coexisting thymoma. Polymyositis (Choice E) refers to an inflammatory myopathy that presents with proximal muscle pain and weakness. It is an inflammatory myopathy not associated with skin findings that is often treated with immunosuppressive therapy. Educational Objective: Dermatomyositis presents with cutaneous manifestations and proximal muscle weakness. Cutaneous manifestations include pink to light purple patches over the upper eyelids (heliotrope sign), pink papules over the dorsal fingers (Gottron papules), and light pink to lilac patches with telangiectasias over the upper back and sun-exposed chest. All patients diagnosed with dermatomyositis should undergo age-appropriate screening to rule out occult malignancy. 4 € ae a Previous Score Report [Ee V al eS Calculator

questionStem: A 19-year-old man is examined in the intensive care unit 3 days after admission for a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 88/min, ventilatory rate is 16/min, and blood pressure is 100/40 mm Hg. Pupils are nonreactive to light. Corneal reflex is absent. Irrigation of the ear canals with cold water results in eye movement only toward the ear being irrigated. On application of noxious stimuli, the patient has only spinal reflex movement. He is not initiating breaths spontaneously above the ventilator. Which of the following findings prevents a diagnosis of brain death in this patient?
correctExplanation: The diagnosis of brain death is determined by the presence of three factors: absence of brainstem reflexes, persistent coma, and lack of spontaneous respirations. Commonly tested brainstem reflexes include the pupillary light response (which tests the optic and oculomotor cranial nerves), the corneal reflex (which tests the trigeminal and facial cranial nerves by lightly touching the cornea with a strand of cotton while observing for blinking or tearing), the pharyngeal and tracheal reflexes (which test the glossopharyngeal and vagus cranial nerves by observing gagging or coughing during endotracheal suctioning), the oculocephalic reflex (which tests the oculomotor, abducens, and vestibulocochlear cranial nerves by assessing for ocular movements during a head turn. Anormal response is eye movement away from the direction of the head turn, whereas an abnormal response is characterized by eye movement with the direction of the head turn, or fixed at midline), and the vestibuloocular reflex. Caloric stimulation, which tests the vestibuloocular reflex, tests the oculomotor, abducens, and vestibulocochlear cranial nerves by assessing for an oculomotor response to irrigation of cold water into one of the ear canals. Cold water irrigation decreases the rate of vestibular afferent signaling within the affected vestibular apparatus, simulating a head turn to the contralateral side. A normal response to cold water irrigation involves tonic deviation toward the ipsilateral ear and horizontal fast nystagmus toward the opposite ear. The fast phase of nystagmus receives input from the dorsal stream of occipitomotor cortex. Absence of fast phase nystagmus suggests an absence of cortical functioning, whereas absence of slow tonic deviation indicates absence of brainstem functioning. Absence of both components of the caloric test is required for the diagnosis of brain death. This patient's caloric testing, which demonstrates slow tonic deviation toward the side of cold water irrigation, may prevent a diagnosis of brain death.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. The corneal reflex (Choice B) tests the trigeminal and facial cranial nerves by lightly touching the cornea with a strand of cotton while observing for blinking or tearing. This patient's corneal reflex is absent, which could be consistent with a diagnosis of brain death. The pupillary light reflex (Choice C) tests the optic and oculomotor cranial nerves by assessing for pupillary constriction in response to light. This patient lacks a pupillary light response, which could be consistent with a diagnosis of brain death. Motor response (Choice D) testing assesses for a motor response to painful or noxious stimuli. The presence of spinal reflex movement in this patient does not indicate an intact motor response. Respiratory effort (Choice E) is assessed with apnea testing by withdrawing the patient from ventilator support. This is typically the final step in diagnosis of brain death. While this patient does not yet have a positive apnea test, lack of spontaneous breaths above the ventilator is consistent with a diagnosis of brain death. Educational Objective: The caloric test is a test of the vestibuloocular reflex, which relies on the oculomotor, abducens, and vestibulocochlear cranial nerves. Cold water irrigation decreases the rate of vestibular afferent signaling within the affected vestibular apparatus, simulating a head turn to the contralateral side. questionStem: A4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he walks predominately on his toes. He was born at 29 weeks' gestation and has a history of hyaline membrane disease and a grade | intraventricular hemorrhage. He takes albuterol for asthma, and his immunizations are up-to-date. He sat up at the age of 9 months and walked at 18 months; he currently uses full sentences when talking. He is at the 50th percentile for both height and weight. Examination shows generalized hyperreflexia, a persistent Babinski sign bilaterally, heel cord contractures, and decreased abduction and external rotation of the hips. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Cerebral palsy is a disorder of nonprogressive central motor dysfunction as a result of impaired fetal or neonatal brain development. The cause is frequently multifactorial, though the most important factors are premature delivery, which may increase the risk for cerebral palsy 80-fold, and low birth weight. Patients who are born prematurely may have also experienced other sequelae of prematurity, including hyaline membrane disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis, and retinopathy of prematurity. Other risk factors include intrauterine infections, antepartum hemorrhage, placental pathology, multiple pregnancy, heavy maternal alcohol use, maternal smoking, and maternal obesity, though for many of these factors, causality has not been established. Cerebral palsy typically presents with upper motor neuron signs (eg, spasticity, hyperreflexia, persistent Babinski sign), dyskinesia, and/or ataxia. Diagnosis includes a thorough history and physical examination along with MRI. Management requires an interdisciplinary team to support the patient's daily functioning.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Multiple sclerosis (Choice B) is a progressive autoimmune demyelinating disease that affects neurons of the central nervous system, resulting in neurologic symptoms that are separated in time and space. Risk factors include female sex, white race, age between 20 to 40 years, residence in temperate climates, and ancestry (HLA-DR2 haplotype). Muscular dystrophy (Choice C), specifically Duchenne type, is an X-linked condition resulting in progressive proximal muscle weakness in male children. Symptoms include an inability to rise from a squatting position and weakness of the lower limb girdle. The adductor muscle group originates from the ischium and inferior pubis and serves the primary role of hip adduction. It is not associated with upper motor neuron signs or premature birth. Myasthenia gravis (Choice D) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by the formation of inhibitory antiacetylcholine receptor autoantibodies. Common symptoms include muscular weakness, fatigue, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens toward the end of the day, along with dysphagia and potential respiratory distress. Patients may present with an associated thymoma. Neurofibromatosis (Choice E) is a hereditary neurocutaneous disorder. Type 1 presents with cutaneous neurofibromas (benign neoplasms derived from neural crest cells), café au lait spots, pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), optic gliomas, and pheochromocytomas. Type 2 presents with cutaneous neurofibromas, bilateral acoustic neuromas, additional schwannomas of the cranial nerves or in the spinal cord, intracranial meningiomas, and neuropathy. This patient has no dermatologic findings. Educational Objective: Cerebral palsy is a disorder of nonprogressive central motor dysfunction as a result of impaired fetal or neonatal brain development. Features include upper motor neuron signs, dyskinesia, and/or ataxia. The cause is frequently multifactorial, though the strongest risk factors are premature delivery and low birth weight. 4 ly Previous Score Report Calculator

questionStem: A42-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 2-month history of generalized weakness. During this period, she has had difficulty climbing one flight of stairs and combing her hair. She also reports double vision that occurs when she reads. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows bilateral ptosis. Muscle strength is 4/5 in all extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Measurement of serum creatine kinase activity

correctExplanation: This patient's presenting findings of intermittent ptosis, diplopia, and proximal muscle weakness are suggestive of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis is a B cell-driven autoimmune disorder characterized by the formation of inhibitory antiacetylcholine receptor autoantibodies. Patients typically experience muscular weakness and fatigue that worsens toward the end of the day, as well as ocular symptoms of ptosis and diplopia. Many patients present with ocular findings and later develop generalized symptoms involving the proximal muscles. Several tests can help to support the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis, including the ice pack test (improvement of ptosis after placement of an ice pack on the eyelids for 2 minutes), the edrophonium test (improvement in muscle strength after administration of the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor), and a repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) study. In this type of study, the motor nerve is repetitively stimulated, and the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) is recorded after each stimulation. In patients with myasthenia gravis, there is a decrease in each CMAP amplitude after the first few stimulations. The diagnosis of myasthenia gravis is confirmed with the detection of serum autoantibodies in addition to a positive RNS study.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Measurement of serum creatine kinase (CK) activity (Choice A) and muscle biopsy (Choice D) may be appropriate in the setting of a suspected myopathy, such as dermatomyositis or drug-induced myopathy. Since myasthenia gravis is a disorder of the neuromuscular junction, CK activity and muscle biopsy would be expected to be normal. Plasmapheresis (Choice B) is a treatment used for patients with myasthenic crisis. Patients with myasthenic crisis may develop weakness of the muscles of the throat, diaphragm, and chest wall leading to dysphagia and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. This patient is not exhibiting signs or symptoms of a myasthenic crisis. MRI of the brain (Choice C) could be useful if this patient's symptoms were caused by a stroke, but proximal weakness in all extremities and bilateral ptosis do not fit with this clinical picture. MRI of the brain in a patient with myasthenia gravis would be expected to be normal. Educational Objective: Common symptoms of myasthenia gravis include muscular weakness, fatigue, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens toward the end of the day, along with dysphagia and potential respiratory distress. questionStem: A37/-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of joint pain. The symptoms initially began with increasing pain in his left knee and have progressed to include his right Knee and left hip. There is no history of trauma. Six weeks ago, he had fever, malaise, and a 5-cm rash with central clearing on his chest that resolved spontaneously after 7 days. He is sexually active with multiple partners and uses condoms inconsistently. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), and blood pressure is 148/90 mm Hg. Examination of the left knee shows no warmth or erythema. Range of motion of the left knee is full and does not produce pain. Range of motion of the right knee is limited by pain; there is a moderate joint effusion. Abduction and adduction of the left hip against resistance produce pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Lyme arthritis, one of several complications of Lyme disease, is caused by disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi infection. B. burgdorferi are transmitted following tick bites, most commonly from Ixodes ticks. Initial manifestations of Lyme disease include the erythema chronicum migrans rash, which is an expanding rash with a central ring-like clearing and targetoid appearance. It generally appears within 1 to 2 weeks of the tick bite. Left untreated, a subset of patients will develop disseminated disease that may result in Bell palsy, meningitis, myopericarditis, or arthritis. Patients may be diagnosed clinically when the characteristic erythema migrans rash is observed in the setting of known or probable recent exposure to a tick in an endemic area. Serologic testing is controversial as it may show false positives or negatives; however, it may be used to support the diagnosis in later stage disease. Patients with Lyme disease are treated with doxycycline or amoxicillin. Most patients with Lyme arthritis will demonstrate response to therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Gonococcal arthritis (Choice A) may present with fever, malaise, and migratory polyarthritis or oligoarthritis. Patients will have purulent arthritis of one or more extremity joints (eg, knees, elbows, or ankles), and synovial fluid analysis will show greater than 20,000 to 50,000 leukocytes/mm?® without organisms, as Neisseria are intracellular. Treatment of gonococcal arthritis includes intravenous antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, along with possible irrigation of the affected joints. Gouty arthritis (Choice B) is an inflammatory arthropathy incited by hyperuricemia, with deposition of uric acid crystals inside the joint and surrounding tissues. This type of arthritis presents following consumption of a purine-rich meal or alcohol (which competes with renal excretion of uric acid). Joint aspirate will show negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals and a leukocyte count of typically less than 50,000/mm‘°. Osteoarthritis (Choice D) is caused by repetitive wear-and-tear injury to a joint with subsequent cartilage degradation, bony sclerosis, and joint pain. Risk factors include age, obesity, and prior intra-articular injury. Treatment options include physical therapy, braces, weight loss, acetaminophen, intra-articular corticosteroid injections, and, if severe, joint replacement. Rheumatoid arthritis (Choice E) is a chronic, progressive, autoimmune disease that primarily leads to destruction of synovial joints. The disease typically presents with symmetric patterns of arthritis, particularly in the wrists and hands, and is treated with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs and tumor necrosis factor-a blockers, such as adalimumab and infliximab. correctExplanation: Delirium is defined by an acute-onset alteration of consciousness and cognition, with symptoms that wax and wane throughout the day. In elderly patients, especially those with underlying dementia, systemic infection can rapidly lead to the development of delirium. Other common causes of delirium include intoxication and adverse effects from medications such as anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, or opiates. All patients with delirium should be evaluated for evidence of systemic infection with urinalysis and culture, chest x-ray, and occasionally with blood cultures, if indicated. Treatment of delirium should focus on treatment of the underlying infection if one is detected, frequent reorientation, maintenance of normal sleep-wake cycles, and placement of the patient in a calm and soothing environment. questionStem: A2/-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of headaches that are dull, constant, and localized to the back of her head. The pain is not relieved by ibuprofen. She has not had fever, nausea, vomiting, or weakness. She has a 5-year history of AIDS currently treated with three-drug antiretroviral therapy. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Examination shows multiple, 1-cm, cervical lymph nodes that are mildly tender. There is no papilledema. Examination of the oropharynx shows thrush. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 25/mm3 (Normal2500), and plasma HIV viral load is 5000 copies/mL. A CT scan of the head with contrast shows five 1- to 2-cm, ring-enhancing lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient has a history of AIDS with low CD4+ count and CT scan showing ring-enhancing lesions, which is suggestive of cerebral toxoplasmosis. Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an AIDS- defining disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii and is the most common cause of multiple ring-enhancing lesions on CT scan of the head in a patient with AIDS. Transmission can occur through the ingestion of oocysts from soil contaminated with cat feces or infected meat, direct transmission between a mother and fetus, or from organ transplantation, which leads to invasion followed by dissemination of the parasite where it typically lies dormant. It is a ubiquitous organism, and nearly 10% of individuals will be seropositive for T. gondii, but the parasite does not usually cause severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. In patients with HIV infection and CD4+ counts less than 100 cells/mm?, however, reactivation can occur with several distinct clinical syndromes of which cerebral toxoplasmosis results in the most morbidity. Cerebral toxoplasmosis typically presents with multiple ring-enhancing lesions scattered throughout the brain. Seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and systemic symptoms are common, as are signs of increased intracranial pressure. Patients with HIV and positive Toxoplasma |gG antibodies are typically treated empirically with a sulfonamide and pyrimethamine if cerebral toxoplasmosis is suspected, but confirmatory diagnosis occurs through a brain biopsy, which will show a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells, along with the presence of the 7. gondii organism.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis will show an increased opening pressure, increased protein, and a mononuclear cell pleocytosis. Ring-enhancing lesions on CT scan of the head are not a feature of cryptococcal meningitis. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (Choice B) can cause a mononucleosis-like syndrome in immunocompetent patients but can cause a variety of other diseases in patients who are immunodeficient, including esophagitis, retinitis, pneumonitis, and colitis. Congenital CMV may present with CNS findings and calcifications on CT scan of the head, but it is not known to commonly cause CNS findings in adults. Patients may present with focal neurologic deficits, vision changes, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and increased intracranial pressure. Neuroimaging will show ring-enhancing lesions similar to those in toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasmosis is more common than CNS lymphoma and should be the presumptive diagnosis for this patient with multiple ring-enhancing lesions. If symptoms do not improve with sulfadiazine or pyrimethamine therapy, CNS lymphoma should be considered. questionStem: A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of low back pain that began 4 hours after he lifted a sofa. His symptoms have gradually become worse, and he now has severe pain with any movement of his back. The pain radiates to the right posterior thigh. He has had no changes in bowel or bladder function. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. On examination, flexion and extension of the waist and twisting movements of the torso increase the pain. There is tenderness over the lumbar paraspinous musculature bilaterally that is more prominent on the right. Straight-leg raising on the right causes pain in the right sacral area at 45 degrees. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities. Sensation is intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.E: Nerve conduction studies of the lower extremities

correctExplanation: This patient's presentation is suggestive of acute onset of low back pain, which lasts up to 4 weeks and may be attributed to musculoskeletal injury from exertion, overuse, or trauma. Symptoms include pain with movement and paraspinal tenderness in the absence of neurologic symptoms or bony tenderness. Most cases resolve with conservative management, which includes activity modification, stretching and physical therapy, over-the-counter analgesics such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, massage, and heat therapy. Certain red flag signs and symptoms should prompt more urgent evaluation for an alternate cause, especially if there is concern for infection, malignancy, spinal cord compromise, or vertebral fracture. These include but are not limited to new fevers, intravenous drug use, focal neurologic deficits (eg, urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bowel incontinence which may suggest cauda equina syndrome), progressive lower extremity neurologic symptoms, current or recent cancer history, advanced age, systemic corticosteroid use, and a significant traumatic mechanism. In this young, otherwise healthy patient with a mild inciting event, the most appropriate initial step in management is ibuprofen therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bed rest for 1 week (Choice A) is not indicated in patients with acute low back pain, as these patients may experience increased pain and slower return to normal function. Activity modification for symptom relief should be advised, with encouragement to continue normal activities of daily living and non-exacerbating exertion. X-rays of the lumbosacral spine (Choice B) and MRI of the lumbosacral spine (Choice C) should be reserved for patients who present with red flag signs and symptoms to evaluate for evidence of infection, malignancy, spinal cord compromise, or vertebral fracture. For otherwise healthy patients with back pain that has persisted for a subacute time course, imaging studies do not generally change management. Nerve conduction studies of the lower extremities (Choice E), including electromyography, should be reserved for patients who experience neurologic symptoms including weakness or altered sensation. This patient's presentation does not warrant additional nerve conduction studies. Educational Objective: Acute low back pain is a common presenting finding in multiple medical settings. General management for pain persisting less than 4 weeks is conservative with over-the-counter analgesics, physical therapy, and nonpharmacologic pain relief options. Initial imaging is not typically necessary in the absence of red flag signs or symptoms suggestive of infection, malignancy, spinal cord compromise, or vertebral fracture. r 4 “ Ps a Previous Score Report etd) V al Lc S Calculator

questionStem: A70-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-month history of progressive swelling that began in his legs and now extends to his lower abdomen. He also has noted fatigue and shortness of breath during this time. He says he lost consciousness briefly while mowing the lawn last week. The patient experienced an episode of chest pain 1 year ago, and coronary angiography at that time disclosed no coronary artery stenosis. He has a 12-year history of severe obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea and has been unable to tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. He also has a 5-year history of hypertension well controlled with hydrochlorothiazide and verapamil. He does not smoke cigarettes. He drinks two 12-0z beers weekly. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 104 kg (230 Ib); BMI is 32 kg/m2. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Examination of the skin over the lower extremities shows pinkish discoloration. There is edema of the lower abdomen and the lower extremities bilaterally. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses regular rate and rhythm. Jugular venous pressure is 8 cm above the sternal notch/clavicle. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Pulmonary hypertension is one cause of right-sided heart failure in patients with no evidence of left-sided heart failure. Signs suggestive of right-sided heart failure include bilateral lower extremity edema, jugular venous distention, hepatosplenomegaly, and abdominal swelling. There are multiple causes of pulmonary hypertension, including genetic causes, connective tissue disease (eg, lupus), HIV, congenital heart disease, left-sided heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea. Transthoracic echocardiography may be used as an initial screening test for evaluation and may suggest the diagnosis. Further studies include high-resolution CT scan, ventilation-perfusion lung scans, right and left heart catheterization, laboratory studies, and polysomnography. Once the underlying cause of pulmonary hypertension has been identified, treatments aimed at symptomatic relief, including diuretic agents, may be used along with treatment of the underlying cause, such as continuous positive airway pressure in obstructive sleep apnea. For this patient, the most likely cause of pulmonary hypertension is poorly controlled obstructive sleep apnea.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cellulitis (Choice A) presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, and induration. Systemic symptoms, including fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis are often present. The two most common pathogens in cellulitis include Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Choice B) is an obstructive lung disease associated with tobacco use characterized by expiratory airflow obstruction. Chronic symptoms are improved with the use of inhaled long-acting beta agonists, inhaled muscarinic antagonists, and glucocorticoids. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease may cause pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure in patients with a significant smoking history. Deep venous thrombosis (Choice C) may cause lower extremity swelling, pain, and discoloration. Symptoms may be acute in nature, and patients are treated with anticoagulation and/or thrombectomy depending on the severity and location of the thrombus. This patient's clinical presentation is not consistent with a deep venous thrombosis. Left-sided heart failure (Choice D) is a commonly encountered clinical syndrome associated with chronic hypertension and coronary artery disease. Physical examination findings include increased jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema, ascites, hepatojugular reflux, pulmonary crackles, and an S3 or Sq gallop. This presentation supports right-sided heart failure; however, this patient lacks clinical evidence of cardiogenic pulmonary edema, which would suggest left-sided heart failure. Educational Objective: Examination findings suggestive of pulmonary hypertension include those of right-sided heart failure: lower extremity edema, jugular venous distention, hepatosplenomegaly, and abdominal swelling. A common cause of pulmonary hypertension is left-sided heart failure; however, other causes include obstructive sleep apnea and chronic venous thromboembolic disease. Obstructive sleep apnea may be diagnosed with polysomnography and is treated with positive pressure ventilation during sleep. o eC 6 € Previous Score Report Lab Values Calculator

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 32-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-month history of episodes of lip smacking, finger fumbling, and alterations of consciousness during which she feels "spaced out." Each episode lasts 30 to 50 seconds. The episodes initially occurred once every 2 weeks but recently have been occurring twice daily. The patient is not aware of her symptoms while she is experiencing an episode but has been told about them by friends and family members. She says she feels tired after the episodes and has noticed mild memory loss and difficulty with word finding since their onset. She takes no medications. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (137 Ib); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Her temperature is 36.1°C (96.9°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 124/82 mm Hg. Physical examination, including neurologic examination, shows no abnormalities. An EEG is obtained and shows epileptiform discharges. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration

correctExplanation: Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures are also called complex partial seizures. As this name suggests, these seizures affect a specific (focal) region of the brain and therefore produce motor or sensory symptoms that are localized to one or a few areas of the body. Patients will be unresponsive during the seizure (impaired awareness). Oral and manual automatisms, as in this patient, are suggestive of a temporal lobe lesion, the most common origin of seizures. Upper limb dystonia and autonomic disturbances such as an epigastric rising sensation can also occur in temporal lobe seizures. Patients may experience visual, auditory, or sensory auras preceding the seizure. Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures are often accompanied by a brief postictal state marked by confusion and fatigue. These seizures will demonstrate localized rhythmic activity with generalized slowing on EEG. The lesion most commonly responsible for temporal lobe epilepsy is mesial temporal sclerosis, also called hippocampal sclerosis. However, a new presentation with progressively worsening frequency and cognitive changes should raise concerns that the cause may be a tumor. MRI of the brain should be ordered to search for a mass lesion. If located, surgical excision of the lesion can be considered.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration (Choice A) can be used to confirm hypo- or hyperglycemia, both of which can cause seizures. However, these tend to be generalized, tonic-clonic seizures or focal motor seizures with intact awareness, respectively. Other signs of hypoglycemia (tremors, palpitations, diaphoresis) or hyperglycemia (osmotic diuresis, dehydration, altered mental status) are present. Measurement of serum prolactin concentration (Choice B) is part of the workup for pituitary adenomas, which present with headache and bitemporal hemianopsia. Seizures are rare and would not localize to the temporal lobe as in this patient. Urine toxicology screening (Choice C) is useful in the workup of suspected substance use disorder or toxin-related seizures. Causes include stimulants such as cocaine, amphetamines, ecstasy (3,4- methylenedioxymethamphetamine), PCP (phencyclidine), and theophylline and toxins such as strychnine. Seizures tend to be generalized, not focal. A chronic, progressive presentation is more consistent with a structural lesion. Lumbar puncture (Choice E) is useful for the diagnosis of meningitis, encephalitis, or leptomeningeal disease, as well as occult subarachnoid hemorrhage, all of which can cause generalized seizures. Focal seizures in the absence of systemic infectious signs, metastatic cancer, or headache and altered mental status, respectively, are not consistent with any of these causes. Educational Objective: Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures, or complex partial seizures, produce localized motor or sensory symptoms. Lesions of the temporal lobe, the most common origin site of seizures, can present with oral or manual automatisms, autonomic disturbances such as an epigastric rising sensation, and upper limb dystonia. Patients may experience visual, auditory, or sensory auras preceding the seizure, and may experience a brief postictal state marked by confusion and fatigue. MRI of the brain should be used to rule out a mass lesion as the cause of new-onset seizures. o eC 6 € Previous Score Report Lab Values Calculator

Symptoms caused by mass effect include abnormal vision (eg, bitemporal hemianopsia), decreased growth (eg, signs of hypopituitarism), and diabetes insipidus. questionStem: A45-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 9-day history of increasingly severe low back pain. The patient says he has experienced intermittent low back pain during the past several years, but it has never been as severe as his current pain. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. He says the pain is constant and localized to the lower back; it does not radiate and is worsened by any type of movement that involves bending. He has not had any recent trauma or falls and has not had incontinence or paresthesia in the legs. He has a history of illicit drug use, including intravenous cocaine twice weekly during the past 4 months. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows localized tenderness in the lumbar area. There are multiple track marks over the upper extremities bilaterally. Results of a complete blood count and basic metabolic panel are within the reference ranges. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 85 mm/h and serum C-reactive protein concentration is 95 mg/L. Urine toxicology screening is positive for cocaine metabolites. MRI of the lumbar spine is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient's current symptoms?

choices.D: Oral administration of a muscle relaxant
choices.E: Oral administration of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug

correctExplanation: Intravenous antibiotic therapy is used for treatment of infection of the intervertebral discs, also known as discitis. Infection may occur from hematogenous spread, as in the case of intravenous drug use, direct inoculation from surgery and/or trauma, and/or spread from overlying soft tissue infection. The most common pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus, and symptoms may include local tenderness, symptoms such as fever and chills, and symptoms and signs including neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies may show leukocytosis and increased inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Diagnosis is confirmed with MRI. Treatment includes surgical debridement with intraoperative cultures to confirm microbiologic diagnosis and antibiotics targeted at the common and likely organisms.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Epidural administration of a corticosteroid (Choice A) is contraindicated in patients with discitis. Epidural corticosteroids are used in the treatment of inflammatory and compressive processes, including disc herniation. Laminectomy (Choice C) is a surgical procedure that removes the vertebral lamina. This procedure may be used in cases of disc herniation or spinal stenosis. The affected area in discitis would not be appropriately managed with an isolated laminectomy. Oral administration of a muscle relaxant (Choice D), including cyclobenzaprine, is used in the treatment of fibromyalgia and muscle spasms. Muscle relaxants are not the first-line treatment for active discitis, though may be used as adjunct for symptom control. Oral administration of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (Choice E) such as naproxen is commonly used in the treatment of acute pain and osteoarthritis. These medications inhibit the COX enzyme. Adverse effects include gastritis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and nephropathy. Physical therapy (Choice F) is commonly used to treat acute back pain. Physical therapy improves muscle weakness, improves flexibility, and aims to prevent future injury to the affected area. Educational Objective: Discitis, or infection of the intervertebral discs, is commonly associated with intravenous drug use, and the most common microorganism is Staphylococcus aureus. An epidural abscess is a localized collection of pus in the epidural space between the dura mater and periosteum. It most commonly occurs in the spine but may occur in the brain. Most patients are elderly, have a history of concomitant infection, and often have a history of immunocompromise (eg, diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, alcohol use disorder). Epidural abscess is more common in patients with a history of intravenous drug use. Infectious organisms usually spread to the epidural space hematogenously, from spinal surgery, or from adjacent osteomyelitis. Staphylococcus aureus is a frequently causative organism, but fungal infections may also occur. Patients present with signs and symptoms of fever, altered mental status, meningismus, localized back pain and tenderness to palpation, along with weakness, numbness, and paralysis below the affected spinal level. Treatment is with broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical drainage of the abscess.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Disc impinging on a lumbar nerve root (Choice B) often presents with severe back pain with associated paresthesia, numbness, pain, and/or weakness of the lower extremities in a dermatomal and myotomal distribution. Fever and focal vertebral tenderness are not features of a herniated disk. Lymphoma (Choice C) may cause low-grade fever and night sweats but would be unlikely to cause high fever and focal tenderness of the spine. Multiple myeloma (Choice D) may cause back pain and focal vertebral tenderness due to the presence of lytic lesions, but patients also typically have characteristic laboratory findings of anemia, renal failure, and hypercalcemia, as well as bone pain in other areas, which is not found in this patient. Additionally, patients with multiple myeloma are often older. Osteoblastoma of the thoracic spine (Choice E) is a benign tumor that may present with focal back pain unresponsive to pain medications. It is unlikely to cause fever and night sweats, as seen in this patient. Syringomyelia of the cervical spine (Choice F) may present with deficits in pain and temperature sensation, along with a lower motor neuron pattern of dysfunction in the bilateral upper extremities. Tuberculous abscess of the spine (Choice G), also known as Pott disease, presents with the stigmata of chronic tuberculosis along with subacute to chronic back pain, fever, chills, and neurologic deficits. X- rays, if revealing of disease, would show evidence of osteomyelitis and lytic or reactive bone lesions. This patient has no history of primary tuberculosis, nor does he have any significant risk factors aside from diabetes mellitus. He smiles eflex is depressed, and the tongue, while at rest, has constant movements on ly decreased. Deep tendon reflexes are absent throughout. correctExplanation: Spinal muscular atrophy is a group of autosomal recessive disorders that lead to the degeneration of motor neurons and result in progressive hypotonia and areflexia. Werdnig-Hoffmann spinal muscular atrophy is the most common subtype and considered the most severe form, with infants experiencing the onset of symptoms within the first 6 months of life. It is characterized by hypotonia, diffuse weakness, and delays or absence of motor development. Notably, higher central nervous system and cerebral function remains intact. Spinal muscular atrophy in general is a type of lower motor neuron disease that affects the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord. Degeneration of these cells results in loss of innervation to muscle. In infants, parents may observe difficulties with feeding, swallowing, and respiratory function. Deep tendon reflexes are absent, and tongue fasciculations are a common finding. Infants often fail to develop head control, an ability to sit up, crawl, or stand. questionStem: A55-year-old man with emphysema is brought to the emergency department because of a 5-month history of weakness and fatigue in his legs. His pulse is 68/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. On pulmonary examination, breath sounds are decreased at the left lung base. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Neurologic examination shows mild dysarthria. LEMS is an uncommon neurologic condition involving formation of antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels at the neuromuscular junction, commonly as a paraneoplastic phenomenon in association with small cell lung carcinoma. Normally, voltage-gated calcium channels at the axonal terminal bouton open following depolarization, allowing calcium influx, and triggering exocytosis of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles into the synaptic cleft. In LEMS, antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels prevent terminal axonal calcium influx and release of acetylcholine to postsynaptic skeletal muscle cells. Patients classically display a triad of muscular weakness, depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes, and autonomic dysfunction. The muscle weakness and areflexia typically improve with exercise as amounts of acetylcholine accumulate in the synaptic cleft. Autonomic symptoms may include orthostasis, decreased salivation, dry eyes, and erectile dysfunction. Ocular and bulbar symptoms may occur later in the disease following onset of proximal muscle weakness and may include dysphagia, diplopia, and ptosis. The diagnosis is confirmed with nerve conduction studies and electromyography with exercise testing.

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (Choice A) is a genetic disorder that presents with slowly progressive, symmetric motor and sensory polyneuropathy that begins in the distal lower extremities, resulting in skeletal deformities such as hammer toes or pes cavus, and may progress to the upper extremities. Patients typically have a positive family history. Inclusion body myositis (IBM) (Choice B) is an autoimmune inflammatory condition affecting the proximal and distal muscles that presents with progressive muscle weakness and increased serum creatine kinase concentration. In contrast to other inflammatory myopathies that have a predilection for proximal muscles, distal weakness of the hands and ankles is a prominent and early finding. IBM does not typically present with autonomic dysfunction or areflexia and is not associated with lung carcinoma. Myasthenia gravis (MG) (Choice C) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by the formation of inhibitory antiacetylcholine receptor autoantibodies. Common symptoms include muscular weakness, fatigue, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens toward the end of the day, along with dysphagia and potential respiratory distress. Patients may present with an associated thymoma. In contrast to LEMS, MG typically displays more prominent involvement of the upper extremities and earlier and more prominent ocular and bulbar findings. Autonomic dysfunction and areflexia are atypical of MG. In addition, muscular weakness in MG worsens, rather than improves, with repeated exertion. Polymyositis (Choice E) is an autoimmune inflammatory condition affecting the proximal muscles. It is closely related to dermatomyositis; however, unlike dermatomyositis, it does not present with cutaneous findings. The muscular inflammation is characterized by endomysial CD8+ inflammatory infiltrate causing damage to the myocytes. Unlike LEMS, polymyositis typically presents with pain and stiffness of the affected muscles. Transient improvement in weakness with repeated exertion does not occur. questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of episodes of visual loss in her right visual field that occur every 2 weeks. The visual loss occurs suddenly and lasts for about 5 to 10 minutes before gradually resolving. She occasionally has severe headache, vomiting, and loss of balance as the visual loss is resolving. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her blood pressure is 115/75 mm Hg. Examination shows intact cranial nerves, including “isuial'aoulty: visu fekissandiceudanmatilty. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely location of the onset of her symptoms?
correctExplanation: After decussating at the optic chiasm, retinal ganglion cell axons carrying information from the right visual field traverse the optic radiations and synapse at the lateral geniculate nucleus. Neurons from the lateral geniculate nucleus travel to the primary visual cortex via the optic radiations. Lesions rostral to the optic chiasm lead to ipsilateral deficits of one eye, whereas lesions caudal to the optic chiasm cause a contralateral visual field defect involving both eyes as in this patient. Thus, this patient's right visual field deficit is attributable to a left-sided area of dysfunction caudal to the optic chiasm. Migraine is a common condition that typically presents with recurrent primary headaches. Some patients experience an aura before or during the headache, which may present with a visual field defect followed by the perception of scintillating shapes or lines and/or paresthesia. For some patients, migraine auras occur in the absence of a headache. The pathophysiology of migraine aura involves the spread of cortical depolarization, the sequential depolarization of neurons, which typically originates in the occipital cortex. This depolarization produces visual field deficits.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Left frontal cortex (Choice A) damage commonly leads to executive dysfunction, depression, motor, and/or speech abnormalities. Right frontal cortex (Choice E) damage typically presents with impulsivity, hypersexuality, and/or mania. If the frontal eye fields are damaged, patients can present with eye movement dysfunction. Visual field deficits are uncommon. Left and right retina (Choices C and G) dysfunction commonly leads to visual field deficits in one eye only. Migraine auras do not involve the retina. Left or right temporal cortex (Choices D and H) lesions may interrupt the inferior branch of the optic radiations. They present with contralateral superior quadrantanopia, a visual defect described as a wedge- shaped loss of vision. Migraine auras originate in the occipital cortex, not the temporal cortex. The right occipital cortex (Choice F) would present with left visual field loss, not right. Educational Objective: Migraine aura is thought to involve sequential depolarization of cortical neurons starting with the occipital cortex. Occipital cortex dysfunction commonly causes contralateral visual field deficits in both eyes. 6 e Previous Score Report Lab Values Calculator

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 62-year-old woman is brought to the physician because of a 3-month history of increasingly severe occipital headaches. She now has a headache each morning on awakening. She has stopped driving because she has had difficulty seeing objects on her left side. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg. Cranial nerve examination shows a left homonymous hemianopia. Funduscopic examination shows papilledema bilaterally. Muscle strength is full. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ in the right upper and lower extremities and 3+ in the left upper and lower extremities. Babinski sign is absent. Sensation is intact. Axial and coronal views of an MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Meningioma is a common, benign central nervous system (CNS) tumor derived from the meninges that occurs along the surfaces of the brain and spinal cord, often in the parafalcine region. They occur in females more often than males and are associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Patients may be asymptomatic or experience seizures or focal neurologic deficits related to the tumor location. Meningiomas are typically benign but can be malignant. Malignant meningiomas may grow rapidly, leading to symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, such as postural headache, nausea, and papilledema. Meningiomas appear as well-circumscribed, extra-axial (outside of the brain parenchyma) masses that compress the parenchyma. They show uniform enhancement on imaging. Definitive diagnosis requires histologic examination of tissue, which will show spindle cells arranged in a whorled pattern with psammoma bodies. Treatment may include antiepileptics or surgical resection to alleviate the tumoral mass effect, if significant. Often, periodic surveillance is all that is necessary.

Essential tremors specifically are exacerbated by stress and improved by small quantities of alcohol. The tremors may progressively involve more body regions over time, including the extremities, head, and voice. The pathogenesis of essential tremor is unknown, though it is commonly heritable. Propranolol and primidone are both effective first-line agents. Propranolol has fewer known drug-drug interactions and a better tolerated adverse effect profile. questionStem: A47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of episodes of involuntary rhythmic jerking of her right arm. The episodes usually last 1 minute and have occurred on six occasions. Twenty years ago, she was hospitalized following a motor vehicle collision because she had loss of consciousness for 30 minutes and confusion for 6 hours. She has had diffuse, throbbing headaches since the collision; the headaches, which resolve with 650-mg aspirin, have decreased in frequency but continue to occur once a month. During the past month, she has had the new onset of a persistent left-sided frontotemporal headache. Her only medication is the aspirin as needed. Symptoms include headache, seizures, signs of increased intracranial pressure, and, rarely, altered vision. Some patients are asymptomatic, while other patients may present with muscle or subcutaneous nodules. Typical manifestations on CT scan or MRI include cystic, ring-enhancing, calcified lesions in the brain parenchyma, meninges, ventricles, spinal cord, and/or orbit. A scolex (larval head) may also be seen on imaging. Treatment includes symptomatic management of increased intracranial pressure and seizures, antiparasitic therapy, and/or corticosteroids.

Patients typically present with severely depressed mental status and are often completely unresponsive. correctExplanation: Surrogate decision-makers (eg, legal guardian, durable power of attorney, or legal next of kin) are responsible for medical decision-making for patients who lack capacity, as in this case. The use of enteral tube feeding in patients with advanced dementia has been found consistently not to result in prolongation of life or increased quality of life and may result in harmful complication related to aspiration pneumonia, tube clogging or dislodgement, infection, and skin ulceration. Despite this evidence, enteral tube feeding is still often offered to patients with advanced dementia, particularly when a particular patient's surrogate decision-maker or family members favor aggressive intervention. Family members who request invasive interventions during end-of-life care often may not understand the invasive nature and potential complications of the requested intervention. When family members request an intervention that is not beneficial and may be harmful, a thoughtful and empathetic discussion of the risks and lack of benefits is most appropriate.

This is not yet necessary in this case. Ultimately, the physician has an ethical obligation of nonmaleficence and may eventually choose to involve the hospital ethics committee if the surrogate decision-maker insists on an intervention that the physician believes is harmful. Placing the tube and beginning enteral nutrition (Choice B) is inappropriate given the lack of demonstrated benefit in this population. Refusing to have the tube placed because of the surgical risk involved (Choice C) is incorrect. While there are a variety of compelling medical and ethical reasons to avoid tube feeding for this patient, outright refusal from the physician is not helpful and is not sensitive to the daughter’s motives for pursuing this intervention. Requesting written documentation of the daughter's power of attorney (Choice D) is not necessary at this time and may lead to a confrontation. As discussed above, a review of the potential risks and benefits of enteral nutrition is more appropriate and likely to dissuade the daughter from this intervention. She is lying still on the stretcher and is unwi blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. Ten seconds after she turns her head toward the le’ abnormalities. This patient most likely has an abnormality at which of the following sites?
correctExplanation: Dizziness and gait instability carries a broad differential diagnosis, and is often divided into central, peripheral, and secondary causes of symptoms to determine a likely diagnosis. Central causes include cerebrovascular accidents such as ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes, tumors of the brainstem and cerebellum, infarction involving the vestibulocochlear nerve, and multiple sclerosis or similar demyelinating disorders. Peripheral causes include benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, labyrinthitis, Meniere disease, endolymphatic fistula, or temporal bone fractures, tumors, or lesions. Secondary or systemic causes can include electrolyte imbalances, hypovolemia, cardiac arrhythmia, infections, and vitamin deficiencies, among other causes. This patient likely has labyrinthitis, an inflammation of the inner ear, often involving the vestibulocochlear nerve and often preceded by an upper respiratory or ear infection. Classic symptoms include vertigo, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, and hearing loss. Treatment is supportive, along with the exclusion of emergent causes of vertigo and ataxia, as the condition is typically self-limited.

Adisorder affecting the acoustic nerve (Choice A), such as an acoustic neuroma, presents with gradual onset of hearing loss and can be associated with an insidious (not sudden) onset of vestibular dysfunction. Adisorder involving the cerebellum (Choices B and E), such as an ischemic stroke, would also result in vomiting, vertigo, and nystagmus, but nystagmus would be multidirectional or gaze-evoked nystagmus, which changes direction according to the patient’s gaze. Neurologic examination for patients with ischemic stroke of the cerebellum would also show other abnormalities such as truncal and/or appendicular ataxia or dysarthria. An infarct in the medulla oblongata (Choice C) can lead to lateral medullary syndrome, which can present with ipsilateral ataxia of extremity movements, gait ataxia, Horner syndrome, and can be associated with nystagmus and dysarthria. questionStem: A90-year-old man comes to the office with his wife because of a 4-week history of mild neck pain. He has not had mities. He h kes no medications. The patient's wife says that he awakens nightly to use the bathroom. He drinks two glasses of wine with dinner dai Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ in the upper and lower extremities bilaterally. Sensation to vibration is decreased over ities. He is unable to tandem walk. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's physical examination findings?
correctExplanation: This patient has physical examination findings consistent with normal aging. Normal aging includes a slow decline of executive functioning, attention span, and problem-solving after age 70 years. The central nervous system is affected greatly by the aging process, and there are characteristic findings consistent with normal aging that every physician should be familiar with. One of the most common neurologic changes to occur is the loss of vibratory sensation, primarily in the distal extremities, as seen in this patient. Other findings include decreased to absent deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) (especially in the ankle), decreased pupillary response to light, presbyopia, and decreased hearing. As a patient ages, their gait often becomes broad-based and their stride shortens. Changes associated with sleep include a decrease in REM sleep and sleep onset latency, and an increase in nighttime awakenings. It is crucial for physicians to be familiar with these changes and be able to distinguish them from pathologic findings.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cervical myelopathy (Choice A) refers to compression of the cervical portion of the spinal cord, most commonly caused by degenerated vertebral bodies, facet joints, and/or herniated intervertebral discs. Motor weakness with lower motor neuron findings at the level of degenerative compression are accompanied by upper motor neuron findings below the level of the compression. Symptoms are most predominant in the upper extremities. Lumbar spinal stenosis (Choice B) refers to the narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal, which results in compression of the lumbar nerve roots or spinal cord. Patients classically present with low back pain that radiates to the buttocks and lower extremities that worsens with spinal extension and improves with spinal flexion. Patients may exhibit weakness and decreased DTRs on examination. Osteoarthritis (Choice C) is a common degenerative condition that is found primarily in elderly patients and frequently affects the weight-bearing joints of the hip or knee. Pain is often worse at the end of the day and after activity. Osteoarthritis does not cause decreased DTRs or decreased sensation. Peripheral neuropathy (Choice D) has many causes, including metabolic, toxic, autoimmune, and/or hereditary neuropathy. Symptoms include paresthesia or pain, and extremity weakness in a “stocking- glove” distribution. Educational Objective: Normal aging includes a slow decline of executive functioning, attention span, and problem-solving after age 70 years. Other findings consistent with normal aging include decreased or absent Achilles reflex, decreased vibratory sensation, and decreased vision and hearing. 4 rZ G € Previous Score Report Lab Values Calculator

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 77-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her husband 2 hours after the sudden loss of vision in her right eye. She has had frequent headaches for the previous 2 weeks and occasional jaw pain when chewing. Her blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg. Visual acuity is 20/400 on the right and 20/20 on the left. Examination of the right eye shows an afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopic findings of the right eye are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient's presenting findings of abrupt onset of monocular vision loss, headache, and jaw claudication are consistent with a diagnosis of temporal arteritis. Temporal arteritis is an autoimmune inflammatory vasculitis of medium and large vessels. Classic findings include symptoms of fever, chills, weight loss, headache, history of preceding transient vision loss (amaurosis fugax), jaw claudication, tenderness of the scalp, and pale optic disc edema. New headaches in an elderly patient should raise suspicion for temporal arteritis. Temporal arteritis frequently occurs in association with polymyalgia rheumatica, which is characterized by stiffness of proximal muscles. Laboratory studies show increased inflammatory markers, including ESR and C-reactive protein, and thrombocytosis. Temporal arteritis is characterized by a predilection for the vessels of the head and neck, and often affects the ophthalmic artery, inflammatory occlusion of which can result in sudden, ischemic damage to the retina. Once vision loss occurs, it is not reversible and is commonly followed by vision loss in the contralateral eye within days or weeks. The diagnosis is confirmed with biopsy of the temporal artery showing granulomatous vasculitis. Treatment with high-dose corticosteroids should occur immediately once temporal arteritis is suspected to preserve vision. Corticosteroid treatment does not generally compromise biopsy results if the biopsy is performed within 1 to 2 weeks.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acute angle-closure glaucoma (Choice A) presents with pain, conjunctival injection, a fixed, mid-dilated pupil, increased intraocular pressure, and no visible fundus abnormalities. Optic disc swelling does not typically occur. - r a SG a Previous
