questionStem: An 8-month-old male infant who was adopted recently is brought to the physician because of poor weight gain. He was born at term and weighed 2410 g (5 lb 5 oz). He was formula fed at birth and has consistently been below the 3rd percenti le for weight. Currently, his diet consists of 16 ounces of iron-fortified cow milk formula, juice, cereal, prepared fruit, and pureed green vegetables. There is no history of vomiting. He has one formed stool daily. He is alert and appears well. He current ly weighs 7002 g (15 lb 7 oz). On examinat ion, he says "mama" and "bye-bye" while waving. He sits unsupported. He is wary of strangers. There are narrow palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a thin upper lip with a "fish mouth" appearance of the oral cavity, and an indistinct nasal philtrum. His ears are normally set, the nasal bridge is flattened, and the tongue is not enlarged. There is a single palmar crease on the left hand. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnorma lities. There is no hepatosp lenomegaly, and no masses are palpated. There is no peripheral edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Alcohol is a proven teratogen, as alcohol use during pregnancy leads to irreversib le fetal neurologic effects and physical malformations in a cluster of symptoms called fetal alcohol syndrome. Because of the failure of cell migration, fetal alcohol syndrome presents with physical abnorma lities such as microcepha ly, facial abnorma lities (small palpebral fissures, thin vermilion border, cleft lip/palate, or smooth or long philtrum), limb deformities, and congenita l heart disease. Patients with fetal alcohol syndrome may demonstrate abnormal bone development (eg, cervical spine fusion) and delayed bone growth. Though alcohol is associated with obstetric complications such as preterm birth and low birth weight that commonly result from the use of substances during pregnancy, the physical malformations, including those seen in this case, are specific to alcoho l use. Growth after birth may be restricted because of eating difficulties caused by the neurodevelopmental effects of alcohol. Fetal alcohol syndrome is a leading cause of intellectual disability in the United States, though this patient is meeting milestones appropriate ly to this point.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Celiac disease (Choice A) is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy that causes inflammatory infiltration of the proximal small bowel, which leads to the malabsorption. This presents symptomatical ly as chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and nutritiona l deficiencies. While it may be a cause of decreased weight gain in children, it is not associated with changes to facial features. Characteristic physical findings of Down syndrome (Choice B) include intellectua l disability, broad, flat, facial features with prominent epicanthal folds, and a single palmar crease. There are similarities between the abnormal facies of patients with fetal alcohol syndrome - - - .

questionStem: A 6-year-o ld boy is brought to the physician by his parents because he continues to wet the bed approx imately five times weekly. He has never had a sustained dry period longer than 7 days. Most of the "accide nts" occur during the first 3 hours of the night and occas ionally during dreams in which he imagines himself urinating. He is afraid to go to friends' houses for sleepovers because of this problem. He worries that his friends would make fun of him if they knew, and he freque ntly feels bad about hims,elf "because I pee the bed like a baby." He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus 1 year ago. It is well controlled with insulin, and he is compliant with the medication regimen. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's bed-wetting?

choices.E: Urinary overflow incontinence secondary to diabetes mellitus

correctExplanation: Primary enuresis refers to episodic urinary incontinence occurring in children older than 5 years. The episodes commonly lead to adjustment problems and low self-esteem. The pathogenesis of primary enuresis most common ly involves a delay in maturation, though it may alternatively be related to a small functiona l bladder capacity or genetic factors. Along with a voiding diary, patients with nocturnal enuresis should undergo a thorough history, physical examination, and urinalysis to rule out medical causes (eg, bladder dysfunction, urinary tract infection). Many patients with primary enuresis spontaneous ly improve, though motivational therapy (eg, rewarding the patient for urinating prior to bed or having incontinence-free nights) may hasten improvement. In patients with persistent enuresis or enuresis associated with emotional problems, management with enuresis alarms or desmopressin is indicated.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice A) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's worry is specific to nocturna l urinary incontinence. Oppositional defiant disorder (Choice B) manifests as a persistent pattern of angry mood, defiant behavior, and vindictiveness that causes distress and impaired functioning in the child or their caretakers. This child's enuresis is not a voluntary behavior. Social phobia (Choice D), also known as social anxiety disorder, refers to an excessive fear of scrutiny, embarrassment, or rejection in social or performance situations leading to significant distress or impaired functioning. This patient's anxiety in social situations is secondary to enuresis.

questionStem: A 77-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician by her daughter beca use of a 3-year history of worsening forgetfulness. The patient says that she has not had any problems and does not know why her daughter is so concerned. She is able to recall zero of three objects after 5 minutes . She has significant deficits in praxis, verbal category fluency, and naming . The remainder of the examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference range. Which of the following neurotra nsmitters is most closely associated with the pathophysiology of this patient's illness?
correctExplanation: Dementia, Alzheimer type, results from decreased cholinergic signaling. Cholinergic neurons, which primarily originate from the locus coeruleus and basal forebrain, project widely to areas including the cerebral cortex to mediate attention, learning, and memory. In dementia, Alzheimer type, a proteinopathy involving amyloid and tau proteins leads to the degeneration of cholinergic neurons. Dementia, Alzheimer type, is the most preva lent dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive decline that begins with short-term memory impairment and decline in visuospatia l abilities, and progresses to apraxia, language abnormalities, and dysexecutive syndrome. The disease culminates in behavioral and personality changes that prevent the patient from performing basic activities of daily living such as bathing. Acety lcholinesterase normal ly hydro lyzes acetylcholine in synaptic clefts. Donepezi l and other cholinesterase inhibitors noncompetitively and reversib ly inhibit acetylcholinesterase activity and thereby increase the amount of synaptic acetylcholine available for neurotransmission. Though donepezil may slow the rate of cognitive decline and modest ly improve functionality, donepezil and the other cholinesterase inhibitors are not curative.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. y-Aminobutyric acid (Choice B), GABA, is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. GABA deficiency is implicated in diseases of central nervous system hyperexcitability but not dementia, Alzheimer type. Dopamine (Choice C) is a monoamine neurotransmitter that mediates reward in the mesolimbic pathway and movement in the basal ganglia. Dopamine excess in the mesolimbic pathway is implicated in psychosis. Dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia leads to parkinsonism. Dopamine is not known to play a significant role in the pathogenesis of dementia, Alzheimer type.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man with Parkinson disease is brought to the physician by his wife for a follow-up examination 6 weeks after pramipexole was added to his regimen of carbidopa- levodopa to manage increasingly severe bradykinesia. The patient reports improved movement and greater stability with walking. His wife says that he has become increasingly suspicious of her and has accused her of infidelity. Last week, she awoke during the night and found him sitting in the living room with his hunting rifle on his knees. The patient had insisted that a prowler or "her paramour" was sneaking around the house, and he intended to "teach him a lesson he won't have to learn twice." The patient has no history of psychiatric illness, but his wife says he has seemed depressed and has had decreased appetite and motivation during the past 4 weeks. The patient just shrugs his shoulders in response to his wife's comment. He has hypertens ion control led with lisinopril and hyperlipidemia controlled with lovastatin. His blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. Examination shows less rigidity and increased arm swing compared with examination results 6 weeks ago. On mental status examination, he is coopera tive and superficially polite. He has a mildly dysphoric mood and restricted affect. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's change in mental status?
correctExplanation: Pramipexole increases dopamine concentrations in several brain areas. In the dorsal striatum, an increased dopamine concentration leads to improvement in Parkinson symptoms. In the ventral striatum, dopamine-enhancing medications may lead to mood dysregulation or depression (commonly manifesting with somatic or neurovegetative symptoms). In the limbic system, an increased dopamine concentration leads to psychotic symptoms such as paranoid delusions, hallucinations, and an incongruent affect (as demonstrated by this patient). Distressing psychotic symptoms in the setting of Parkinson disease treatment are typically managed with antipsychotic medication or a decreased dose of the inciting medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Delusional disorder (Choice B) is characterized by the presence of one or more delusions (fixed, false beliefs) for a month or longer without other psychotic symptoms. This patient does not demonstrate one circumscribed delusion, instead presenting with general paranoia (against his wife, her "paramour," a prowler). Further, the onset of psychotic symptoms correlates with the initiation of pramipexole. Major depressive disorder (Choice C) includes 2 or more weeks of five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worth lessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor retardation, suicida l thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A 25-yea r-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her mother, who reports that the patient has been threatening her at home during the past 2 weeks. The patient has a 5-year history of schizophrenia. Her psychiatric symptoms had been "fairly" well controlled with oral quetiapi ne for 6 months, but she reports that she stopped taking her medication 6 weeks ago because it was sedating her. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status exam ination shows an agitated mood and a guarded affect. She appears to be responding to internal stimuli. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacothe rapy?

choices.B: Switch from quetiapine to amitripty line

correctExplanation: Schizophrenia is characterized by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms (eg, alogia, apathy, flattened affect). Treatment requires long-term antipsychotic medication. In patients with a partial response to an antipsychotic, a dose increase should be considered. However, intolerable side effects may limit the maximum acceptable dose. Quetiapine is an atypica l antipsychotic medication that primarily antagonizes dopamine-2 receptors and serotonin receptors. Quetiapine also antagonizes histamine receptors, adrenoreceptors, and muscarinic receptors, leading to sedation, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic side effects (eg, dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation). This patient experiencing the combination of intolerable sedation (leading to nonadherence) and incomplete control of psychotic symptoms should be trialed on a less sedating antipsychotic medication. Aripiprazo le is an antipsychotic medication with a lower affinity for histamine and acetylcho line receptors and is therefore less likely to cause sedation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Increasing the dosage of quetiapine (Choice A) would likely worsen this patient's sedation. She has already self-discontinued quetiapine because of sedation, so increasing the dosage would make her even less likely to adhere to the medication regimen. Switching from quetiapine to amitriptyline (Choice B) or bupropion (Choice D), antidepressant medications, would not address this patient's psychotic symptoms. This patient should be switched to a different antipsychotic medication. Switching from quetiapine to chlorpromazine (Choice E) would be less likely to resolve the patient's sedation. Chlorpromazine is a low­ potency typical antipsychotic that antagonizes histamine receptors, adrenoreceptors, and muscarinic receptors. It commonly causes sedation.

questionStem: An 86-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician because of confusion , forgetfu lness , and lethargy for 6 weeks. She lives by herse lf and has been functio ning inde pendently . She has hypertens ion, hypercho lestero lemia, and osteoarthritis of the lumbar spine and hips. Her drug regimen includes hydrochlorothiazide, captopri l, naproxen , gemfibrozi l, and lovastat in. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 87/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Reflexes bilaterally are brisk, and muscle strength in the upper and lower extremities is exce llent. On menta l status examination , she is oriented to person but not to time and place and is unable to remember three objects after 2 minutes; she cannot perform serial sevens and is frustrated when she cannot answer proverb or judgment questions . Laborato ry studies show: Hematocrit 44% Leukocyte count 9600/mm 3 Serum Na+ cI - K+ HCO -3 Ca 2+ Urea nitrogen Creat inine 121 mEq/L 86 mEq/L 3.0 mEq/L 28 mEq/L 9.6 mg/dL 20 mg/dL 2.0 mg/dL Toxicology screening is negative. A CT scan of the head shows mild d iffuse cerebra l atrophy with no lesions. An x-ray of the chest shows normal findings. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the change in mental status?

choices.B: Adverse effect of hydrochlorothiazide therap Yi
choices.C: Adverse effect of lovastat in therapy

correctExplanation: Electro lyte derangements such as hyponatremia or hypernatremia can cause altered menta l status. Hyponatremia can be acute or chronic. Acute hyponatremia occurs in 24 to 48 hours and commonly presents with symptoms of nausea, malaise, lethargy, obtundation or coma, and seizures secondary to cerebra l edema, as water is drawn into the neurona l cells in the setting of hypotonic interstitia l fluid. Given the rapid decline in sodium, symptoms can even present with sodium concentrations of 130 mEq/L. In chronic hyponatremia, however, symptoms generally do not present until the hyponatremia has become significant (usually less than 120 mEq/L). Symptoms include fatigue, nausea, forgetfu lness, lethargy, and confusion. Hydroch lorothiazide and other thiazide diuretics can induce • ·•• - ••• - ·- - - • ·•• - -· ·-. •• • - ·- - •••••••• ·- •••• - • ·-. - • - ·- •••• -■- r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous Next Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 5 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Psychiatry Self-Assessment Correct Answer: B. Electrolyte derangements such as hyponatremia or hypernatremia can cause altered mental status. Hyponatremia can be acute or chronic. Acute hyponatremia occurs in 24 to 48 hours and commonly presents with symptoms of nausea, malaise, lethargy, obtundation or coma, and seizures secondary to cerebra l edema, as water is drawn into the neurona l cells in the setting of hypotonic interstitia l fluid. Given the rapid decline in sodium, symptoms can even present with sodium concentrations of 130 mEq/L. In chronic hyponatremia, however, symptoms generally do not present until the hyponatremia has become significant (usually less than 120 mEq/L). Symptoms include fatigue, nausea, forgetfu lness, lethargy, and confusion. Hydrochlorothiazide and other thiazide diuretics can induce hyponatremia because of impaired urine dilution. Since they act on sodium-ch loride symporters in the distal tubule, they do not affect the medullary gradient or the action of antidiuretic hormone. Therefore, these patients can lose sodium in excess of water leading to euvolemic (but also hypovolemic) hyponatremia. The loss of excess solutes in relation to the loss of water also explains this patient's hypokalemia and hypochloremia. Treatment of diuretic-induced hyponatremia involves discontinuing the causative agent, restoring euvolemia if the patient is not euvolemic, and restricting free water intake.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adverse effect of captopril therapy (Choice A) is incorrect. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, such as captopril, are used in the treatment of hypertension, diabetic nephropathy, and congestive heart failure. Adverse effects include cough, hypotension, acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and angioedema. This patient has hypokalemia, making hydrochlorothiazide-induced hyponatremia the more likely cause of her hyponatremia and altered mental status. Adverse effect of lovastatin therapy (Choice C) is incorrect. Statins are used in the treatment of hyperlipidemia, particularly in patients with clinical signs or symptoms of atherosclerotic cardiovascu lar disease. A common side effect of statins is myopathy, which can present with fatigue and muscle weakness. However, statins do not cause hyponatremia and are unlikely to cause altered mental status. A cerebral infarction (Choice D) is caused by occlusion of a cerebral artery and presents with focal neurologic symptoms, such as hemiparesis or aphasia. It would be unlikely to present solely with mental status changes, particularly in the absence of changes on a CT scan of the head. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice E), presents with impairments in language, memory, perception, motor skills, attention, orientation, problem-solving, and executive function. Lethargy would be uncommon ear ly in the disease, and this patient's electrolyte abnormalities are more likely contributing to her altered mental status than a primary neurologic disease, making an adverse effect of hydrochlorothiazide the most likely cause of her change in menta l status. Educational Objective: Thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide, can cause clinical ly significant hyponatremia. Chronic hyponatremia can present with lethargy, fatigue, nausea, forgetfulness, and confusion. Treatment includes discontinuing the causative medication and restricting free water intake until sodium concentrations return to normal.

questionStem: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, has had episodes of anxiety, bloating, fatigue, irritability, and breast tenderness for the past 2 years. Her symptoms begin about 10 days before menses and cease with the onset of menses. Physical examina tion is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in patient care?

choices.A: Reassura nce and reexam ination in 6 months
choices.B: Instruction to keep a diary of symptoms for the next two menstrual cycles
choices.D: Measureme nt of serum thyrox ine (T 4), thyroid-stimulating hormone , and prolactin concentratio ns

correctExplanation: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) consists of affective and somatic symptoms occurring in the week before menses. According to the DSM-5, patients must demonstrate at least five symptoms. The symptoms must include at least one mood symptom (affective !ability, marked irritability, depressed mood, or anxiety) and at least one of the following symptoms: anhedonia, concentration difficulties, decreased energy, hypersomnia or insomnia, increased or decreased appetite, a sense of being overwhelmed, and physical symptoms (eg, breast tenderness, muscle or joint pain, sensation of bloating, weight gain). The symptoms must begin to improve within a few days after menses onset and resolve during the week after menses. The diagnosis is established by the patient's prospective documentation of symptoms in relation to at least two menstrual cycles. The pathogenesis is likely related to modulation of neurotransmitters such as serotonin secondary to changes in estrogen and progesterone concentrations. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are indicated in patients with moderate to severe PMDD, whereas patients with mild PMDD may benefit from counseling about stress reduction and lifestyle changes.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Reassurance and reexamination in 6 months (Choice A) would be inappropriate in this patient who is likely to have a PMDD diagnosis and may benefit from active management with medications or stress reduction techniques. Behavior modification therapy (Choice C) emphasizes reinforcement and punishment of certain behaviors. It is commonly utilized in autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. However, this patient is not demonstrating problematic behaviors that require modification. Measurement of serum thyroxine (T 4), thyroid-stimulating hormone, and prolactin concentrations (Choice D) are unnecessary in patients who meet diagnostic criteria for PMDD. Mood changes related to thyroid dysfunction are accompanied by other physical examination signs of thyroid disease (eg, skin and hair changes) and are not typically episodic.

questionStem: A 48-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter 2 hours after she fell at home. Physical exam ination shows ecchymoses over the left hip and left shoulder but is otherwise normal. During evaluation, the daughter pulls the physician aside and explains that her mother has drunk excessively over the past 12 years. She freque ntly consumes several bottles of wine alone at home each day. She also reports that her mother has been forgetting to take cooking pots off the stove. When the physician continues with the evaluation, the patient behaves as if she has never met the physician before now. On cognitive examination, she recalls zero out of three objects after 5 minutes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's cognitive decline?
correctExplanation: Patients who chronically abuse alcohol typically demonstrate a significant thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency caused by poor nutritional intake, thiamine malabsorption, and impaired cellular utilization of thiamine. Over time, thiamine deficiency can result in damage and atrophy of the mammillary bodies, visible on MRI of the brain, which manifests as Wernicke encephalopathy. The typical clinical presentation of Wernicke encephalopathy is a triad of acute altered mental status, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, and ataxia. The symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy are reversible but incre,ase the risk for developing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (also known as Korsakoff psychosis) in chronic alcohol users if not immediately treated with high-dose thiamine. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is an irreversible condition that features anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with the consequent tendency to confabulate, or verbalize false stories or memories, to compensate for the inability to remember. This patient demonstrates an inability to form new memories after the amnesia-causing event (anterograde amnesia).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Choice A) is a human prion disease that presents with rapidly progressing dementia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, cerebellar dysfunction, corticospinal tract dysfunction, basal ganglia dysfunction, and stimulus-induced myoclonus. This patient does not demonstrate stimulus-induced myoclonus or cerebellar, corticospina l, or basal ganglia dysfunction. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice B), is the most prevalent dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive decline that begins with short-term memory impairment, progresses to apraxia and language abnormalities, and culminates in behavioral and personality changes preventing the patient from performing basic activities of daily living. Anterograde memory impairment is common, but this patient's young age is inconsistent with dementia, Alzheimer type.

questionStem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father as a new patient for a well-child examination. On entering the physician's office, the patient immediately climbs onto the physician's lap and begins talking with the physician. Her father says that his daughter has shown poor learning ability and has outbursts in school. He also says she is highly sensitive to sound. Examination shows a small, upturned nose, small chin, and long philtrum. Muscle tone is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Williams syndrome results from a sporadic or inherited deletion of contiguous genes on chromosome 7q11.23, including the elastin gene. Patients typically present with an overly friendly demeanor, emotiona l dysregulation, intellectual delay, elfin facies (strabismus, flat nasal bridge, short nose, long philtrum, wide mouth), short stature, vascular and cardiac valve abnormalities seconda ry to elastin dysfunction, structura l abnormalities of the urinary tract, and endocrine abnormalities (eg, hypothyroidism). Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing confirming a deletion on chromosome 7q 11.23. !Management involves surgica l correction of vascula r, cardiac, or other functionally significant structu ral abnormalities and antihypertensive medication if such develops.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cornelia de Lange syndrome (Choice A) results from the sporadic deletion of cohesin complex genes, which normally direct prenatal development. It is characterized by growth delay, intellectual disability, facial dysmorphia (microcephaly, arched eyebrows, small upturned nose, widely spaced teeth), and malformations of the extremities. Down syndrome (Choice B) results from trisomy of chromosome 21 and presents with characteristic physical features including broad, flat, facial features with prominent epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease. Patients with Down syndrome also present with cognitive impairment, cardiac abnormalities (eg, atrial septal defect), gastrointestinal abnormalities (eg, duodenal atresia, imperforate anus), ophthalmologic abnormalities (eg, refractive errors), and hearing loss. Prader-Wi lli syndrome (Choice C) results from the absence of paternal expression of genes on chromosome 15. Children typically present with hyperphagia (and potential obesity), short stature, impaired cognition, motor delays, and hypogonadism. Smith-Magenis syndrome (Choice D) results from microdeletion or mutation of a transcriptional regulator gene (RA/1) and is

questionStem: A 77-year-o ld woman comes to the physician at the request of an attorney prior to writing an advance directive. She says that she wants to have an advance directive in order to avoid putting an unnecessa ry burden on her children. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She immigrated to the USA from Poland 20 years ago. She has only an elementary school education. She was employed in a cleaning service for a hotel but stopped working 5 years ago. She lives alone and is able to perform activities of daily living independently. She participates in social activities at her church. All of her close friends are also from Poland. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. On mental status exam ination, she is nervous . She is alert and is oriented to person. She knows she is in the physician's office but does not recall the street name correctly. She knows the month and day of the week but is not sure of the exact date. She knows her address. She can recall two of three words after 5 minutes. She can subtract 7 from 100 using her fingers but is unable to subtract 7 from 93. She is unable to spell the word "world" backwards. She can draw the hands on a clock to show 10 minutes to 2 o'clock and can slowly copy a drawing of two intersecting pentagons. She demonstrates that she understands the meaning of a standardized story. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step with respect to this patient's advance directive?

choices.A: Discussion of her preferences for care
choices.C: Repeat her mental status examinat ion with an interprete

correctExplanation: Though some cognitively impaired patients may lack capacity to make decisions about their care, cognitive ly impaired patients should not be assumed to lack decisional capacity. Though this patient illustrates mild abnormalities on brief cognitive testing (which may indicate normal aging changes in a patient with a limited education), these findings do not necessarily preclude her from making end-of­ life decisions. To meet the criteria for decisional capacity, patients must express a consisten t choice, demonstrate an understanding of the risks and benefits of the choice, demonstrate an appreciation of the significance of the choice for their personal circumstances, and illustrate an ability to reason through the options. Therefore, to assess this patient's decisional capacity and potentially write her advance directive (if the physician believes the patient possesses decisional capacity), the physician should discuss the patient's preferences for care and assess the four decisional capacity criteria specific to these decisions.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A second examination in one week (Choice B) would be unnecessary in this patient. A fluctuating cognitive course (eg, delirium) is unlikely in this patient with mild cognitive impairment who is consistently alert, attentive (difficulty with serial ?sand spelling "world" is likely secondary to this patient's limited education given her ability to attend to and understand a story), and able to verbalize a desire to write an advance directive.

questionStem: Six hours after undergoing an appendectomy, a 4 ?-year-old man repor ts a moderately severe, diffuse headac he. He has no other symptoms. He has not ingested food or drink for 2 days . His pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Bacte rial meningitis G) Occipital neuralgia
choices.B: Brain abscess H) Post-traumatic headac he
choices.C: Caffeine withdrawal I) Subdural hema toma
choices.D: Cluster headac he J) Tension-type headac he

correctExplanation: Headaches can be differentiated into primary and secondary headaches (eg, substances, infection, neoplasm, trauma). Headache features that raise concern for serious secondary causes include fever, focal neurologic deficits, abrupt onset, history of malignancy or trauma , and positional exacerbation. Caffeine withdrawal typically presents with headache, fatigue, depressed or irritable mood, difficu lty concentrating, gastrointestinal distress, tachycardia, hand tremor, or flu-like symptoms. The headache is common ly diffuse and pulsating, varies from mild to severe in intensity, begins within 24 hours of last caffeine consump tion , and improves once withdrawal resolves. Acute management may include over-the-counter analgesics or the administration of caffeine. Patients desiring to abstain from caffeine should gradually taper their use to prevent severe withdrawal symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd K. Bacteria l meningitis (Choice A) typically presents with fever and signs of meningeal irritation (nausea, irritability, confusion, anorexia, photophobia, headache, and nuchal rigidity). This patient does not demonstrate a fever or signs of meningea l irritation other than headache. Brain abscess (Choice B) typically presents with fever, focal neurologic deficits, headache, and altered mental status. This patient does not demonstrate a fever, focal neurologic deficits, or altered mental status. Cluster headaches (Choice D) are primary headaches that typica lly present with short-lived , unilatera l, severe pain in the orbital, supraorbital , or tempora l region of the head and are accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, miosis, ptosis, lacrimation, nasal congestion). This patient endorses a diffuse headache and does not demonstrate autonomic symptoms. Hypertensive encephalopathy (Choice E) refers to malignant hypertension causing diffuse brain dysfunction including severe headache, vision · - ••- - - . .. . .. • - -· ..... - - .. ••

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of difficulty sitting still for more than 1 hour. He says that he has a nearly intolerable sensation of restlessness in his legs when watching movies or during long flights. His symptoms resolve when he stands up and takes a few steps. He also has had difficulty falling asleep because of his symptoms and states that he thinks he moves around a lot once he falls asleep because his wife often complains that he kicks her in bed. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Deep tendon reflexes are normal in all extremities. Sensation is intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacothe rapy?
correctExplanation: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common movement disorder characterized by an urge to move the lower extremities when sitting or lying down to sleep. During sleep, many patients with RLS demonstrate periodic movements of the lower extremities. The pathogenesis is incomplete ly understood, but alterations in dopamine metabolism and cellular iron influx and efflux may be involved. Caffeine along with antihistamine, dopamine antagonist, and antidepressant medications common ly exacerbate RLS. All patients with RLS should undergo iron studies. Patients with iron deficiency require iron repletion. In patients without iron deficiency who report chronic and severe symptoms, dopamine agonists such as ropinirole are indicated.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hydroxyzine (Choice A) is an antihistamine medication utilized for allergic reactions and off-label for anxiety. It common ly exacerbates RLS. Modafinil (Choice B) is commonly utilized to address daytime sleepiness in patients with narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea, and shift­ work sleep disorder. It has no proven efficacy in RLS. Trazodone (Choice D) is a serotonin modulator, and zolpidem (Choice E) is a nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic medication. Both are utilized to treat insomnia but are not helpful in RLS. Educational Objective: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common movement disorder characterized by an urge to move the lower extremities when lying down to sleep. During sleep, many patients with RLS demonstrate periodic movements of the lower extremities. . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because her husband is concerned that she has been having difficulty remembe ring things around the house. During the past 6 weeks, she has been forgetting to do her usual household chores. She does not think that she has a problem. She says that she does her best but often feels fatigued, especial ly when moving around a lot. She has had numbness of both legs and intermittent blurred vision during the past year. Physical examination shows pallor of the optic discs. Deep tendon reflexes at the knees and ankles are brisk bilatera lly. On mental status examination, she has an upbeat mood and affect. She is oriented to person, place, and time. She has difficulty remem bering the names of recent U.S. Presidents. There is no evidence of auditory or visual hallucinations. A T2-weighted MRI of the brain shows numerous small plaques in the periventricular white matter. A lumbar puncture is done. Which of the following findings is most likely on cerebrospina l fluid analysis?
correctExplanation: Multiple sclerosis, the most prevalent immune-mediated demyelinating disease, can present initially with lesions in several central nervous system (CNS) locations. According to the McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis diagnosis, patients must have evidence of demyelinating lesions that are separated in time and location. This evidence can be based on subjective symptoms or imaging evidence. This patient demonstrated several episodes of optic neuritis separated in time, along with dysfunction of the dorsal column­ medial lemniscus tracts (decreased sensation), corticospinal tracts (hyperreflexia), frontal lobes (incongruent ly bright affect), and medial temporal lobe (decreased recall memory), representing separation in space. Fatigue and symptom exacerbation with exercise are common in multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain typically shows focal white matter hyperintensities in the periventricular region, cortex, subcortical region, cerebellum, or spine. Oligoclonal bands of immunoglobulins, indicating immune overactivation, can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid but are not necessary for diagnosis. Treatment includes corticosteroids for symptomatic management of acute flares and long-term disease-modifying treatments such as interferon or monoclonal antibodies, which decrease the frequency of future episodes.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreased glucose (Choice A) is demonstrated in bacterial and fungal meningitis or encephalitis. Eosinophilocytosis (Choice C) is consisten t with eosinophilic meningitis secondary to parasitic infections. This patient's focal neurologic deficits and chronic course along with the absence of headache, encephalopathy (eg, decreased alertness, disorientation), or systemic signs of infection are more consisten t with multiple sclerosis.

questionStem: A 57-year-o ld lawyer is brought to the emergency department by police after he interrupted a church service by loudly proclaim ing that he is the Messiah. Police say that he became angry and physically confronta tional when he was asked to leave and continued to insist that he was the Messiah when police intervened . On arrival in the emergency department, he is expansive and talks loudly. He appears well groomed. On questioning, he says he has never been sick and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He refuses to allow a physical examination and becomes irritable with the nurses. He dema nds to see the person in charge of the hospital, noting he has figured out a way to save the hospital millions of dollars. On mental status examination, he talks rapidly and abruptly shifts from topic to topic. He reports hearing the voice of God telling him that He is pleased with him. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Bipolar disorder is a mood disorder that features acute episode,s of mania. This patient's career as a lawyer indicates he is high functioning at baseline, signifying that his current behavior is an episodic change from baseline. Acute mania typically manifests with an expansive or euphoric or irritable mood, increased energy, a decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, rapid speech and thinking (as evidenced by this patient's pressured speech with a flight of ideas), irresponsibility (as evidenced by this patient's disruption of a church service), and grandiose thinking (as evidenced by this patient's confidence that his plan can save the hospital millions of dollars). Some patients demonstrate associated psychotic symptoms (eg, hallucinations, delusions). This patient's belief that he is the Messiah constitutes a grandiose de lusion. Type 1 bipolar disorder is this patient's most likely diagnosis. Though patients with type 1 bipolar disorder need to demonstrate a history of mania to meet diagnostic criteria, patients with type 2 bipolar disorder must demonstrate major depressive episodes in addition to hypomanic episodes (less severe and shorter episodes of mania without psychotic features). Management requires mood stabilizing therapy (eg, mood stabilizers or mood-stabi lizing antipsychotics) for acute mania. Once acute mood episodes resolve, patients with bipolar disorder should continue mood stabilizer maintenance therapy to prevent future episodes of mania or depression.
incorrectExplanation: nd E Delusional disorder (Choice B) is characte rized by the presence of one or more delusions for a month or longer without other psychotic symptoms. Mania symptoms are atypical. Dysthymic disorder (Choice C), more common ly known as persistent depressive disorder, refers to depression symptoms lasting longer - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A 32-yea r-old man is broug ht to the emergency depa rtme nt 2 hours after the onset of chest pain, palpitatio ns, and agitation. He has a history of cocaine abuse and has been treated in the emerge ncy department six times during the past 4 months for episodes of agitation and hallucinations. He has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. On arrival, he is agitated but cooperative. His temperatu re is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 130/min, and blood pressu re is 160/100 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Urine toxico logy scree ning is positive for cocaine. An ECG shows new ST-segme nt depress ions in the anterior leads, which were not found on ECGs obtained at previous visits. Which of the following medications is contraindicated in this patient?
correctExplanation: Cocaine is an addictive recreationa l drug that causes euphoria, restlessness, and increased sympathe tic tone (tachycardia, hypertension, pupillary dilation). Cocaine blocks the presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine, serotonin, and dopamine, which increases the concen tration of these substances in the synaptic cleft. The increased norepinephrine causes tachycardia and hypertension through activation of sympathetic adrenoceptors, leading to increased cardiac chronot ropy and peripheral vasoconstriction. It can also cause coronary artery vasospasm, which presents with chest pain and new ECG changes (eg, T wave inversions, ST elevations or depressions). ~-Adrenergic blocker therapy in cocaine intoxication can lead to unopposed a1-adrenergic activation, which can lead to marked hypertension and further increase the risk for coronary vasospasm. Therefore, in this patient, administering ~-adrenergic blocker monotherapy with metoprolol would be contraindica ted.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Aspirin (Choice A) is an antiplatelet agent used in the primary and seconda ry prevention of acute coronary syndromes. It should be given as soon as possible when a patient presents with signs and symptoms of myocardia l ischemia, such as chest pain, diaphoresis, nausea, and ECG changes. Aspirin would be appropriate in this patient and is not contraindi cated in cocaine intoxication. Diazepam (Choice B) is a benzodiazepine that is used in the treatment of anxiety, seizures, and alcohol detoxification. It can also be used to decrease the agitation associated with cocaine intoxication and is indicated in this patient. Diltiazem (Choice C) is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used in the treatment of hypertension and atrial fibrillation. questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of recurrent thoughts that she has sexually abused her 5-year-old daughter. She says that she examines her daughter's perineum several times daily looking for evidence of abuse. Examination of the child by her pediatrician has shown no evidence of abuse. The patient believes that she is going crazy. She reports that she was sexually abused as a child. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she appears tense, anxious, and mildly depressed. She cries as she describes her worrisome thoughts. There is no evidence of hallucinations . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is an anxiety disorder typica lly characterized by obsessions that the patient attempts to neutralize with compu lsions. Obsessions are unwanted, intrusive thoughts (eg, thoughts related to violence, sex, or contamination) or urges (eg, to commit violence) that increase anxiety. Compulsions are rigidly applied repetitive behaviors (eg, checking, washing) or mental activities (eg, counting, repeating words) that relieve anxiety related to obsessions. By definition, the compulsions are excessive or do not realistica lly address the obsessive fears, and patients commonly recognize the irrationality of their compulsions. The pathogenesis of OCD is likely multifactorial, related to genetics, stress, or dysfunction of striatal and thalamic circuits. Treatment includes high doses of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRls, eg, fluoxetine) or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with a focus on exposure to the discomfort of suppressing the compulsion after experiencing the obsession.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acute stress disorder (Choice A) refers to intrusive thoughts, hyperarousal, avoidance, or negative mood and thoughts that occur within 1 month of a traumatic event such as a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. This patient has no history of a traumatic event within the past month. Delusional disorder (Choice B) is characterized by the presence of one or more delusions for a month or longer without other psychotic symptoms. Patients typically lack insight into their delusion, which they accept as truth. As such, delusiona l thoughts are usually ego­ syntonic and nondistressing. This patient is instead experiencing distressing, intrusive, ego-dystonic thoughts that she is likely able to identify as untrue . . . - - -••·- .. ·- .. - - - . - .. -· . ·- ... ···••-• .. ••- ... •- -· ··- ..

questionStem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. His mother states that he has had increasingly impulsive behavior and aggressive outbursts during the past year. His kindergarten and first grade teachers expressed concern about his ability to follow directions and socialize with peers. At the age of 3 years, he received treatme nt for lead exposure. Language development is appropriate; toilet training milestones have been met. His mother states that he is a picky eater. He has no history of serious illness. His mother believes that he is angry about his parents getting a divorce. He is alert and fidgety. He is at the 5th percentile for height and weight. His pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 97/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no dysmorphic features . The thyroid gland is not enlarged. Pulmonary and abdomina l examinations show no abnormalities. The upper and lower extremities are thin. Muscle tone is normal. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk. He is easily distractible, impulsive in observed play, and oppositional when his mother attempts to redirect him. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) presents with chronic symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity or inattention that occur in more than one setting and impair academic, social, or emotional function. Children with predominant hyperactivity symptoms are unable to sit still and may have difficulty taking turns (postulated to result from a dysregulated dopamine reward pathway), whereas children with predominant inattentive symptoms tend to daydream, process information slowly, and demonstrate difficulty in completing tasks (related to norepinephrine dysregulation). ADHD is associated with soft neurologic abnorma lities such as brief reflexes. For diagnosis, physicians must establish that the patient is functional ly impaired in severa l settings, so parents and teachers must fill out behavioral rating scales. Stimulants, which include amphetamine salts and methylphenidate, are first-line agents for treatment that increase synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Projective testing by the school psychologist (Choice B) would involve the patient interpreting ambiguous stimuli (eg, Rorschach testing) as a persona lity test. This patient does not demonstrate a pathologic persona lity and this testing is inappropriate at this time. Thyroid function tests (Choice C) would assist in diagnosing thyroid dysfunction, which may present with hyperactivity. However, this patient does not demonstrate tachycardia or physical examination signs of thyroid dysfunction (eg ,skin, hair, or eye changes). \ j • - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- i.

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 30 minutes after his friends noticed that he had become confused and unsteady . His friends reported tha t he "may have been trying to get high." Glucose and naloxone administered en route to the emergency department produced no change in his condition. On arrival, he is lethargic , and his speech is slurred. His temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. His gait is ataxic. Results of urine toxicology screening are pending. A CT scan of the head shows no abnormalities. The patient falls asleep for 1 hour, and a second neurologic examination on awakening shows full alertness and a normal gait. Which of the following substances is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Inhalant abuse (eg, toluene, nitrous oxide, spray paint, glue) is common in children and adolescents. The effects typica lly begin within seconds of use and persist for approximately 30 minutes, representing a faster onset and resolution compared with other recreationa l drugs. Inhalants exert effects on multiple organ systems: dermato logic (eg, perioral or perinasal dermatitis with erythro- or pyoderma), otolaryngologic (eg, nosebleeds, halitosis), ocular (eg, conjunctiva! infection), cardiac (eg, dysrhythmia, tachycardia), gastrointestinal (eg, nausea, anorexia), respiratory (eg, wheezing, coughing, sneezing), and neuropsychiatric (eg, headache, ataxia, anosmia, slurred speech, mood swings, hallucinations). Severe inhalant toxicity can manifest with tachydysrhythmias and respiratory depression, and ultimate ly seizures or coma. Treatment is primari ly supportive, though some inhalants have specific antidotes (eg, methylene blue for nitrites). Prevention is key; schoo ls shou ld monitor the use of solvent-based products, and parents and children should be educated about the risks of inhalants.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Alcohol (Choice A) is a central nervous system (CNS) depressant that can cause slurred speech, emotional !ability, behaviora l disinhibition, ataxia, and memory lapses. However, alcohol is typically metabolized over the course of hours, not minutes. Cocaine (Choice B) is a CNS stimulant that causes euphoria and increases sympathetic tone, leading to tachycardia and hypertension, pupillary dilation, and restlessness (rather than lethargy). Also, cocaine is typical ly metabo lized over hours, not minutes. Heroin (Choice C) causes symptoms of CNS depression including sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia, and hypotension. However, heroin is typical ly metabo lized over the course of hours, not minutes. Also, if the patient were intoxicated with opioids, his lethargy would be expected to rapidly improve with naloxone therapy.

questionStem: A 20-year-o ld woman comes to the physician with her husba nd because of increasing fatigue and social withdrawal. The patient reports that she has always worried about her appearance and how other people perceive her. She has difficulty shopping and states, "Every time I go into a grocery store, I feel like I might not get out alive." During the past 3 months, she has induced vomiting 6 to 10 times weekly when she feels "panicky" after eating "bad foods ." Her husband reports that she becomes anxious and irritable when she has not exercised. She has not had a menstrua l period for 6 months. Her husband expresses frustration with her problems and says that her obsessive worrying and poor self-image are ruining their marriage. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is thin and meticu lously groomed. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 48 kg (105 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m2. Her tem perature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 50/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. Physical examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. The patient states that her recent weight loss of 6.8 kg (15 lb) has made her feel less anxious and that she plans to lose more weight. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by an intense fear of gaining weight, decreased self-worth related to body weight, and consequent restricting (eg, fasting, exercising) or binge eating/purging behavior (eg, vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse) leading to insufficient nutrition. Patients with anorexia nervosa often have a BMI less than 17 kg/m 2, though patients with mild anorexia may demonstrate a BMI greater than 17 kg/m 2(normal BMI is 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m 2). Amenorrhea is common and reflects insufficient nutrition. Alternatively, patients with bulimia nervosa do not typically demonstrate severe malnutrition that leads to amenorrhea or a low BMI. Physical examination of patients with anorexia nervosa can show dry, scaly skin and fine hair or hair loss caused by decreased protein stores. Patients who vomit to purge can demonstrate parotid gland enlargement from salivary gland overstimulation, dental caries from gastric hydrochloric acid erosion of enamel, and scars on the knuckles secondary to abrasions from the incisors when inducing vomiting. The loss of gastric hydrochloric acid leads to hypoch lorem ia and metabolic alkalosis. In severe cases, signs of hypovolemia such as tachycardia and hypotension may be present. Treatment of anorexia nervosa is through a combined medical and psychiatric approach and involves correcting fluid and electrolyte derangements along with behavioral and pharmacologic therapy.

questionStem: A 4-year-o ld girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of frequent temper tantrums and extreme irritability over the past 6 months. She was born at 35 weeks' gestation and had jaundice at birth. Her 17-year-old mother reports that her daughter refuses to listen to her and will not eat foods she previously ate. The mother appears sad and states that she is overwhe lmed. The patient is at the 15th percenti le for height and weight. Physical examination shows no abnorma lities. She is very active during the examinat ion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Measurement of serum albumin concentrat ion
choices.D: Measurement of urine amino acid concentration

correctExplanation: Normal 4-year-old children play with other children , play make-believe , tell stories , understand time and counting , stand and hop on one foot, and cut their own food with supervision. Typical preschoo l-age children also demonstrate defiant behavior and are picky eaters. When children demonstrate difficult behaviors, parents should utilize ignoring and other parenting skills. Teenage parents commonly possess inadequate parenting skills and may increase their attention to the child during tantrums, reinforcing the tantrum behavior. Young parents typically benefit from parenting classes.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Play therapy (Choice A) can help children with anxiety, adjustment disorder, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). This patient demonstrates age-appropriate behavior. Measurement of serum albumin concentration (Choice C) or urine amino acid concentration (Choice D) assists in assessing a patient's nutritional status or aberrant protein metabolism, respectively. This patient demonstrates age-appropriate behavior and no evidence of nutritional or metabolic derangements. MRI of the brain (Choice E) assists in diagnosing neurologic causes of behavior difficulties (eg, genetic syndromes). This patient demonstrates age-appropriate behavior and has no physica l signs of a genetic syndrome. Methylphenidate therapy (Choice F) treats ADHD. This patient does not demonstrate inattention or hyperactivity, and her impulsive tantrum behaviors are a e-a ro riate.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 57-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of memory loss for 3 months. Examination shows a very sluggish patient with a flat affect who talks slowly and in a whisper. Initially, she replies to all mental status tests, "I don't know" or "I can't remem ber." As the physician shows a warm and supportive manner, her responses improve, so that eventual ly she recalls the main event in the news the previous evening and is able to recall two out of three objects after 5 minutes. She is told the third object. When retested just before leaving 10 minutes later, she recalls all three. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?

choices.F: Major depressive disorder with atypica l features

correctExplanation: Symptoms of major depressive disorder (MOD) include 2 or more weeks of at least five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor retardation, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. In patients with MOD with atypical features, neurovegetative symptoms typically manifest as hypersomnia and hyperphagia. Patients with MOD with atypical features may also demonstrate situational improvements in mood, oversensitivity to interpersonal rejection, or leaden paralysis (a heavy sensation in the extremities leading to extreme psychomotor retardation). The underlying pathogenesis is believed to arise from personality and temperament characteristics that promote emotional and behavioral dysregulation in response to stressful situations such as interpersonal rejection. This patient's subjective memory loss and severe psychomotor retardation that improve as she develops a rapport with the physician likely represents a functional neurologic disorder (reflecting the conversion of emotional distress into neurologic symptoms), which is frequently comorbid with depression. When the patient's fear of interpersonal rejection by the physician decreases, her distress and consequent psychological need to convert her distress into a neurologic symptom dissipates. Treatment of atypical depressive disorder involves antidepressant medication and psychotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Communicating hydrocephalus (Choice A) refers to hydrocephalus secondary to inadequate reabsorption of cerebrospinal fluid. Patients typically present with positional headaches, nausea, vomiting, and vision changes (signs of increased intracranial pressure). Memory loss in the absence of other hydrocephalus symptoms that improves over the course of minutes is atypical.

questionStem: A 21-year-o ld college student is brought to the emergency department by her roommates because of a 4-day history of progressive general ized weakness and muscle cramps. She has been unable to eat solids for 2 days. Her last bowel movement was 4 days ago. Her roommates report that, during the past year, they have heard her vomiting in the bathroom after meals. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. The patient is oriented to person, place, and time and says that she feels tired. Her temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft, and bowel sounds are decreased. Muscle strength is decreased throughout. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Bulimia nervosa (binging/purging type) involves cycles of uncontrollable eating and compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, laxative, or diuretic overuse that occur at least once a week for 3 months or more. Unlike patients with anorexia nervosa, patients with bulimia nervosa typically have a normal BMI and do not demonstrate amenorrhea. Patients with the binging/purging type of anorexia or bulimia nervosa can demonstrate dental caries from gastric hydrochloric acid erosion of enamel, parotid gland swelling from salivary gland overstimulation, and scars on the knuckles secondary to abrasions from the incisors when inducing vomiting. The loss of gastric hydrochloric acid leads to hypochloremia and metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalemia is common, as increased bicarbonate leads to renal proton-potassium exchange and consequent potassium secretion. In severe cases of bulimia nervosa, signs of hypovolemia such as tachycardia and hypotension may be present. Hypovolemia leads to increased aldosterone concentrations, resulting in further potassium secretion. As potassium is involved in the membrane potential of muscle cells (including skeletal, smooth, and cardiac muscles), hypokalemia typically leads to general weakness, muscle cramps, fatigue, palpitations, or decreased gastrointestinal motility. Treatment of bulimia nervosa is through a combined medical and psychiatric approach, and it involves correcting fluid and electrolyte derangements alongside behavioral and pharmacologic therapy.

questionStem: A 23-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by police after he had to be removed in handcuffs from an airliner on which he had been a passenger. The airline attendants report that the patient shouted that he was a pilot and demanded to fly the plane, because he was too busy to wait for "those idiots that the airline calls pilots to take off." The patient reports, "I felt exquis ite and perfectly glorious until those Keystone Cops started harassing me." He states that he has been brought to the hospita l by "peons" in the past who failed to understand his essential superiority to "normal man." He says he has racing thoughts and boundless energy and has been sleeping only 2 hours nightly for the past week. He adds that he recent ly quit his job as a software engineer because he is now in complete control of the US government. He takes no medications. He has increased his alcohol consumption to six beers daily for the past 3 days. He does not use illicit drugs. He is wearing bright, mismatched clothing. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . On mental status examinat ion, his mood is expansive and irritable, and his speech is loud and rapid. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Bipola r disorder is a mood disorder that features acute episodes of mania. Acute mania typically manifests with an irritab le or euphoric mood, increased energy, a decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, rapid speech and thinking, irresponsibility (as evidenced by this patient's demand to fly the plane), and grand iose thinking. Some patients demonstrate associated psychotic symptoms (eg, grandiose delusions, hallucinations). Management of acute mania requires mood stabilizing therapy (eg, mood stabilizers or mood stabilizing antipsychotics). Atypical antipsychotics (eg, quetiapine, olanzapine), which antagonize dopamine receptors and modulate serotonin activity, possess mood stabilizing properties and demonstrate effectiveness for acute mania over the course of days. Alternatively, for acute bipolar depression, the most effective medication choices are lurasidone, quetiapine, lamot rigine, and fluoxetine-o lanzapine. Once acute mood episodes resolve, patients with bipolar disorder should continue mood stabilizer maintenance therapy to prevent future episodes of mania or depression.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Diazepam (Choice A) may be utilized in conjunction with mood stabilizers or antipsychotic medications to promote sleep, which quickens the resolution of acute mania. However, acute mania requires treatment with a mood stabilizing medication. Fluoxet ine (Choice B) and sertraline (Choice E) are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors utilized for unipolar major depressive disorder. In patients with bipolar disorder, these medications may worsen mania or convert depression to mania.

questionStem: A 20-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by his parents because he has not moved or spoken for 60 minutes despite encouragement. He has had similar episodes over the past 6 months. His parents say that he has always been shy and a loner. He has not looked for a job since graduating from high school 2 years ago. He appears unkemp t and has long finger nails. He is mute and maintains a rigid posture during the examination. He resists passive movement of his extrem ities. Physica l examination shows no other abnormalities. A CT scan of the head is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Catatonia is a neurobehavioral syndrome marked by the inability to move or speak (stuporous subtype) or the inability to stop moving or speaking repetitively (excited subtype) that typically arises from an exacerbation of a psychiatric disorder such as bipolar disorder or schizophrenia. Patients with the stuporous subtype of catatonia typically present with immobility, mutism, muscle rigidity, waxy flexibility (maintaining limb position after the limb is moved by the examiner), negativism (resistance to instruction), staring, and/or posturing. Patients with the excited subtype typically demonstrate hyperactivity, purposeless movements, verbigeration (repetition of words/phrases), and echolalia (repetition of other people's words). Treatment requires benzodiazepine medications or, if refractory to benzodiazepines, electroconvulsive therapy. According to the DSM-5, patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (eg, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder) demonstrate at least two of the following five symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms (eg, flat affect, apathy, alogia). To meet the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia, patients must demonstrate functional deficits, and the total duration of symptoms must exceed 6 months. This patient demonstrates apathy (not looking for a job and poor hygiene) and consequent impairment in social function and can be assumed to possess a chronic psychotic disorder.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Absence seizures (Choice A) are generalized seizures that manifest as transient staring episodes and an associated loss of consciousness without postictal confusion. Absence seizures typically last a few seconds, not an hour, and are not associated with muscle rigidity. Brief psychotic disorder (Choice B) is characterized by at least one acute psychotic symptom (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. questionStem: A previously well-functioning 14-year-o ld boy is apprehended for steali ng a compact disc from a store. A court-ordered evaluat ion shows the stealing to be the latest in a series of self-defeating behaviors over the past 2 months that include incomplete homewor k assignments and truancy. He states that he has difficulty concentrating and awake ns frequentlly at night. During an interview with his family, the teenage r seems oblivious to the obvious marital discord between his parents. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Adjustment disorder refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. The emotiona l disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stressor and a significant impairment in daily school, work, or social functioning. Patients may internalize or externalize their distress, resulting in depression or anxiety symptoms or conduct disturbances (acting out), respectively. Patients with adjustment disorder do not meet criteria of anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. This patient has some anxiety/depression symptoms (eg, difficulty concentrating and sleeping) and conduct disturbances (eg, truancy) with a clear stressor and without meeting the criteria for anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. As adjustment disorder is typical ly self­ limited, the treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Antisocial persona lity disorder (Choice B) is a cluster B personality disorder that arises from a deficit in empathy, resulting in pervasive violations of others' rights, aggression, and a hostile and manipulative attitude toward others. Personality disorders are only diagnosed in patients older than 18 years, and this patient does not yet demonstrate a persistent pattern of transgressive behavior. Conduct disorder (Choice C) refers to a persistent pattern of violating others' rights, including aggression, deceitfu l behaviors, and property destruction. Patients must demonstrate this behavior for 12 months, whereas this patient has been acting out for the past 2 months. Dysthymic disorder (Choice D), more common ly called persistent depressive disorder, refers to at least three depression symptoms (including depressed mood during more days than not) that have endured at least 2 years. This patient demonstrates two depression symptoms (impaired concentration, insomnia) for 2 months only. .

questionStem: A 42-year-o ld man with obsess ive-compu lsive disorder comes to the physician because of only partial symptomat ic relief with adequate trials of clomipram ine and fluoxet ine. He has fewe r but persiste nt contamination obsessions and conducts fewe r hand-washing rituals. He asks what else can be done to relieve his symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is an anxiety disorder typically characterized by obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts that produce anxiety) that the patient attempts to neutralize with compulsions (repetitive behaviors). By definition, the compulsions are excessive or do not realistically address the obsessive fears, and patients commonly recognize the irrationality of their compulsions. Treatment includes high doses of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRls) or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), also referred to as behavior therapy, with a focus on exposure to the discomfort of suppressing the compulsion after experiencing the obsession. Suppressing the compulsion teaches the patient that they can cope with the anxiety related to their obsessions and leads to natural habituation (decrease) of their anxiety. In patients who opt to try medication first and experience a partial response, physicians may augment with an antipsychotic medication (eg, risperidone) or CBT.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Seclusion and restraint (Choice A) is utilized on patients with acute physical agitation that presents an imminent danger to self or others. This patient is not an imminent danger to himself or others. SPECT scan of the brain (Choice B) may assist in diagnosing dementia, Alzheimer type, and other neurodegenerative diseases but is not typical ly utilized to confirm OCD diagnoses. This patient appears to meet OCD criteria and does not require additiona l diagnostic testing. questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty falling asleep for 3 years. She reports that it has been even more difficult to fall asleep during the past month. Five weeks ago, her cat of 4 years was hit by a car and died. She has a generally poor appetite but has not had any recent changes in weight or appetite. She has worked as a registered nurse on the overnight shift at a skilled nursing care facility for 5 years. She says that she has never missed a day of work in 3 years, althoug h she rarely feels like getting out of bed. She states that she prefers night work because it involves less contact with families. She does not enjoy her job even though she is respected for her work and regularly receives good evaluations. She is neatly dressed. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 120/65 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormal ities. On mental status examination, she is pleasant and polite. She says she felt sad when her cat died but states that she cannot recall a time when her life did not seem sad to her. When asked about her social life, she says she has never been in a romantic relationship and states that "no one would really want me." Results of laboratory studies are within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassura nce that this is normal bereaveme nt
choices.F: Supplementat ion with a multivitamin and iron

correctExplanation: Persistent depressive disorder, previously called dysthymia, refers to at least three depression symptoms that have endured for at least 2 years. By definition, patients must endorse a depressed mood on more days than not. Other symptoms of persistent depressive disorder include neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbances, appetite disturbances), impaired concentration, low self-esteem, and hopelessness. This patient also demonstrates anhedonia as evidenced by a lack of enjoyment of her job or socializing; however, she does not have at least five symptoms of major depressive disorder, making persistent depressive disorder the most accurate diagnosis. Emerging evidence indicates that persistent depressive disorder should be managed similarly to major depressive disorder: antidepressant medication plus psychotherapy is most effective. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are generally the first-line medications given their low side-effect burden. However, bupropion is also a reasonable option, and its activating effects may be useful in this patient with difficulty getting out of bed.

questionStem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for a physical examination prior to participating in school sports. Her parents are concerned about her academ ic performance because she has received mostly B's and C's. Her parents and older brother attended Ivy League colleges. Every time they try to discuss applying to colleges, she becomes angry and tearful and goes to her room, slamming the door and refusing to talk about it. They try to talk to her through the closed door, but she will not cooperate. They have arranged alumn i interviews for her at their own alma maters, and they are concerned that this negative attitude will impact her interviews. When they contacted her guidance counselor about their concerns and observations, he was surprised and reported that she has been diligently working on her applications with his help. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 30th percent ile for weight. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examinat ion, she is cooperative but reticent. Her speech is articulate and coherent. Wh ich of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Parental expectations exert a strong influence on children's wel l-being. Unrealistically high expectations common ly lead to the child feeling disappointed and inadequate. These feelings may be internalized (eg, lead to depression) or externalized (eg, acting out, such as slamming the door). This patient's emotional dysregulation and uncooperative behavior when her parents communicate or imply high expectations about her academic performance is an age-appropriate reaction. Parents should critical ly examine whether their expectations are realistic and communicate acceptance to their child to avoid these emotiona l difficulties.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adjustment disorder with anxious mood (Choice A) or depressed mood (Choice B) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress manifested as anxiety or depression symptoms, respectively, within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. This patient does not demonstrate anxiety or depression symptoms. As well, her uncooperative behaviors are specific to situations when her parents communicate their high expectations, whereas patients with adjustment disorder demonstrate consistent depression, anxiety, or conduct disturbances. Dysthymic disorder (Choice C), more common ly known as persistent depressive disorder, refers to depression symptoms lasting longer than 2 years. This patient does not endorse depressive symptoms and has not illustrated behavior changes for more than 2 years.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man who is a resident of a skilled nursing care facility is brought to the emergency department because of sweating and increas ing confusion for 2 days. He underwent a below-the-k nee amputat ion 4 weeks ago for osteomyelitis. He has a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glybur ide. He also is receiving acetaminophen and codeine for pain, allopurino l for gout, and haloperido l for nighttime agitation. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1 °F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Muscle tone is increased. The patient is too disoriented to respond appropriate ly to questions. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit Leukocyte count Serum Na+ Glucose 50% 8000/mm 3 with a normal differentia l 154 mEq/L 175 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient who has received high-potency antipsychotic medication (haloperidol). NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction (eg, tachycardia, sweating). Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especia lly high-potency antipsychotics) and antidopaminergic nausea medications. Rigidity results from dopamine antagonism in the nigrostriatal pathway, while autonomic dysfunction and hyperthermia may result from dopamine antagonism in the hypothalamus. Characteristic laboratory abnorma lities include leukocytosis and increased serum creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and alkaline phosphatase concentrations (caused by prolonged muscle rigidity and consequent myocyte damage). Electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypo- or hypernatremia, hypocalcemia) may also be demonstrated. Treatment is supportive and includes discontinuation of the offending medication, hydration, cooling blankets, and benzodiazepines, if needed, for agitation.
