questionStem: A 47-year-o ld woman comes to the physician to request a sedative to help calm her nerves. She has had extreme anxiety and difficulty eating and sleeping since she received the diagnosis of breast cancer 10 days ago. She is married and has two children, and she worries constantly about what will happen to them if she dies. She regularly volunteers at the school library, but she has been unable to go because of her anxiety since her diagnosis. She has not felt depressed, guilty, or suicidal. She has no other history of serious medical or psychiatric illness. There is no family history of psychiatric illness. Physical examination shows a healing incision over the breast biopsy site. On mental status examination, she is anxious but shows a full range of affect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Adjustment disorder refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. The emotional disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stresso r and a significant impairment in daily school, work, or social functioning. Patients may internalize or externalize their distress, resulting in depression and anxiety symptoms or conduct disturbances, respectively. Patients with adjustment disorder do not meet criteria of anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. This patient has some anxiety and depression symptoms (anxiety, insomnia, decreased appetite) with a clear stresso r and without meeting the criteria for anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. As adjustment disorder is typically self-limited, the treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acute stress disorder (Choice A) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts or memories, changes in arousal and reactivity (eg, hypervigilance ), avoidance of reminders of trauma, and negative mood/thoughts that occur within 1 month of a traumatic event such as physical or sexual violence. This patient has not experienced a violent event and is not reporting intrusive thoughts, avoidance of reminders of her stressor (she is instead constant ly worrying about the stressor), or a depressed mood. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice C) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's anxiety is specific to her new diagnosis. • I I• I • • I I I• I• I • • I I I I • •II • • I

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician by her family 1 week after the sudden onset of bizarre behavior that began after she had a disagreement with her supervisor at work. The supervisor told her fam ily that she became confused and began to accuse him of monitoring her phone calls and watching her every move because he wanted to fire her. Her work performance had been fine. She told her husband that she heard the voices of her coworkers talking about her when she was driving home from work 2 days ago. She used cocaine briefly 5 years ago. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she is oriented to person and place but not to date. She is unsure why she is being evaluated, and her answers to questions are incomprehensib le at times. She admits to being worried and depressed about her coworkers being "after her." Laboratory studies are within normal limits, and toxicology screening shows traces of marijuana. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct

correctExplanation: This patient meets the diagnostic criteria for brief psychotic disorder. Brief psychotic disorder is characterized by the acute onset of one or more psychotic symptoms (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. This patient is experiencing a paranoid delusion, disorganized speech, and auditory hallucinations. Risk factors for brief psychotic disorder include stressful life events and personality disorders. Treatment may include hospitalization and antipsychotic treatment depending on symptom severity and functional impairment, though some symptoms or the entire presentation may resolve without medications.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adjustment disorder (Choice A) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress within 3 months of an identifiable stressor and may be associated with anxiety, depression, or conduct disturbances. Psychotic symptoms would be atypical. Cocaine-induced psychotic disorder (Choice C) refers to psychotic symptoms secondary to cocaine use. The onset of this patient's psychotic symptoms years after cocaine use is inconsistent with cocaine-induced psychotic disorder. Post-traumatic stress disorder (Choice D) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts and memories of trauma, hyperarousal, avoidance of trauma reminders, or negative mood/thoughts resulting from a traumati c event (such as a life-threatening motor vehicle collision) and lasting more than one month. questionStem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of behavior problems since starting preschool 3 months ago. Her parents report that she was adopted at 2 weeks of age and little is known about her biologic parents. Her teachers report that she is more active than her peers, is easily frustrated, and has frequent tantrums. She is not yet toilet trained. She is at the 20th percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows a thin upper lip, a narrow philtrum, and bilateral palmar creases. Her gait is normal. On mental status examination, she speaks clearly, communicating in two- to three-word phrases. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Alcohol is a proven teratogen, since alcohol use during pregnancy leads to irreversible fetal neurologic effects and physical malformations in a cluster of symptoms called fetal alcohol syndrome. Fetal alcohol syndrome is a leading cause of intellectual disability in the United States and would explain this patient's behaviora l problems. Because of the failure of cell migration, fetal alcohol syndrome also presents with physica l abnormalities such as microcephaly, facial abnormalities (small palpebral fissures, thin vermi lion border, cleft lip and palate, smooth or long philtrum), limb deformities, and congenital heart disease. Patients with fetal alcoho l syndrome may demonstrate abnormal bone development (eg, cervical spine fusion) and delayed bone growth. Though alcohol is associated with obstetric complications such as preterm birth that commonly result from the use of substances during pregnancy, the physical malformations including those seen in this case are specific to alcohol use.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (Choice A) is defined as a pattern of inattention or hyperactivity that persists in at least two settings. Patients may demonstrate symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following instructions, difficulty completing tasks, or a poor attention span in school. Interrupting others, fidgeting, and not waiting one's turn may be symptoms of hyperactivity. This patient's behavioral problems are only seen at school and her unique physical characteristics are not seen in ADHD. Characteristic physical findings of Down syndrome (Choice B) include intellectua l disability, broad, flat, facial features with prominent epicanthal folds, and a single palmar crease. There are similarities between the abnormal facies of patients with fetal alcohol syndrome and Down syndrome, but this patient's combination of growth retardation and characteristic physica l features are most suggestive of fetal alcohol syndrome.

questionStem: A 22-yea r-old college student comes to the physician because of depressed mood, restlessness, irritability, and an inability to concentrate since being raped 1 week ago. She has had difficulty sleeping because of recurrent nightmares about the rape and has not been able to study or attend classes . At times, she feels like the world around her is not real. Physical examination shows no abnormal ities. On mental status examination, she is anxious and tense. She is unable to remembe r the details of the rape and becomes distressed and does not want to talk about it. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Acute stress disorder refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts or memories, changes in arousal and reactivity, avoidance of reminders of trauma, and negative changes in mood or thoughts that occur within 1 month of a traumatic event. The inciting traumatic event is defined as a serious physically or sexually violent experience. Intrusive memories may manifest as daytime flashbacks, nightmares, or dissociative experiences (eg, derealization as in this patient). Changes in arousal and reactivity may manifest as hypervigilance, easy startle, anxiety, restlessness, or decreased concentration. This patient's selective amnesia represents a negative alteration in cognition. Treatment common ly includes trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy rather than medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Brief psychotic disorder (Choice B) is characterized by at least one acute psychotic symptom (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. This patient's belief that the world around her is not real is stress-related rather than rigid, signifying that the belief represents derealization rather than a delusion. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice C) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's anxiety is specific to the rape. Major depressive disorder (Choice D) includes 2 or more weeks of five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor retardation, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). This patient does not meet the symptom or duration criteria for major depressive disorder. Post-traumatic stress disorder (Choice E) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts and memories of trauma, hyperarousal, avoidance

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man with cancer of the tongue comes to the physician 2 days after an episode of anxiety and panic while being fitted with a mask in preparation for radiation therapy. He reports similar symptoms during MRI of the brain; he says he was unable to tolerate being confined to such a small space and felt panic and the need to escape. On physical exam ination, the tongue is enlarged and tender. On mental status examination, he is anxious when descr ibing being confined. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient targets which of the following neurotransm itters?
correctExplanation: Specific phobia is a psychiatric disorder featuring anxiety about a certain situation or object that leads to avoidance behavior. Common phobias include flying, anima ls, and enclosed spaces. To meet diagnostic criteria, the anxiety symptoms must be persistent (lasting longer than 6 months), and patients must demonstrate significant distress or socia l and occupational impairment. Long-term cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the most effective treatment, though short-term benzodiazepines may be utilized in certain patients whose feared situations occur infrequently (or patients without access to CBT). Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of the ionotropic y-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAA) receptor, permitting the increased influx of chloride ions and decreased neuronal excitability in brain regions responsib le for fear such as the amygdala.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Medications that increase acety lcholine (Choice A) signaling (eg, cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezi l) are utilized in dementia and myasthenia gravis. Acety lcholine antagonists (eg, benztropine) lead to relief of drug-induced parkinsonism along with sedation, urinary retention, and constipation. These medications are not utilized to treat acute anxiety. Dopamine (Choice C) agonists (eg, pramipexo le) are utilized for symptomatic treatment in Parkinson disease, while dopamine antagonists (eg, antipsychotic medications) are utilized to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. These medications are less effective than benzodiazepines in treating acute anxiety. Norepinephrine antagonists (Choice D) (eg, ~-adrenergic block,ers such as proprano lol) are common ly utilized for performance anxiety but not specific phobia. Norepinephrine agonists (eg, stimulant medications, clonidine) are commonly used to treat attention­ deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Clonidine is also utilized off-labe l to treat anxiety, though benzodiazepines are the most effective option fo

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of decreased libido over the past 2 years. He describes his marriage as good. He is able to achieve erection only through masturbation. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. He uses marijuana daily. His pulse is 72/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 120/90 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 1 µU/ml, thyroxine (T 4) concentration of 7 µg/dl, and triiodothyronine (T 3) concentration of 125 ng/dl. Urine toxicology screening is positive for marijuana. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cannabis use has been associated with erectile dysfunction. The pathogenesis is believed to involve both peripheral vascular endothelial dysfunction and dysregulated endocannabinoid signaling in the hypotha lamus. Testicular atrophy and decreased libido related to cannabis use have been found in animal studies, though human studies of the relationship of cannabis and libido have demonstrated mixed results. Erectile function may be sufficient to allow for nocturnal erections and erections from direct penile stimulation but insufficient to permit the level of rigidity required for penetration. Management of erectile dysfunction requires addressing the underlying cause. To assist in determining the underlying cause and potentia lly addressing the problem, patients with erectile dysfunction who use cannabis should be advised to discontinue cannabis use.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Individual psychotherapy (Choice B) and marital therapy (Choice C) assist in addressing psychogenic causes of erectile dysfunction, which typically present with intact nocturnal and masturbation-induced erections. Marital therapy is unlikely to be helpful given the good relationship between the patient and his partner. This patient should first attempt discontinuing cannabis; if discontinuing cannabis does not lead to improved sexual function, then individual psychotherapy should be considered to address potentia l performance anxiety or another psycho logical cause. Levothyroxine therapy (Choice D) treats sexual dysfunction secondary to hypothyroidism. This patient demonstrates normal thyroid function tests. Sildenafi l therapy (Choice E) promotes vasodilation in the arteries of the corpora cavernosa. In patients with erectile dysfunction secondary to psycho logical causes or substance use, these underlying problems should be addressed first.

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because she is anxious and concerned that she is contaminating her hands with HIV whenever she touches a door handle. She realizes that this is irrational but nevert heless has to wash her hands repeatedly with household bleach. She estimates that she washes her hands 10 times daily for 10 minutes at a time. Exam ination shows cracked and bleeding hands . Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is an anxiety disorder typica lly characterized by obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts that produce anxiety) that the patient attempts to neutralize with compulsions (repetitive behaviors). By definition, the compulsions are excessive or do not realistica lly address the obsessive fears, and patients commonly recognize the irrationality of their compulsions. This patient's worry about contamination represents an obsession, while her repeated hand washing represents a compulsion. Treatment includes high doses of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRls, eg, fluoxetine) or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with a focus on exposure to the discomfort of suppressing the compulsion after experiencing the obsession. SSRls have the lowest side effect burden of antidepressant medications. Clomipramine (a tricyclic antidepressant) and venlafaxine (a selective serotonin­ norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor antidepressant) are effective second- line agents.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Bupropion (Choice A) is an antidepressant that increases synaptic norepinephrine and dopamine. It common ly causes increased anxiety as a side effect and is not a first-line medication for OCD. Buspirone (Choice B) is a serotonin modu lator utilized to treat generalized anxiety disorder. It has no proven efficacy in OCD. Haloperido l (Choice D) is a typica l antipsychotic medication utilized to treat schizophrenia. It has no proven efficacy in OCD. lmipramine (Choice E) is a tricyclic antidepressant without proven efficacy for OCD and an increased side effect burden compared with . -- - -- -- - -- -·

questionStem: Immediately after undergo ing operative repair of a right knee dislocation, a 42-year-o ld woman has severe pain. She has a history of heroin addiction and has been receiving therapy through a comm unity-based methadone maintenance program . Her methadone maintenance dose has remained constant for 2 years. She has no other history of medical or psychiatric illness. On examinat ion, she rates her pain as a 10 on a 10-point scale, a level that is consistent with that reported by other patients who have undergone this operative procedure. Admin istration of which of the following is most appropriate at this time?

choices.A: A decreased methadone dose and additiona l analges ia on a set schedule
choices.B: A decreased methadone dose and patient-control led analgesia
choices.C: An increased methadone dose and additiona l analgesia on a set schedule
choices.D: The patient's usual methadone maintenance dose and patient-controlled analgesia
choices.E: The patient's usual methadone maintenance dose only

correctExplanation: Methadone is an opioid receptor agonist with a long half-life. While it can be used to treat acute pain, it is often used to treat patients with opioid use disorder. While methadone is common ly dosed once daily when used to treat opioid use disorder, it only provides analgesia for 6 to 8 hours. Therefore, it is not solely efficient for the management of postoperative pain. Current recommendations for acute pain management in patients on methadone maintenance therapy include continuing the baseline methadone dose and supplementing pain control with other non-opioid and opioid agents as needed. Pain control may be more difficult in patients on chronic methadone therapy, as they common ly have cross-to lerance to other opioids. Therefore, continuing this patient's baseline methadone dose and adding a regimen of patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) would be appropriate to allow for sufficient pain relief. As her acute pain declines, the PCA can be weaned.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A decreased methadone dose and additiona l analgesia on a set schedule (Choice A) would not effectively treat this patient's pain. A decreased dose of methadone would likely exacerbate her pain, and a set schedule of pain medication would not be adequate or flexible enough to control her pain. A decreased methadone dose and patient-controlled analgesia (Choice B) may control this patient's pain but would likely cause her to use an increased amount of intravenous opioids as compared with a regimen with her baseline dose of methadone. An increased methadone dose and additional analgesia on a set schedule (Choice C) may control this patient's pain but would complicate weaning of her medication regimen back to her baseline methadone dose. Additional ly, this patient has been on a stable dose of methadone and adjusting her dose may interfere with her substance use disorder treatment.

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of a 3-month history of social withdrawa l and subtle but increasingly odd interpersonal interactions, such as blinking to avoid direct eye contact. He also has a 1-month history of intermittent daydreaming and episodes of talking to himself. His behavior was first noticed by his teacher and the school nurse, who notified his parents. The patient says that when in quiet locations, he hears vague, distorted sounds. He talks to himself to calm himself and to make the sounds disappear. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His maternal uncle has bipolar disorder, and two paternal uncles have schizophrenia. The patient does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is alert and fully oriented; he appears shy and has a flat affect. He says his mood is "okay." Further testing is most likely to show which of the following results in this patient?

choices.E: Hyperphospho rylation of the Tau protein

correctExplanation: According to the DSM-5, patients with schizophreniform disorder must demonstrate two of following: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or disorganized behavior (known as positive symptoms), or negative symptoms (eg, flat affect, apathy, alogia). To meet diagnostic criteria, patients must demonstrate symptoms for greater than 1 month and less than 6 months. Two-thirds of patients with schizophreniform disorder ultimately develop schizophrenia. Cognitive impairment is commonly one of the early signs of schizophrenia. Schizophrenia has been postulated to result from excessive pruning of glutamatergic synapses in the cerebral cortex during development, explaining the negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia. Patients commonly experience deficits across several cognitive domains including attention, working memory, verbal learning and memory, and executive function. However, basic cognitive functions such as orientation commonly remain intact. Antipsychotic medications address positive symptoms but do not significantly improve negative or cognitive symptoms. Cognitive training may assist with cognitive deficits.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abnormal amyloid precursor protein (Choice A) and hyperphosphorylation of the Tau protein (Choice E) are pathologic findings in dementia, Alzheimer type, not schizophrenia. Amyloid plaques are extracellular protein accumulations while tau forms intracytoplasmic and extracellular protein tangles. Adolescent patients are too young to develop dementia, Alzheimer type. Decreased auditory acuity (Choice C) and decreased visual fields (Choice D) are atypical of schizophrenia. Patients with schizophrenia typically experience deficits in higher-order functions mediated by the frontal lobes such as cognition and motivation (eg, cognitive and negative symptoms).

questionStem: Three weeks after voluntarily enter ing a residential treatment facility for alcoholism, a 27-year-o ld woman is being prepared for discharge. She requests medication to control her urge to drink alcohol and decrease her risk for relapse. Prior to admission, she drank 6 to 12 glasses of wine nightly. She tried to quit drinking several times but says her urges to drink returned after 2 to 3 days of abstinence. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. Physical and mental status exam inations show no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Alcohol use disorder refers to an addiction to alcohol that must meet at least two criteria, including an inability to cut back on drinking, drinking more than expected, excessive time spent drinking, alcoho l cravings, persistent drinking despite physical or mental problems related to drinking, and persistent drinking despite negative socia l consequences. Patients with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder may benefit from daily medication. Commonly utilized medications for alcohol use disorder include naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram, and gabapentin. Naltrexone, a long-acting opioid receptor antagonist, blocks the rewarding effects of drinking alcoho l and thinking about alcohol, thereby preventing alcohol cravings.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Buprenorphine (Choice A) is an opioid receptor partial agonist utilized as an opioid replacement therapy in opioid use disorder. It is not useful in alcohol use disorder. Bupropion (Choice B) is an antidepressant medication that increases synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine and is postulated to antagonize nicotine receptors. It is useful in nicotine use disorder but not alcohol use disorder. As a result of its lowering of the seizure threshold, bupropion increases the risk for alcohol withdrawal seizures. Levomethadyl acetate (Choice C) is an opioid receptor agonist similar to methadone. It is utilized as an opioid replacement therapy in refractory opioid use disorder but would not be helpful in alcoho l use disorder. Naloxone (Choice D) is a short-acting opioid receptor antagonist. Its maximum duration of action is approximately 2 hours, which would necessitate multiple doses daily to prevent alcohol cravings. questionStem: As a condition of employment, a newly hired police officer has agreed to avoid the use of all illicit drugs bo th on and off duty and to provide random urine samp les for drug screening. Although he has not used any drugs in the past month, his urine samp le shows a definite positive reaction. Which of the following drugs would most likely account for this finding?
correctExplanation: The psychoactive component of cannabis is f1-9 tetrahydrocannabino l (THC). THC is lipophilic and therefore distributes widely across body tissues (eg, adipose tissue, heart, lungs, and liver). As a resu lt of its wide distribution and slow release from body stores, THC has a long half-life and may lead to positive urine toxico logy screening up to 50 days after the last use. Patients who regularly use cannabis are more likely to demonstrate persistent ly positive urine drug screenings.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cocaine (Choice A), heroin (Choice B), LSD (Choice C), and methamphetamine (Choice E) are not as widely distributed as cannabis and possess shorter half-lives. Urine drug screens are typically negative a few days after the patient's last use. Educationa l Objective: Compared with other recreational drugs, cannabis has a long half-life. In chronic users, urine toxicology screenings may remain positive up to 50 days after the patient 's last use.

questionStem: A 19-yea r-old man is brought to the physician by his parents because of changes in his behavior during the past 6 months. During this time, he has been obsessed with what he calls "the ultima te truth of the universe" and has spent most of his time in his room alone. His parents say that he has always been serious, curious, and quiet. The few friends he had stopped interacting with him because of this behavio r. The patient explains that he needs to solve "the ultimate and consummate algorithmic result." He has no history of serious illness . He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 98 kg (217 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m 2. His pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 116/77 mm Hg. Physical examination shows abdominal striae. On menta l status examination, he describes his mood as "transfixed. " He has a blunt affect. His thoug ht process is disorganized, and he continues to talk about the equation. There is no evidence of suicidal ideatio n. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Urine toxicology screening is negative . A CT scan of the head shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: According to the DSM-5, patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders demonstrate at least two of the following five symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms (eg, flat or blunted affect, apathy, alogia). Delusions, hallucinations, and disorganization are referred to as positive symptoms. To meet the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia, patients must demonstrate functional deficits, and the total duration of symptoms must exceed 6 months. This patient demonstrates delusional thinking (a fixed belief that he needs to solve a problem of the universe), disorganized thinking orspeech, and negative symptoms (isolating to his room, a blunted affect). Many patients with schizophrenia are social ly anxious prior to the onset of psychotic symptoms. Management requires antipsychotic medication (eg, ziprasidone, an atypical antipsychotic). Antipsychotic medications antagonize the dopamine receptor, addressing excessive dopaminergic signaling in the mesolimbic pathway (postu lated to underlie positive psychotic symptoms), though they do not address the negative or cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Buspirone (Choice A) is a serotonin modulator utilized to treat genera lized anxiety disorder. Clonazepam (Choice B) is a benzodiazepine medication utilized to treat acute episodes of anxiety. Neither would address psychotic symptoms.

questionStem: A 42-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examinat ion for insurance purposes. When asked for an emergency contact, he gives the name of his mother but says that she lives in another state and that he has not seen her for 5 years. He lives by himself and says that he has no friends. He spends most of his free time alone in his apartment cutting out articles about animals from magazines and newspapers that he plans to use in the future. He has worked the graveyard shift of his company for 10 years with few absences. On two occasions, he was offered a day shift but refused. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He is wearing mismatched socks, and his glasses are tied to a piece of twine he wears around his neck. Physical examinat ion shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. His thoughts are goal directed but difficult to understand because of his frequent use of idiosyncratic metaphors. He reports no auditory or visual hallucinations. He can recall three of three objects after 5 minutes and describes events of the past several years without difficulty. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Schizotypal personality disorder is a cluster A personality disorder, the odd or eccentric cluster. The disorder is characterized by odd behavior and thinking and a constricted affect. Patients with schizotypa l personality disorder may have strange, overly metaphorical or magical thinking, though they fluctuate in the degree of their conviction about these beliefs (which differentiates these beliefs from the fixed delusions of schizophrenia). The strange beliefs may also manifest as eccentric appearance as in this patient. Patients may experience somatosensory illusions or other abnormal perceptions. Patients with schizotypal personality disorder may appear to lack interest in cultivating relationships (eg, work graveyard shifts) and, because of an inability to interpret others' motivations, may be deeply distrustful and anxious around others. Personality disorders are persistently maladaptive ways of relating to the self and to society that typically appear by early adulthood.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Agoraphobia (Choice A) refers to the fear of leaving one's home. Though this patient lacks an interest in socializing, he leaves his home to work the graveyard shift. . - - -- - - - - -- -- - ~ - ~ -- -- - - -- - - - ·

questionStem: A 47-yea r-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of anxiety and difficulty falling asleep. He attributes his symptoms to the stress related to his 21-year-old daughter's weddi ng plans. He divorced his wife 11 years ago because he felt more sexually attracted to men than women. He has had a monogamous homosexua l relationsh ip for 7 years. He relates that he is happier now than when he was married, but he has been having some doubts recently. He would like to bring his partner to the weddi ng and accompa ny his daughter down the aisle, but the groom's parents are protesti ng his attendance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Adjustment disorder refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. The emotiona l disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stressor and a significant impairment in daily school, work, or social functioning. Patients may internalize or externalize their distress, resulting in depression and anxiety symptoms or conduct disturbances, respectively. Patients with adjustment disorder do not meet criteria of anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. This patient is experiencing distress and anxiety symptoms related to the possibi lity of difficulties with his daughter 's fiance 's parents at his daughter 's wedding because of his sexual orientation. As adjustment disorder is typical ly self-limited, the treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Exhibitionistic disorder (Choice B) is a paraphilia characterized by sexual arousal related to the exposure of the patient's genitalia that causes clinically significant distress or functional impairment. This patient does not demonstrate evidence of exhibitionistic disorder. Though this patient experiences sexual attraction to men, there is no evidence that he possesses a gender identity different from his assigned gender as a man. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice D) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's anxiety is specific to his daughter's wedding. questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman with major depressive disorder is brought to the physician by her daughter for a follow-up examination. During the past 6 months, she has received trials of citalopram, fluvoxam ine, and escitalopram with no improvement in her symptoms. Four weeks ago, she was switched from fluoxetine to sertraline therapy because the fluoxetine caused excessive tiredness . Her daughter reports that the patient is "slightly better, but not dramat ically so." She has had a decreased appetite resulting in a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss during the past 3 months. Today, her eyes are closed throughout most of the visit. She appears cachectic and disheve led. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 43 kg (95 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m2. Physical examinat ion shows poor skin turgor and severe psychomotor retardat ion. On menta l status exam ination, she respo nds to few of the physician's questions and uses only brief responses . There is no evidence of suicida l ideation or psychot ic symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Add buprop ion to her current medicat ion regimen
choices.B: Add olanzapine to her current medication regimen
choices.C: Switch from sertraline to nortripty line
choices.D: Switch from sertraline to paroxet ine

correctExplanation: Symptoms of major depressive disorder (MOD) include two or more weeks of at least five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia (eg, decreased interest in socia lizing), guilt or worth lessness, difficu lty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. This patient's functional impairment is so severe that she is minimal ly interactive and appears disheveled. Her neurovegetative symptoms have led to physical deterioration, including significant weight loss and nutritiona l compromise. The patient requires admission to the psychiatric unit to prevent further physica l deterioration and so she can receive an inpatient course of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). ECT utilizes electrical current to induce a generalized seizure under general anesthesia, which is postulated to increase monoamine activity and promote neurogenesis. Indications include depression that is refractory to multiple medication classes and depression associated with catatonia, nutritional compromise and dehydration, psychotic features, or persistent suicida l intent. Depression may begin to improve immediately after the first ECT session, whereas antidepressant medication takes weeks to work. Further, ECT has an increased effectiveness compared with antidepressant medications. Adverse events common ly include transient memory loss and the risks of general anesthesia (eg, cardiovascu lar events, postoperative confusion).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adding bupropion or olanzapine to an antidepressant regimen (Choices A and B) are augmentation strategies utilized in patients with a significant partial response to the initial antidepressant. This patient minimal ly responded to sertraline. Further, these augmentation strategies typically take weeks to be effective, whereas this patient is nutritiona lly compromised and requires rapid treatment.

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld man is admitted to the hospital because of extreme hyperactiv ity for 2 days. He is unable to conduct an intelligent conversation because of flight of ideas. He is started on haloperidol therapy (10 mg daily). Two days later, he has difficulty breathing, uncontrollable tightening of his face and neck muscles with spasm, and a rolling up and locking of his eyes. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Acute dystonic reactions are involuntary, painful muscle spasms that occur most frequent ly in response to potent dopamine-2 (D2) antagonists such as typical antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol). Common presentations include torticollis (head tilted to the side and down), retrocollis (head tilted back), opisthotonos (arching of the back), and oculogyric crisis (upward deviation of the eyes). Patients rarely present with laryngospasm and strider. The underlying pathophysio logy is an imbalance in the dopaminergic-cholinergic pathways of the basal ganglia. Risk factors for development include male sex, young age, recent cocaine use, and a history of previous acute dystonic reaction. Acute dystonic reactions are treated with diphenhydramine or benztropine, which are both anticholinergic medications that work to restore the proper balance in the dopaminergic and cholinergic pathways.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bethanechol (Choice A) is a muscarinic receptor agonist that promotes bladder and gastrointestinal motility because of its stimulation of smooth muscle. It does not act on skeletal muscle and would therefore be unhelpful in acute dystonic reactions. Chlordiazepoxide (Choice B) is a benzodiazepine medication most commonly utilized for alcohol withdrawal. Clonazepam (Choice C) is a benzodiazepine medication commonly utilized to treat anxiety and rapid-eye movement sleep behavior disorder. Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam may also be utilized to treat antipsychotic-induced akathisia. However, these medications do not restore the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia and are therefore ineffective for an acute dystonic reaction. Propranolol (Choice E) is a ~-adrenergic blocker medication utilized to treat performance anxiety and antipsychotic-induced akathisia. However, propranolol does not restore the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia and is therefore ineffective for an acute dystonic reaction. questionStem: A 27-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by police after he threatened to commit suicide in jail. He was arrested 3 days ago for the murder of his girlfriend. Two years ago, he completed a 5-year prison sentence for assault. He was treated in a psychiatric hospital for conduct disorder at the age of 15 years. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He has a history of drinking excessive amounts of alcohol and using illicit drugs. He is cooperative with the hospita l staff but becomes irritable when the police officer who is guarding him attempts to interact with him. His tempera ture is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 132/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for multiple scars over the face. On questioning, he says that he got the scars in fights. On mental status examination, there is no evidence of depression or psychosis. His speech is clear and slow, and he says, "If you don't release me and I am sent back to jail, I will find a way to kill myself!" Metabolites of which of the following neurotransm itters are most likely to be decreased in this patient's cerebrospinal fluid?
correctExplanation: Antisocial persona lity disorder is a cluster B persona lity disorder, the emotiona l or dramatic cluster, that arises from a deficit in empathy, resulting in pervasive violations of others' rights, aggression, and a hostile and manipulative attitude toward others. Similar to other cluster B personality disorders, patients with antisocial personality disorder struggle to regulate their emotions in that their frustration tolerance is low and they frequently behave impulsively. Deficient serotonin signaling secondary to genetic polymorphisms in the serotonin transporter has been found in patients with antisocial personality disorder and borderline persona lity disorder, another cluster B personality disorder characterized by impulsive self-harm behaviors. It is postulated that deficient serotonin leads to a propensity toward a dysphoric affect, which usually leads to self-harm behavior in women (reflecting borderline personality disorder) and violent behavior toward others in men (reflecting antisocia l personality disorder). These patients may also be chronically bored and hence sensation seeking, leading to a high rate of substance abuse and gambling. These persona lity traits lead to deficits in personal (extreme egocentrism) and interpersonal (empathy, intimacy) functioning. Personality disorders are persistently maladaptive ways of relating to the self and to society that typica lly appear by early adulthood.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acetylcholine (Choice A) is a neurotransmitter that mediates attention, learning, and memory. questionStem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after s he became agitated and disruptive on an airplane. She was screaming and using profanity, and the plane was forced to land. On arrival, she is agitated and hypervig ilant, and her speech is rapid and pressured. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows warm dry skin. The pupils are 8 mm bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Acetylcholine activity in the brain mediates attention and motivation, and periphera l acetylcho line mediates smooth muscle contraction. Diphenhydramine, an antihistamine medication with strong anticho linergic activity, is commonly utilized off-label for acute episodes of anxiety (eg, secondary to flying). Anticholinergic agents commonly cause delirium (as evidenced by this patient's agitated behavior) along with smooth muscle dysfunction (decreased function of sweat glands and pupillary muscles leading to this patient's flushed skin and mydriasis, respectively). Anticho linergic toxicity typically manifests as delirium, sedation, hallucinations, ataxia, mydriasis, visual disturbances (cycloplegia, or loss of accommodation), dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, constipation, and flushed skin. Management includes discontinuation of the offending agent, supportive care with gentle sedation, fluids, and prevention of hyperthermia, seizure, or arrhythmias. In severe cases, treatment with pyridostigmine, a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, may be initiated.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acetaminophen overdose (Choice A) most common ly presents with nausea, vomiting, lethargy, and acute liver failure (manifesting with right upper quadrant tenderness, jaundice, encepha lopathy, bleeding complications, and increased hepatic transaminases). Tachycardia, mydriasis, and warm dry skin are more consistent with anticholinergic-induced delirium. Benzodiazepine overdose (Choice C) typical ly presents with central nervous system (CNS) depression, slurred speech, ataxia, emotional !ability, and memory lapses. Agitation, tachycardia, and warm, dry skin would be atypical. . - . -. - - . -. - . . -. . --. - -. .

choices.D: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

correctExplanation: This patient meets the diagnostic criteria for brief psychotic disorder. Brief psychotic disorder is characterized by the acute onset of one or more psychotic symptoms (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. This patient is experiencing a religious delusion, disorganized behavior (eg, agitation, sitting alone in a corner rocking back and forth, stabbing herself), and visual and auditory hallucinations. Risk factors for brief psychotic disorder include stressful life events and personality disorders. Treatment may include hospitalization and antipsychotic treatment depending on symptom severity and functional impairment, though some symptoms or the entire presentation may resolve without medications.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Adjustment disorder (Choice A) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress within 3 months of an identifiable stressor and may be associated with anxiety, depression, or conduct disturbances. Psychotic symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations are atypical. Bereavement (Choice B), or uncomplicated grief reaction, refers to a person's emotiona l response after a loved one dies and can include sadness, shock, anguish, guilt, difficulty concentrating, decreased interest in usual activities, preoccupation with thoughts and memories of the deceased, and neurovegetative symptoms such as sleep, appetite, and energy disturbances. Hallucinations of the deceased may also occur. Complex religious delusions, disorganization of behavior, and hallucinations other than hallucinations of the deceased are atypical. • I I• I • • I I I• I I• I • • I I• I •

questionStem: An 82-year-old man is brought to the physician by his daughter because of progressive problems with his memory during the past 3 years. She became concerned when his electricity was turned off recently after he failed to pay the bill. The patient says that he is not concerned about his memory and that his daughter worries too much. He has no history of serious medical or psychiatric illness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination, including neurologic examination, shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he has a euthymic mood and reactive affect. He makes numerous paraphasic errors, and his thought process is circumstantial. He recalls one of three words after 5 minutes. He is able to remember his date of birth, the name of his high school, and the year he was married. The patient's drawing of the intersecting triangles in Figure 1 is shown in Figure 2. His Mini-Mental State Exam ination score has decreased from 26/30 1 year ago to 23/30 today. This patient's cognitive disorder is most likely associated with mutations in genes encoding which of the following?

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man with angina pectoris comes for a follow-up examination. His wife reports that he is concerned that his neighbors have been watching and videotaping him over the past 3 months. He has no history of these concerns prior to this time. He has suggested to his wife that they build a 14-foot fence to stop this surveillance, but she is not concerned that they are being videotaped. He believes that the neighbors might have followed him to his appointment today, but he does not believe that they would come into the office and speak to the office personnel. His medications include metoprolol and aspirin. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is guarded and hypervigilant. He is oriented to person, place, and time. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.C: Mood disorder due to a general medical condition

correctExplanation: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more delusions (fixed, false beliefs) for a month or longer without other psychotic symptoms (eg, hallucinations). Patients typically lack significant negative symptoms (eg, alogia, apathy) or functional impairment. The onset of psychotic symptoms in patients older than 45 years is often consistent with delusional disorder (or a medical cause of psychosis) rather than schizophrenia. The disorder may present suddenly or gradually. Patients typically lack insight into their illness and may resist seeking psychiatric help, though antipsychotic medication and psychotherapy are the preferred treatments.

Brief psychotic disorder (Choice A) is characterized by at least one acute psychotic symptom (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. Mood disorder due to a general medical condition (Choice C) refers to depression or mania secondary to a medical disease. This patient does not demonstrate symptoms of depression or mania, instead presenting with an isolated delusion. Schizotypal personality disorder (Choice D) is a cluster A personality disorder, the odd or eccentric cluster. The disorder is characterized by odd or magical behavior and thinking, along with a constricted affect. Rigid delusions are more consistent with delusional disorder. As well, patients with personality disorders demonstrate a persistent pattern of interpersonal difficulties that typically begins early in life. questionStem: A 19-year-old college sophomore comes to the physician because of episodes of shortness of breath, palpitations, and sweating that have awakened him from sleep several times over the past 2 months. He says that the episodes are so alarming that he thinks he is going to die and is afraid that he has a serious illness. He reports episodes of sadness since he broke up with his girlfriend 3 weeks ago. He does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. He requests a bronchodilator inhaler. His pulse is 80/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Panic attacks feature acute fear or anxiety that peaks within minutes and is associated with four additional physical symptoms or associated mental states. These additional symptoms may include heart palpitations or tachycardia, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, the sensation of choking, gastrointestinal distress, paresthesias, sweating, chills, trembling, derealization, the fear of dying, or the fear of losing control. These episodes may occur during calm or anxious states, in the daytime or nighttime. The pathogenesis involves genetic factors, an anxious temperament, and stressful life events. In patients with an initial episode of panic symptoms, a thorough history and physical examination along with a basic laboratory workup and a potential ECG should be performed. Panic disorder is a relatively common psychiatric disorder characterized by recurrent panic attacks that are unexpected and associated with worry about future panic attacks or avoidance of panic attack triggers. Treatment of panic disorder typically includes antidepressant medication and/or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with a focus on graded exposure to the feared situation.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Adjustment disorder (Choice A) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress within three months of an identifiable stresso r and may be associated with anxiety, depression, and/or conduct disturbances. Separation anxiety disorder (Choice F) refers to excessive fear of separation from an attachment figure. This patient's panic attacks started before his relationship breakup. A number of preventive measures have been recommended for prevention of otitus externa, including use of earplugs while swimming, use of hair dryers on the lowest settings and head tilting to remove water from the ear canal, and avoidance of self-cleaning or scratching the ear canal. Acetic acid 2% (Vosol) otic solutions are also used, either two drops twice daily or two to five drops after water exposure. However, no randomized trials have examined the effectiveness of any of these measures.

This patient has CHF, as indicated by his dyspnea, orthopnea, cephalization on CXR, and Kerley B lines. Although diuretics will lead to some symptomatic relief, the question asks which drug will improve the patient's survival. ACE inhibitors are the only drug that will reduce mortality and prolong survival in moderate to severe CHF.
SCC in the vaginal and perineal region is most commonly caused by HPV infection.

Acute rheumatic fever can cause mitral valve regurgitation early and mitral stenosis later in life. The patient has an S4 due to left ventricular hypertrophy best heard at apex with patient in left lateral decubitus position and high atrial pressure.
This patient has exercise-induced and allergen-induced asthma. His asthma is not well-controlled on an albuterol inhaler alone, thus a daily inhaled corticosteroid should be added to his regimen.
This is tinea versicolor, which is best treated with topical selenium sulfide.

Nicotine patches are not contraindicated in patients with angina pectoris, nor should the dosage be lowered below recommended levels. Nicotine gum has not been shown to be superior to nicotine patches, and in fact patients are more likely to become addicted to the gum than the patch. Physicians counseling patients to cut back on cigarette use is associated with greater cessation failure rates compared to urging them to quit altogether. Transdermal nicotine in combination with a behavior modification program is a very effective method for achieving tobacco cessation.

Cluster headache is characterized by attacks of severe orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain, accompanied by autonomic phenomena and/or restless or agitation. The unilateral autonomic symptoms associated with cluster headache, such as ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, and nasal congestion, occur only during the pain attack and are ipsilateral to the pain. The stereotypical attacks may strike up to eight times a day and are relatively short- lived. Another clinical landmark of the cluster headache syndrome is the circadian rhythmicity of the attacks. Cluster headache is strictly unilateral, and the symptoms remain on the same side of the head during a single cluster attack. However, the symptoms can switch to the other side during a different cluster attack (so-called side shift) in approximately 15 percent of cases. In contrast to migraines, patients with cluster headaches are restless and prefer to pace about or sit and rock back and forth. The attacks of cluster headache can be so vicious that patients may commit suicide if the disease is not diagnosed or treated.

This is not a good question. This patient is having an acute gout attack. Corticosteroids (e.g. prednisone, prednisolone) and NSAIDs (e.g. indomethacin or naproxen) are both reasonable first line agents for treatment of acute gout. Colchicine is a reasonable second line agent in patients with relative or absolute contraindications to both NSAIDs and corticosteroids, and in those in whom colchicine has effectively treated a gout flare previously. Historically, urate-lowering medications were thought to worsen acute gout flares, but recent evidence suggests that allopurinol (Zyloprim) can be started during an acute flare if it is used in conjunction with an NSAID and colchicine. Patients receiving a urate-lowering medication should be treated concurrently with an NSAID, colchicine, or low- dose corticosteroid to prevent a flare.

The question asks which one will have prevented mildly elevated AST/ALT. Of the answer choices only alcohol causes mildly elevated AST more than ALT. There is no carrier or chronic state of hepatitis A, so this asymptomatic patient likely does not have hepatitis. There is no reason to suspect that this patient has hemochromatosis, diphtheria, or tetanus. Smoking does not directly affect liver function or produce a rise in liver enzymes, and ALT is typically elevated more than AST in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, which must be what answer choice D is getting at.

This patient is showing signs of normal aging and does not require further evaluation. Certain memory performances on cognitive testing, like procedural, primary, and semantic memory, are well-preserved with age. Skills, ability, and knowledge that are overlearned, well-practiced, and familiar, like vocabulary or general knowledge, remain stable or improve up to 0.2 standard deviations per decade through the seventh decades, but even these processes can begin to decrease with further aging. The ability to recognize familiar objects and faces, as well as to maintain appropriate visual perception of objects, remains stable over the lifetime. Episodic and working memory and executive function are the specific domains of cognition most affected by "normal" aging. These are late-life changes, occurring after the sixth decade and have a linear or accelerating decline with further aging. Processing speed decreases with age and can have a global effect on the testing performance of other neurocognitive domains in any timed test. Executive function is critical to engagement in purposeful, independent, and self-preserving behavior and is necessary for an older person to successfully manage their own medical illnesses. Executive function declines with age, and more dramatically after age 70. Attention span decreases with even simple attentive tasks. In particular, there is decrease in the ability to focus on a task in a busy environment and ability to perform multiple tasks at one time. Problem- solving, reasoning about unfamiliar things, processing and learning new information, and attending to and manipulating one's environment show a steady decline (by about -0.02 standard deviations per year) after peaking around age 30. Language abilities (verbal fluency and the ability to name objects) demonstrate some late-life decline, particularly after age 70.

Both GERD and peptic ulcer disease (PUD) are in the differential diagnosis for this patient’s symptoms. The diagnosis of GERD is based on clinical symptoms alone with esophageal testing reserved for refractory cases. H. pylori infection is common and should be ruled out in a patient with symptoms suspicious for PUD. The test is also non-invasive, and the consequences of untreated PUD can be grave.
ACE inhibitors are always beneficial in MI with EF < 40%.

In patients near a threshold for treatment based on total CV risk and in patients above a threshold for treatment, repeating measurements every three years is recommended. According to many community practice standards of care such follow-up studies are performed yearly.

Fecal impaction is the likely diagnosis, especially as constipation is a common side effect of the oxybutynin the patient is taking for urinary incontinence. Oxybutynin blocks not only the muscarinic M3 receptor subtypes, but also the M1 receptor subtypes. This action accounts for the common adverse effects associated with oxybutynin: new-onset constipation, dry mouth, flushing, and heat intolerance.

Both overflow incontinence and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) are in the differential diagnosis for this patient’s symptoms. Overflow incontinence typically presents with continuous urinary leakage or dribbling in the setting of incomplete bladder emptying. Associated symptoms can include weak or intermittent urinary stream, hesitancy, frequency, and nocturia. When the bladder is very full, stress leakage can occur or low-amplitude bladder contractions can be triggered resulting in symptoms similar to stress or urgency incontinence. BPH is a histologic diagnosis that becomes more prevalent with age, although some men with BPH are asymptomatic. Approximately 50 percent of men at age 50 and up to 80 percent of men at age 80 have lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) attributable to BPH. Common manifestations include storage symptoms (increased daytime frequency, nocturia, urgency, and urinary incontinence) and voiding symptoms (slow urinary stream, splitting or spraying of the urinary stream, intermittent urinary stream, hesitancy, straining to void, and terminal dribbling). Post-void residual urine volume determination is useful in men with evidence of urinary obstruction or suspected neurologic involvement of the genitourinary tract and prior to initiation of an anticholinergic drug (which may decrease bladder contractility). Normal men have less than 12 mL of residual urine, but most urologists are not concerned unless the post-void residual volume is greater than 100 to 200 mL. In addition to being a possible indicator of BPH, a large residual volume is probably associated with increased risk of infection and is a precursor to bladder decompensation.

This patient most likely has a scaphoid fracture. Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal bone fracture and typically occur from a fall onto an outstretched arm with the wrist in dorsiflexion. Suspect a scaphoid fracture in any patient with wrist pain following a fall. When a definitive diagnosis cannot be determined at presentation and a scaphoid fracture is suspected on clinical grounds, even if radiographs are negative, the patient should be placed in a volar wrist splint or preferably a thumb spica splint or cast until a definitive imaging study can be performed.

This patient has diminished renal function as indicated by her elevated creatinine, which according to the Cockroft-Gault equation is approximately a GFR of 38. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) revised its labeling of metformin, which previously had identified metformin as contraindicated in women and men with serum creatinine levels ≥1.4 mg/dL (124 micromol/L) and ≥1.5 mg/dL (133 micromol/L), respectively. The use of metformin is contraindicated in patients with an eGFR <30 mL/min, and the initiation of metformin is not recommended in patients with an eGFR between 30 and 45 mL/min. For patients taking metformin whose eGFR falls below 45 mL/min, the benefits and risk of continuing treatment should be assessed, whereas metformin should be discontinued if the eGFR falls below 30 mL/min. Thus while metformin is not absolutely contraindicated in this patient, this is the best of the answer choices presented. It is possible also that this question was written based on previous guidelines that contraindicated metformin at lesser degrees of renal impairment.

A physician cannot revoked a person’s driver's license (only the department of motor vehicles can do that). But the family can ensure that the patient does not have access to car keys until a formal evaluation can be completed.

This patient likely has a viral pharyngitis without meeting the criteria for strep pharyngitis. He does not have a fever, tonsillar exudates, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and he has a cough. Viral pharyngitis requires only supportive treatment, including use of warm saline gargles. A patient with a very high Centor score would be treated for strep pharyngitis without need for a confirmatory test, a patient with an equivocal score should be given a rapid strep test, and any patient testing negative should be given a throat culture in order to prevent rheumatic heart disease in case of a false negative. Infectious mononucleosis should be suspected in patients 10 to 30 years of age who present with sore throat and significant fatigue, palatal petechiae, posterior cervical or auricular adenopathy, marked adenopathy, or inguinal adenopathy. An atypical lymphocytosis of at least 20 percent or atypical lymphocytosis of at least 10 percent plus lymphocytosis of at least 50 percent strongly supports the diagnosis, as does a positive heterophile antibody test. This patient’s clinical picture is not suspicious enough for mono to warrant a monospot test.

This patient has a macrocytic anemia, which is commonly caused by either a folate or vitamin B12 deficiency. It take years to develop vitamin B12 deficiency versus a few months to develop folate deficiency.

Individuals with suspected iron deficiency should have laboratory testing that is stratified for their age and possible related conditions. For infants without risk factors for (or evidence of) lead toxicity, a complete blood count may be sufficient. For children and young adults, it is appropriate to obtain a reticulocyte count, review the RBC indices and/or the blood smear, and test the stool for occult blood. For individuals with other medical conditions, it is appropriate to measure iron studies (serum ferritin, total iron binding capacity [TIBC]), and serum iron. This 55 year old woman should have her ferritin checked to determine whether she has iron deficiency anemia likely due to poor diet or occult blood loss.

The most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in the elderly is GI blood loss. The physician started with the best initial/least invasive therapy, a trial of iron supplementation. Her lack of response indicates that there is ongoing blood loss. Thus the best next step is a colonoscopy. Other causes for lack of improvement with iron supplementation (in addition to ongoing blood loss) could be nonadherence to iron or celiac disease.
It is not certain whether she is telling the truth. Thus the physician should speak to both at the same time in order to assess the validity of his concerns.

This patient has elevated free T4, symptoms of hyperthyroidism, and neck tenderness with decreased uptake on RAIU scan, which indicates subacute thyroiditis. In subacute thyroiditis the thyroid gland is typically slightly or moderately diffusely or asymmetrically enlarged, and nearly always tender. In some cases, the pain is so severe that the patient cannot tolerate palpation of the neck. Both thyroid lobes are involved from the beginning in most patients, but the pain, tenderness, and enlargement can be unilateral or start on one side and later spread to the other side days or even weeks (so called “creeping thyroiditis”) later. Temperature elevations also can occur. Subacute thyroiditis is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis. In most patients, clinical manifestations (the presence of neck pain, often radiating upward to the jaw, marked thyroid tenderness, and a diffuse goiter) are sufficient to establish the diagnosis. Symptoms and signs of hyperthyroidism may or may not be present, but the serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is usually suppressed (typically <0.1 mU/L) and free thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) concentrations elevated, particularly in the early stages of the illness. Serum TSH, free T4, and T3 should be measured in all patients in whom there is a clinical suspicion of subacute thyroiditis. We also typically measure an erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein (CRP) level and obtain a radioiodine or technetium imaging study. A high erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or CRP measurement and a low radioiodine uptake (usually less than 1 to 3 percent) during the hyperthyroid phase help confirm the diagnosis.

This is a bad question, as the CDC recommends PPSV23 for everyone 2 years of age and older at increased risk of disease, which explicitly includes those who smoke cigarettes or have asthma. Thus the correct answer is C, he should receive the flu vaccine and the PPSV23 vaccine, but because he has completed all of his childhood vaccinations, which include Hib, he does not need another Hib vaccine.
This patient with lower back injury and symptoms of radiculopathy likely has either a muscle strain or a disc herniation, and should be initially managed with NSAIDs.
This is a clinically depressed patient who should be screened for suicide.
For an overweight person, the greatest decrease in SBP occurs with at least 10% weight loss.

Food stuck in a patient’s throat with a 20 year history of GERD that has not improved with PPIs should prompt an EGD to rule out complications of long term GERD, for example Barrett's esophagus, adenocarcinoma, or esophageal stricture.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of diffuse abdominal cramps and worsening constipation. Her last bowel movement was 4 days ago, and the stool was hard. She has a long-standing history of constipation. She typically has one bowel movement every other day, but this pattern varies from two bowel movements daily to one bowel movement weekly. She has stopped using a laxative because of diarrhea resulting in fecal incontinence. Colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnorma lities. She has major depressive disorder with anxiety treated with sertraline and lorazepam . She does not appear to be in distress. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 152/84 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender. Bowel sounds are decreased. Rectal exam ination shows no masses or stool; test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

correctExplanation: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is diagnosed using the Rome-IV criteria, which includes the presence of abdominal pain at least once weekly that is associated with (generally relieved by) defecation, along with a change in stool appearance, or stool frequency (at least two of three is required). IBS is further subdivided into IBS with constipation (IBS-C), with diarrhea (IBS-D), or mixed (IBS-M). IBS often presents with intermittent abdominal pain that is relieved by bowel movements and associated alterations in bowel habits with intermittent episodes of diarrhea and/or constipation. Stress management may improve bowel habits in patients with IBS, which is often associated with concomitant anxiety. In this patient, fiber supplementation may help with constipation and improve regularity of bowel movements. Features that are suggestive of underlying organic pathology rather than IBS include the presence of occult blood or melena, nocturnal diarrhea, worsening abdominal pain, weight loss, or a family history of inflammatory bowel disease or colon cancer.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. X-rays of the abdomen (Choice A) can show increased stool burden in patients with constipation but would not change management. X­ rays are poorly sensitive and nonspecific for bowel pathology and would not be appropriate in this patient. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (Choice B) would be appropriate in patients with acute abdominal pain and an abdominal examination concerning for intra-abdominal pathology, such as in patients with fever, vomiting, focal abdominal tenderness, rigidity, --- -- ---- -- - -- -- - - -- - -- - - - -- - - -- --- ·

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 4-year-o ld girl is brought to the physician because of a sore throat and temperatures to 38.8°C (101.8°F) over the past 24 hours. She attends preschool, and several other students have similar symptoms. She appears ill. Examination shows erythema of the tonsils with exudate. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A rapid streptococca l antigen test is negative, but throat cultures grow Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). Which of the following character istics of the rapid streptococcal antigen test best explains these results?
correctExplanation: The rapid streptococcal antigen test results in this case of streptococcal pharyngitis are best explained by a low sensitivity of the test. Sensitivity is the ability of a test to detect a disease if it is present. A test is described as sensitive if it has a high likelihood of disease detection and therefore a low likelihood of a false negative. A test with poor sensitivity, if negative, does not provide strong evidence or confidence that the patient does not have the disease. In contrast, a highly sensitive test allows the clinician and the patient to be confident that a negative test means that the patient is disease free. In the case described, the rapid streptococcal antigen test demonstrates a low sensitivity and is of limited use to the physician for ruling out a streptococcal infection. However, the test is still useful because, if positive, it will prevent a more expensive and involved test from being required.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Likelihood ratios are ratios of either the true positive rate to false positive rate or false negative rate to true negative rate. In this case, the test's low sensitivity, not its low likelihood ratio (Choice A), best explains the results. Low negative predictive value (Choice B) indicates a low probability that a patient with a negative test result truly does not have the disease. In this case, because the patient's true disease status is known rather than just predicted, negative predictive value is not applicable. Since this patient's rapid streptococca l antigen test was negative, a low positive predictive value (Choice C) is not applicable in this case. Positive predictive value is the likelihood that a person has a disease, given a positive test. A positive predictive value is of greater importance in confirmatory testing.
