questionStem: A 34-year-o ld woman , gravida 1, para 1, comes to the emergency department because of a 7-hour history of moderate diffuse lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and temperatures to 38.3°C (101 °F). She says she felt well until this morning. One week ago, she had an uncomplicated spontaneous vagina l delivery of a female newbo rn at term. Her postpartum vaginal bleeding had been decreasing daily until today, when she began passing some blood clots and soaking through a sanitary pad every 2 hours. Her current temperature is 37.9°C (100.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 102/66 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. On examination , the abdomen is soft and diffusely tender to palpation of the lower quadrants; there is no rebound tenderness or guard ing. The uterine fundus is firm, tender, and palpable inferior to the umbilicus. Her hematocrit is 29% and leukocyte count is 15,200/mm 3 (15.2 x 109/L). Pelvic ultrasonography shows echogenic material in the uterine cavity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

correctExplanation: Postpartum hemorrhage is a relatively common complication of childbirth. While some postpartum vaginal bleeding can persist for up to 8 weeks following delivery, late or secondary postpartum hemorrhage occurs more than 24 hours after delivery and is characterized by significant uterine bleeding, such as the passage of clots or bleeding that soaks a menstrual pad in less than 1 hour. A common cause of secondary postpartum hemorrhage is retained products of conception, which can become infected and cause a postpartum endometritis. Endometritis presents with fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, and leukocytosis, as in this patient. Ultrasonography can identify the retained products of conception by disclosing echogenic material in the uterine cavity. Treatment for retained products of conception includes cervical dilation and curettage to remove the products. This patient would also need antibiotics to treat an associated infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Methotrexate therapy (Choice B) is used in the treatment of gestational trophob lastic disease and ectopic pregnancy. Gestational trophoblastic disease can present with secondary postpartum hemorrhage but is also commonly associated with increased ~-human chorionic gonadotropin concentration, bilateral adnexal masses, and multiple diffuse echogenic clusters on ultrasonography. Ectopic pregnancy can also present with vaginal bleeding but would be unlikely in this patient who had a normal delivery 7 days ago. Methylprednisolone therapy (Choice C) is used to treat a variety of allergic, inflammatory, and autoimmune disorders. However, it plays no role in the treatment of secondary postpartum hemorrhage or retained products of conception.

questionStem: A 36-year-o ld man with HIV infection comes to the emergency department because of a 1-hour history of nausea and sharp , intermittent pain in his right midback that radiates to his right flank. He has had two episodes of vomiting during this time . His only medica tion is atazanavir. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. On examination, there is tende rness to percussio n of the right costovertebra l angle. No abdomina l tenderness is noted. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglob in Leukocyte count Platelet count Serum Na+ K+ c I­ Hco -3 Glucose Creatinine Urine RBC WBC Nitrites Leukocy te esterase Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.D: Measurement of serum uric acid concentration

correctExplanation: 14 g/dL (140 g/L) 17,000/mm3( 17 x 109/L) 250,000 /mm3 (250 x 109/L) 140 mEq/L (140 mmol/L) 4.5 mEq/L (4.5 mmol/L) 100 mEq/L (100 mmol/L) 25 mEq/L (25 mmol/L) 100 mg/dL (5.55 mmol/L) 0.9 mg/dL (79.56 µmol/L) 10-20 /hpf 1-2/hpf negative negative CT scan of the abdomen is most likely to confirm the ureterolithiasis in this patient with right flank pain and hematuria. Risk factors for the development of nephrolithiasis include diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome, male sex, and prior gastric bypass. Calcium­ containing stones, including calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate, are the most common varieties, although kidney stones may also ·- ..... -·. ·- - - •• - . ·- . - . - -· - ... . ··- ··- • - • - - ·- ···- ...... ·- - -r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous Next Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 26 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Emergency Medicine Self-Assessment Correct Answer: B. CT scan of the abdomen is most likely to confirm the ureterolithiasis in this patient with right flank pain and hematuria. Risk factors for the development of nephrolithiasis include diabetes mellitus, metabo lic syndrome, male sex, and prior gastric bypass. Calcium­ containing stones, including calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate, are the most common varieties, although kidney stones may also be composed of cystine, struvite, and uric acid. The typical presentation of kidney stones that have become lodged in the ureter (ureterolithiasis) includes severe, intermittent, sharp flank pain with either gross or microscopic hematuria, leukocytosis, and occasionally evidence of a concomitant urinary tract infection. While abdominal, plain x-rays were traditiona lly used for diagnosis, urate stones are radiolucent, and given the availability and sensitivity of advanced imaging, a noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen is now the preferred imaging modality for definitive diagnosis. Acute management depends on the size and location of the stone, in addition to complicating factors such as abnormal anatomy or the concurrent presence of a urinary tract infection. Staghorn calculi, which occur commonly in the setting of infection with urease-producing bacteria, often must be surgical ly removed. Additionally, stones larger than 6 mm often require intervention because they are unlikely to pass on their own. For smaller stones in clinical ly stable patients, treatment is hydration and pain control. Medications such as tamsulosin may be used to augment stone passage. At times, urine should be strained to assess the passage of the stone, though data and practice patterns on this are mixed.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abdominal x-ray series (Choice A) is not the preferred imaging modality for diagnosing renal stones because it is not as sensitive as abdominal CT scan. Additiona lly, uric acid stones may be missed because they are radiolucent. Cystoscopy (Choice C) is typically done in the evaluation of hematuria after an abdomina l CT scan has already been conducted to rule out nephrolithiasis. It would be premature in this patient. Measurement of serum uric acid concentration (Choice D) is not necessary in this patient because he does not have evidence of a gout flare. While some kidney stones are composed of uric acid, serum uric acid measurement does not reliably predict the composition of any kidney stones. Urine culture (Choice E) should be performed in patients who are suspected to have a urinary tract infection in addition to ureterolithiasis. Laboratory findings consistent with diagnosis of a urinary tract infection include pyuria, positive nitrites, or positive leukocyte esterase on urinalysis. Educationa l Objective: Nephrolithiasis is a relatively common condition, and most stones are composed of calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate. When stones become lodged in one of the ureters, this condition is known as ureterolithiasis. Diagnosis is made with a noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen. Acute management depends on the size of the stone and the presence of complicating factors such as concurrent ascending urinary tract infection or altered anatomy.

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after collapsing near the completion of a 26-mile run in warm, humid weather. On arrival, he is obtunded and warm. His temperature is 40.5 °C (104.9°F), pulse is 120/min and regular, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 85/50 mm Hg. Examination shows moist, clammy skin. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 55% Leukocyte count 15,000/mm 3 (15 x 109/L) with a shift to the left Platelet count 55,000/mm 3 (55 x 109/L) Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine Alkaline phosphatase AST ALT Creatine kinase 50 mg/dL (17.8 mmol/L) 2.5 mg/dL (221 µmol/L) 100 U/L 500 U/L 500 U/L 1000 U/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Heat stroke is characterized by an increased body temperature that occurs when the body is exposed to high environmental temperatures and high humidity, and it commonly occurs in young athletes or in elderly patients with impaired thermoregulatory capacity. Excessive heat exposure and increased core body temperature leads to cardiovascular and neurologic dysfunction with secondary tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Vasodilation of superficia l blood vessels may lead to multi-organ system failure, including hepatic and renal ischemia, rhabdomyo lysis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treatment includes cooling of the patient with fans or ice water, continuous core temperature monitoring, and support of airway, breathing, and circulation. Heat stroke generally requires neurologic symptoms to be diagnosed (collapse, in this case), whereas heat exhaustion presents similarly but with an intact neurologic examination.
incorrectExplanation: nd E.

questionStem: A 60-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency depart ment because of a 12-hour history of moderate, diffuse abdominal pain and vomiting. Two weeks ago, she underwe nt a sigmoidectomy for perforated diverticulitis. Her postoperative course has been otherwise uncomplicated. She has not had fever, diarrhea, or pain with urination. Her last bowel movement yesterday was normal. She has not passed any flatus today. Her medications are ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and oxycodone-acetaminophen. On arrival, the patient is in moderate distress. She is awake and alert. Her temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnorma lities. The abdomen is moderately distended and diffusely tender to palpation in all four quadrants. The surgical incision is clean, dry, and intact. Bowel sounds are decreased. An x-ray of the abdomen shows multiple loops of distended small bowel with air-fluid levels throughout; no air is noted in the rectum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Bowel obstruction is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with previous abdominal surgery presenting with abdominal pain and obstipation. Obstruction of the bowel occurs from partial or complete blockage of the bowel lumen and typically presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Partial obstruction allows a degree of continued flatus with diminished stooling, and complete obstruction will result in obstipation (no passage of stool or flatus). Obstruction has many potential causes, although the most common are postsurgical peritoneal adhesions and hernias. On physical examination, patients typically present with abdominal tenderness, distention, tympany to percussion, and borborygmi (high-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds). Potential complications include bowel rupture and necrosis, which can result in sudden-onset peritoneal signs such as rebound tenderness and guarding. X-ray of the abdomen typically discloses multiple air-fluid levels in the setting of dilated bowel loops. Management requires bowel rest, insertion of a nasogastric tube for decompression, and intravenous hydration followed by surgical intervention if the obstruction does not autoreduce. Partial obstruction may resolve with monitoring, supportive care, and bowel rest, whereas complete obstruction or any complicated partial obstruction generally requires management through exploratory laparotomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complete blood count (Choice A) can be done as part of routine blood work prior to possible surgery or hospitalization, but it would not change or assist in the management.

questionStem: A 68-year-o ld man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of abdom inal cramps after eating. He has also noticed a 2.3- kg (5-lb) weight loss during this time. He has had occasional loose stools but does not report any blood. He has hypertension and congestive heart failure. Medications are metopro lol, digoxin, and amlodipine. His medical records from 6 months ago show a left ventricu lar ejection fraction of 20%. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival, he appears thin and uncomfortable. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/72 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Cardiopu lmonary examination discloses an S3 and bilateral basilar crackles. The abdomen is soft with minimal genera lized tenderness to palpation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?

choices.E: Upper gastrointest inal series with small bowel follow through

correctExplanation: CT angiography is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), recent weight loss, and postprandial abdominal pain most likely has nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia. Mesenteric ischemia can occur secondary to thrombosis of the mesenteric artery or can result from low-flow cardiac states leading to intestinal hypoperfusion. The blood supply to the intestines is primarily derived from the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). Following a meal, the blood flow to the intestines increases to aid in the digestive process. In nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia, constriction of the mesenteric artery in combination with a decreased cardiac output leads to a supply-demand mismatch and subsequent intestina l ischemia. This is often experienced as postprandia l pain which may make some patients avoid eating altogether, thereby leading to weight loss. The diagnosis is made by CT angiography, which shows narrowing of the mesenteric vessels and their branches. When the condition is secondary to HFrEF, therapy is aimed at improving cardiac function.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abdomina l ultrasonography (Choice A) can be used to evaluate the abdominal aorta and flow through its main branches, which include the SMA, IMA, and celiac trunk, but advanced cross-sectional imaging with CT angiography is more sensitive and specific for mesenteric ischemia. Barium enema (Choice B) is used infrequent ly in current clinical practice, but it can occasionally help to diagnose malrotation or volvulus. It is not helpful in the diagnosis of mesenteric ischemia. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of dizziness, numbness, and neck pain. She was participating in a vigorous aerobics class when she began to have sharp pain on the right side of her neck that spread to the back of her head, followed by a sensation of spinning and left-sided numbness. She is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Her temperatu re is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 90/min and regular, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Examination shows mild narrowing of the right palpebral fissure. The right pupil is 2 mm, and the left pupil is 4 mm; both pupils are reactive to light. Ocular movements are full. Funduscop ic examination shows no abnormalities. The palate does not elevate on the right, and the tongue protrudes in the midline. Muscle strength is full. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout. Babinski sign is absent. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the entire left side of the body and right side of the face. Sensation to vibration and proprioception are intact. There is an intention tremor of the right upper extremity. Her gait is mildly ataxic. Her speech is mildly slurred. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vertebral artery dissection is the most common cause of stroke in young, healthy patients and can be caused by spontaneous dissection or can be secondary to trauma. Even mild trauma such as quickly turning the neck, exercise, or chiropractic activities can be associated with vertebral artery dissection. Patients can present with symptoms such as neck pain, Horner syndrome, cranial neuropathies, dysarthria, and ataxia. Horner syndrome is characterized by the triad of ipsilateral miosis, ptosis (eg, narrowed palpebral fissure), and anhidrosis. Horner syndrome can arise from lesions along a sympathetic pathway. Vertebral artery dissection is associated with lateral medullary infarction or Wallenberg syndrome, characterized by ipsilateral ataxia of extremity movements and gait ataxia, and can be associated with nystagmus and dysarthria.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Carotid artery occlusion (Choice A) can cause decreased flow to the brain or embolic events resulting in cerebrovascular ischemia. Patients can have a carotid bruit on examination. Carotid plaques can embolize to cause ocular ischemia, contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, or homonymous hemianopsia. Cerebral vasculitis (Choice B) is rare and can present with neurologic deficits, headache, seizures, or coma. Symptoms of dizziness, neck pain, cranial nerve deficits, ataxia, and dysarthria are more consistent with vertebra l artery dissection.

questionStem: A 54-year-o ld man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 30 minutes after his wife found him lying unresponsive on the bed. His fingerstick blood glucose concentration was 20 mg/dl (1.11 mmol/L), so she called 911. His medicat ions are glimepiride and metformin. He has no known drug allergies. At the scene, paramedics could not obtain intravenous access and transported him to the hospita l. On arrival, the patient is diaphoretic and moaning softly. He does not cooperate w ith the examination. His temperature is 34.8°C (94.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 134/86 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Cardiopu lmonary examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. No skin rashes are noted. Now, fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 15 mg/dl (0.83 mmol/L). The nurses continue to have difficulty obtaining intravenous access. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while awaiting intravenous access?
correctExplanation: Intramuscular administration of glucagon is the most appropriate step in management of this diabetic patient with severe hypoglycemia and no intravenous access. The treatment of severe hypoglycemia in a diabetic patient requires administration of either carbohydrates or glucagon. If intravenous access is available, carbohydrates can easily be given as 50% dextrose. However, in this case, intramuscular glucagon is a fast and safe way to reverse hypoglycemia in a patient with impaired consciousness and no intravenous access. After administration of glucagon, the patient must be closely monitored and intravenous access obtained because the effect of glucagon is transient. After intravenous access is available, a continuous infusion of glucose will likely be necessary. Any patient with hypoglycemia taking long-acting oral hypoglycemics ( sulfonylureas in this case) requires prolonged monitoring or admission because rebound hypoglycemia is common.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Application of a warming blanket (Choice A) should be included in the supportive care of this patient after his underlying problem has been addressed. Any delay of glucagon administration in this patient will increase his chances of death. While the patient's respiratory rate is low, bag-valve-mask ventilation (Choice B) is not necessary at this time given the adequate oxygen saturation of 96%. It is more important to address the underlying cause of this patient's symptoms, which is severe hypoglycemia. -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A 47-yea r-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramed ics 15 minutes after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was the restrained driver. The patient was traveling at about 5 miles per hour (8 km/hr) in a parking lot when his car struck a parked vehicle. Paramedics say that the damage to both vehicles was minimal. The, patient says he consumed two beers earlier in the evening. On arrival, he is awake, alert, and fully oriented. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Examination shows tenderness and swelling of the right elbow but no other abnormal ities. The physician recomme nds that an x-ray of the elbow be performed. The patient says that he would prefer to leave; he is able to verba lize the risks of leaving using his own words. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in manageme nt?

choices.A: Allow the patient to leave against medica l advice
choices.C: Detain the patient until his blood alcohol concentratio n is measured
choices.D: Discharge the patient with a diagnosis of elbow contusion
choices.E: Obtain x-rays despite the patient's wishes

correctExplanation: Patient autonomy is one of four common medical ethical principles, along with beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Autonomy posits that patients have the right to make their decisions provided that they have the capacity to do so and that they have been provided with appropriate information for use in making such a decision. A consenting adult with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse some or all aspects of medical care even if such a decision may result in short- or long-term morbidity or mortality. In this case, the patient is declining further work-up and treatment of a musculoskeleta l injury induced by a motor vehicle collision. Provided that this patient has capacity and that the caring physician has explained the benefits, risks, and alternatives of not performing the x-ray of the elbow, the patient may elect to refuse and then be allowed to leave against medical advice.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. It is not necessary to call the police (Choice B) in this case because the patient has demonstrated lawful behavior in the emergency department since arrival. It is not the physician's role to determine whether the police need to be involved in the motor vehicle collision, and disclosing such would be a breach of patient privacy. If the patient had assaulted providers who wished to pursue legal action, or if he had committed a reportable offense (eg, discharged a firearm), calling the police may be appropriate. Detaining the patient until his blood alcohol concentration is measured (Choice C) or obtaining x-rays despite the patient's wishes (Choice E) violates the ethical principle of patient autonomy. Because this patient demonstrates decision-making capacity by being able to verbalize the risks of leaving in his own words (and is not suspected to be impaired), there is no justification to detain the patient or perform tests against his will.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after losing consciousness while eating at home. During the past month, she has had intermittent 1-minute episodes of vertigo, nausea, double vision, and numbness of the left side of her face. She has a 20-year history of hypertension treated with enalapril. On arrival, she is intubated and mechanical ly ventilated because of poor respiratory effort. She is unrespons ive to commands. Her temperatu re is 37.1 °C (98.8°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 160/94 mm Hg; she is overriding the ventilator with respirations of 14/min. The pupils are pinpoint. There are no horizontal eye moveme nts spontaneous ly or on doll's eye (oculocephal ic) maneuver. There are no spontaneous movements of the extremities except for occasiona l extensor posturing. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. A complete blood count and serum electrolyte and glucose concentrations are within the reference ranges. A CT scan of the head within 2 hours of arrival shows no abnorma lities. Wh ich of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient is showing signs of brainstem dysfunction including altered level of consciousness, poor respiratory effort, posturing, and negative oculocephalic maneuver on examination. Dysfunction of the brainstem can also present with cranial nerve dysfunction, dizziness, vertigo, and gait instability, symptoms that the patient had been experiencing prior to this acute episode. The Babinski sign, or extensor plantar response, is an upper motor neuron sign that indicates damage to the corticospinal tract, a descending motor tract located in the central nervous system. The Babinski sign is present when the lateral part of the plantar surface of the foot is firmly stroked and the hallux extends (moves rostrally) while the other toes abduct. The doll's eye (oculocephalic) maneuver refers to the brainstem reflex that occurs in normal adults in which the examiner moves the patient's head, and the eyes move in the opposite direction to hold the patient's gaze on an object. In a negative oculocephalic reflex, the patient's eyes remain midline, which indicates severe brainstem dysfunction. The cause of brainstem dysfunction in this patient is likely brainstem ischemia, which is often not disclosed on CT scan when acute. MRI is more sensitive for diagnosis. Patients with brainstem ischemia can have a stuttering course, which this patient experienced with mild intermittent symptoms prior to this presentation.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Brain stem demyelination (Choice A), such as in central pontine myelinolysis, can occur when there is rapid correction of hyponatremia. - - - - -- ...

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 40 minutes after he sustained a stab wound to the chest during an altercation. He has no history of serious illness and no known allergies. He takes no medications. His last meal was 12 hours ago. On arrival, he is awake and alert and speaks in a clear voice. He appears anxious and is in respiratory distress . His pulse is 130/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 80/58 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. He receives 100% oxygen by nonrebreather face mask. Examination shows jugular venous distention. There is a 2-cm wound over the left anterior chest wall but no active bleeding. Decreased breath sounds are heard over the left hemithorax . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Tension pneumothorax can be a complication of a penetrating thoracic trauma and occurs when air is able to enter the pleural space but is prevented from exiting. Increasing amounts of trapped air in the pleural space compress the lung parenchyma, creating an inability for the lung to expand and causing it to collapse. As the pneumothorax progresses and continues to increase in size, it can result in tracheal and/or mediastina l deviation away from the affected hemithorax. It can result in decreased venous return to the heart, which manifests with hypotension and obstructive shock. Tension pneumothorax is characterized by absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion caused by the increased air in the intrathoracic space displacing normal lung parenchyma. In cases of acute tension pneumothorax, evacuating the accumulated air via needle decompression and aspiration permits expansion of the lung and eliminates tension on the mediastinal structures, resolving obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression is followed by tube thoracostomy, which promotes expansion of the lung, prevents reaccumu lation of air, and promotes healing of the pleural defect.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Intravenous administration of 0.9% saline (Choice A) can be helpful for patients with hypotension secondary to distributive shock such as anaphylaxis or sepsis. This patient's tension pneumothorax is causing an obstructive shock, and fluid administration would not resolve the deficit. Pericardia ! window (Choice C) or pericardiocentesis (Choice D) would be indicated in cases of traumatic pericardia! effusion causing cardiac tamponade. Tamponade presents with hypotension, jugular venous distention, distant heart sounds, and pulsus paradoxus. This atient has decreased breath sounds, tach nea, and h oxia, makin neumothorax more likel .

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of lower back pain that began after he moved heavy boxes of books and furniture 1 day ago. He has been taking acetaminophen with no relief of pain. Physical examination shows tenderness over the lumbar paraspinal muscles on palpation. Perinea! sensation is intact, and rectal tone is normal. Muscle strength is full and sensation is intact in the lower extremities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.E: No further diagnostic testing is indicated

correctExplanation: Lumbosacra l strain commonly occurs following strenuous exertion and is characterized by dull, aching lower back pain that does not radiate to the lower extremities and which is not accompanied by neurologic deficits. Most adults with acute lower back pain of less than 1 month's duration do not require imaging, which is of limited diagnostic value and leads to unnecessary testing, medical expenses, and radiation exposure. Imaging may be useful for the diagnosis of persistent back pain, pain that is accompanied by severe or progressive neurologic deficits, or pain that is suspected to be secondary to certain disease entities, such as vertebral metastasis, spinal stenosis, osteomyelitis, spinal epidural hematoma or abscess, or vertebral fracture. Any patient with red flags of back pain such as neurologic symptoms to suggest cauda equina or conus medullaris syndrome, history of malignancy, traumatic injury, midline tenderness, accompanying fever or infectious symptoms, or history of immunocompromise may benefit from acute imaging. However, most patients with acute lumbosacral strain can be managed conservatively with heat or ice, massage, and light exercise provided the history and examination are reassuring and lacking red flags.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Measurement of postvoid residual volume (Choice A) may be helpful for the detection of urinary retention in the setting of spinal cord injury, cauda equina syndrome, or conus medullaris syndrome. This patient's lack of other neurologic symptoms renders such a diagnosis unlikely. MRI of the lumbar spine (Choice B) may be useful for the detection of myelopathy secondary to epidural metastasis, abscess, or radiculopathy. MRI is of limited diagnostic value for nonspecific lower back pain or lumbosacral strain and is not necessary for this patient. questionStem: A 26-yea r-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of shortness of breath and moderate right-sided chest pain. She reports shortness of breath when walking up a flight of stairs this morning and when walking with friends at a shopping mall earlier. She also has a 2-day history of nonproduc tive cough. She has sickle cell disease. Her medications are hydroxyurea and acetami nophen with codeine as needed. The patient was hospitalized for treatme nt of a painful vase-occl usive crisis 1 year ago. On arrival , she is in mild respiratory distress. BMI is 21 kg/m2. Her temperatu re is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 104/min and regular, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 91 % that improves to 95% on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. Fine crackles are heard at the right lung base. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglob in 8.9 g/dL (89 g/L) Hematocrit 25.2% Leukocyte count 12,600/mm 3 (12.6 x 109/L) Platelet count 457,000 /mm3 (457 x 109/L) A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's current condition?
correctExplanation: Infection is the most likely precipitant of this patient's acute chest syndrome (ACS). ACS occurs as a result of vaso-occlusion within the pulmonary microvasculature and is diagnosed in patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) who present with a new pulmonary infiltrate in the setting of fever or other new respiratory symptoms, including cough, shortness of breath, increased work of breathing, tachypnea, or hypoxemia. While ACS is a distinct clinical syndrome, it is common ly precipitated by another illness such as bacterial or viral pneumonia, asthma exacerbation with hypoventilation, or fat embo li, among others. It is both impractical and nearly impossible to distinguish ACS from pneumonia, so nearly all patients receive antibiotics to treat bacterial pneumonia. Additional ly, the use of either simple transfusion or exchange transfusion may be a component of therapy. Further treatment involves maintaining normoxia with supplemental oxygen or the use of noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, judicious use of fluids, and aggressive pulmonary hygiene measures, including the use of an incentive spirometer. Patients with a pulmonary embolism should be placed on full anticoagulation while all others should receive prophylaxis against venous thromboembolism. Pain should be managed aggressive ly.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aplastic crisis (Choice A) presents with anemia and a low reticu locyte count indicating inadequate erythropoiesis, but does not present with fever, pulmonary symptoms, and a new infiltrate on chest x-ray. In patients with SCD, aplastic crisis can be precipitated by infection with parvovirus B19. Embolism (Choice B) should always be considered in patients with ACS, but thrombi found within the pulmonary vasculature are more likely to form in situ rather than represent emboli from the veins of the lower extremities. Fat emboli may also precipitate ACS, but these are not visualized on CT angiography and there is no treatment other than supportive care. Hypoventilation (Choice C) can precipitate ACS, but this patient 's prodrome with cough and shortness of breath is more suggestive of pneumonia than hypoventilation in isolation. Similarly, thrombosis (Choice E) can precipitate ACS, but this patient's symptoms prior to presentation suggest an alternative cause. Educational Objective: ACS is diagnosed in patients with SCD who present with a new pulmonary infiltrate and either fever or new respiratory symptoms. There are myriad precipitating causes, but infection is among the most common. In addition to treating any suspected underlying cause, further therapy should aim at maintaining normoxia, treating pain, and avoiding ongoing sickling with the use of simple or exchange transfusion.

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld woman with rheumatoid arthritis comes to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of fever, severe malaise, and joint stiffness. She has severe stiffness and pain in the wrists, hands, and knees. She also has a history of hypertension and hypercholeste rolemia. Her medications are prednisone, etanercept, enalapril, hydroch lorothiazide, and ibuprofen as needed . She is sleepy but easily aroused. Her temperatu re is 38.4 °C (101.2°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. The upper and lower extremities are cool to the touch; there is mottling over the lower extremities. There is no jugular venous distention. Crackles are heard over the left lung base. Cardiac examination shows a hyperdynamic precordium. A grade 2/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard at the base; there is no S3 or S4. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Platelet count Prothrombin time Serum Na+ K+ Urea nitrogen Creatinine Albumin 9.5 g/dL (95 g/L) 20,500/mm 3 (20.5 x 109/L) 90,000/mm 3 (90 x 109/L) 16 sec (INR=1.5) 135 mEq/L (135 mmol/L) 4.2 mEq/L (4.2 mmol/L) 35 mg/dL (12.5 mmol/L) 1.2 mg/dL (106.1 µmol/L) 2.1 g/dL (21 g/L) An ECG shows sinus tachycardia but is otherwise unchanged from a prior ECG. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Sepsis can be complicated by shock and multiorgan failure with a high mortality rate. Septic shock is characterized by vasop legia (impaired response of the vasculature to vasoconstricting stimuli) with markedly decreased systemic vascu lar resistance, increased cardiac output (tachycardia, hyperdynamic ventricular function), oliguria, and lactic acidosis. Fever, tachypnea, and leukocytosis also support a diagnosis of sepsis. I C) Non-ST-e levation myocard ial infarction D) Pulmonary embolism E) Sepsis Correct Answer: E. The patient's presentation is most consistent with sepsis complicated by distributive shock. Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory syndrome that results from a dysregu lated and exaggerated immune response to an infection. Sepsis can be complicated by shock and multiorgan failure with a high mortality rate. Septic shock is characterized by vasop legia (impaired response of the vasculature to vasoconstricting stimuli) with markedly decreased systemic vascu lar resistance, increased cardiac output (tachycardia, hyperdynamic ventricu lar function), oliguria, and lactic acidosis. Fever, tachypnea, and leukocytosis also support a diagnosis of sepsis. Hypotension, cool mottled extremities, and end-organ dysfunction indicate the presence of shock. The patient's risk for developing a severe infection is increased by use of daily corticosteroids and a tumor necrosis factor a blocker for her rheumatoid arthritis.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cardiac tamponade (Choice A) can result in obstructive shock caused by compression of the cardiac chambers. Findings suggestive of cardiac tamponade include hypotension, jugular venous distention, distant heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, and a low-voltage ECG. Gastrointestinal bleeding (Choice B) may result in hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock, and the use of ibuprofen and corticosteroids are risk factors for gastrointestinal bleeding. The presence of fever and leukocytosis and the absence of any reported history of bleeding make sepsis a more likely diagnosis. The initial management for both septic and hemorrhagic shock is fluid resuscitation. Non-ST-elevation myocardia l infarction (Choice C) may lead to cardiogenic shock because of impaired ventricular contraction and inadequate cardiac output. Typical findings include jugular venous distention, pulmonary crackles, and a weak pulse. Measuring troponin concentration and performing echocardiography can support or refute the diagnosis. Pulmonary embolism (Choice D) can cause an obstructive form of shock in which the right ventricle fails as it contracts against greater resistance in the pulmonary vasculature. This results in diminished left heart return and cardiac output, with the consequence of decreased perfusion to the right ventricle and further loss of function. Educational Objective: Septic shock refers to the presence of persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate fluid resuscitation in the setting of infection. It is characterized by vasoplegia and increased cardiac stroke volume and pulse, and it may progress to multi-organ dysfunction.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 23-year-o ld woman comes to the emergency departme nt because of a 3-day history of severe left lower abdom inal pain and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She is sexually active with multiple male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Her last menstrua l period was 2 weeks ago. Her temperatu re is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/85 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows tenderness to palpation in the left lower quadrant. Pelvic examination shows cervical motion tenderness and left adnexa l tenderness. There is foul-smelling white discharge. A urine pregnancy test is negative . Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis can both cause vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PIO). Risk factors include adolescence, multiple sexual partners, and not using barrier contraception such as condoms. Vaginitis typica lly presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus. Cervicitis presents with similar discharge, but also with an erythematous, friable cervix and cervical motion tenderness on examination. When infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, PIO with purulent and foul­ smelling cervical discharge, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and systemic symptoms such as fever can result. If left untreated, PIO can become complicated by a tuba-ovarian abscess, as in this patient, presenting with focal tenderness and a possible fluctuant mass on physical examination. The diagnosis can be confirmed with pelvic ultrasonography, which would demonstrate a complex, heterogeneous, multilocular mass within the adnexa. Treatment includes antibiotics and surgical management.
incorrectExplanation: nd 0. Blood cultures (Choice A) are used to diagnose bacteremia in septic patients. While they may be utilized in this febrile, tachycardic patient with a likely infection, they will not confirm the diagnosis of tuba-ovarian abscess. Urinalysis (Choice B) and urine culture (Choice C) can be used to evaluate urinary tract infections, such as cystitis or pyelonephritis. Urinary tract infections commonly present with dysuria, urinary frequency or urgency, and suprapubic discomfort, as well as fever and costovertebral tenderness in pyelonephritis. This sexual ly active patient with cervical discharge and adnexa l tenderness more likely has PIO complicated by a tuba-ovarian abscess. questionStem: A previously healthy 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of progressive redness and swelling of his right knee for the past 3 days. His temperat ure is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 134/7 4 mm Hg. Examination shows a 1.5 x 3-cm area of swelling and fluctuance over the anterior aspect of the right knee. A photograph is shown. Range of motion of the knee is full. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Incision and drainage of the affected area

correctExplanation: Abscess formation occurs in the settin Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 42 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Emergency Medicine Self-Assessment Correct Answer: B. Abscess formation occurs in the setting of an acute inflammatory response to an infectious organism, resulting in an organized collection of pus, necrotic cellular debris, and infectious organisms present on histology. A bacterial abscess presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, fluctuance, and purulent drainage, often following inoculation from an injury such as a spider bite, puncture, or abrasion. Systemic symptoms including fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis are often but not necessarily present. Most commonly, abscess formation is acute and results from a bacterial infection of the skin. The two most common pathogens to cause bacteria l infections of the skin are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). S. aureus is most likely to cause a bacteria l abscess. It also causes impetigo, erysipe las, and folliculitis. Other less common organisms include C/ostridium perfringens, which infects an open wound and causes necrotizing fasciitis, Enterococcus faecalis, which causes nosocomial infections, and Pasteurel/a multocida, which causes infections secondary to cat and dog bites. Incision and drainage would be appropriate therapy for an abscess to release pus and debris to control the source of the infection. While the patient may also require oral antibiotics, without incision and drainage the oral antibiotics will not effectively penetrate the abscess wall; thus, it is the most important next step.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Biopsy of the affected area (Choice A) is not necessary in this case. Skin biopsy is performed when there is diagnostic uncertainty about the cause of a skin finding and can be used to obtain a sample for culture. It involves surgically removing a small core of skin and submitting it for pathology in formalin or for tissue culture in sterile saline. In this case, the diagnosis of bacterial abscess is clinical, and a biopsy is unnecessary. Oral antibiotic therapy (Choice C) is inadequate in this case without appropriate surgica l drainage of the bacterial abscess. While the patient may receive oral antibiotic therapy following incision and drainage, the bacterial source control provided by the surgical procedure is more critical than antibiotic therapy alone. Topical corticosteroid therapy (Choice D) is used to treat inf lammatory processes of the skin including dermatitis, psoriasis, and lichen planus. While the presence of erythema around the abscess clear ly indicates inflammation, treating this inflammation with topica l corticosteroids without treating the underlying cause, a bacterial abscess, will be ineffective. X-ray of the right knee (Choice E) is not necessary in this case because there is no suggestion of bony involvement of the infection. X­ ray of the right knee will not provide any information about the soft tissue surrounding the abscess. Imaging is unnecessary in this case, but if x-ray evaluation of the soft tissue was necessary, an MRI would be more appropriate. Educational Objective: A bacterial abscess presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, fluctuance, and purulent drainage, often following inoculation from an injury. S. aureus is the most common ly identified organism. Incision and drainage is the first step in controlling the source of the infection and, without it, antibiotics alone will be inadequate.

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband after she fell at home. She has a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Medications are metformin and insulin. On arrival, she is somnolent. Her temperatu re is 37.7°C (99.9°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 78/40 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturat ion of 98%. Basilar crackles are heard at the left lung base. The remainder of the examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 13.2 g/dl (132 g/L) Serum Na+ K+ c 1- HC0 3- Glucose 142 mEq/L (142 mmol/L) 3.9 mEq/L (3.9 mmol/L) 100 mEq/L (100 mmol/L) 15 mEq/L (15 mmol/L) 90 mg/dl (5 mmol/L) Blood cultures and a chest x-ray are ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The patient is presenting with shock, and the most appropriate next step is isotonic fluid resuscitation by administration of 0.9% saline. Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory syndrome that results from a dysregulated and exaggerated immune response to an infection. Sepsis can be complicated by shock and multi-organ failure with a high mortality rate. Septic shock is characterized by vasoplegia (impaired response of the vasculature to vasoconstricting stimuli) with marked ly decreased systemic vascular resistance, increased cardiac output (tachycardia or hyperdynamic ventricular function), oliguria, and lactic acidosis. The presence of hypotension, tachycardia, and altered mental status indicate an acute shock state, and the patient requires emergent volume resuscitation. Isotonic crystalloid solutions are effective, inexpensive, and readily available in most medical settings.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Urine toxicology screening (Choice A) does not take precedence over immediate fluid resuscitation. It may be considered as part of the evaluation for the underlying cause of the patient's fall and somnolence, and it could rule out toxic ingestions that may be contributing - .

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 37-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has passed black, tarry stools during the past 4 hours. He had one episode of severe dizziness and palpitations when he arose from the toilet. He has not had abdominal pain or nausea. He has no history of ulcers. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. He appears pale. His pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 85/50 mm Hg while supine. Abdominal examination shows no tenderness. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. His hematocrit is 37%. After intravenous administration of 2 L of 0.9% saline and transfusion of 3 units of packed red blood cells, his pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Upper endoscopy is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis in this patient with signs and symptoms of upper gastrointestina l bleeding (UGIB). Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is often separated into upper and lower GI bleeding. Patients with UGIB often present with dizziness or light-headedness, nausea, epigastric pain, and melena. Occasiona lly, as in the case of varicea l bleeding, hematemesis may accompany these symptoms. Laboratory findings may show an increased blood urea nitrogen concentration, but the decrease in hemoglobin concentration often lags behind clinical ly significant bleeding. Treatment should initially focus on resuscitation with crystalloids and erythrocyte transfusion as needed. All patients are started on an intravenous proton pump inhibitor, and patients with cirrhosis and suspected variceal bleeding should receive octreotide and antibiotics. Major causes of UGIB aside from esophageal varices include Mallory-Weiss tear, peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, esophagitis, and angiodysplasia. Rare causes include Dieulafoy lesion, gastric antra l vascular ectasia, and aortoenteric fistula. After patients have been stabilized, upper endoscopy should be performed both to determine the cause of bleeding and to intervene on any lesions that are amenable to treatment, such as bleeding ulcers or visibly bleeding blood vesse ls.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. CT scan of the abdomen (Choice A) is insensitive for evaluating the cause of gastrointestinal bleeding. Resuscitation followed by endoscopy should general ly be performed first. If no cause of bleeding is identified, then CT angiography may be able to localize brisk bleeds that exist at locations distal to the duodenum. Colonoscopy (Choice B) is the intervention of choice when patients are suspected of having a source of lower GI bleeding such as diverticulosis or angiodysplasia, which often presents with hematochezia rather than melena.

questionStem: A 2-year-o ld boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents 1 hour after he had a genera lized tonic-clonic seizure. The seizure lasted approximate ly 1 minute, and the child was lethargic for approximately 15 minutes afterward. He is now behaving normally. For the past 2 days, he has had a fever, runny nose, and loss of appetite. He has no history of seizures. On examination, he is awake, interactive, and smiling. His rectal temperatu re is 39.1 °C (102.4 °F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnorma lities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Segmented neutrophils Bands Lymphocytes Which of the following interventions is the most appropr iate next step?

choices.A: Admiss ion to the hospital for observat ion

correctExplanation: 12 g/dL (120 g/L) 12,000/mm 3(12 x 109/L) 56% 6% 38% Febrile seizures are a common presentation in infants or young children. Simple and uncomplicated febrile seizures are generalized and defined as lasting less than 15 minutes and not recurring within a 24-hour period, whereas complex febrile seizures are focal, prolonged, and recurring. It is important to differentiate febrile seizures secondary to a viral illness from a bacterial central nervous system infection, which can also present with fever and seizure, but patients are typically ill-appea ring and may have signs of meningismus. In patients with febrile seizures that have spontaneously resolved, active treatment with benzodiazepines is not necessary and the fever can be treated symptomatically with antipyretics (eg, acetaminophen). Most children who present with simple febrile seizures can be discharged safely as long as they have returned to baseline and parents are given anticipatory guidance and strict return precautions. Children with focal or prolonged seizures may require further observation, intervention, or diagnosis, especially if there is delayed recovery to baseline or a prolonged postictal phase.

He has had one episode of vomiting during this time. He describes the pain as a pressure; it radiates to his shoulders. He rates the pain as a 7 on a 10-point scale. The patient says he has had three similar episodes of pain during the past 3 months; previously, they occurred only on exertion and resolved after 15 minutes of rest. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. His medications are aspirin, metformin, and enalapri l. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. His temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 154/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of chest pain, shortness of breath, and nausea that began while he was sitting and working at his desk. He has had one episode of vomiting during this time. He descr ibes the pain as a pressure; it radiates to his shoulders. He rates the pain as a 7 on a 10-point scale. The patient says he has had three similar episodes of pain during the past 3 months; previous ly, they occurred only on exertion and resolved after 15 minutes of rest. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. His medicat ions are aspirin, metformin, and enalapr il. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. His temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 154/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Physical findings are normal. Laboratory studies, including serum troponi n concentration, are within the reference ranges. An ECG and chest x-ray show no abnorma lities. Aspirin, nitroglycerin, and morphine are administered; 15 minutes later, he rates the pain as a 2 on a 10-point scale. The patient is observed in the emergency department. Repeat serum troponin concentrat ion 4 hours later is within the reference range . Now, all of the patient's symptoms have resolved. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: CT scan of the chest with pulmonary embolism protocol in the emergency department
choices.D: Primary care physician follow-up within 1 week

correctExplanation: Exertional chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath that improves with rest is suggestive of stable angina pectoris, caused by cardiac ischemia from insufficient perfusion during exertion through narrowed atherosclerotic coronary arteries. This patient presents with symptoms consistent with unstable angina, defined by angina symptoms that are new, occur at rest, or are worsening in severity. Unstable angina is a type of acute coronary syndrome, which requires urgent diagnostic workup including serial ECGs, troponin testing, cardiology consultation, and myocardial perfusion testing, stress testing, or cardiac cathete rization. Nitroglycerin is a potent venodilator that decreases cardiac preload and myocardial oxygen demand, making it a first-line therapy in the treatment of angina pectoris along with aspirin, which inhibits platelet aggregation. Patients with unstable angina are stratified on the basis of the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) score, which assists in identifying the need for therapeutic anticoagulation and coronary angiography. In this patient with improving chest pain, a normal ECG, and serial troponin concentrations within the reference range, the most appropriate next step in management is urgent myocardia l perfusion testing.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. CT scan of the chest with pulmonary embolism protocol (Choice A) would not be appropriate diagnostic workup in this patient. Pulmonary embolism typically presents with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxia, tachypnea , hemoptysis, or syncope. This patient is presenting with chest pain with similar episodes during exertion that is relieved with aspirin, nitroglycerin, and morphine, which is more consistent with anginal chest pain. Emergent cardiac catheterization (Choice B) would be appropriate in cases of acute myocardial infarction, which would present similarly with anginal chest pain but would have ECG changes showing ST-segment elevation and increased concentrations of serum troponin. This patient's diagnostic work-up shows no abnorma lities, making acute myocardial infarction unlikely. This patient may require cardiac catheterization because his TIMI score is high; however, it (or a noninvasive stress test) should occur urgently within 3 days, as opposed to emergently. Primary care physician follow-up within 1 week (Choice D) would not be an appropriate next step in management. This patient is presenting with symptoms concerning for unstable angina, which requires urgent cardiac diagnostic testing and cardiology consultation. Educational Objective: Unstable angina is a type of acute coronary syndrome, which requires urgent diagnostic work-up including serial ECGs, troponin testing, cardiology consultation, and a myocardial perfusion test, stress test, or cardiac catheterization.

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 25 minutes after susta ining a gunshot wound to the abdomen. She is hyste rical and is unable to give any other history. Her pulse is 100/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. Examination of the chest shows no abnorma lities. Abdomina l examinat ion shows an entrance wound in the right lower quadrant and no exit wound; the abdomen is mildly tender but not distended. Bowel sounds are hypoact ive. X-rays of the chest and abdomen show a bullet in the left paraspinal area. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Explora tory laparotomy involves the surgical evaluation of the peritoneal cavity and is commonly employed in the diagnosis and managemen t of abdominal trauma, bowel obstruction, peritonitis, and undifferentiated cases of acute abdomen. In penetrating abdominal trauma, evaluation of the depth of the wound tract is quickly done to determine whether it has violated the peritoneum. Gunshot wounds are particularly high-ene rgy and can cause severe intra-abdomina l injury including hemo rrhage and viscus perforation. Laparotomy of the abdomen is indicated for hemodynamically unstable patients (eg, tachycardia and hypotension) presenting after penetrating abdomina l trauma because it permiits the control of hemo rrhage and the repair of identified injuries. In stable cases, imaging precedes surgical intervent ion.

Observation (Choice A) could potentially be appropriate for a patient who is hemodynamica lly stable and with a superficia lly penetrating wound not violating the peritoneum. It would be inapprop riate in this borderline unstable patient with a severe penetrating wound with likely intra-abdomina l injury. questionStem: A 27-yea r-old man is brought to the emergency departme nt 2 hours after he was involved in a head-o n motor vehicle collision. He was the unrestrained front-seat passenger. Examination of the right lower extrem ity shows discolo ration and a dislocated knee. Sensation is absent from the knee to the toes. There are no palpable pulses distal to the femoral artery. No motor activity is present. Which of the following is the most approp riate next step in management?

choices.A: Measureme nt of ankle brachia! indices

correctExplanation: Posterior knee dislocation may occur secondary to posteriorly directed force against the proximal tibia, such as in the setting of motor vehicle accidents. Posterior knee dislocation places traction on the popliteal artery and branches of the sciatic nerve. Such an injury can result in potential neurovascu lar insufficiency to the leg distal to the level of the injury, resulting in permanent l oss of function if untreated. Arterial injuries sustained during a posterior knee dislocation can include dissection, rupture, thrombosis, and intramural hematoma; pseudoaneurysms can also occur. Imaging, including arteriography or CT or MR angiography, is useful to investigate the presence of underlying arteria l injuries and to facilitate operative repair planning. Prompt reduction of the knee dislocation serves to limit the extent of injury by relieving neurovascular traction, thereby minimizing damage to and restoring nerve function and arterial flow. Pursuit of imaging studies should not delay the reduction of the dislocated knee.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Measurement of ankle brachia! indices (Choice A) is useful for the diagnosis of peripheral arterial disease and of traumatic arterial injury, but it should not be performed prior to reduction of the knee in this scenario, where clear pulse and neurologic deficits exist. Venous duplex ultrasonography (Choice B) is useful for the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis or chronic venous insufficiency. Nerve conduction studies (Choice C) are useful for the diagnosis of nerve injury or demyelinating diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, or Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Venography (Choice D) employs a contrast agent to evaluate flow and anatomical abnormalities of venous structures. It is not useful for the evaluation of o liteal arter in'ur in the settin of osterior knee dislocation.

questionStem: A 23-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after he was bitten by a rattlesnake on the left hand. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He has no known allergies. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 114/min, respirations are 23/min, and blood pressure is 134/76 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Physical examination shows swelling, discoloration, and severe tenderness of the left hand. The physician administers Crotalidae Polyvalent Immune Fab Ovine (CroFab) antivenin. Fifteen minutes later, the patient becomes obtunded and flushed. His temperature now is 38°C (100.4 °F), pulse is 138/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 75/34 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 85%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Anaphylactic shock, a severe type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction, presents following exposure to an allergen. It is caused by widespread lgE-mediated mast cell degranu lation and is characterized by histaminergic responses within multiple organ systems leading to flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and vasodi lation, which can lead to airway obstruction and circulatory collapse. It is general ly acute in onset following a specific exposure and general ly does not self-resolve. If not managed promptly, death can occur from hypoxia and/or distributive shock. Anaphylaxis is a form of distributive shock, which is characterized by a primary reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR). This reduction in SVR is secondary to lgE-mediated histamine and cytokine release. Cardiac output increases to compensate for low SVR in the early stages of distributive shock. If the inciting state is not appropriate ly treated, further decompensation can occur, resulting in progressive hypotension and insufficient perfusion with associated end-organ damage. After the administration of epinephrine, fluid resuscitation should be initiated to increase intravascular volume to support adequate organ perfusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute serum sickness (Choice A) is a type Ill (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction in which antibodies to foreign proteins are produced and immune complexes deposit in membranes, leading to tissue damage. It typically presents with fever, urticaria, arthralgias, proteinuria, and lymphadenopathy 5 to 10 days after exposure. Anaphylaxis is typica lly an immediate and acute reaction. questionStem: A 67-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 60 minutes after the sudden onset of shortness of breath. She also has had a 2-day history of swelling of her abdomen and legs. She received the diagnos is of carcinoma of the right breast 6 years ago and underwent lumpectomy followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus well controlled with diet. On arrival, she is in severe respiratory distress. Her pulse is 122/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Examination shows jugular venous distention. Heart sounds are distant. A pericardia! rub is heard best at the second to fourth left intercostal spaces. The abdomen is distended and nontender. The liver is enlarged. There is 2+ edema of the lower extremities. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia and ST-segment elevations throughout all leads. An x-ray of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Bedside cardiac ultrasonography is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This patient has a history of breast cancer and now presents with tachycardia, jugular venous distention, pulmonary edema, and hypotension with a pericardia! friction rub, hepatomega ly, and ST elevations on ECG. Together this is concerning for pericardia! tamponade, likely seconda ry to malignancy. Further assessment with bedside ultrasonography should be the next step. Characteristic findings on echocardiography include a pericardia! effusion, collapse of the right atrium at the end of diastole, and a collapse of the right ventricle in the early part of diastole. Additional ly, pulsus paradoxus, which is a clinical finding defined by a drop in the systolic blood pressure of greater than 10 mm Hg with inspiration can also be visualized on echocardiography as changes in the volume of the left and right ventricles with respiration. As a result of increased diastolic filling pressures and equalization of diastolic pressures between the left and right heart, other potential findings include congestive hepatopathy and tender hepatomegaly from flow reversa l within the hepatic veins, and pulmonary edema.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Cardiac catheterization (Choice B) is appropriate for patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). This patient may also have acute coronary syndrome, but an echocardiography should be performed prior to catheterization as decompression of the pericardium via a pericardiocentesis should be performed first.

questionStem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after having a genera lized tonic-clonic seizure at home. The seizure began after she awoke from a nap and lasted approx imately 3 minutes. She was drowsy afterward. This morning, her parents noted that she had mild rhinorrhea. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Development has been appropr iate for age. On examinat ion, she is alert and respons ive. Her temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. There are copious nasal secretions. The neck is supple. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Muscle strength is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's seizure?
correctExplanation: This infant's generalized tonic-clonic seizure, which occurred in the setting of a febrile, upper respiratory illness, is consistent with a diagnosis of simple febrile seizure. Febrile seizures typica lly occur in children between the ages of 6 months and 6 years and may be simple (generalized and lasting for less than 15 minutes) or complex (focal, recurrent, or lasting longer than 15 minutes). The majority of febrile seizures are simple, and neither require treatment nor carry a significantly increased risk for future epilepsy. A careful history and physical examination are necessary to distinguish benign, febrile seizures from complex seizures resulting from viral or bacterial central nervous system infections.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. CT scan of the head (Choice B) is useful for identifying an intracranial mass lesion or hemorrhage. This child does not display focal neurologic signs or altered mental status to suggest an underlying intracrania l pathology. Anticonvulsant therapy (Choice C) is useful in the management of epilepsy. Simple febrile seizures are typically self-limited and do not carry a significantly increased risk for future epilepsy. EEG (Choice D) is useful for the diagnosis of epilepsy. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures lasting less than 15 minutes in the setting of a febrile illness do not require evaluation with an EEG. Recurrent seizures or those occurring outside of a period of febrile illness should be evaluated with an EEG. Lumbar puncture (Choice E) may be useful for the diagnosis of meningitis or encephalitis. questionStem: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-hour history of fever, severe headac he, and neck and back pain. He appears acutely ill and lethargic. His temperature is 40°C (104 °F). When he attempts to flex his neck, he has severe neck pain and automat ically flexes his thighs. Examination shows small petechial hemorrhages over his abdomen and thighs. He is oriented to person but not to place or time. Cerebrospina l fluid analysis in this patient is most likely to show which of the following sets of findings?
correctExplanation: This patient demonstrates findings of acute meningococcal meningitis including fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash. This patient also demonstrates Brudzinski sign, in which flexion of the neck induces hip flexion. Meningococcal meningitis is caused by infection with Neisseria meningitidis, the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in teenagers and young adults. Clusters of infections may be seen among young adults sharing close living quarters such as college dormitories or military barracks. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis of bacterial meningitis demonstrates increased leukocytes with a neutrophil predominance, increased protein, and decreased glucose concentration. The appearance of the fluid is often cloudy and additiona l studies such as gram stain and bacterial culture will often be positive. Thus, the CSF findings in this patient are most likely to show cloudy fluid with a leukocyte count of 2600/mm 3 with 70% segmented neutrophils, increased protein (258 mg/dl), and decreased glucose (10 mg/dl).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Clear fluid with a low leukocyte count, whether 10/mm 3 (Choice A) or 28/mm 3 (Choice B), is not generally seen in bacterial meningitis. Clear fluid with a norma l glucose concentration (Choice C) does not represent the typical findings seen in bacterial meningitis. In bacterial meningitis, the neutrophils recruited to the CSF in respo nse to the infection utilize glucose to perform their metabolic activities, resulting in a decreased glucose concentration within the CSF. Cloudy fluid with 250/mm 3 leukocytes, 90% monocytes, increased protein, and decreased glucose (Choice D) is consistent with a viral, fungal, or mycobacterial meningitis. In contrast, bacterial meningitis will have a predominance of neutrophils.

questionStem: A 42-year-o ld woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of moderate, intermittent right upper abdomina l pain that radiates to her right shoulder blade. The pain typically occurs 30 minutes after eating and is associated with nausea and vomiting. She says she has not eaten much today but continues to have pain. She also had a tem perature of 38.3°C (101 °F) earlier. She has no history of similar symptoms. She has mild asthma treated with an albutero l inhaler as needed . She has no history of operative procedures and has no known drug allergies. Her current temperature is 38.1 °C (100.5°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 136/72 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. The abdomen is soft; there is tenderness to palpation of the right upper quadra nt. The patient ceases inspiration during palpation of the right upper quadra nt. Risk factors for developing gallstones include female gender, multiparity, increasing age, and obesity. High rates of gallstone formation are also seen after periods of rapid weight loss, though the mechanism by which this occurs is not fully understood. Acute cholecystitis occurs secondary to obstruction of the cystic duct from a gallstone, which results in subsequent inflammation of the gallbladder wall. Risk factors for developing gallstones include female gender, multiparity, increasing age, and obesity. High rates of gallstone formation are also seen after periods of rapid weight loss, though the mechanism by which this occurs is not fully understood. Acute cholecys titis typically presents with fever, abdominal pain, and tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant, often in a patient with a history of biliary colic and cholelithiasis. The pain may also radiate to the right shoulder or interscapular region. It may be distinguished from biliary colic by its constant rather than intermittent nature and associated findings of fever and leukocyto sis. Abdominal ultrasonography is the first-line diagnostic examinat ion for the evaluation of potential acute cholecystitis. Characteristic ultrasonography findings of acute cholecystitis include gallbladder wall thickening and hyperemia, pericholecystic fluid, presence of gallstones, a dilated cystic duct or common bile duct, and a sonographic Murphy sign (pain with compression directly over the gallbladder). Treatment includes supportive therapy, intravenous fluids, intravenous antibiotics, and urgent surgical resection of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy). Intravenous antibiotic therapy should cover Gram-negative rods and anaerobes, making piperacillin­ tazobactam therapy the most appropriate next step.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Endoscopy and colonoscopy (Choice A) are used to evaluate gastrointestinal bleeding, which can present with fatigue, hematemesis, hematochezia, and melena. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography can be performed if there is concern for choledocholithiasis, but antibiotics are a more appropriate initial next step. Ketorolac therapy (Choice B) may be useful in managing this patient's pain. However, it is more pertinent to start antibiotic therapy as soon as possible to prevent complications of acute cholecystitis, such as abscess formation or bacteremia. Methylprednisolone therapy (Choice C) is used in the treatmen t of allergic, autoimmune, and inflammatory conditions, such as autoimmune hepatitis, Crohn disease, or ulcerative colitis flares. This patient has localized right upper quadrant pain, associated with fever, leukocytosis, and mildly increased bilirubin and hepatic transaminase s, making acute cholecystitis the more likely diagnosis. Placement of a nasogastric tube (Choice E) is utilized in small bowel obstruction, which presents with nausea, emesis, abdominal pain, distension, and constipation or obstipation, most commonly in a patient with a history of previous abdomina l surgery. While this patient is having nausea and emesis, her pain is localized to her right upper quadrant, making acute cholecys titis more likely. Educationa l Objective: Acute cholecystitis occurs secondary to cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone. It presents with fever and right upper quadrant abdominal pain, in addition to leukocytosis, and potential mild hyperbilirubinemia and transaminitis. Treatment includes supportive therapy, intravenous fluids, antibiotics, and urgent surgical resection. Antibiotic therapy should include coverage of Gram­ negative rods and anaerobes, such as that provided by piperacillin-tazobactam therapy.

questionStem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics because of a 1-day history of generalized weakness and confusion . Medical history includes mild dementia , hypertension, and osteoporosis . Medications are alendronate , atenolol, and donepezil. On arrival, the patient appears ill. She is oriented to person but not to place or time. Her temperature is 35.4 °C (95.7°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 76/50 mm Hg. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows: Leukocyte esterase 2+ WBC 50-100 /hpf RBC 10-2Wh~ A central venous catheter is inserted while the patient is lying supine. Ceftriaxone and 0.9% saline (2 L) are administered during the first hour. After fluid resuscitation , central venous pressure is 2 mm Hg (N=3-8 ). Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this finding?

choices.C: Failure to place the patient in Trendelenburg position
choices.D: Improper placement of the central venous cathete

correctExplanation: This patient demonstrates persistently decreased central venous pressure despite fluid resuscitation , which is suggestive of vasodilation caused by septic shock. The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock defined septic shock by a vasopressor requirement to maintain mean arterial pressure greater than 65 mm Hg or a serum lactate concentration greater than 2 mmol/L despite fluid resuscitation. This patient presents with findings concerning for a urinary tract infection as a source, with a urinalysis demonstrating increased WBCs and leukocyte esterase . This is the likely cause of the patient's probable bacteremia and sepsis, which predisposed her to developing septic shock. Septic shock is characterized by profound circulatory dysregulation causing abnormal peripheral vasodilation , which results in decreased systemic vascular resistance, decreased mean arterial pressure, and consequent organ hypoperfusion and dysfunction.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Anaphylaxis from ceftriaxone (Choice A) is typically accompanied by respiratory and cutaneous findings such as wheezing, flushing, or urticaria.
